# BOOK THE FIRST

## TREATISE.

<margin>1 Corinthians 2:7.</margin>
<margin>The Introduction of Arbatel. <note>Referring to the "Arbatel de Magia Veterum," a highly influential 16th-century manual of spiritual magic that emphasized piety and the help of benevolent spirits.</note></margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'C' decorated with floral patterns and a small bird-like figure.</image-desc>
It is a widely held opinion that "Magic" is a Persian term; indeed, Porphyry and Apuleius <note>Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher; Apuleius was a 2nd-century Roman writer. Both were key authorities for Renaissance thinkers on the subjects of ancient religion and theurgy.</note> appear to support this claim. They state that in the Persian language, the word signifies the same thing as Wisdom, Philosophy, and the Priesthood. Consequently, a **Magus** is the same as a wise Philosopher and a Priest. In a broader sense, however, Magic is divided into two parts, following the nature of Wisdom as described by the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul. Fludd is framing his defense of magic within a strictly Christian, biblical context.</note>. He identifies one as human or worldly wisdom, which he says is mere foolishness [1 Corinthians 3:19]. The other is divine wisdom, which is further divided: first, into **natural wisdom**, insofar as that Wisdom operates within nature and causes all created things—following the sentiment of the royal Psalmist <note>Referring to King David; see Psalm 19:1, "The heavens declare the glory of God."</note>—to declare the glory of the Creator. The second division is **supernatural and mystical wisdom**, which is the Apostle’s focus when he says, *We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery* <note>original Latin: "Sapientiam Dei loquimur in mysterio."</note>, which God has revealed to us through His Spirit. That which is human and worldly—which others call ceremonial magic—is impious and hateful both to God and to godly men. However, so that you may understand these concepts more systematically, Wisdom in general is described in the following manner, according to the opinion of *Arbatel* in his supreme study of Wisdom:

# Concerning the Highest Good, etc.

->A A 3<-

<meta>catchword: Is it</meta>

To those who are truly Wise, it clearly seems that Magic in its entirety should not be rejected by Christians simply because one portion or species of it deals with the most wretched things, which are abominable to the Christian soul. If, I say, "worldly wisdom"—which is the fruit of human invention—is "foolishness" (according to the words of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19: "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God."</note>) and leads to the worst ends, it does not follow that the *true* wisdom—sent by God into the world through divine inspiration for the benefit of His creatures—should be rejected on account of the diabolical follies of that other kind. Nor should it be relegated by Christian men to perpetual oblivion as if it were a thing to be discarded, for nothing in the whole world can be found that contains more wisdom, whether divine or natural.

As for that "knowledge of evil" <note>original: "scientia mali"</note> which was the cause of Adam's fall (for indeed, having dealings with the serpent, he was deceived and thus tasted of the tree of both evil and good), I desire from my heart, along with all Christians engaged in the true and sincere Wisdom of God, that it be thrust down into the abyss to its master, the Devil. It was he who, in the beginning, breathed this craft into the world like a foul vapor for the ruin and destruction of humanity, so that no trace of such a "mystery of iniquity" might be left to human posterity.

Therefore, for a better distinction between these two species, authors have called the good science ***Magic***, but the evil one directly ***Cacomagic*** <term>Cacomagic: From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'magia'; specifically referring to "black magic" or sorcery involving demons.</term>.

That which is named ***natural*** is intended for revealing and investigating the mysteries of nature, both celestial and terrestrial. Thus, through the mediation of this science, the ***Magi***—who are the most accurate explorers of nature—by applying active things to passive ones with a learned and expert hand, eventually produced things for the world that the common people regarded as miracles. They were accustomed to perform works that sometimes surpassed all admiration, as trustworthy authors have recorded. Sometimes this art even leads toward supernatural mystery, bringing the incorruptible Spirit of the creature—or the <term>quintessence</term> itself, which is most full of the divine ray—out of darkness into the sight of mortals by means of true, rather than counterfeit, chemistry. 

By this means, the ***Ancient Magi*** brought so many great things to light. These were not ***Cacomagi*** (as the ignorant suppose), who are practiced in the most wretched and "Cacomagical" wisdom, but the truly ***Wise***. These are the men who received the gift of Wisdom from God, such as those three Magi, or Wise Men, who followed his star from the East when Christ was born. I speak of those three kings who foretold that Christ, the Savior of the world, was to be born. 

It should be known, however, that there were anciently four celebrated schools of this natural Magic throughout the entire world: namely the ***Indian, Persian, Chaldean, and Ethiopian***. In the ***Indian*** school among the ***Brahmins*** <note>original: "Brachmanas"</note>, the fame of Hiarcha was greatest; of Tespion among the ***Gymnosophists*** <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known for asceticism and nudity.</note>; of Buddha among the Babylonians; of Numa Pompilius among the Romans; of Zamolxis among the Thracians; of Abbaris among the Hyperboreans; of Hermes among the Egyptians; and of Zoroaster, son of Oromasus, among the Persians. 

It was from this part of the world that those three kings came, seeking the newborn Christ to adore him with gifts. Interpreters of the Gospels explain that these men were Philosophers of the Chaldeans, of the same kind as ***Hiarcha the Indian, Buddha the Babylonian, and Zoroaster the Persian***. These men were called "kings" because Plato testifies in his *Alcibiades* that the sons of Persian kings were instructed in the mysteries of this natural magic, so that they might learn to administer and distribute the affairs of the commonwealth after the image of the world's own governance. Cicero seems to support this opinion of Plato, saying in his *Books on Divination* that ***no one among the Persians was adorned with the royal diadem who had not first learned Magic.*** This seems to be the reason why these Eastern kings were most learned in Wisdom, or "good Magic," seeking the name of Magi and Wise Men, which is why they are described as ***MAGI*** by the ***HOLY SPIRIT*** in the Gospel.

<summary>This page distinguishes "Natural Magic" (divine wisdom used to explore nature and alchemy) from "Cacomagic" (evil sorcery). It argues that the Biblical Magi were actually philosopher-kings trained in this noble tradition of natural science.</summary>

# Treatise

<margin>Aphorisms of the Arbatel <note>Referring to the *Arbatel de magia veterum*, a highly influential manual of spiritual magic first published in 1575.</note></margin>

Magic, or Wisdom, in a general sense is the knowledge of either:

*   **The Good**, which is true Wisdom, of which one type is:
    *   **Theosophy** <term>Theosophy: From the Greek 'theos' (god) and 'sophia' (wisdom); here meaning the direct knowledge of God and divine things.</term>
        *   Knowledge of the Word of God, and the ordering of life according to the Word of God.
        *   Knowledge of God’s governance through Angels, whom Sacred Scripture calls "watchers" <note>original: "vigiles"</note>, and the understanding of the mysteries of angels.
    *   **Anthroposophy** <term>Anthroposophy: Literally "human wisdom," focusing on the study of the human being and the natural world.</term> given to man by God.
        *   The knowledge of natural things and the wonders contained within them; this belongs to natural Philosophy.
        *   Prudence in human affairs, which is the subject of moral and Political Philosophy.

*   **The Evil**, which is "Pseudo-wisdom" <note>original: "Pseudosophia," meaning false or sham wisdom.</note>, or that human wisdom which is false and fraudulent; and this is twofold:
    *   **Cacodosophy** <term>Cacodosophy: From the Greek for "evil teaching" or "wicked doctrine."</term>
        *   Contempt for the Word of God and living according to the will of the Devil.
        *   Ignorance of God’s governance through the Angels.
        *   Despising the guardianship of Angels and becoming companions of Devils.
        *   Idolatry and Atheism.
    *   **Cacodemonia** <term>Cacodemonia: The practice of dealing with evil spirits (cacodemons) for harmful ends.</term> which is occupied with a cunning used for the destruction of the human race; its species are:
        *   **Poisoning** <note>original: "Veneficium," a term that encompasses both chemical poisoning and harmful sorcery.</note>, which is concerned with drugs, cups, and love-potions <term>philters: potions intended to induce love or lust.</term> prepared for human harm.
        *   **Necromancy** <term>Necromancy: Historically the art of conjuring the spirits of the dead for divination, here categorized as traffic with "unclean spirits."</term>, fashioned by dealings with unclean Spirits through the rites of an unlucky and wicked curiosity, illicit incantations, and prayers.
        *   **Theurgy**, which seems to be guided by good angels and divine power, yet under the names of God and Angels, it is bound by the wicked deceptions of Demons. <note>The author warns that this form of magic is a "wolf in sheep's clothing," using holy names to mask demonic influence.</note>
        *   **The science of illusion** <note>original: "Scientia præstigiatrix," referring to the creation of phantasms or "prestigiation."</note>, by means of which Magi produce phantasms and even many miracles; and this is done partly through fumigations, lights, potions, rings, images, and mirrors, with which are mixed Necromantic incantations, curses, and the deceits of Demons.

It defines various occult practices like Necromancy and Theurgy, specifically framing the latter as a deceptive form of demonic manipulation.</summary>

### Concerning the Highest Good, etc.

In light of this, it appears clear to the Wise that the whole of Magic should not be rejected by Christians simply because one portion or species of it is occupied with the worst things, which are abominable to the Christian soul. If, I say, worldly Wisdom—which is the fruit of human invention—is foolish (according to the words of the Apostle <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 3:19: "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God."</note>) and leads to the worst ends, then that true Wisdom is not to be rejected. True Wisdom was sent into the world by God through divine inspiration for the benefit of His creatures; it should not be banished into perpetual oblivion by Christian men because of the diabolical nonsense of that "other" kind. Indeed, if this true Wisdom were taken away, nothing would remain in the whole world of either divine or natural Wisdom. As for that "knowledge of evil" which was the cause of Adam's fall (for he, having dealings with the serpent, was deceived, and thus tasted of the tree of both good and evil), I desire from my heart, along with all Christians practiced in the true and sincere Wisdom of God, that it should be thrust down into the abyss to its master, the Devil. For it was originally inspired into the world by the cunning of its said master like a rising vapor, intended for human ruin and destruction, so that no trace of such a mystery of iniquity might be left to human posterity.

Therefore, for a better distinction between these two types, authors have called the good science *Magic* <note>original: *Magia*</note>, while the evil kind is directly called *Cacomagic* <term>Cacomagic: From the Greek *kakos* (evil) and *mageia* (magic); refers to black magic or sorcery intended to harm.</term>.

**Natural Magic**, as it is named, is intended for revealing and investigating the mysteries of nature, both celestial and terrestrial. Through this science, the *Magi*—who are the most accurate explorers of nature—eventually produced things for the world that the common people regarded as miracles. They did this by applying active things to passive things <term>Applying actives to passives: A fundamental concept in Renaissance natural magic; the idea that a practitioner can produce "wonders" by bringing together natural substances that have a hidden sympathy or complementary power.</term> with a learned and expert hand. As trustworthy authors have recorded in their writings, they were accustomed at times to perform works beyond all admiration. Sometimes this art even leads to the supernatural mystery by bringing the incorruptible Spirit of the creature—the "quintessence" <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, believed by alchemists to be the medicinal or spiritual core of matter.</term> itself, most fully filled with the divine ray—out of darkness into the sight of mortals through true (and not counterfeit) chemistry. By this means, the *ancient Magi* (not *Cacomagi*, as the ignorant suppose) brought so many great things to light. These were not men practiced in the worst "Cacomagical" wisdom, but truly Wise men—those who received the gift of Wisdom from God. Such were those three Magi, or Wise Men, who followed the star from the East when Christ was born: those three kings, I say, who foretold the birth of Christ, the Savior of the world.

It should be known that in ancient times there were four schools of this natural Magic famous throughout the whole world: namely, the **Indian, Persian, Chaldean, and Ethiopian**. In the Indian school among the Brahmans, there was the great fame of Hiarcha; of Tespion among the Gymnosophists <note>Gymnosophists: Meaning "naked philosophers," an ancient Greek term for Indian holy men who practiced asceticism.</note>; of Buddha among the Babylonians; of Numa Pompilio among the Romans; of Zamolxis among the Thracians; of Abaris among the Hyperboreans; of Hermes among the Egyptians; and of Zoroaster, son of Oromasius, among the Persians. It was from that part of the world that those three kings came, seeking the newborn Christ to adore Him with gifts. Interpreters of the Gospels explain that these men were philosophers of the Chaldeans, of the same kind as Hiarcha the Indian, Buddha the Babylonian, or Zoroaster the Persian. And these were called "kings" because Plato testifies in his *Alcibiades* that the sons of the Persian kings were instructed in the mysteries of this natural magic, so that they might learn to administer and distribute the affairs of the state according to the image of the world's governance. Cicero seems to support this opinion of Plato, saying in his *Books on Divination*: **"No one among the Persians was adorned with the royal diadem who had not first learned Magic."** This appears to be the reason why these Eastern kings were most learned in good Wisdom, or Magic; they sought the name of Magi and Sages, and thus they are described by the HOLY SPIRIT in the Gospel as *Magi*.

It traces the history of Magic through ancient global schools and identifies the biblical Three Wise Men as practitioners of this noble, natural science.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of "Natural Magic" by addressing its critics, specifically the French theologian Marin Mersenne. It argues that true magic is a branch of divine wisdom (Theosophy) involving the study of God's governance through angels, and begins a specific defense of the medieval scholar Roger Bacon.</meta>

# A Treatise

Is the name of Magic or the Magi to be held in such hatred among mortals, when the Sacred Scriptures seem to celebrate and remember it with such honor? <note>The author refers to the "Magi" or Three Wise Men in the Nativity story as a justification for the term.</note> Or should anyone be believed who, because of one evil branch of Magic, attempts to uproot the good also from the memory of mortals? Is it as if, because of the sins of the worst men, the good must also be completely extirpated and fundamentally removed along with the evil?

But there are those who use the term "Magic" without any distinction throughout the entire thread of their works, always in the worst sense—that is, they take it to mean *Cacomagic* <term>Cacomagic: From the Greek "kakos" (evil), referring specifically to "black" or demonic magic.</term>—hardly understanding that there is no difference between natural Philosophy and natural Magic, and consequently no difference between a *Magus* and a *Philosopher*. Even Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus, did not deign to mention this kind of Magic when he said that *Apollonius of Tyana was a Magus, or a Pythagorean Philosopher* <note>original Latin: "Apollonium Tyaneum fuisse Magum, seu Philosophum Pythagoricum." Jerome was a 4th-century Church Father; Apollonius was a famous 1st-century sage.</note>.

Can you not also perceive, with open eyes and contrary to their own opinion, from the higher branch of the previous distinction, that true Wisdom (which is the knowledge of good) has in its *Theosophical* <term>Theosophical: From "Theosophy," meaning "divine wisdom" or knowledge of God and the celestial hierarchy.</term> nature the duty to teach not only the knowledge of the Word of God (that is, eternal Wisdom), but also that by which we are taught how God governs all things through the mediation of Angels? For this reason, they are called "Watchers" in the sacred pages, and through this wisdom, we are made participants in the Angelic mysteries. Are not those also included through a single branch of Cacomagic who are swept away by ignorance of God's governance through Angels, and, despising the protection of Angels, make themselves—willingly or unwillingly—companions to Devils? Yet we have this confirmed by the Holy Scriptures: namely, that *God carries out His Word through the mediation of His Angels with the strongest power, and that it is the duty of Angels to perform what is pleasing to God, and that everyone has their own good Angel before the face of the Father who is in heaven*.

<margin>Psalm 103:4</margin>
But why should we create further doubt regarding this matter, since the Holy Bible itself seems to resonate with this subject everywhere? And yet a certain monk called Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a famous French mathematician and theologian who vigorously attacked "magical" thinking in the 17th century.</note> has unknowingly, I know, fallen into that pit of Cacomagic. For he seems to deny the powers of Angels and their governance under God in the world, as well as the guardianship assigned by God over us. He seems to call those "impious Magi" who feel this way, and by this reasoning—in his denial of the protection of the good Angels—he makes himself a companion of Devils.

But since this "good" author, according to his own ill-pleasure, sharply rebukes European men—men most famous for their learning and even unblemished in the Roman religion, being dressed in religious habits and untouched in the honesty of their lives—falsely accusing them of impious Magic (truly called cacomagic), let the readers see through what follows whether these men are truly such as they are accused by Marin. Let their writings be produced before the throne of the tribunal, so that you may understand what they can bring forth in their masters' cause, by which they might declare their masters either innocent or guilty of Cacomagic. In this way, you may conclude whether they are truly to be held as impious Cacomagicians or as natural Magi, in no way inconsistent with divine laws. And first, I will explain the accusation against *Roger Bacon* <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher known for his early advocacy of the scientific method.</note> introduced by *Marin Mersenne*; then I will give Bacon's own response, and so I will proceed with the rest.

->From Column 971 of Mersenne.<-

> It should be noted, however, that Roger Bacon wrote one book on Necromantic images, another on incantations, two on Alchemy, and countless others on Astrological mysteries. So cautious is the rival of the human race <note>A common historical epithet for the Devil.</note> that he deludes even this otherwise most learned man and leads them into error; their familiarity is certainly the more dangerous because they better conceal the poison of insane doctrine with various conjectures and the intricacies of reasoning. By their custom, even the elect, if it were possible, are cast into the danger of their salvation, not to say their destruction.

<header>Concerning the Highest Good, etc.</header>

### Roger Bacon: speaking for himself from the booklet on the *Power of Art and Nature*.

<note>original: "Robert. Baco." The text refers to Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the famous English philosopher and Franciscan friar often mistakenly called "Robert" in early modern texts.</note>

Although nature is powerful and wondrous, yet Art—using nature as its instrument—is more powerful than natural force alone, as we have seen in many things. Anything, however, that exists outside the operation of Nature or Art is either not human, or it is a fabrication and occupied with deceptions. Because of this, it is a most wicked occupation when a man despises the laws of Philosophy and, against all reason, invokes nefarious Spirits so that through them he might fulfill his will. And in this lies the error: that they believe Spirits are subject to them, and that Spirits are compelled by human will. This is impossible, for human power is far inferior to that of the Spirits. Or they err even more in this: that through certain natural things they use, they believe evil Spirits are either summoned or put to flight. And they err further when, through invocations, prayers, and sacrifices, men strive to appease them and bring them forth for the benefit of men; for without comparison, it would be easier to obtain from God or from good Spirits whatever a man ought to consider useful. But the evil Spirits do not assist favorably in these useless matters, except insofar as it is permitted by God (who rules and governs the human race) because of the sins of men. Therefore, these ways are outside the teachings of Wisdom; indeed, they work better to the contrary, and those who truly practice Philosophy have never cared for these methods.

And elsewhere: And thus many secrets of Nature and Art are thought to be Magic, and Magi foolishly trust in spells and characters <term>Characters: In this context, "characters" refers to mystical symbols, sigils, or astrological signs believed to hold occult power.</term>, thinking that these provide power to them. For the sake of pursuing these things, they abandon the work of Nature and Art because of the error of spells and characters. Thus, both kinds of these men are deprived of the utility of Wisdom, forced by their own foolishness. Therefore, those things contained in the books of the Magi are all to be kept at a distance—even if they contain something true—because they abuse so many falsehoods that one cannot discern between the true and the false.

<note>original: "Hæc ille pro se ipso."</note> Thus he speaks for himself, and there throughout his whole admirable booklet, he declares the power of art and nature—that is, the mysteries of Natural Magic.

What do you say, O just Judges? Is this religious man guilty, according to the opinion of that Monk, or not guilty? I shall say no more on this matter, since the integrity of this good man shines forth more clearly than the midday light (despite his slanderer). But now let another be brought forward: let it be an Abbot, a man of no small esteem in the Roman Church: Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German Benedictine abbot, lexicographer, and chronicler who was famously accused of demonic magic due to his cryptic writing.</note>, I say—an Abbot known to all the learned and most celebrated for his profound knowledge, who has not only himself but also other religious men speaking on his behalf. The accusation, or rather the judgment against him, is as follows:

### From Column 42 of Mersenne, in Volume 1.

I gladly leave aside the other rhapsodies and "name-makings" of the Rabbis, just as I do those things which Cornelius <note>Referring to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous occult philosopher and contemporary of Trithemius.</note> has in the place cited, and the things in Trithemius’s *Steganographia* <term>Steganographia: Trithemius's most famous work. It appears to be about summoning spirits to communicate over distances, but was later revealed to be a complex treatise on cryptography (secret writing).</term> which are most worthy of the flames, etc.

### Trithemius for himself in his Letter to Cornelius Agrippa.

> We ask and pray that you always exercise your labor toward better things and demonstrate the light of true Wisdom—by which you are greatly and divinely illuminated—even to the ignorant. Let the consideration of any scoundrels (take note, Mersenne!) not draw you back from your purpose: of whom it is truly said, "the weary ox treads the ground firmly," <note>original: "bos lassus fortiter figit pedem." A Latin proverb meaning that those who are slow or "tired" (intellectually dull or reactionary) can be stubborn and difficult to move.</note> etc.

Thus he speaks for himself, by which he desires to show the world that the whole endeavor of a Christian man lies in the acquisition of the light of true Wisdom, by which he may be divinely illuminated, so that in that light, he may see the light.

### Abbot Sigismund appears on behalf of Trithemius, as in Column 440 of Marin’s work.

I, Lord Sigismund, Abbot of the Monastery of Seon of the Order of Saint Benedict, confess and attest that all things written in the three books of the *Steganographia* of Trithemius are natural and pertain to Natural Magic, even if they are not understood because of the various characters, numbers, and modes of conjuration by which he seems to propagate Demonic Magic—even though, under those names, he only hides natural secrets, etc.

Tractatus

Thus says Sigismund: Judge therefore whether this Abbot <note>Referring to Johannes Trithemius, discussed on the previous page.</note> is guilty of Cacomagia <term>Cacomagia: derived from Greek, meaning "evil magic" or "black magic," as opposed to "natural magic."</term> or not. Let us move to the third who is called into question as a wicked Magician: this is Marsilio Ficino, a Priest, whom [Mersenne] pursues with this kind of accusation.

->From Column 1704 of Mersenne.<-

> He objects that Marsilio Ficino—a Catholic man and most learned—attributes the powers of Music to the stars, so that through songs superior influences might be attracted. I respond indeed that Ficino is not Catholic where he brings forth and approves those Magical and Astrological trifles.

## Marsilio Ficino responds for himself in his Apology at the end of his book *On Life from Heaven* <note>original: "cœlitus." This refers to the third book of Ficino's *De vita libri tres*, titled *De vita coelitus comparanda* (On obtaining life from the heavens).</note> in this way:

> Magic or images are not indeed approved by Marsilio, but he is merely narrating what Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was a major Neoplatonic philosopher whose works Ficino translated and interpreted.</note> himself says while interpreting him. This his writings clearly declare if they are read with an even mind. Nor have I asserted even a single word here concerning profane Magic, which relies on the worship of Demons, but I have made mention of Natural Magic, which captures the benefits of the celestial bodies through natural things for the prosperous health of bodies. This faculty surely seems as much to be granted to those using their talents legitimately as medicine and agriculture are granted by right—and even more so, the more perfect it is, joining heavenly things to earthly ones by industry. And from this workshop <note>original: "officina." Here used metaphorically to mean the school or practice of the Magi.</note> the Magi, first of all, immediately adored the newborn Christ. Why therefore do you fear the name of "Magician" so dreadfully, a name graceful in the Gospel, which does not sound of sorcery and poisoning, but of a Wise man and a Priest, etc.

These are the stones, Guicciardini, <note>Likely referring to a member of the influential Guicciardini family of Florence, acting as a patron or interlocutor.</note> for defending the reputation of his Master against the detractor. Whether this good man is worthy of such an accusation, I leave to your judgments.

But now the writings of that "Arch-magician" (as he says), Cornelius Agrippa, are produced for accusation and judgment. But he, who is the accuser of his brothers, continues thus:

->From Column 39 of Mersenne. In the verso.<-

> Agrippa, forgetful of himself and an Arch-magician most addicted to Magic, devises various names of Angels, etc.

His own writings are produced, excusing their master. In the first place, his innocence is shown by his *Declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences* and that book he wrote, *On the Excellence of the Word of God*, which is that sole and unique mystery which the Wise have sought with such vehemence and diligence. Then we read in his "Letter to the Reader" the marrow of his *Occult Philosophy* in these words:

> *I do not doubt that the title of our book, "On Occult Philosophy or Magic," by its variety will entice many to read it, among whom several of slanted opinion, weak in mind, and many also malicious and ungrateful toward our talent will approach. These, in their rash ignorance taking the name of Magic in a worse sense, will cry out—scarcely having seen the title—that we teach forbidden arts, sow seeds of heresy, are a stumbling block to pious ears, a scandal to noble minds, and that I am a sorcerer, superstitious, and demonic because I am a Magician. To these I would respond thus: that among literate men, "Magician" does not sound like sorcerer, superstitious, or demonic, but like a Wise man, a Priest, and a Prophet. The Sibyls <note>Prophetic women in ancient Greece and Rome who were later interpreted by Christians as having predicted the coming of Christ.</note> were Magicians, and therefore prophesied so clearly about Christ. Indeed, even the Magi, from the wonderful secrets of the world, recognized Christ the author of the world as born, and were the first of all to come to adore Him. The very name of Magic is accepted by Philosophers, praised by Theologians, and not unwelcome even to the Gospel itself. I believe those censors of such stubborn arrogance would sooner forbid themselves the Sibyls, the Holy Magi, or even the Gospel itself than receive the name of Magic into favor, etc. I confess that our Philosophy, besides Magic itself, teaches many superfluous things and things curious for display.*

<meta>This page continues the defense of Renaissance occult philosophers, specifically focusing on Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa. It explains the "riddle" of why these authors mixed apparently superstitious or "black" magic with their philosophical works: as a protective veil to hide natural secrets from the uninitiated.</meta>

# On the Highest Good, etc.

*...to teach wonders while at the same time abandoning them as vain, yet not being ignorant of their causes. Those things which can be done for the benefit of men—to turn away evil events, to destroy sorceries <note>original: "maleficia," often referring to harmful or "black" magic</note>, to cure diseases, to drive away phantoms, to preserve the skill of life, honor, and fortune, without offense to God or injury to religion—who would not judge them as useful as they are necessary, etc.*

Agrippa answers thus for himself: I also commit him, along with the others, to the judgment of just judges.

From these things it appears clearer than the Sun that these most learned men, although they mix spurious and impure ceremonial things with the pure, nevertheless their entire intention revolves around true Magic, around true and holy Wisdom, around that true and unique Highest Good of the Philosophers, and not Cacomagia <term>Cacomagia: derived from Greek, meaning "evil magic" or "black magic," as opposed to natural or divine magic.</term>, since they by unanimous consent hold Cacomagia (as it is right to gather from all their assertions) in hatred.

<margin>From column 470.</margin>
But perhaps curious readers will desire to know the reason why these authors are accustomed to mixing spurious, superfluous, and prodigious or necromantic things with true Wisdom and naked truth. To them I respond: because they were unwilling, at first glance, to cast pearls before swine, nor did they wish for their roses to be found without thorns. Therefore they wrote in such a way that they would be understood only by the wise; for the wise man reads one thing and understands another. Hence Abbot Sigismund <note>Likely referring to a contemporary defender of the occultist Johannes Trithemius.</note> says: *“Although Trithemius has characters, numbers, and various modes of conjuration by which Demonic Magic seems to be propagated, nevertheless under those names he hides only natural secrets, etc.”* This is also what Agrippa seems to intend: by confessing that although his Philosophy contains vain and superstitious things along with the truth, he nevertheless warns us to leave the vain things behind, with the caution that we should by no means be ignorant of their hidden causes. From this he argues that a mystery is contained under a fiction, a spiritual thing under the "rind" or the literal word, and a holy character under the name of an angel. 

And they did this after the example of the ancient philosophers, among whom Socrates did not want the secrets of nature to be committed to the skins of goats and sheep <note>i.e., written on parchment</note>, lest they be understood by any unworthy person. And Aristotle, in his *Book of Secrets* <note>Referring to the "Secretum Secretorum," a popular medieval treatise attributed to Aristotle.</note>, says: *“He who would communicate the secrets of art and nature should be considered a breaker of the celestial seal.”* And the whole crowd of philosophers agrees on this: *that they hid nothing in their philosophy except the secret of the art,* and [the philosopher] says it is not permitted for him to reveal it to anyone, because if it were done he would be cursed, which would also move the indignation of God. And elsewhere he says *that he has hidden the mysteries of natural science not from the learned and true sons of the art, but from the unworthy.* 

But to come to the words of Roger Bacon (whom Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French priest and mathematician who frequently criticized occultism.</note> makes guilty of Cacomagia), Bacon himself calls him insane who wished to disclose any secret to the world except through riddles and enigmas, or to commit them to writings by which they would be hidden from the world and scarcely understood by the studious and wise. And Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist.</note> says: *“This mystery is covered and hidden, and wherever it is, it is called by a thousand names; it is also sealed nor is it open except to the wise, and yet the thing is one, and the way of operation is unique and linear.”* And that truly wise Arbatel <note>The reputed author of the "Arbatel de magia veterum," a 16th-century manual of spiritual magic.</note> (though he is also falsely held to be an evil magician), speaks thus in his primordial Aphorism: *“He who wishes to know secrets, let him know how to keep secrets secretly; let him reveal what is to be revealed, seal what is to be sealed, and give not that which is holy to dogs nor cast pearls before swine; observe this law and the eyes of your mind shall be opened to understand secrets.”* Thus he spoke. And Solomon says: *“It is for a wise man to conceal a matter.”* And Christ says: *“Speak to them in parables,”* etc.

Here therefore, Readers, judge whether such a great crime is to be imposed upon these good men as Marin Mersenne has published to the world with his outcries, and whether the name of magic is to be held in such great hatred, if it be considered in its sincere and simple nature.

# Treatise

These are the words of Sigismund: Judge, therefore, whether this Abbot <note>Referring to Johannes Trithemius, a famous abbot and cryptographer accused of magic.</note> is guilty of evil magic <term>Cacomagia: From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'mageia' (magic); specifically malevolent or demonic sorcery.</term> or not.

Let us proceed to the third person who is called into question as a wicked Magician, and that is Marsilio Ficino, the Priest, whom he pursues with this kind of accusation.

->From Column 1764 of Mersenne.<- <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a French mathematician and theologian who often critiqued Renaissance magic while corresponding with the greatest scientists of his age.</note>

He objects that Marsilio Ficino—a Catholic man and most learned—attributes the powers of Music to the stars, so that through songs, superior influences might be attracted. I respond indeed that Ficino is not acting as a Catholic where he brings forward and approves those magical and astrological trifles.

->Marsilio Ficino, in his Apology at the end of his life,<-
->responds for himself from heaven thus:<- <note>Ficino wrote an 'Apologia' to defend his 'Three Books on Life' from charges of heresy and magic.</note>

> That magic or images are not indeed approved by Marsilio, but he is merely narrating what Plotinus <note>Plotinus: A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated into Latin.</note> himself says while interpreting him. This his writings clearly declare, if they are read with an impartial mind. Nor have I asserted a single word here concerning profane Magic, which relies on the worship of Demons, but I have made mention of natural Magic, which seeks celestial benefits through natural things for the prosperous health of bodies. This faculty surely seems as much to be granted to those using it lawfully as medicine and agriculture are granted by right—and even more so, as it is more perfect, joining celestial things to earthly ones by its industry. And from this workshop, the Magi, first of all men, adored Christ immediately upon his birth. Why then do you fear the name of Magician so dreadfully? It is a name gracious to the Gospel, which does not signify a sorcerer <note>original: "maleficum"</note> or a poisoner, but a Wise Man and a Priest, etc.

Petrus Guicciardini <note>A member of the influential Florentine Guicciardini family and a supporter of Ficino.</note> offered these stones <note>i.e., these arguments</note> to defend his master’s reputation against the detractor.

Whether this good man is therefore worthy of such a great accusation, I leave to your judgments.

But now, the writings of that "Arch-magician," as he calls him, Cornelius Agrippa, are produced for accusation and judgment. But he who is the accuser of his own brothers proceeds thus:

->From Column 39 of Mersenne. In v.<-

Agrippa, forgetful of himself and an Arch-magician most addicted to Magic, devises various names of Angels, etc.

->His own writings are produced, excusing their master.<-

In the first place, his own innocence is indicated by his *Declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>Agrippa’s famous 'De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum', where he ironically attacks all human knowledge, including magic.</note> and that book which he wrote on the *Excellence of the Word of God*, which is that sole and unique mystery which the Wise have sought with such vehemence and diligence.

->Then we read in his Letter to the Reader the very marrow<-
->of his Occult Philosophy in these words:<- <note>Agrippa’s 'De Occulta Philosophia libri tres' (Three Books on Occult Philosophy) is the most influential compendium of Renaissance magic.</note>

> I do not doubt that the title of our book, *On Occult Philosophy* or *On Magic*, might by its variety allure very many to read, among whom some of perverse opinion and weak mind, and many even malicious and ungrateful toward our talent, will approach. These men, in their rash ignorance taking the name of Magic in its worse sense, will—hardly having glimpsed the title—cry out that we teach forbidden arts, sow the seeds of heresies, are a stumbling block to pious ears, a scandal to noble talents; that I am a sorcerer, a superstitious man, a demonic man, because I am a Magician. To these I would respond thus: that among literate men, the word Magician does not sound as a sorcerer, nor as one superstitious or demonic, but as a Wise Man, a Priest, and a Prophet. The Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses of the Greek and Roman world, whom Renaissance Christians believed had predicted the coming of Christ.</note> were female Magicians, and therefore prophesied most clearly concerning Christ. And now, the Magi also recognized Christ, the author of the world, as having been born through the wonderful secrets of the world itself, and they were the first of all to come to adore him. The name of Magic itself is accepted by Philosophers, praised by Theologians, and even not unwelcome to the Gospel itself. I believe those censors of such persistent arrogance would sooner forbid themselves the Sibyls, the Saints, or even the Gospel itself before they would receive the name of Magic into favor, etc. I confess that our Philosophy, besides Magic itself, teaches many things that are superfluous and curious for the sake of show.

# On the Highest Good, etc.

> *...to teach wonders, while at the same time leaving these things aside as vain, yet not being ignorant of their causes. But those things which can be done for the benefit of men—to avert bad outcomes, to destroy sorceries, to cure diseases, to exterminate phantoms, to preserve the dexterity of life, honor, and fortune, without offense to God and without injury to religion—who would not judge those to be as useful as they are even necessary, etc.*

Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous theologian and occult writer whose "Three Books of Occult Philosophy" is a cornerstone of Renaissance magic.</note> answers these things for himself: whom I also commit, along with the others, to the judgment of those critics.

From these things it appears "brighter than the sun" that these most learned men, even if they mix spurious and impure ceremonial matters with pure ones, nevertheless their entire intention is centered around **True Magic**, around **true and holy Wisdom**, and around that true and only **Highest Good of the Philosophers**, and not <term>Cacomagia: From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'mageia' (magic); specifically malevolent or demonic sorcery.</term>, since they—by unanimous consent—hate "Cacomagia" (as is right to gather from all their assertions).

But perhaps curious readers will desire to know the reason why these authors were accustomed to mixing spurious, superfluous, and "prodigious" or necromantic things with **True Wisdom** and the naked truth. To them I respond: because they did not wish, at first glance, to "throw pearls before swine," nor did they want their "roses" to be found without "thorns." They wrote, therefore, in such a way that they might be understood only by the wise; for the wise man reads one thing and understands another. Whence Abbot Sigismund says: <margin>From column 470.</margin> *Although Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and polymath accused of demonic magic due to his complex systems of cryptography.</note> possesses characters, numbers, and various modes of conjuration by which he seems to propagate Demonic Magic; nevertheless, under those names he only hides natural secrets, etc.* 

Agrippa also seems to intend this: by confessing that although his Philosophy contains vain and superstitious things alongside the truth, he nevertheless warns us to leave the vain things aside, with this caution: that we should by no means remain ignorant of their hidden causes. From this he argues that a mystery is contained under a fiction, a spiritual matter under the "bark" or the letter, and a holy character under the name of an "angel." And they did this following the example of the ancient and antique philosophers, among whom Socrates did not wish the secrets of nature to be committed to the skins of goats and sheep <note>Meaning parchment or books available to the public.</note>, lest they be understood by anyone unworthy. 

And Aristotle, in his *Book of Secrets* <note>The 'Secretum Secretorum', a popular medieval treatise attributed to Aristotle, though likely written in Arabic in the 10th century.</note>, says: *That he who would communicate the secrets of art and nature would be held as a breaker of the celestial seal.* And the whole crowd of philosophers agrees on this: *that they have hidden nothing in their philosophy except the secret of the art,* and he says it is not permitted for him to reveal it to anyone, because if it were done, he would be cursed, which would also move the indignation of God. And elsewhere he says *that he has hidden the mysteries of natural science not from the learned and true sons of the art, but from the unworthy.* 

But to come to the words of Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English friar and scientist known as 'Doctor Mirabilis', who was frequently accused of magic.</note> (whom Mersenne makes guilty of "Cacomagia"): he himself calls that man insane who wished to disclose any secret to the world except through riddles and enigmas, or to commit them to writings by which they would be hidden from the world, and scarcely understood by the studious and wise. And Morienus <note>An 8th-century legendary alchemist and hermit.</note> says: *This mystery is covered and hidden, and wherever it may be, it is called by a thousand names; it is also sealed, nor is it open except to the wise, and yet the thing is one, the way of operation is one and linear.* 

And that truly wise man, Arbatel <note>The 'Arbatel de Magia Veterum', a 16th-century manual of spiritual magic emphasizing piety.</note> (although he also is falsely held to be an evil magician), speaks thus in his primary Aphorism: *He who wishes to know secrets, let him know how to keep secrets secretly; let him reveal what is to be revealed, and seal what is to be sealed; do not give that which is holy to dogs, nor throw pearls before swine; observe this law and the eyes of your mind shall be opened to understand secrets.* These are his words. And Solomon says: *It is the part of a wise man to conceal a matter.* And Christ says: *Speak to them in parables, etc.*

Judge here, therefore, O Readers, whether such a great crime is to be imposed upon these good men as Marin Mersenne has published to the world with his outcries, and whether the name of "Magic" is to be held in such great hatred, if it be considered in its sincere and simple nature.

# BOOK TWO.
->In which<-
# THE NATURE OF THE KABBALAH,
## AND ITS FOUNDATION
## IS REVEALED.

<margin>Reuchlin, Book 1 <note>original: "Reuchl. l 1." Refers to Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist who was the first non-Jew to deeply study the Kabbalah and introduce it to the Christian intellectual world.</note></margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring floral scrollwork and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>
Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabala"</note> (to draw its definition from the very nature of the word itself) is the reception by the ear of the mystery of God and nature from another. Or put another way: Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the life-giving contemplation of God and of the separate forms <note>In this context, "separate forms" refers to angels or spiritual intelligences that exist apart from physical matter.</note>; those who obtain this through heavenly inspiration are rightly called Kabbalists. And although this Hebrew name seems not to have been known except in the time of the Christians, it is nevertheless most certain that this art is quite ancient. There are those who wish to trace its origin only from the time of Moses; however, if the matter is considered with a slightly more accurate gaze, we perceive that it was propagated even from the age of Adam. To him, first of all, such a great secret was revealed by the Creator himself, which afterwards in the succession of time was handed down as if from father to son—not indeed to just any elder, but to both the elder and the younger by birth, whom God wished to admit: as the sacred scriptures testify. Hence God seemed to show greater favor to Abel than to Cain, which is why the offering of the former was pleasing to him, while that of the latter was rejected; this also happened by divine will to Jacob, with Esau being excluded.

<margin>Wisdom 10, 11 <note>Refers to the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon, chapters 10 and 11.</note></margin>
The subject of this mystical science was that mystical wisdom so celebrated from the times of Adam even to the time of the Apostles. The Wise Man <note>Traditionally identified as King Solomon.</note> seems to confirm this through successive accounts: *Wisdom guarded Adam and gave him the power to contain all things. From her Cain perished; she healed the earth submerged by waters, and guided the just Noah. She preserved and guarded the just Abraham. She freed Lot fleeing from the fire descending upon the Five Cities <note>The Pentapolis, the group of five cities including Sodom and Gomorrah.</note>. She led Jacob, a fugitive from his brother’s wrath, through straight paths, and showed him the kingdom of God, and gave him the knowledge of holy things. She did not abandon the just Joseph, but freed him from sinners. She freed the Israelites from Egyptian servitude. She entered into the soul of Moses, through which he stood against terrible kings with portents and signs. She led the Israelites on a wondrous path, and was a covering for them by day and a light of stars by night. She carried them through the Red Sea. She directed the works of the travelers by the hands of the holy prophet, and they stood against their enemies. For them, water was given from the rock, etc.*

Finally, the Apostles themselves acknowledge that this is their very "hidden mystery" which had its beginning from the dawn of the world. "We speak," says the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in 1 Corinthians 2.</note>, "a mystical wisdom in a mystery, as it were, a hidden one, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and God revealed to us through the Spirit." Solomon declares the reason why God does not walk with those who are not gifted with this kind of gift: <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> *Wisdom,* he says, *establishes the friends of God and prophets; for God loves no one except him who dwells with Wisdom.*

And hence it was that Abel’s offering was acceptable to God, while that of Cain was rejected; so also Jacob was beloved by God, while his elder brother Esau was held in hatred. For this reason, from the time he received the mystical blessing from his father Isaac—and not before—God appeared to him with His angels, first in dreams and then later face to face. From that time, according to the covenant made with Abraham and Isaac his fathers, [He was] with the house of the Israelites...

# Concerning the Highest Good, etc.

<margin>Genesis 41:38</margin>
...always walked, as was declared from the place cited above: but this mystical science was not communicated or revealed to all Israelites, but only to one or another among the entire multitude by a hidden tradition. It was through this that they were made participants in holy wisdom. But Joseph, whom Jacob pursued with such great love that he was hated by his brothers, possessed the gift of dreaming true dreams and of revealing and uncovering hidden things. This gift was so exalted, through the revelation of that mystical spirit, that even the Egyptians were moved by the truth and broke forth into this opinion of him: *Can we find another like this man, in whom is the spirit of God? There is no one as prudent and wise as you.* <note>original: "Anne inuenire possumus huic similem in quo spiritus Deorum sit? Nemo est prudens & sapiens sicut tu." A quote from Pharaoh regarding Joseph in Genesis 41:38.</note> Then afterwards, this mystery reached Moses by Kabbalistic succession, as he was a vessel chosen by God. In his time, driven by necessity and at the command of Jehovah <term>Iehoua: An older Latin transcription of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</term>, this gift was communicated to the seventy elders, and so it was spread among the multitude. And in the following age, that power given by divinity was placed in Joshua, and thus communicated by succession to the Judges of the house of Israel. From them it passed to King David and his son Solomon—to whom that divine gift of acquiring the way was revealed by his father—then later to the prophets and the priests Ezra and the Maccabees. And finally, Christ, filled with that spirit more than all men, taught the way of acquiring this mystical wisdom to the Apostles, who also left it to their successors until the end of the world.

If this were not a mystery hidden by Kabbalistic tradition, to be revealed by a father to his only son, or by a faithful teacher to a worthy disciple, why would Isaac have taken it so heavily that he had given this gift to Jacob against his will? Concerning this it is said, "Isaac trembled with a violent shuddering," etc. And also, why would Esau have received this trickery of his brother so bitterly, crying out in a marvelous way? For it is said that when Esau heard his father's words, he roared with a great cry and, being dismayed, said: *Bless me also, my father! And he said: Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing. To which he replied: He has supplanted me, lo, this second time; and now he has snatched away my blessing. And again to his father: Have you not reserved (he said) a blessing for me also?* <note>original: "auditis Esau sermonibus... Nunquid non reseruasti (ait) & mihi benedictionem..." This recounts the biblical narrative of Jacob stealing Esau's blessing in Genesis 27.</note> Hence it was that Esau hated his brother Jacob for a long time and intended death for him, just as Cain struck his brother Abel with death for the same reason—namely, because he perceived that God was on his side, but against himself and his sacrifices.

But so that we may now arrive at a methodical division of the Kabbalah taken in a general sense, we say that:

->Kabbalah is divided into<-

*   **The True and Essential**, of which there are two species:
    *   **Cosmology or Breseth** <note>original: "Breseth" refers to *Bereshit*, the Hebrew word for "In the beginning," the first word of Genesis. Here it refers to the study of the creation of the physical world.</note>, which explains the powers of {the Heavenly and the Terrestrial}.
    - **Mercaua** <note>original: "Mercaua" refers to *Merkavah*, the "Chariot" of Ezekiel's vision, representing the study of the divine realm and the throne of God.</note>, which is either {Notariaca or Theomantica <note>Theomantica: A term for divine prophecy or communication with the divine.</note>}.
*   **The Superstitious and Spurious**, of which there are three species:
    *   **Gematria**, which is also called Arithmetic: concerned with the {transmutation of syllables and words, and the calculation of number-characters}.
    *   **Notariaca**, expressing letters in place of whole words.
    *   **Temurah**, or the commutation of letters, such as when one letter is accepted in place of another.

# Treatise

Just as it was stated regarding Magic, that there is a divine wisdom upon which true sciences depend, and another worldly wisdom which the Apostle calls vanity and foolishness: so indeed must it be said of the art of Kabbalah. One kind comes from the true wisdom sent from heaven, while the other stems from the deceptive and unstable invention of men—a thing fashioned and refashioned. For the gift of that true wisdom is the subject of the first kind of Kabbalah, which is either revealed immediately to men through inspiration, or its Kabbalistic mystery is uncovered through the teaching of a faithful master. Conversely, the second kind, derived from human invention, is vain, uncertain, and inconstant, produced and fashioned according to the imagination of its inventor.

<margin>Wisdom 7:17, 18, 19</margin>
<margin>Wisdom 7:20</margin>
And although the inventor may perhaps have understood the logic of his own invention very well, and attempted to hide and conceal the truth of the mystery beneath it (like a spirit beneath the literal text), he nevertheless acted most wickedly in this: by using superstitious ceremonies of that sort, he led man away from the truth into a kind of Theurgy <term>Theurgy: A type of ritual magic intended to invoke the presence of divine spirits or gods.</term>, rather than directing them toward the desired goal, as will be discussed more extensively below. The species of true and essential Kabbalah known as "Cosmological" deals with natural things, both of heaven and earth, and it typically explains and unfolds the laws and secrets of the Holy Bible through philosophical reasoning. From this, it is clear that Cosmological Kabbalah and Natural Magic share the same subject matter, about which we have spoken at length in our preceding discourse on magic. However, that species called *Merkavah* <note>original: "Marcaua." Refers to Merkavah or "Chariot" mysticism, focusing on the throne of God and the celestial hierarchy.</note> deals with mysteries far more sublime—namely those which pertain to the divine nature and the condition of angels. It also treats the secrets of characters and formal elements, whether fiery or luminous. A branch of this, called *Notariakon* <note>original: "Notariacam." A method of shorthand or using the letters of words to uncover hidden names and meanings.</note>, deals with the virtues, names, and seals of angels, and also uncovers the conditions of demons and souls. So too does the "Theomantic" species <term>Theomantic: From "Theomancy," a form of divination or prophecy involving the direct study of divine names.</term> scrutinize the mysteries of the divine majesty, the various emanations according to their properties, and the sacred names of God. Those Kabbalists who truly know these things say they possess wonderful powers, so that whenever a person wishes, he may foreknow all future things, command all of nature, hold authority over demons and angels, and perform miracles. Indeed, it is believed that by means of this species, Moses performed those signs described in Exodus. The entire and sole subject of this study is that spirit of wisdom who (as the holy page witnesses) is the worker of all wonders. Solomon confessed that, with this spirit assisting him, he possessed perfection in these two complete species of Kabbalah. For he acknowledges the entire power of Cosmology in these words:

> *Wisdom gave me knowledge of the things that are; from her I was given certain knowledge of the constitution of the world and the powers of the elements; the beginning, the end, and the midpoint of times; the changes of the solstices and the varieties of the seasons; the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars, etc.* <note>A translation of Wisdom 7:17-19.</note>

By these words, he proves that by means of true wisdom, he possessed knowledge of the mysteries of heaven, and consequently was most perfect in his understanding of the higher cosmological parts. Then he continues:

> *Wisdom was given to me to know the natures of living creatures and the rages of wild beasts, the differences between plants and the medicinal powers of roots, etc.* <note>A translation of Wisdom 7:20.</note>

By this, he concludes that he had certain knowledge of nature, both of the lower terrestrial things and the higher celestial things. From these words, one may clearly see that Solomon acquired the most perfect Cosmological science in the first species of essential, true Kabbalah.

<margin>Wisdom 7:20, 21</margin>
That he was also expertly practiced in the second species—indeed, in the branches of both forms of Kabbalah—he seems to acknowledge in the following verse, where he says:

> *God gave me knowledge of the powers of the winds, and the thoughts of men, and I learned whatever things are hidden and unforeseen; for Wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me.* <note>A translation of Wisdom 7:20-21.</note>

Thus he speaks, where by "the power of the winds" he understands both angels and winds, as it is said: *Who makes your angels winds, etc.* This is very easy to discern because he speaks also of the internal mystery of man himself, namely of his

# On the Highest Good, etc.

<margin>Wisdom 9</margin>
...by his contemplation, which was not granted even to the devil to grasp or understand—as it is revealed and known to God alone—nevertheless, through the mediation of His Wisdom, it was granted to man to discern these same things. Finally, the last clause of that verse indicates that he possessed knowledge not only of the hidden state of Angels, Demons, and souls, but even of the counsels and secrets of God himself; for through the mediation of wisdom, he knew both whatever things are hidden and those which are manifest and revealed. And Solomon seems to confirm this elsewhere, saying: *Who shall search out the things that are in the heavens, and who shall know the counsel of God, unless God has given wisdom and sent his Holy Spirit from the highest places?* <note>original: "Quæ in cælis sunt quis inuestigabit & consilium Dei quis nouerit nisi Deus dederit sapientiam, & miserit Sanctum Spiritum suum è locis altissimis"</note> Furthermore, just as Jacob was taught by Isaac, and Isaac by Abraham, so indeed was Solomon instructed by David in the acquisition of this mystical wisdom. Solomon himself describes this most clearly and exactly as *a certain pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty God and the brightness of eternal light, etc.* <note>original: "emanationem quandam claritatis omnipotentis Dei synceram & splendorem lucis æternæ &c."</note>

<margin>Wisdom 7:22</margin>
This, therefore, is the sole and unique true subject of all Magic as well as Kabbalah: namely Wisdom, the Word, Christ, and the name of **Jesus** alone; for there is no other name in heaven or on earth in which we may be saved except this unique name **Jesus**, in which all things are contained, for Christ Jesus is all in all.

But let us now come to the spurious branch of Kabbalah, which seems to be nothing but a fiction or a false image invented by human minds for their own pleasure. For although this may be able to contain some mystery within it, devised by the inventor, nevertheless—on account of the vanity and superstitious condition of that Jewish science—it causes a man to wander further from the laws of truth than it serves to draw him out or free him from the darkness in which he is immersed. Indeed, those who have been seriously occupied with this branch of Kabbalah have perceived it to be nothing other than a mere rhapsody of superstition, and a kind of Theurgic <term>Theurgy: A form of ritual magic intended to invoke the presence of divine spirits or to achieve union with the divine.</term> magic. And although some Jewish Kabbalists boast that this spurious art is derived from God for the perfection of human life, the salvation of men, the worship of God, and the truth of science; nevertheless, in itself it appears to be a very uncertain art, established upon no firm foundations. Thus, such inventions seem to tend more toward the hiding and, as it were, the taking away of the true mystery (as has been said) than toward its detection or for the benefit of men. For example, the first species of this is called <term>Gematria</term>, insofar as it is fashioned as a kind of numerical measurement of earthly characters in relation to one another; it is also frequently called **Arithmetic**, as it consists in the calculation of numbers. Furthermore, in its **Geometric** arrangement, a transformation of syllables is made according to the intention of the artist. Similarly, its second species is called <term>Notariaca</term> <note>Also known as Notarikon; a method of shorthand where single letters stand for whole words.</note>: it works through the meaning of a word via a single letter alone, without the joining of syllables. Finally, the last species consists in the various commutation of letters, namely by using one letter in place of another, according to the hidden intention of the author. From this comes that well-worn axiom of the Kabbalists: that it is the duty of the Kabbalist *to read one thing, and to understand another*, <note>original: "aliud legere, aliud intelligere"</note> so that a truly wise man can scarcely, if at all, reach the intention of the inventor or the interpreter.

But if a true Artist could comprehend the nature and various properties of the formal, luminous, or essential letters according to the figure and image of their various appearances in <term>Hyle</term> <note>From the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter or the underlying substance of the physical world.</note>, then he himself understands—and that beyond any further doubt—what those truly holy letters are, which are the characters of the divine Word itself or of holy Wisdom, by whose mediation all things were made into diverse species at creation. When these are well understood, as being of one identity in essence, it will not be difficult to know why Wisdom is an emanation of divine light, why it is more excellent than the sun and all the stars when compared in light, why all things are cut from a single spiritual rock, why Christ Jesus is said to be all in all, and infinite other questions arising from these fiery and truly holy letters.

# Treatise

...can be very easily resolved by those who understand their properties best.

Why, then, does that man Mersenne condemn and despise both types of <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that explores the nature of God and the universe; here, Fludd distinguishes between a "true" divine version and a "corrupt" human version.</note> with such vehemence, as if they were a single branch? Or why does he seem to reject the good along with the evil? We see that the man has not changed his judgment at all from that which he held regarding magic; for he condemns the whole of Kabbalah for the sake of a single fault in one of its parts, just as he condemned the entirety of magic because of the lack of a "pure essence"—a fiction added by false artists. But let us see what this author says in his contempt for Kabbalah and the Kabbalists.

->From Mersenne, Column 1696.<-

> *Indeed, I relegate these imaginings to the Kabbalists and <term>merchants of nonsense</term> <note>original: "nugiuendulos." Mersenne uses this derogatory term to describe Kabbalists as peddlers of worthless trifles.</note> of this sort, etc.*

->Robert’s Examination.<-

Wherein he seems to hold and esteem Kabbalists in general as merchants of nonsense.

->From Column 202 of Mersenne.<-

> *As for the trifle that a sevenfold influence proceeds from a well, he learned this, I believe, from those merchants of nonsense who are called Kabbalists and Rabbis, against whom we have fought elsewhere. What if, by that "earthly well," he actually means God himself, the Greatest and Best, the fountain of all goodness? Yet he ought to have explained that more clearly.*

->From Column 214 of Mersenne.<-

> *We do not need the trifles and errors of the Kabbalists to understand Holy Scripture, whether literally or mystically; they obscure and infect it rather than interpret it. Therefore, the "supramundane fountain" belongs to those same trifles, along with many other things we have reported above.*

It is clear from these passages that this monk <note>Referring to Marin Mersenne, who was a member of the Order of Minims.</note> calls the mysteries of Kabbalah "trifles" without exception, and calls the Kabbalists themselves "merchants of nonsense" in general. He fails to consider that he himself is the prince of all such triflers—indeed, an outstanding one—who, by failing to grasp the true meaning of the Kabbalists, seems to ignorantly contaminate the truth with his own fictions. For "the Venetian" <note>Francesco Giorgio Veneto (1460–1540), a Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist whom Fludd is defending.</note> speaks of a <term>sevenfold influence</term> <note>The idea that divine power flows down through seven stages or spheres.</note> proceeding from a well (as he puts it), learned from those he calls merchants of nonsense, the Kabbalists and Rabbis. Then he proceeds thus: *What if, by that earthly well, he means God himself, the Greatest and Best, the fountain of all truth? etc.* Here, therefore, you see this man condemn that exquisite thing as a trifle with his immature judgment—a thing he himself clearly does not understand, as can be perceived by his question, *"What if...?"* But to come to the point: Why do you think, Mersenne, that God the Greatest and Best is understood by an "earthly well"? Do you wish to take the corporeal for the spiritual, or earth for heaven? Or did the patriarch Jacob say that the earthly stone which he set up as a pillar was God the Greatest and Best, or the house of God? Was that material rock which Moses struck God, or was it a spiritual rock issuing from the material one, by means of which (as the Apostle witnesses) the Israelites were sustained in the desert? Is the earth God, which is to be opened so that it may bring forth a Savior, or the Savior to be produced? Certainly, we understand the "living waters," and the "spiritual rock," and the "fountain of life," which I—together with the Venetian—most rightly call Christ, the Word, Wisdom, and indeed that supramundane fountain of the Kabbalists, even though you believe the "supramundane fountain" belongs to Kabbalistic trifles. That mystical and parabolic poet says:

> There is a hidden stone buried in the deepest fountain,
> It is despised by fools, etc.
> <note>original: "Est lapis occultus & in imo fonte sepultus, / Spernitur à stultis, &c."</note>

Does not Holy Scripture also speak in many places of the "stone rejected by the builders"? But let us look into the words of the Venetian himself with a slightly more curious eye, so that we may see whether the Venetian or rather Mersenne is to be considered the merchant of nonsense. From Problem 156: *And they came to Beersheba, together with the father, namely...*

# On the Highest Good, etc.

namely, that he and the son of Isaac lived there, receiving from that **well of sevenfold influence** <note>original: "puteo septenarii influxus"</note> everything necessary and everything desirable. For that well is called by the wise men **Col**, *that is, the whole*, etc. If **Mersenne** had correctly understood this discourse of the **Venetian** <note>Francesco Giorgio Veneto (1460–1540), a Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist whose work Mersenne heavily criticized.</note>, he would not have considered him a **merchant of nonsense** <note>original: "nugivendulo." A derogatory term Mersenne used to describe Kabbalists.</note>, but rather a truly wise man, since he explained in very few words a great sea abounding in all delights: the deepest well (I say) **Col**, encompassing everything that can be imagined in this entire world. I mean **Christ**, the savior of the world, all in all, without whom there is no truth in the world: the fountain of life, the spiritual rock in which there is all abundance and fullness. From that (he says) *well of sevenfold influence*, etc.

But what this *sevenfold influence of the well* means, this "faithful corrector" of the Venetian <note>Mersenne</note> does not say a single word, nor can he speak to the point. From this it is clear how great his knowledge is in the true <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, adapted by Christian thinkers to explore the divine structure of the universe.</note>—he who is ignorant of the reasoning behind the perfection of the number seven among the wise. For the wise are not accustomed to counting like **common mathematicians**, but in a more subtle way. For example: on the first, second, and third day, the perfection of the universal world was completed; and yet the perfection of each of these three unities proceeds from the influence of the Word, or the various emanations of wisdom or divine splendor (differing from one another in property and effect, though one and the same in essence). Now, 1, 2, and 3 make 6; if another unity is added to this, it produces the fourth day in which the sun was created. Thus, 1 added to 6, or four to 3, finally draws out the number seven—a number, I say, which after the number three is the most perfect of all. It is (I say) the solar day, the day of the Sabbath and of rest, which is the sign of the completion of the entire work of creation.

Now, these four operations were completed by as many emanations or influences: of which 3 is the sign of the triple property in the divine essence that informs and gives life to all things; and the number 4, being the square of the root 2, is the material number representing the informed aquatic spirit of the world. But 4 joined with 3 constitutes the complete composition of the whole world, in which the holy emanation is mixed with the worldly spirit, according to that saying of the royal **Psalmist**: *He is clothed in Light, as if with a garment.* Does not Wisdom itself seem to affirm this elsewhere, saying, *that by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their powers by the spirit from his mouth*? Hence the wise man confessed that **Wisdom built her house upon 7 columns**, as if he had said that she built her own dwelling or church, fitting for herself, by seven outpourings or emanations: and thus the said divine spirit *placed his tabernacle in the sun.*

But **Marinus** <note>Marin Mersenne</note> will reply: "What does this have to do with a well of sevenfold influence, since you speak of the world and I speak of a well?" To him I say: the "little world" <note>The Microcosm, or the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> is everywhere, since that incorruptible spirit is all and in all, though more in one place than another. Hence **Moses** was said to have received the depicted fabric of the world by the demonstration of the finger of God. Did not **Esdras** <note>Ezra, the biblical scribe associated with mystical visions.</note> also acknowledge this same thing revealed to him divinely and described symbolically? And the scriptures indicate that **Solomon** was instructed in all the mysteries of the creation of the world by **Wisdom** herself as his teacher—she whose role it is to build new heavens and new lands. Must not "living waters" also be extracted from a stone well, and consequently an earthen one, through the operation of triple wisdom upon quadruple matter? By means of these, with that same Wisdom assisting, new heavens and a new earth can be created, bringing with them everything necessary and desirable to man. If that material **Mosaic** cliff which he struck produced a universal spiritual cliff or rock, overflowing with all fullness and necessities, why should living waters not also be extracted from the stone of **Jacob’s** land? For according to the Patriarch, that was the house of God and the dwelling place of wisdom, which is the fountain of life, from which alone (and from no other) living waters are accustomed to gush forth. Jehovah commanded Moses to strike the dry rock with his staff so that waters might gush from it: and Christ says, *seek, knock, and you shall find.*
