But we do not wonder that the ungrateful world has persecuted the Professors of the true arts along with Truth itself. However, for your sake, we will briefly answer these questions: namely, what do we do? What can we do? And whether we actually exist? In the writings of John, therefore, we read that God is the supreme Light, and we walk in that Light, because we show that Light (even if the Lantern is closed) to the world. But you, worldly man who denies this, you are ignorant or you do not see; it is necessary to know that Jesus inhabits your vile body. You have this from the Apostle. But Jesus knows the thoughts of all; if you adhere to Him, you will eventually become one spirit with Him, and when you are of such a kind, who prohibits you from knowing the disputes of men, both the depraved and the good, just as Solomon did? And this you shall receive from me based on what has been said before. And this is why we do not answer everyone, clearly because of the deceitful minds of some; for those who are alienated from God are contrary to us: and who is so foolish as to allow a passing stranger to enter someone else's hearth? But if you object that this union is only to be expected in the future world, behold, you show yourself a worldly man in this way, who by your ignorance extinguishes the light; you are not even ashamed to say the Apostle lied, in whose writings these things are held more clearly in these words: "so that nothing is lacking to you in any grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ." But you will say this is by no means to be understood regarding this life. What then does the following verse mean: "Who will also confirm you until the end"? For in the kingdom of God there is no end; therefore, the glory of the Lord and the glorious Jesus will be seen regarding this temporary state. If anything further is asked concerning our true duty: we endeavor to lead the lost sheep back to the true fold. You miserable mortals labor in vain, you who have entered a foreign way, rather than (as the Apostle wills) by laying down the tabernacle <note>original: "deponendo tabernaculum." A biblical metaphor for the body or the physical self.</note>—which way is not achieved by dying according to the opinion of the common people, but as Peter wills when he says, "just as Christ taught me": namely, when He was transfigured on the mountain. If this "laying down" had not been secret and hidden, the Apostle would not have said, "as Jesus taught me," nor would the Supreme Truth have said, "tell this to no one." For according to the common way, dying in the common manner was known to everyone from the beginning of the world. Therefore, be transmuted! Be transmuted from dead stones into **Living Philosophical Stones**. The Apostle demonstrates the way when he says: "let the same mind be in you which is in Jesus." He even explains that mind in the following words: namely, when in the form of...*

### THE KEY
## TO FLUDDIAN PHILOSOPHY
## AND ALCHEMY.
-> OR <-
### THE RESPONSE OF ROBERT FLUDD, ESQUIRE,
### AND DOCTOR OF MEDICINE, TO THE EPISTOLARY
-> Exercise of the Theologian Pierre Gassendi. <-

-> In which: <-
*The empty objections of the monk Marin Mersenne <note>A French polymath often called the "father of acoustics" and a staunch critic of alchemy</note>, and his unjust complaints, unfairly directed at Robert Fludd, are examined and removed: the severe and thunderous judgment of François de La Noue <note>original: "Franciscus Lanovius," a scholar who wrote against Fludd</note> concerning Fludd is refuted and reduced to nothing: the erroneous detection of the principles of Fluddian philosophy, made by Pierre Gassendi, is corrected and weighed in an equal balance of justice: and finally, those six impieties which Mersenne devised against Fludd are washed away and wiped clean by the waves of sincere truth.*

-> Truth conquers above all things, 1 Esdras 3:12. <note>original: "3. Esdr. 3. 12." In the Latin Vulgate, this refers to the book known as 3 Esdras; in English Bibles, this is usually found in the Apocrypha as 1 Esdras.</note> <-

It serves as Robert Fludd’s formal "Address to the Reader," transitioning from the general defense announced on the title page to a personal appeal for a fair hearing against his critics, Marin Mersenne and Pierre Gassendi.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal banner featuring an intricate repeating pattern of knotwork and floral motifs inside rectangular frames.</image-desc>

# TO THE PRUDENT READER AND
## TO HIM WHO RESTS UPON THE WINGS OF JUSTICE,
### GREETINGS.

*Kind reader, you see here a judgment from my adversaries regarding me and my books that is so sharp and heavy that, unless you provide a similar response and measure them with that same measure—discerning whether I am being weighed down by the eyes of justice or by a judgment that is true or false—I would not know what to do or where to turn. But with arguments (unless I am mistaken) drawn from the treasury chest of Truth, I shall open this case of mine to you—for you are a just judge who does not turn a blind eye—so that finally your sentence may gladly absolve me from the judgment of these accusers. I ask you, therefore, again and again, to judge this controversy of ours and deliver a just sentence. If, according to the assertions of my adversaries, I deserve the charge of those six impieties <note>Mersenne had specifically listed six "impieties" or heretical errors he claimed to find in Fludd's philosophy, including accusations of magic and deifying the soul.</note> they have cast upon me, and must undergo that heavy judgment they have imposed, then I will certainly submit myself willingly. But truly, before I seriously involve myself in the deeper aspects of this case, I will briefly point out who is the proclaimer of this severe sentence in such a sharp trial; who is the usurper of the judge's office; and finally, who and of what sort that giant-like accuser of mine <note>original: "Giganteus ille meus Accusator." Fludd uses this "giant" imagery to characterize the overwhelming nature of the attacks against him.</note> shall be. In the meantime, however, I humbly beseech you that while I plead my case before your tribunal, you remain a fair judge, weighing it in the equal scales of justice, and that you persist in the holy duty of your goodness toward the Truth*
->*and entreat.*<-

<summary>Robert Fludd appeals to the reader's sense of fairness, asking for an impartial judgment as he prepares to defend himself against the "six impieties" and harsh criticisms leveled by his rivals.</summary>

He frames Mersenne as a cowardly instigator who cannot fight his own battles.</meta>

# TREATISE
## THE FIRST SECTION
### OF THIS WORK.

<margin>This section is divided into three parts, of which</margin>
The First argues for Mersenne’s cowardice and his insufficiency in responding to Fludd.
The Second opens and reveals the biased judgments of the adversaries.
The Third responds to the less important points raised against Fludd in Mersenne’s letter.

---

->PART I OF THE FIRST SECTION.<-

Before I apply my mind and pen to the controversy itself, I believe it will not be irrelevant or contrary to your judgment (kind Reader) to indicate the natures and conditions of my adversaries; likewise, in what points they agree, or where they differ from one another, as far as I have gathered from their writings. I will begin the web from the very root of all this evil and the present contention, so that I may then ascend in a more direct order to its trunk and branches.

The proclaimer of sentences of imaginary impieties—minted only by the deceptive stroke of his imagination—and the source and origin of this entire controversy, is a certain brother of the Order of Minims of Saint Francis <note>The Order of Minims (Ordo Minimorum) is a Roman Catholic religious order of friars founded by St. Francis of Paola; Mersenne was a prominent member.</note>, named Marin Mersenne. He is a man more prone to litigation and quibbling than well-versed in the deeper secrets of either God or Nature. Indeed, since he loves to join a council uninvited and stick his finger into other people’s business, and presumes to deliver a judgment that is too sharp and hardly befitting Christian modesty (with no respect held for anyone), he is ultimately unable to defend or sustain his own rash censure—interwoven with intolerable insults and therefore called into controversy by the one judged and condemned—by himself and without the help of friends (whose aid he implores to respond). This can be gathered not only from the words of his friends themselves, but even from the stupid and dull betrayal of his own pen.

->From this Letter of Lanovius <note>François de La Noue (Lanovius), a correspondent of Mersenne.</note>.<-

> I cannot but strongly approve of the plan you have taken to submit to the judgment of other men, lest you seem to have rushed your opinion in your own cause. Yet it is to be lamented for your sake that I am among those whom you considered fit for this task, as I cannot sustain it with the dignity it deserves.

->Again in the same place.<-

<margin>...dissolved, etc.</margin>
> Nothing is to be feared from those "Floods" <note>original: "Fluctibus"—a pun on Robert Fludd's surname, suggesting his arguments are merely shifting waves or foam.</note>, which of their own accord dissolve into foam and become the playthings of the winds.

->From Gassendi’s preface, chapter 1.<-

> What you request in the first place is that, after I have seen the books which Robert Fludd released against you at the last fairs, I should explain to you what I think of them.

Furthermore, it is clear from this chapter and the following one that Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a famous French philosopher and scientist who was recruited by Mersenne to refute Fludd.</note> wrote against me at the urgent instigation of Mersenne, and not of his own accord.

->From his chapter 3, these words.<-

> Come then, since you ask it by the right of friendship, that I should somehow finally open my mind to you in this matter; there is no reason for me to hesitate. For I ought not to remain silent like a singer who is asked to perform, preferring to seem inept rather than fail to comply with a friend. I would only wish to say this one thing by way of preface: that I never sell my trifles and conjectures as the absolute truth itself. For although you almost forbid me from being a Pyrrhonian <note>A Skeptic; referring to the school of Pyrrho of Elis which doubted that absolute truth could be known.</note>, and are always accustomed to press me as if I had something to offer dogmatically <note>original: "dogmaticōs" — to speak with the authority of established doctrine.</note>, etc.

Here you see (Reader) how Gassendi first descended into the arena of this Theological-Philosophical controversy at the instigation and provocation of that man. For this monk-soldier (as we see from the result) perceived himself to be too powerless to respond to those objections brought by me against him in the book titled *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "Sophia cum Moria certamen" — Fludd's 1629 work attacking Mersenne.</note>. That my response also exceeds his grasp, we prove both by his own words and by those described by Gassendi.

->Gassendi, page 11.<-

> A key must be held by which his hidden meaning may be opened; for they are perpetual riddles with which he addresses you. How can those things which he says be subjected to examination, unless they are first understood? Must we contend in the manner of the Andabatae <note>Gladiators who fought in helmets without eye-holes, effectively blindfolded.</note> so that one strikes toward the North, and another receives blows in the South? Allow me, therefore, first to draw out from Fludd's various works what principles of his philosophy he establishes and follows. For thus, finally, it will be very easy to hunt down his mind, etc.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Fludd persists in his character assassination of Marin Mersenne. He focuses on the dynamic between Mersenne and his defender, Pierre Gassendi, portraying Mersenne as an intellectual lightweight who requires a "minder" to handle the complexities of Fludd’s philosophical and occult system.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>Fludd’s Response.</header>

### In which he argues for the ignorance of his friend, and shows that it is impossible for him, without the friend's help and assistance, to respond to or refute the arguments Fludd leveled against him.

#### Mersenne’s own confession in his own Letter.

Behold, since Fludd, in responding to me, wished to hide himself still in the senses of Scripture as if in lurking-places, my friend Gassendi has led him out, and so traced his Cabala <note>The "Cabala" or Kabbalah refers to a tradition of Jewish mysticism that Fludd and other Renaissance thinkers integrated into Christian philosophy to explain the relationship between God and the universe.</note> that I consider myself satisfied by this exposure alone. For from this it is clearer than the sun <note>original: "Sole clarius"</note> how truly, and not through slander, I had objected to many of his points.

#### And elsewhere in the same letter.

Gassendi invites me to a fuller response; yet he himself so skillfully touched upon everything that what he left for me to do is of no great importance.

->By these words, therefore, he seems to suggest his own impotence and insufficiency for making a further response.<-

#### And again in the same place.

After sharing advice with friendly and learned men, many persuaded me to respond with nothing, for they saw such writings were altogether unworthy of a response, etc. Having heard the others, I wished also to consult my friend Gassendi by letter, etc. I asked him to write back seriously what he thought of those works. For I conjectured that he, given the curiosity he has for grasping all Philosophy, had certainly also penetrated that philosophy under which Fludd hides his Impieties, etc.

By this conclusion to his speech, he seems expressly to denote his own ignorance regarding Fludd’s foundations; and yet he does not hesitate to judge—and finally condemn—those things, and even his Cabala (even though he is least qualified). But because his ignorance of those foundations of mine has been published by me to the world with the most deserved right, he makes a complaint to his friends, praying that they bring him help in this so harsh a case. Finally (which is the most childish thing of all), he is so far deluded that he even permits it to be publicly promulgated, and makes it known to all, that he once falsely claimed and vainly usurped the name of a great Philosopher for himself: namely, in his *Volume on Genesis*. For now, by my aforementioned response, he seems so cast down that he publicly argues his own poverty in Philosophy, and like a boy, or at least some novice in the secrets of nature, he openly requires to be taught and instructed by Lanovius <note>François de La Noue, another critic of Fludd.</note>, and especially by Gassendi. Indeed, in this conflict of his, he appears so prostrated in spirit as if he were another Job, who, as if in his death-throes, calls together his friends for the sake of consolation.

### This is gathered from the citations below. And first, regarding his instruction.
#### Gassendi, pages 271 and 272.

I add only this: if anything from conjecture (mind you, conjecture) should happen to please you, it is my wish that you use it skillfully against Fludd. I have not so much collected many things as touched upon a few, since my sole aim was that, by exposing the mind of the adversary, I might smooth the way for you to march against him. Therefore, this remains your work: to fight most vigorously for Religion and for Nature. Only take care, as I was saying, that your famous gentleness of manners is not sharpened into bitterness while writing, etc.

Furthermore, in many other pages of his treatise, Gassendi points out to Mersenne—as if with a finger—the places assigned by his Analytical inquiry, by which he might proceed against me. For example:

#### Gassendi, page 32.

Unless you interpret Fludd in this way, I believe the greatest part of his Philosophy will remain hidden from you, etc.

#### And page 32.

Repeat if you like what he disputes against you in the second book of the contest. But since the chief mystery of Alchemy <note>original: "Alchymiæ"</note> lies hidden here: I therefore point out a few things, etc.

#### And page 89.

Since he has arranged this contest into four books, like certain battle lines, let us skim through them in the order he disposed them. While you play the Antagonist, you will strive for victory. It is enough for me to wish to indicate with my finger in which part I think he is most equipped.

### Regarding the second point: for his consolation. From Mersenne’s Letter.

Fludd wrote two works against me a year and a half ago, in which, since he seemed to repeat the same Impieties, it cannot be said with how many insults and reproaches he provoked me. After sharing advice with friendly and learned men, etc. some thought, etc. that the judgment of the most learned men should be collected, so that from it might appear how unworthily and undeservedly Fludd had dealt with me, etc.

->Hence he himself received consolation of this sort from his friends.<-

#### Gassendi, page 87.

You will therefore act sincerely in my opinion when, according to your modesty, you declare that the Folly <note>original: "Moriam" (Folly), a reference to Erasmus’s *Praise of Folly* and St. Paul.</note> which he attributes to you is Wisdom <note>original: "Sophiam" (Wisdom).</note> before God. You are truly a Christian: but even Christ himself was called not only crazy, but even possessed by a Demon: and his primary followers were shouted at for being driven to insanity or being soaked in wine. You know truly how the Savior was always gentler than a sheep: how the Apostles even rejoiced whenever they were held worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus. And let him call your commentaries on Genesis both a Babylonian Volume and most famous fictions: why should you not bear this patiently? You who, besides illustrious examples, have as a witness the integrity of your own conscience. You also have, I know well enough, the support of many good men, etc.

Here then you see (Just Reader) how effectively this friend of that "second Job" strives to provide him consolation.

### Conclusion.

I conclude, therefore, that I was greatly deceived in my opinion. For I thought my business was with a Philosopher, a Cabalist, an Alchemist, and a profound natural Magician: seeing as he wrote about all these things boldly, and as if with a certain mastery, in his Volumes; but, as can be seen from the aforementioned, the reality speaks otherwise. But who (I ask) does not blush not only to fight fiercely and like a lion with big words against all Artists—even those most skilled in the sciences they profess—but also to treat them inhumanely, and having held no respect for piety, to condemn them utterly? No one, surely; unless it be someone like this man of ours, a boastful and reckless Thraso <note>Thraso is the "Braggart Soldier" character from Terence's Roman comedy *Eunuchus*; Fludd uses the name to label Mersenne as a cowardly blowhard.</note> who has hardly known the Arts superficially, much less driven deep roots into them. For does not he who, being timid and weak, dresses himself in a wolf-skin...

<meta>The catchword "tam" (so) at the bottom indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Fludd mocks Mersenne for relying on Pierre Gassendi’s intellectual support, arguing that Mersenne's own letters prove he is an amateur in philosophy and alchemy who requires "consolation" like a biblical Job. Fludd concludes that Mersenne is not a true scholar but a "Thraso"—a boastful but ignorant character from Roman comedy.</summary>

<keywords>Robert Fludd, Marin Mersenne, Pierre Gassendi, Alchemy, Cabala, Job, Thraso, polemic, philosophy, Genesis, Folly vs Wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 73 ---
<meta>Continuing from page 6, Fludd intensifies his critique of Marin Mersenne’s intellectual independence. He portrays Mersenne as a man who possesses a vast library of knowledge but lacks the internal architecture to synthesize it, forcing him to rely on the "protection" of Pierre Gassendi and François de La Noue (Lanovius).</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>To the Mersennian Letter, Part I of the First Section</header>

...have we found and uncovered something so hidden? Do we not hear the wind and sounds without a mind? I speak from experience: for certain things seem to be, even though they are not. How unhappy am I, then—to use the bombastic words of Lanovius with the proposition changed—to have fought a battle in the public field of Philosophy with an inglorious enemy? For what glory will be mine, or what honor, to have defeated an adversary so unwarlike <note>original: *imbellem*; Fludd is mocking Mersenne for being "unfit for combat" in a philosophical sense</note>, who is held to so humbly implore the help or aid of Masters—or rather, common and vulgar assistance—to respond on his behalf?

Certainly, whoever reads his works will feel that he has indeed scanned more volumes of learned men, both recent and ancient, than either Gassendi or Lanovius, whom he chose as his Tutors and Masters; yet he seems to possess less of a steady and judicious mind than they do. What more is there to be said, then, except that we believe he has collected stones or gems of great enough price in the treasury-chest of his memory, but was utterly ignorant of how to adapt them into an elegant and uniform structure? This treasury of the learned, I say, appears to be rich enough (as one can gather from his writings), but he is unknowing and insufficient in using those materials decently for his purpose. For otherwise, he would not have wished to be taught by men who (in my judgment) are not to be placed ahead of him in doctrine, nor would he have yielded his place to them so that they might respond for him.

Truly, I do not pursue the man with hatred or envy; but moved rather by piety and commiseration toward him, I pray from my heart for a sounder mind in a sound body <note>original: *mens sana in corpore sano*, a famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal</note> for him, so that with that mind as his guide, he may learn to keep silent when not provoked. Instead, let him manfully, by himself and without the advice of learned friends, all fear removed, attack the adversary who causes him trouble. For if anyone, because of an injury done to him or some private cause, desired to descend into the arena of combat and therefore provoked his Adversary: would he not rightly and deservedly be proclaimed unwarlike and faint-hearted if afterward, when he had to fight for himself, struck by a certain fear, he revealed the whole matter to his friends and sought their help, suppliantly begging that they go out into the field armed on his behalf and be willing to fight? Absolutely. For he would offer himself as a laughingstock to almost everyone. 

Therefore, if Mersenne had fought strenuously for his cause in his own person, as becomes a Philosopher, calling no one else to his aid, it would have been honorable for him; and the honor or glory of that epistolary response (if there is any in it) would be attributed neither to Gassendi nor to Lanovius, but to the man himself whose duty it was to perform it. For it is a laudable and magnanimous deed to preside over one’s own cause (especially if someone stands as the Author of the dispute or contention) by oneself, with no one else intervening, and to propound and defend it vigorously. But was it a beautiful thing in a Philosopher, especially one so pompous, or worthy of praise, to say—and what is even worse—to emit these words into public to his own disgrace?

<margin>Mersenne in the dedicatory letter.</margin>
"Although my Gassendi invites me to a more abundant response, he himself touched upon the matter so skillfully that what he left over is of no great importance."

->Also:<-

<margin>ibid.</margin>
> "Behold, since Fludd, in responding to me, wished to hide himself still in his senses of Scripture as if in lurking-places, my Gassendi has led him out and so uncovered his Cabala <note>Fludd uses "Cabala" to refer to his mystical interpretation of the universe, based on Jewish Kabbalah but integrated into his Christian Neoplatonism</note> that I consider myself satisfied by this exposure alone, etc."

For by these words, he teaches that he is unfit and powerless to respond, and he hints that although he himself could not deal with me, his Gassendi has penetrated my Philosophy and Cabala. From this, he even sought the doctrine and assistance of Lanovius (as appears from the end of the same Letter) to explain the principles of my Cabala.

I say, therefore, since this adversary of mine is of such a weak condition, I have until now disdained to give him a response. For those things which he proclaims regarding those six Impieties <note>Mersenne had accused Fludd of six specific theological errors or "impieties"</note> charged against me, he confesses he drew from the Gassendian source and from the judgment of Lanovius. Therefore, in the future, I shall dismiss the disciple and manfully engage (relying, of course, on the truth) with the Masters themselves, who run so boldly and with such confidence to their friend's aid.

***

## SECTION I. PART II.

->Here they judge me severely; yet he, who should be judged with a heavier judgment, is excused.<-

->From Mersenne’s Letter.<-

"Robert Fludd seemed to me to have sprinkled his volumes with innumerable impieties and errors; therefore he wrote two things against me, in which it cannot be said with how many insults and reproaches he provoked me. Therefore some of my friends thought that the censure of the most learned men should be collected, so that from it it might appear how unworthily and undeservedly he had dealt with me. But in the name of everyone, it will suffice to place here the Judgment of the most learned Lanovius."

->From this Letter of Lanovius:<-

"Therefore it did not befit Your Reverence, as far as I judge, to so dissemblingly tolerate the insane voices and sounds without mind of Robert Fludd, the doctor-soldier <note>original: *medico-militis*; a jab at Fludd’s dual identity as a physician and a polemicist</note>, that you should remain entirely silent; but neither was it in keeping with the greatness of your soul to test your strength with an unequal and inglorious enemy."

->To these things Fludd says:<-

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
Christ says: *Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, and do not see the beam in your own eye?* But Mersenne, not content that he has torn me apart with biting reproaches without any provocation given, and defiled me with stains of scandal and infamy solely for the sake of something unknown, still proceeds to harshly rebuke and blame me if I produce anything a little more sharp in defense of my good name. 

He certainly notices the speck in my eyes, but he does not even think of the beam in his own eye: for he, hiding the injury done to me by him behind a veil of forgetfulness, remembers only my words produced in my own defense against him. And although by divine law an eye is required for an eye, he, if I repay anything (though sparingly enough) for his great malevolence toward me, immediately cries out and tries to defile me with an unspeakable crime. As if all the inhabitants of the Christian world were his slaves, so that however many intolerable insults they were afflicted with by him, they were nevertheless forced to revere and cherish his Reverend Paternity!

<margin>Mersenne column 714, Commentary on Genesis. He seems to brand me with the stigma of Atheism.</margin>
That the curses and insults previously vomited out by him against me are far heavier and sharper than my words is clear from our contest of Wisdom against Folly <note>A reference to Fludd's work *Sophia cum Moria certamen* (The Contest of Wisdom with Folly), published in 1629</note>.

<summary>Fludd mocks Mersenne for relying on the intellectual "bodyguards" Gassendi and Lanovius, comparing Mersenne to a coward who calls for backup in a duel. He further defends himself against charges of impiety and atheism by accusing Mersenne of hypocrisy, using the biblical "mote and beam" analogy.</summary>

<header>Fludd’s Response,</header>

To this passage, I say this: You see with what great malice our Author here continues to rage against Robert, though no just occasion was given to him. He calls the things in Robert’s works "trifles," even though they do not disagree with the Holy Scriptures in the least, and he includes Robert himself, along with many learned men, in the number of Atheists. And although he sees that our Philosophy everywhere rests upon the testimonies of the sacred writings, yet, having brought forward no reason to the contrary, he judges it false. In this way, he busies himself with the Jews to "release Barabbas," but strives to keep Christ—who is the only truth—forever bound in darkness. From this it is clearly established that I am neither worthy of the name "Atheist," nor have I given any shameful scandal to anyone in this place.

Column 1744 <note>Fludd is citing specific columns in Mersenne's massive work, *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim* (1623)</note> contains this: "So that you might achieve this, Fludd, call upon a Spirit or a Demon: for you teach the form of summoning such a thing."

Column 1743 has this: "That Robert Fludd, the heretical-magician, seems to me to be insane," etc.

Column 4, in Problem V: "O the wonderful blindness of the man, who with impunity not only treats such foul and horrendous Magic; but," etc.

And again in the same place: "Will anyone call you a Catholic, James <note>Addressing King James I of England</note>, as long as you see such nefarious books and Magicians roaming in your Kingdom?"

Column 222, Problem 5, has this: "In which place that Robert betrays himself as being enough of a Magician, or writing Magic."

Furthermore, in many other places, he calls Fludd a Magician.

And again in the same place: "But at some point I will write more extensively (God helping) against his impious errors."

Column 40, on Problem 5, says: "This is the distinguished doctrine which he propagated from the 'Waves' <note>original: *de Fluctibus*; a pun on Fludd’s Latinized name, Robertus de Fluctibus</note> quickly; unless he seriously repents, he is to be submerged in eternal waves."

Likewise in the same place: "Would he not have earned greater praise from the devils if he had proposed the masks of fantasy, and Ghosts, and Harpies, and Fates, Eumenides, Gorgons, Furies, Witches, Centaurs, Arimaspians, Dog-milkers, Satyrs, Fauns, Nymphs, and a Crowd of the rest, whether true or fictional? O the wonderful blindness of the man, who in Europe, among Christians, has dared not only to handle such foul and horrendous Magic with impunity, but even impudently to publish it to the light."

Regarding these places, Robert says in folio 73 of *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*: "Surely the mind of that Gigantic man—whatever kind it may be toward me, a miserable Pygmy, falling into the dangerous snares of such a great Philosopher and 'Catholic,' or rather an egregious slanderer and impostor—is easy to gather from these very Texts of his. Is he not like the one who said: *I will ascend into the heavens, and I will be like the Most High*? But nothing that is 'like' is the 'same.' For the Most High said 'let it be,' and immediately they were made. This Impostor says 'let it be' or 'it is,' as if his will stood in place of reason; and yet, once his speech is made, there is almost nothing in what he says. At first glance (I say), it seems to be something; but in the end, nothing at all appears. It is a Thrasonic <note>original: *Thrasonica*; referring to Thraso, a boastful soldier in Roman comedy</note> cloud (not to call him a scoundrel) which is suddenly reduced to nothing by the appearance of the solar truth. For by truth, as if by a Lydian stone <note>The Lydian stone, or touchstone, was used to test the purity of gold</note>, virtue is distinguished from vice, light from darkness, God from the devil, etc."

Will you find in these things, Candid Reader, any crime of treason? Or is there in any way anything published in this place of such ignominy and infamy that it equals the aforementioned texts? These things, therefore, I leave to be determined by your judgment. But I shall proceed.

Columns 671 and 672 speak thus: "The books of Charron *On Wisdom* swarm with Atheism; as do Machiavelli's *The Prince* and *The Republic*; Cardano's *On Subtlety* and his *Judgment of the Stars*; the dialogues of Campanella and Vanini. It would be a worthwhile effort for Fludd’s books either to perish entirely, or at least to be accurately purged. For they more than once insinuate the mortality of the soul, or sow other errors that can lead to Atheism."

To those things, Robert says only this: "While Mersenne seems to hunt for the crimes of heresy and Atheism in others, he many times, though unknowingly, casts himself into their abyss." That is all.

Column 1744: "Wherefore that Robert Fludd, the heretical-magician, seems to me to be insane, when he says the World is like a map of nature brought forth."

To which I say: Observe, I pray, the disposition of this diligent and troublesome man, who, having omitted all sciences of greater importance—or at least barking against them like a dog, yet not knowing how to bite—has arrived at a more irrational science.

Column 1744 says this: "I challenge that Robert, a soldier armed in his own judgment, who believes himself—or at least pretends—to be a learned <term>speaker</term> <note>original Greek: *παγόρην* (pagoren); likely referring to a public orator or someone who addresses an assembly</note>; that Fludd, I say, with all his 'waves' and his formal and material pyramids, and with his soul of the world," etc.

To this, I say: "Let Fludd perish in his own waves, if he should so lightly cast himself into the impetuous waves of a Marine impostor just to satisfy the appetite of his envy," etc.

Again in the same place: "I omit almost infinite things which you chatter with the insane people like yourself; unless you renounce them, I do not know what Hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness</note> Hippocrates, or even your Paracelsus, could use to cure you, etc. So that you might better achieve this, call upon your Geomantic Astrology, or rather your Spirit or Demon, whom even a nursing or babbling child would mock."

To these things Fludd says: "I feel, Marine <note>Fludd punning on Mersenne's name *Marin*, Latin for 'sea-like'</note>, that your nature is so violent, insane, and pestilential that, like a rabid dog, you bespatter everyone, and especially me, with your foamy saliva, having no regard for respect."

Column 1744 says this: "If you do not wish to cast away your trifles, with which your books swarm, and especially your heresy; and if you do not abjure your errors, you will be tormented in eternal flames."

To those things I say: "This is that Lydian Stone (Touchstone) to whose trial (O boastful Mersenne!) you are reduced, so that from it, it may appear to the whole world whether you are truly a genuine or rather a Pseudo-Catholic."

And Column 717: "Whether Robert is a Magician or not—for I do not judge the man’s soul, it is God who tests the reins and the hearts—truly, for the example of others and the edification of Christians, he ought to be afflicted with no less punishment than a Magician."

To this, Robert says: "O unjust judge! For this unworthy Monk, when he ought to have imitated Christ by virtue of his office, does not blush to profess himself the son of the devil at the first glance: let him be punished, he says, whether he acted justly or unjustly. Thus did those most wicked Jews cry out against the innocent (the cause having been weighed not at all): *let him be crucified, let him be crucified,* etc."

Furthermore, in many places of his volume, he fastens the labels of stupidity, ignorance, and impudence upon Fludd. Sometimes he calls me an "impotent squire," in mockery of that Nobility which I claim for myself by the highest right from an ancient lineage: and he delights to tear me apart with a thousand other insults.

Finally, having taken arguments from his own confession, I have left it to the whole world to judge whether he himself can be acceptable to God or not.

Do I not clearly see from these things (Just Reader) how much that adversary was indulging himself in his own cause?

# Fludd’s Response,

To this point I say: You see with what great malice this Author of ours continues to vent his rage against Robert, given no just occasion, calling those things in his works "trifles" which in no way disagree with the Holy Scriptures, and including Robert himself, along with many learned men, in the number of Atheists! And though he sees that our Philosophy rests everywhere upon the testimonies of the sacred writings; nevertheless, bringing no reason to the contrary, he judges it false. In this way, like the Jews, he strives to set Barabbas free, but seeks to keep Christ—who is the only Truth—forever bound in darkness. From this it is clearly established that I am neither worthy of the name of Atheist, nor have I given any shameful scandal to anyone in this place.

*Column 1744 has this:* So that you might achieve this, Fludd, call upon a Spirit <note>original: *Genium*</note> or a Demon: for you teach the form for summoning such a thing.

*Column 1743 has this:* That Robert Fludd, the Heretic-magician <note>original: *Hæretico-magus*</note>, seems to me to be insane, etc.

*Column 4, in Problem 5:* Oh, the wonderful blindness of the man, who would not only treat such foul and horrendous Magic with impunity; but, etc.

*And again in the same place:* Will anyone call you "Catholic," James <note>Refers to King James I of England, whom Mersenne is addressing to complain about Fludd</note>, as long as you see such wicked books and Magicians roaming about in your Kingdom?

*Column 222, problem 5, has this:* In which place that Robert betrays that he is enough of a Magician, or that he writes Magic.
Furthermore, in many other places he calls Fludd a Magician.

*And again in the same place:* But at some point more at length (with God's help) against his impious errors.

*Column 40, on Problem 5, says this:* This is the distinguished doctrine which he defends regarding the Waves <note>original: *de Fluctibus*; a pun on Fludd's Latinized name, Robertus de Fluctibus</note>; unless he seriously repents, he will soon be submerged in the eternal waves.

*Also in the same place:* Would he not have earned greater praise from the devils if he had proposed the masks of fantasy, and Ghosts, and Harpies, and Fates, Furies, Gorgons, Fiends, Witches, Centaurs, one-eyed Arimaspi, dog-milkers <note>original: *Cynomolgas*; a legendary race of dog-headed people</note>, Satyrs, Fauns, Nymphs, and the whole Crowd of the rest, whether fictional or real? Oh, the wonderful blindness of the man who, in Europe and among Christians, has dared not only to handle such foul and horrendous Magic with impunity, but even to publish it impudently to the light.

*In which places Robert, on folio 73 of "The Contest of Wisdom with Folly" <note>original: *Certaminis Sophia cum Moria*</note>, says only this:* Truly, what the mind of that Gigantic man is, and how it stands toward me, a wretched Pygmy—who has fallen into the ruin and snares of such a great Philosopher and Catholic, or rather, such an egregious slanderer and impostor—may be gathered from these very Texts of his. Is he not like the one who said: *I will ascend into the heavens, and I will be like the Most High*? But nothing that is "like" is the "same." For the Most High said *let it be*, and immediately things were made. This Impostor says *let it be*, or *it is*, as if his will stood for reason; and yet, once his speech is made, there is almost nothing in what he says. At first glance (I say) there seems to be something; but in the end, nothing at all appears. It is a boastful <note>original: *Thrasonica*; referring to Thraso, a braggart soldier character from Roman comedy</note> cloud (not to call him a scoundrel <note>original: *nebulo*; Fludd is punning on *nebula* (cloud) and *nebulo* (scoundrel)</note>) which is suddenly reduced to nothing by the appearance of the solar truth. For by truth, as if by a Lydian stone <note>original: *lapide Lydio*; a touchstone used to test the purity of gold</note>, virtue is distinguished from vice, light from darkness, God from the devil, etc.

Will you find in these things, Honest Reader, any crime of high treason? Or is there, in any matter published in this place, anything of shame and infamy equal to the aforementioned texts? These things, therefore, I leave to be determined by your judgment. But I shall proceed.

*Columns 671 and 672 speak thus:* The books of Charron *On Wisdom* swarm with Atheism; as do Machiavelli's *The Prince* and *The Republic*; Cardan *On Subtlety* and *The Judgment of the Stars*; the dialogues of Campanella and Vanini. It would be worthwhile for Fludd's works either to perish entirely, or at least to be accurately purged. For they more than once insinuate the immortality of the soul <note>Mersenne likely meant the *mortality* of the soul, or Fludd is highlighting Mersenne's confusion</note>, or scatter other errors that can lead to Atheism.

To these Robert says only this: While Mersenne seems to hunt for the crimes of heresy and Atheism in others, he many times, though unknowingly, casts himself into their abyss. This is the whole of it.

*Column 1744. Wherefore* that Robert Fludd, the Heretic-magician, seems to me to be insane when he says that the Hand is like a map of progeny and nature.

To which I say: Observe, I pray, the disposition of this diligent and troublesome man, who, having omitted all sciences of greater weight—or at least barking against them like a dog but not knowing how to bite—has arrived at a more irrational science.

*Column 1744 has this:* That Robert, a soldier armored in his own judgment <note>original: *cataphractarium*; referring to a heavy armored cavalryman</note>, who believes himself to be learned in all things <note>original: *παvδοξα* (pandoxa); all-reputed or all-knowing</note>, or at least pretends to be; that Fludd, I say, with all his waves and his formal and material pyramids, and with his soul of the world, I provoke, etc.

To this I say: Let Fludd perish in his own waves if he should cast himself so lightly into the impetuous waves of a Marine impostor <note>A pun on Mersenne's name, Marin, and *marinus* (of the sea)</note> to satisfy the appetite of his envy, etc.

*Again in the same place:* I omit almost infinite things which you chatter with those insane people like yourself, which unless you repudiate, I do not know what Hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity to treat madness</note> Hippocrates, or that Paracelsus of yours, could use to cure you, etc. So that you might better achieve this, call upon your Geomantic Astrology, or rather your Genius or Demon, which even a child still sucking or babbling would laugh at.

To this Fludd says: I feel your Marine nature to be so violent, insane, and pestilential, that, in the manner of a rabid dog, you bespatter everyone, and especially me, with your foamy saliva without any respect.

*Column 1744 has these:* If you do not wish to cast away your trifles, with which your books swarm—especially heresy—and to abjure your errors, you will be tortured in eternal flames.

To these things I say: This is that Lydian stone, to whose examination (O boastful Mersenne!) you are reduced, so that it may appear from there to the whole world whether you are truly a real or rather a Pseudo-Catholic.

*And column 717: Whether* Robert be a Magician or not—for I do not judge the mind of a man; it is God who tests the reins and the hearts—truly, for the example of others and the edification of Christians, he ought to be punished with no less a penalty than a Magician.

To this Robert says: O unjust judge! For this unworthy Monk, when by his office he ought to have imitated Christ, does not blush at the first glance to profess himself a son of the devil: Whether I have acted justly (he says) or unjustly, let him be punished. Thus those worst of Jews cried out against the innocent (the cause being not at all weighed): *let him be crucified, let him be crucified*, etc.

Furthermore, in many places of his Volume, he strikes Fludd with accusations of foolishness, ignorance, and impudence. Sometimes he calls me an "impotent squire," in mockery of that Nobility which I claim for myself by the highest right from an ancient lineage: and he delights to shred me with a thousand other insults.

Finally, with arguments taken from his own confession, I have left it to the whole world to judge whether he himself can be acceptable to God or not.

Do you not clearly perceive from these things (Just Reader) how much that adversary indulged himself in his own cause...

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Robert Fludd is defending his reputation against the attacks of Marin Mersenne. He has just argued that he is no atheist and that his philosophy is rooted in Scripture. On this page, he enlists the support of Pierre Gassendi to show that even Mersenne's friends find Mersenne's language unnecessarily harsh and libelous.</meta>

# To Mersenne's Letter, Part III of Section I.

Did my adversary act justly by speaking and proclaiming to everyone that I had provoked him with so many insults and reproaches? And did his friends (as he calls them) act rightly toward me when they said that Fludd had dealt unworthily and undeservedly with Mersenne (as Mersenne himself tells it)? Finally, I would like you to judge, if you please, whether Lanovius <note>François de La Noue, a friend of Mersenne</note> is a fair or unfair judge by asserting quite foolishly that everything in my response is full of insults. Indeed, as becomes a just judge, he ought to have weighed Mersenne's words against mine with an equal balance.

I conclude, therefore, that if I had written nothing for myself in this defensive style <note>original: "stylo Apologetico"</note>, then I would have acknowledged myself guilty of Mersenne's accusation before both God and men. For he who is silent is seen to consent. But truly, among his other friends, I hold Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a famous French philosopher and scientist</note> deservedly excused; for he, being noble and putting aside all partiality, recognizes and confesses that there was great indiscretion in Mersenne—however much his friend—to provoke an adversary with such spurs of ignominy, and to stir up and exacerbate his anger with so many marks of intolerable insult. And so that the fairness of his right judgment may appear more clearly, I am pleased to note his words here.

->Gassendi, page 9.<-

Your zeal (my dear Mersenne) by which you are carried away, while it ought to be commended, yet it cannot be hidden from you how very harsh it is for one living in the Christian world to be called an Evil Magician <note>original: "Cacomagum"</note>, a Heretical-Magician, or a teacher and propagator of foul and horrendous Magic. To hear that such a teacher must not be tolerated with impunity, and to provoke the Prince <note>Referring to King James I of England</note> to take punishment upon him, even using threats: that for this reason he should soon be submerged in eternal waves, etc.; to say nothing of the Atheism and Heresy which you also charge against Fludd. These are surely things that could have irritated the patience of a Rufinus or a Saint Jerome. For the one, while he requires patience in other matters, cries out that he who bears or ignores the crime of even one heresy is not a Christian. The other says: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy." What would they have done regarding the crime or suspicion of Atheism, or Evil Magic? etc. These are his words.

I wish Mersenne would learn that honorable and Christian discipline of his master and friend, which is full of morality and civility. Nor should he, having erred in such a gross manner, scorn to be taught by a friend devoted to greater modesty. Similarly, I wish he would lend an ear to these words of the same friend, which overflow with truth.

->Gassendi, pages 20 and 144.<-

As far as I am concerned, I neither hold him to be an Evil Magician, nor do I believe him to be an Atheist at all; yet I suspect he disagrees with our Religion, and therefore he ought to be called by us "heterodox" <note>original: "ἑτερόδοξος" (heterodoxos), meaning "of a different opinion"</note>, that is, a Heretic. That he is not an Atheist is clear from the fact that he perpetually sings the praises of some divine nature, and employs the testimonies of Sacred Scripture, not just occasionally, but everywhere. He admits a God, by whom he wants all things to be made, cherished, driven, and governed, etc. Thus says Gassendi.

By these words, he clearly teaches that no one can be justly regarded as an Atheist who acknowledges God. But leaving such superficial matters, I will now descend to the investigation of Mersenne's Letter itself, and its very meat or marrow; in which some things are to be held by any reader as collateral and more superfluous, while others are more essential or real. Concerning each of these in its own order.

---

### SECTION I. PART III.

->In which the less important points, which do not much pertain to the infamy and scandal of Fludd, are refuted.<-

**W**hat is contained in Mersenne's Letter, we divide into less and more important points. We call those "less important" which do not directly aim at or lead to the staining of our honest reputation. And since we have already responded to several of these in the things alleged before, we will pass over them in this place to say a few words about the rest. Those which are esteemed as "more important" are namely those six Impieties falsely imputed to me by my adversaries. And toward removing those, and wiping away their stain, I will apply strenuous effort in the fourth section of this Treatise.

To refute each less important point in its order and reduce it to nothing, I shall proceed in this part of this section.

->Text 1. Mersenne in his Letter:<-

> When in the Volume of my Commentaries on Genesis I was censuring various impieties against God, both ancient and modern, it happened that I simultaneously noted Robert Fludd (also known as Robert de Fluctibus), an English Physician, who, having published many large Volumes, seemed to me to have sprinkled them with innumerable impieties and errors, etc.

->To which Fludd responds:<-

I advise him to take the beam out of his own eye before he judges the speck in his brother's <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:3-5</note>. For how (I ask) is it possible for anyone to pass judgment directly on any matter unless he first understands it? He who does not truly know piety himself, how can he dispute about impieties without injury? But indeed, I have proved from Mersenne’s own mouth that he himself, while acting as the herald or proclaimer of such a sentence, was polluted by those six impieties of his. Nay, seven, which God hates and His soul detests; namely, a lying tongue, Pride, a bloodthirsty Nature, a wicked Imagination, false Testimony, Lying, and the devising of Strife among brothers <note>A reference to the seven things God hates in Proverbs 6:16-19</note>. All this, I say, I have proved and demonstrated clearer than the noonday light in Mersenne, in Book 5 of *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "de Sophiae cum Moria certamine"</note>, chapter 3. Regarding that passage, I find that neither he himself, nor any of his friends speaking for him, has responded in the slightest, nor can they respond. For the demonstration is so evident to anyone's eye that it can be refuted by no one.

As for the "errors" found in my Volumes, I say I hardly know what they are? But since Mersenne is such a good inquisitor, I have truly—as a reward for such great labor of his—expended similar diligence upon his own Volume. Having made an investigation, I discovered that he himself committed almost innumerable and truly real errors in it; not imaginary and apparent ones like those seen by a man who, like a blind man, does not know how to judge colors. Indeed, I will say boldly that I can find and note an error on almost every page of his Volume, where he has not stolen the subject word-for-word from other authors. And this I promise in good faith to put into action, if anyone assigns me some leaf for the sake of a trial. Therefore, this naked assertion of Mersenne's is vain without a demonstration of the matter itself.

->Text 2. Mersenne in the same place:<-

Fludd erred in this, that in volume 2, pages 135 and 164, he teaches [concerning] hammers struck upon the same anvil. <note>This refers to the famous story of Pythagoras discovering musical ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers, a point of scientific/mathematical contention between Fludd and Mersenne.</note>

<meta>Continuing from page 8, Robert Fludd continues his defense against the accusations of the French priest and mathematician Marin Mersenne. In the previous section, Fludd cited Mersenne's specific insults, including labels like "heretical magician." Here, Fludd brings in the testimony of Pierre Gassendi to show that even Mersenne's own friends found his attacks excessively harsh.</meta>

To my adversary <note>Referring to Marin Mersenne</note>, who says and broadcasts to everyone that I provoked him with so many insults and reproaches: did those friends of his (as he calls them) act justly with me when they said that Fludd dealt with Mersenne unworthily and undeservedly (as he himself tells it)? Finally, I would like the judges to decide, if they please, whether Jean de Launoy <note>Jean de Launoy (1603–1678) was a French historian and theologian who supported Mersenne.</note> is a fair or unfair judge by asserting quite foolishly that everything in my response is full of insults. Surely, as befits a just judge, it was proper for him to weigh Mersenne’s words against mine with an equal scale.

I conclude, therefore, that if I had written nothing for myself in a defensive style, I would then have acknowledged myself guilty of Mersenne's accusation before both God and men. For "he who is silent is seen to give consent." However, among his other friends, I rightly hold Pierre Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655) was a philosopher and scientist who, though a friend of Mersenne, attempted to mediate this dispute.</note> excused, for he—honestly and with all partiality set aside—recognizes and confesses that there was great indiscretion in Mersenne (friend of his though he may be) to provoke an adversary with such spurs of ignominy, and to stir up and exacerbate his bile with so many marks of intolerable insult. And so that the fairness of his upright judgment may appear more clearly, I am free to note his words here.

->Gassendi, page 9.<-

> Your zeal (my Mersenne) for which you are carried away, while it ought to be commended, nevertheless cannot be hidden from you: for it is quite harsh for one living in the Christian world to be called an "Evil Magician" <note>original: "Cacomagum"</note>, a "Heretical Magician," or a teacher and propagator of foul and horrendous Magic. To hear: that a teacher of this kind should not be tolerated with impunity, and to provoke the Prince <note>Referring to King James I of England.</note> to take punishment from him, even using threats: that for this reason he must soon be submerged in eternal waves, etc.; to say nothing of the Atheism and Heresy which you also charge against Fludd. These are surely the things that could have irritated the patience of Rufinus or Saint Jerome. For the former, while he requires patience in other matters, cries out that he who bears or ignores the crime of even one heresy is not a Christian. The latter indeed said, "I do not wish anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy." What would they have done regarding the crime or suspicion of Atheism, or Evil Magic? etc. Thus he wrote.

->Gassendi, page 20 and 144.<-

> As far as I am concerned, I neither hold him for an Evil Magician, nor do I believe him to be an Atheist at all; I suspect, however, that he disagrees with our Religion, and therefore he ought to be called by us a Heretic, that is, a <term>heterodox</term> <note>original Greek: ἑτερόδοξος, meaning "of a different opinion" or "unorthodox."</note> person. That he is not an Atheist is clear even from this: that he perpetually sings the praises of some divine nature, and uses the testimonies of Holy Scripture, not just a few times, but everywhere. He admits God, by whom he wants all things to be made, nourished, moved, and governed, etc. Thus says Gassendi.

By which he clearly teaches that no one can be justly reputed as an Atheist who acknowledges God. But leaving aside such superficial matters, I shall now descend to the Letter of Mersenne itself, and to the investigation of its very pulp or marrow, in which some things are to be held by any reader as collateral and more superfluous, while others are more essential or real. Concerning each of these in its own order.

***

# SECTION I. PART III.

## In which the less principal matters, which do not pertain much to the infamy and scandal of Fludd, are refuted.

We divide the contents of the Mersennian Letter into the "less principal" and "more principal" matters. We call those "less principal" which do not directly aim at or lead to the staining of our honest reputation. And since we have already made a response to some of that kind in the previously cited passages, we will therefore pass over them in this place to say very few words about the rest. Those which are estimated as "more principal" are namely those six Impieties falsely imputed to me by my adversaries. And toward removing those, and wiping away their stain, I shall work strenuously in the fourth section of this Treatise.

To refute and reduce to nothing each "less principal" matter in its order, I will proceed in this part of this section.

### Text 1. Mersenne in his Letter.

> When I was criticizing various impieties against God, both ancient and modern, in the Volume of my *Commentaries on Genesis*, it happened that I simultaneously noted Robert Fludd <note>original: "Robertum à Fluctibus"</note>, the English Physician, who—having published many large Volumes—seemed to me to have sprinkled them with innumerable impieties and errors, etc.

### To which Fludd responds.

I warn him to "remove the beam from his own eye" before he judges the "speck in his brother's eye." <note>A reference to Matthew 7:3-5.</note> For how (I ask) is it possible for someone to pass judgment directly on any matter unless he first understands it? He who did not truly know piety himself, while he acted as the herald or proclaimer of a sentence of that kind, was himself polluted by the dregs of those impieties. Indeed, seven of them, which God hates and his soul detests: namely, a lying tongue, Pride, a bloodthirsty nature, an evil imagination, false testimony, lying, and the engineering of contention among brothers. <note>A reference to the "seven things detestable to God" in Proverbs 6:16-19.</note> This, I say, I proved entirely, and demonstrated more clearly than the midday light in Mersenne in Book 5 of *The Struggle of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "de Sophiae cum Moria certamine," published in 1629.</note>, Chapter 3. Regarding that passage, I do not find that either he himself, or any of his friends speaking for him, has responded even a little bit, or is able to respond. The demonstration is so evident to anyone's eye that it can be refuted by no one.

As for the "errors" found in my Volumes, I say I hardly know what they are. But since Mersenne is such a good "Inquisitor," I have surely—as a reward for such great labor of his—spent similar diligence on his own Volume, and upon investigation, I discovered that he himself committed almost innumerable and truly real errors in it, not imaginary and apparent ones to a man of that sort, who (like a blind man) truly does not know how to judge colors. Indeed, I will say boldly that I can find and note an error on almost every page of his Volume, where he has not gathered his subject matter word-for-word from other authors. And this I promise in good faith of my actions, if anyone assigns me some leaf for the sake of trying me. Therefore, that naked assertion of Mersenne's is vain without a demonstration of the matter itself.

### Text 2. Mersenne in the same place.

Fludd erred in this: that in Volume 2, pages 135 and 164, he teaches that when hammers are struck upon the same anvil:

# Fludd’s Response

For their weights, even if they maintain the same ratio among themselves as those numbers 12, 9, 8, and 6, nevertheless they are far from producing the musical harmonies <note>original: "consonantias"</note> signified by those numbers; rather, they produce nearly the same sound in terms of pitch.

->To this, I respond:<-

*The things I proposed in that same place are not without their own foundations. For we read these things first in the Philosophical Pearl <note>The "Philosophica Margarita" (1496) by Gregor Reisch, a famous encyclopedia of the time</note>, which in effect we also find in Boethius and others. These are the words: "Pythagoras the Philosopher learned the proportions of sounds by experiment. For while he was for a long time agonizing in his mind by what method he might learn the measures of harmonies, at last, by a fatal nod <note>i.e., by divine providence or fate</note>, passing by a blacksmith’s shop, he noticed a single harmony coming from the various sounds of the hammers. He approached, examined the weight of the hammers: and since there were five hammers, he found the first to be double the weight of the fourth, which rang out with the harmony of an Octave <term>Diapason [an octave ratio of 2:1]</term>. He found that same hammer to be in a ratio of four-to-three <term>Sesquitertium [a 4:3 ratio]</term> to the second, against which it thundered a Fourth <term>Diatessaron</term>. And again, that same one being in a ratio of three-to-two <term>Sesquialter [a 3:2 ratio]</term> to the third, it harmonized as a Fifth <term>Diapente</term>. He found the second and third to maintain a ratio of nine-to-eight <term>Sesquioctave [a 9:8 ratio]</term>, sounding a whole tone. The fifth hammer, however, which was discordant with all the others, he rejected." These are their words. Furthermore, various other authors most skilled in the science of Music also seem to agree with this assertion of the aforementioned Philosophers. But Mersenne concludes that all of these men are liars, as if there were not the same relationship between Geometric and Arithmetic proportion—namely, between a weight of three dimensions and an interval of numerical value. But I will say to Mersenne that which he himself, I confess, has so far ignored: namely, that a figure of three dimensions, of one and the same weight but varying in shape, is observed to give forth different sounds. As for the rest: I have fulfilled what I promised in my "Brief Explanation of Music and Other Sciences"; namely, I have revealed the worlds, such as the Technical History of the Artists in the Macrocosm <note>Fludd is referring to his massive work, "Utriusque Cosmi Historia"</note>. Not that I was finding something brand new; rather, I promised that I would explain to the best of my ability that which has been considered proven by preceding centuries. I confess, however, that I have added some things to the Mathematical sciences which were not common, but known only to a very few. But those things are trivial and of little moment, and consequently to be passed over in silence.*

->Text 3. Mersenne, in the same place.<-

In that which he concludes by the force of his principles—that a living body is far lighter than itself when dead—he errs. For it is repugnant both to experience and to truth. Therefore, by my own right, I demand that Fludd's principles be declared false and useless. Yet it is established by experience, which we have performed most accurately, that a dead body is no heavier than a living one; since we found a living dog of 17 pounds, and a hen of 52 ounces, to be of the same weight—indeed, even less—after death.

->To this, Fludd responds:<-

We are playing with a bubble <note>An idiom meaning "we are wasting time on trifles"</note>. Mersenne certainly deserves extraordinary praise for bringing a matter of such great weight to light: that a dead dog and a dead hen had the same, or rather a somewhat lesser weight, than when they were alive, and that therefore Fludd's principles are false. From this he seems to conclude at the same time against those principles that fire and air are not light, and do not by their own accord hold a body up, and that a body is not carried upward by a natural inclination. Therefore, fire, by its own effort while it is being kindled, is not raised upward against the light disposition of its body. Therefore, a maid-servant, suffocating a cat by pressing her feet into its belly and throat, does not find the vital power of the cat resisting, and the body of the one treading upon it raised upward for a little while. Therefore, air drawn in and retained in the lungs or a bladder does not make a man more difficult to submerge. Therefore, air returned into water and thickened is not heavier with respect to its location than when it was contained in its simple and subtle nature in a similar location. But truly, so that I may demonstrate by common experience that this axiom of Mersenne’s is uncertain and inconsistent, let him look at the "Weather-glass" <note>original: "speculum Calendarium," Fludd's name for his thermoscope, a precursor to the thermometer</note> (named quite often in my Volumes, and hardly unknown to any curious person in Europe), and he will find that the air enclosed in the glass is condensed by the force of external cold, and by condensation is reduced into a narrower space; whence it happens that the more that internal air is contracted by the presence of cold, the more the water contained in the lowest vessel is raised. From this it is clear that cold is the cause of the condensation of air, and that contracted air requires a narrower place than when it was dilated. Hence it follows, therefore, that air condensed by cold is heavier, and consequently, that those dead through the extinction of heat and the dominance of cold are heavier—unless perhaps, on account of the compression made in the agony of death, the vessels are also constricted and the enclosed air is expelled, as can be seen in certain killed animals. For where the vessels, at the moment of death and after death, are left open, there it is necessary that they be filled with thick and heavy air due to the presence of dominating cold, which was being driven out during life by the action of the heat present. But that subtle air, in the same vessels, is lighter than thick air, no one (I think) will doubt.

*But now (diligent Reader), I will recite a faithful story to you. A certain Vintner, a young man living in the city of Westminster at the sign of the Dog, so abounded and swelled with fat <note>original: "adipe"</note> that he could scarcely, or not at all, be moved or carried by himself without the help of three men in a certain chair made industriously for such work. By chance, being infested by some lethal disease, this man, monstrous on account of the mass of his fat, died. For when the body of the deceased was opened by a surgeon, they found in it an almost ineffable abundance of fat. When his pious wife, refusing the great price offered to her by the surgeon for his fat, wished to commit her whole husband to the earth, then the funeral was found to be so grave and heavy that seven or eight porters were required to commit it to the grave and hide it in the earth. Nor, certainly, would they have performed that work without wooden wheels, by which the corpse was more easily carried. This is known to almost the entire city of London, and confirmed by the testimony of many thousands watching and admiring.*

The reason for this thing (unless I am mistaken) was the extreme coldness of the fatty mass which, once the heat was driven out, condensed the air contracted in its pores after death. For that fat was nothing other than air gradually coagulated by the conflict made between hot and cold. From these things, therefore, it is clear how experiment can contradict experiment, by reason of the diversity of the subject, either in the capacity of the passages, or in the composition of the matter, or in the presence of greater or lesser cold or heat. Finally, I have found that iron filings, exposed to a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note> for three days, are rendered quite spongy, and for that reason, after their extraction from the furnace and their cooling, I noticed they were a little heavier and more ponderous than they were before their placement, since the matter, having been made more spongy and gradually cooling, attracted into its porous and loose substance thick air condensed by the action of cold. You see here, therefore (Reader), whether on account of that assertion of Mersenne, these principles of Fludd are found to be false and useless—principles affirming that cold thickens and consequently makes heavier and presses downward; but on the contrary, that heat attenuates more and makes lighter, and by consequence carries upward by natural inclination.

### Regarding Mersenne’s Letter. Member I. Part II.

->Text 4. Mersenne, in the same place.<-

Since Fludd enumerates many other authors, I will bring forward only those upon whose authority he relies in his books. Among these, *Pseudo-Trismegistus* <note>original: "Pseudo-Trismegistus"; Mersenne uses the prefix "Pseudo" to suggest that the works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus are forgeries</note> holds the first rank. Fludd seems to make his *Pymander* <note>A foundational Hermetic text dealing with the nature of God and the cosmos</note> and other treatises equal to the authority and truth of Holy Scripture. I believe Fludd would lower his estimation of them significantly if he were to read *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon, the scholar who proved in 1614 that the Hermetic texts were written in the early Christian era, not in ancient Egypt</note> in his first exercise on the *Annals*.

->*Fludd’s Response*<-

> Why is there a need for so many words? If truth corresponds to truth, why should we reject the truth found in *Hermes Trismegistus*? Why should I not compare it with the truth found in the Scriptures? Has *Mersenne* never learned that truth has been excluded from the sacred page by his own kind simply because it was received from a "vile place" <note>i.e., a non-Christian or pagan source</note>? Is not the truth always the same, wherever it is found? Therefore, from a huge pile of chaff, the grains of wheat—however few—must always be gathered as long as they are true and good. Truly, any writing in which not even a crumb of truth is found is foolish and utterly empty. Therefore, whatever is good, even if brought forth by an author however meager and sterile, must be embraced; and conversely, whatever is evil must be ignored. 
> 
> As for what pertains to *Hermes Trismegistus*, I believe indeed that *Mersenne* understands their "marrow" <note>original: "medullam"; the inner essence or hidden meaning</note> no more than he understands the writings of *Francesco Giorgio* <note>original: "G. Veneti"; Giorgio was a Venetian monk and Christian Kabbalist</note>, whose subject matter (however unknown to him) he has taken it upon himself to judge and correct with such great rashness. But let us hear, I pray, the reason for the name *Pseudo-Trismegistus*? Because, forsooth, *Casaubon* said so. But certainly, this proves nothing. For it is nothing new in this present age for the blind to lead the blind. Furthermore: how can someone judge without injury a matter that is utterly unknown to him? "Let the cobbler stick to his last" <note>A Latin proverb meaning one should not comment on things outside their expertise</note>; let not the "ass play the lyre." 
> 
> As for *Casaubon*, there is no reason for us to dwell on his assertions, since he is equally ignorant of the matter being discussed. It was fitting for *Casaubon* to look after his own *Annals* and monuments of antiquity, rather than to rashly judge the mysteries of God and Nature. For I dare to constantly affirm that he did not understand even a page of *Hermes Trismegistus*. But it is written that the wisdom of God is mere foolishness to the worldly; and for that reason, the chosen are held in hatred by the worldly. Why then should it be a wonder, or why should we dwell on an ungrateful world?

->Text 4. Mersenne, in the same place.<-

I add *Paracelsus* <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note>, regarding whom let Fludd learn what the chemists themselves think from *Goclenius* <note>Rudolf Goclenius the Younger, a professor of medicine</note>, who speaks thus in his book *Morosophia*: *one thing I cannot pass over (namely the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross of which he speaks) is that he not only cites Theophrastus Paracelsus, but even strives to prove his own institution and efforts from his writings; although it is more than well-known that he [Paracelsus] was most devoted to evil and illicit arts, insulting to nature, harmful to men, and blasphemous toward God, etc.*

->*Fludd’s Response*<-

In this way, of course, *Mersenne* has written as the absolute truth that *Fludd* is a <term>Cacomagus [an evil magician]</term>, a leader of heretics, an atheist, and a blasphemer; yet *Fludd’s* conscience bears witness that he is innocent of these crimes. What of it? Is it true just because a malevolent man said so? But to the text:

However much *Paracelsus* may be held as impious and insulting by the envious and malignant, it is nevertheless certain that in the age in which he lived, he brought admirable cures to a happy conclusion, and did so beyond the grasp of the common people. For this reason, he was hated by malignant and envious men, especially the Galenic doctors <note>Followers of the ancient Roman physician Galen, representing the medical establishment of the time</note>. But why not? Is it not written of *Christ* himself that the Jews, driven by their malice, spread the word that he was a <term>Cacomagus</term> and healed the sick by the power of *Beelzebub*? 

I long to know whether the things accomplished or published by *Paracelsus* and the brothers of the *Rosy Cross*—namely, the admirable cures of desperate diseases and other wonders—were done by the power of God and the secret force of Nature implanted by God, rather than by the operation of the devil? Truly: if *Moses*, *Joshua*, *Samuel*, *Elijah*, and *Elisha*—even *Christ* himself and his *Apostles*—were walking the earth today and performing miracles in their usual way, I believe they would immediately be considered <term>Cacomagi</term> by the malignant men of this age, to be burned in the flames as quickly as possible, or punished by some other most cruel kind of death. Truly, there is a great error in the men of the present age: while they believe that God has granted all his power to the Devil and to evil magicians, they believe he has hidden the lawful magic (whether natural or supernatural) of the ancient chosen ones from pious men; indeed, they believe he has denied it to them entirely. Thus, if any wonders happen today, they immediately think those things proceed only from impious Magi, and not at all from the pious.

As for what concerns the brothers of the *Rosy Cross*, what should I say? For they themselves, in their Letter published by *Joachim Frizius* <note>A pseudonym likely associated with the defense of the Rosicrucians</note>, respond quite abundantly on their own behalf, however concisely, to men of that sort who so sharply rail against them:

->From the Letter, folio 51. Concerning the Highest Good.<-

> He who increases knowledge, increases also sorrow, because in much knowledge there is much indignation: we speak from experience. For all the worldly people, and the boastful braggarts, the vainglorious, the pompous, the talkative, and the empty, blaspheme us undeservedly; they even speak evil of us regarding matters unknown to them. But we do not wonder that the ungrateful world has persecuted the professors of the true arts along with the Truth itself, etc.

By these few things, it seems to me that a precise response is given to *Mersenne*, *Casaubon*, *Goclenius*, and unworthy men of that sort; and it seems to satisfy the pious and worthy.

I found nothing in his entire Letter, besides those things cited above, worthy of a response: therefore, I shall descend to the examination of the severe and "high-thundering" judgment of *Franciscus Lanovius*.

***
