# Fludd’s Response, MEMBER II. PART 1.

### François de La Noue wrote a letter to Marin Mersenne, the title of which is as follows:
## TO THE REVEREND FATHER MARIN MERSENNE,
### The Judgment of François de La Noue regarding Robert Fludd.

From the very marrow of this letter, we have gathered—through a sufficiently strict investigation—first the condition and nature of the man passing judgment, and afterwards his effectiveness in attempting to refute Fludd’s principles. Therefore, we shall discuss these two parts (God willing) in their proper order.

->Part I.<-

To you (benevolent Reader, whom I have chosen as the Judge in this cause of mine), I shall faithfully present the nature and condition of this "Judge" of ours, just as I have received it from his own words and mouth. I shall get straight to the point. When I seriously reflected upon the haughty words and spirit of La Noue in his *Judgment of Robert Fludd*, it seemed to me—or at least to the eyes of my mind—that he presented the appearance of a certain Schoolmaster <note>original: "Pædagogi"; Fludd is mocking La Noue as a petty classroom tyrant rather than a serious scholar</note> armed with a switch at his belt instead of a sword; a sight terrible indeed to boys and beginners, but more ridiculous than formidable to those who are grown and nourished in the mystery of Minerva <note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom; Fludd means those initiated into deeper philosophical truths</note>. Indeed, we have gathered into this little bundle the man’s haughty words, which indicate his proud condition as well as the imbalance of his heart.

->La Noue in his letter to Mersenne.<-

"Since, however, our patience is tested by such insolent boldness, I do not think we owe such a duty of silence to Religion that we should allow the truth to be endangered alongside our own virtue. For this reason, it was not fitting for your Reverence (so far as I can judge) to tolerate the insane voices and mindless sounds of the Soldier-Physician <note>original: "Medico-militis"; a jab at Fludd’s profession as a doctor and perhaps his defensive posture</note> Robert Fludd so dissemblingly that you remained entirely silent. Nor was it in keeping with the greatness of your soul to test your strength against an unequal and inglorious enemy."

->And further.<-

"Truly, so that I may not let you lack my support, the ignorance and impudence of your adversary compels me; I shall not fear to uncover it, since he himself has defamed his own unworthiness in his public writings. I shall do so briefly, and as far as it is permitted for a Theologian to spend his labor in cleaning up such filth, etc."

->And again.<-

"He translates the Scriptures partly ineptly, and against their genuine and proper sense, and partly impiously, in order to establish his ridiculous and erroneous dogmas, etc."

->Then here.<-

"He occasionally carps at the Philosophy of Aristotle; but content with having cast an insult in a word, he abstains from a more laborious refutation: for an insult is as easily despised as it is lightly and rashly thrown by an unpraised and unskilled man, etc."

->Then afterwards.<-

"He says it is not his place to judge whether Fludd is a Magician <note>original: "Magus"; in this context, it carries a negative connotation of forbidden or black magic</note>, but for no other reason does he incline toward the contrary view, except because of the lack of skill that Fludd displays."

->And again.<-

"In the Kabbalah <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, which Fludd integrated into his Christian philosophy</note> he has betrayed his vanity and ignorance; nor is it possible for one to be very skilled in Hebrew who blunders and hallucinates as shamefully as Fludd does."

With these (Candid Reader) and other words full of reproach—which I omit here for the sake of brevity—he has moved against me, led more by a malignant mind and a hateful and angry passion than by reason. He thought, perhaps, that with his grand words, full of disgrace and infamy, he could strike some sort of fear and dread into me and deter me entirely from the duty of responding. For in these words (as you see) he calls me insolently bold, a broadcaster of insane voices and mindless sounds, vile, inglorious, impudent, ignorant, unworthy, one who translates the scriptures ineptly and impiously for my ridiculous dogmas, unpraised, unskilled, vain, contemptible, etc.

But observe (I pray, good Reader) the remarkable persistence of this man, and his shameful and hateful immodesty in slandering and pouring out insults and railings against anyone. Have you ever heard an argumentative little woman <note>original: "muliercula dicaculæ"; a derogatory comparison to a nagging or gossiping woman</note> speaking against someone more harshly than our La Noue? Is anyone more ready to inflict contumely? Is anyone, finally, more skilled in the art of brawling? I would wish, therefore, that the Old Hags of Paris <note>original: "Parisienses Vetulae"</note> might learn from this Master of theirs the faculty of scolding and of wordy or windy defamation, because he alone seems to excel in it. Yet, are such things becoming of an honest Theologian or an upright Philosopher? Do they suit Christian modesty and scholarly morality? Christ teaches us to do good for evil; this man, on the contrary, though given no handle against me, strives to move every stone of impiety and malice against me. Christ says: *judge not and you shall not be judged*; but this man proceeds not only to judge, but even to condemn me with an unjust judgment. For he condemns only me, and not my adversary, as if the latter had dealt with me far more worthily. For he [Mersenne], being in no way provoked by me, is the author of our dispute; but I was compelled to speak and respond only on my own behalf, to defend my good reputation. And therefore this unjust Judge, being too indulgent in his friend’s cause, goes about condemning me. For he asserts that I received his friend Mersenne with immoral words, when he himself sins far more grievously in the same regard. For I wish someone would see whether, in that quite ample response of mine to Mersenne, there exist as many insults uttered by me against him as La Noue has heaped upon me in this tiny bit of paper containing his letter? And yet he says: "in that work of Fludd's, all things are full of insults." Hypocrite, says Christ, *first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to pull the mote out of your brother’s eye.* But leaving aside all these superficialities of his, which are like false images, I shall scrutinize the deeper marrow of his judicial letter and pluck out the very kernel, so that, a proper inquiry having been made, his "Gigantic" strength (if it be truly such) may come to light, and it may appear more clearly to the world whether it is sufficient and strong enough to subvert the foundations of Fludd's Philosophy. And I shall dispatch this inquiry, or this examination of mine, in a few words: because to detect and scatter falsehoods by the light of truth, not many things are required.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s rebuttal of François de La Noue. Having previously criticized La Noue’s character, Fludd now addresses the specific charges: that his philosophy is a modern invention, that he misuses Scripture, and that his interests in alchemy and magic are blasphemous or forbidden.</meta>

# Regarding the Judgment of La Noue, Member II. Part II.
<note>Member II refers to the second major section of Fludd's multi-part response to his critics.</note>

B 3
<meta>catchword: damna-</meta>

## Text 1. La Noue.

First, his entire system of natural philosophy <note>original: "physiologiæ"; in this period, "physiology" referred to the general study of nature and the physical world, not just biology</note>, which he claims to have fashioned anew and for which he sought authority from divine sources, is—aside from being inconsistent—unstable at its very foundation.

## Fludd.

It will be a Herculean labor for La Noue to prove this with any precision. But let us proceed to his reasoning.

## Text 2. La Noue.

Because he translates the Scriptures partly in an inept manner, against their genuine and proper sense, and partly in an impious manner, to establish his own ridiculous and erroneous dogmas.

## Fludd.

He says that I have translated the Scriptures against their proper sense, but he proves nothing; therefore, he is hardly to be believed. On the contrary, I have clearly indicated—using many passages of Scripture and indeed the harmonic consensus of the entire sacred codex—that the foundations of my philosophy do not disagree with those of Moses. I showed this in my response to the second and third texts of chapter 2, book 1, of *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "Sophiæ cum Moria certamine"; this was a book Fludd published in 1629 specifically to defend himself against Mersenne</note>. From this, it can be seen that it was never my intention to claim that I discovered or "fashioned" these principles anew, since I candidly attribute them to Moses as their Father. Furthermore, regarding the sense of the Scriptures: how shall we better draw it out than through a multitude of sacred authorities and testimonies sounding the same note? Is it not according to the consensus of all that Book opens Book, Text opens Text, and Passage elucidates Passage? We conclude, therefore, that here his entire force is directed toward refuting Fludd’s principles; however, any Wise person can discern at first glance how weak that force truly is.

->Now he turns to Fludd's Chemistry.<-

## Text 3. La Noue, ibid.

Indeed, the fact that he draws the authority of these same Scriptures into the mysteries of Chemistry is sacrilegious and blasphemous; nor is it necessary to add anything to the censure of the Sorbonne <note>The Faculty of Theology at the University of Paris, the highest authority for Catholic orthodoxy at the time</note>, by which the very similar impiety of Khunrath <note>Heinrich Khunrath (1560–1605), a German physician and "theosophical" alchemist whose work "The Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom" was condemned by the Sorbonne in 1625</note> was condemned. For both are in the same category.

## Fludd.

How unjust is this Judge, who, having understood the cause not at all, plunges himself into judgment with such rashness. What the nature of my Alchemy truly is, I shall explain briefly here, and with a fuller pen in the fourth member of Part 2 of this Treatise. I acknowledge, then, that my Alchemy is concerned with the knowledge and acquisition of the cornerstone <note>original: "lapidis angularis"; Fludd is playing on the dual meaning of the "cornerstone" as Christ and the "Philosopher's Stone" of the alchemists</note>; which stone such pseudo-builders as Mersenne and La Noue reject and deride to their own ruin. Was it sacrilegious and blasphemous in the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles—indeed, in all those established in sacred and Christian philosophy—to so greedily seek the possession of that stone? But concerning this subject, we shall speak more widely below (as has been said).

Finally, I do not take it as granted that Khunrath is truly and before God guilty of a crime, sacrilege, or blasphemy simply because he was condemned by the censure of the Sorbonne. Rather, his judges—who dare to condemn anyone with such security and audacity while the matter is entirely unknown to them—will be condemned before God, who is the sole searcher of hearts and things. They pay no heed to those words of the Savior: <margin>Matthew 7</margin> Judge not, and you shall not be judged; condemn not, and you shall not be condemned. For with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged, and with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again. I would have them know, therefore, that the Lord will judge all things according to the truth, and He will not permit unjust judges to go unpunished.

I conclude, however, that he merely says it is sacrilegious and blasphemous to draw Holy authority into the mysteries of Chemistry, yet he proves nothing. But how could he prove it? He is utterly ignorant of the very subject he ought to prove. Here, therefore (candid Reader), you can see the depth of this man’s knowledge in true Alchemy.

->Now he passes to the Investigation of Fludd's Magic.<-

## Text 4. La Noue, ibid.

He may be deservedly suspected of Magic, for besides reviving forbidden arts already long ago proscribed by the Church, he establishes them as far as he can. The things he invents regarding the discovery of each person's genius or spirit <note>original: "Dæmone"; in the Platonic tradition Fludd followed, this referred to a personal guardian spirit or guiding intelligence, not an evil entity</note> are sufficient to create this suspicion. This is greatly increased by the devotion he professes toward Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous Renaissance occult philosopher</note> and scoundrels of that sort who are infamous for Magic. It is not our place to judge whether he has defiled himself with this disgrace; and I would prefer to lean toward the negative side on account of the ignorance he displays, rather than pronounce anything rashly.

## Fludd.

Note the opinion of our Judge. First he says Fludd is "deservedly suspected" of Magic; and soon, forgetting himself, he excuses him from that crime because of the "ignorance" he notices in him. But how poorly those things hang together! And consequently, how inconsistent this Man of the Bench <note>original: "Tribunalista"; a mocking term for someone acting like a high-court judge</note> is with himself! For if I am deservedly suspected of Magic, it follows that I am indeed a Magician. If not, I am held as such undeservedly. But in his conclusion, he argues that I am not such a thing because of my excessive ignorance; consequently, therefore, I cannot be deservedly suspected of such a matter. As for my Magic, that shall be answered in full later in the objection to Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi, another major critic of Fludd</note>.

## Text 5. La Noue, ibid.

But concerning his writings, we can and must say safely and without offense to anyone that they are to be entirely abolished and struck from the hands of men, as they savor, at the very least, of a condemned curiosity.

## Fludd.

Behold the unique judgment of this high-sounding and vainglorious Judge, by which he concludes that my writings are to be deleted and abolished. But I wish this severe and angry Judge would abstain from the exile and excommunication of my books until the cause has been heard by just ears and weighed by a healthy mind. If not, why should we care for such a judgment? Especially from one who is utterly ignorant of the very thing he chooses to judge. Nor do I believe that the learning or the reputation of François de La Noue is so eminent among the literate of Europe that they would so easily allow my writings to be struck from their hands based on his irrational opinion. For the majority of them understand what Fludd has written and perceive his meaning—which is entirely hidden from La Noue. And that is the reason why he believes they...

...to reek of a condemned curiosity, things which in themselves are true and honest, and not unworthy of a Christian man. Therefore, to the rest.

->Now he proceeds to my *Universal Medicine*.<-

### Text 6. La Noue, in the same place.

I leave it to the sons of Aesculapius <note>A poetic term for physicians, after the Greek god of healing</note> to discuss what, or how much, this *Universal Medicine* <note>original: "Medicina Catholica"; Fludd’s massive work on the intersection of medicine, astrology, and theology</note> contributes toward the attainment of health. Certainly, it cannot be denied that it falls back into those errors which we have briefly recounted; and generally, it is certain that it retains—according to the old proverb—trifles more tasteless than those of a tasteless countryside.

->**Fludd.**<-

According to his usual custom, this "terrible judge" condemns, vituperates, and annihilates; but he proves nothing worthy of condemnation. Indeed, regarding my *Universal Medicine*, he presumes to judge like another Apelles the Shoemaker going beyond his last <note>original: "Apelles Sutor ultra crepidam"; a reference to the Greek painter Apelles who told a cobbler not to judge parts of a painting above the shoes he made. It means one should not judge things outside their expertise</note>, however much it exceeds the capacity of his judgment. Furthermore, it is clear from these words of his that he has never read that volume of mine, or perhaps, having glanced through it in passing, he by no means understood it. But truly, is anyone more an enemy to knowledge than the ignorant? Hence it is so easy for him to deny everything therein with general words, however true they may be, and to trumpet them as false and futile; even though men far more skilled than he in Medicine and Philosophy, as well as Theosophy, are accustomed to hold them as good and certain after a diligent reading.

We conclude, therefore, that whatever he has written against me in that letter of his, he has taken entirely from Gassendi's <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher and scientist who was one of Fludd’s primary intellectual rivals</note> response—if you except the insults—merely changing the words; but from his own reading (as it seems to me), he has nothing. Therefore, his judgment is rejected as easily as it is rashly and lightly cast.

->Now he passes to *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*; let us see if he speaks with a more prudent style.<-

### Text 7. La Noue, ibid.

*The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "Sophiæ cum Moria certamine"; Fludd’s 1629 defense against Marin Mersenne</note> contains nothing worthy of such a splendid title. If he attributes "Wisdom" to himself, he is far wrong. It would have been better if, having made an exchange, he had assumed "Folly," whose persona he sustains so well that it suits no man more equally. The list of authors he has prefixed has an appearance that might entice the unwary to waste good hours badly; there is not even a shadow of truth beneath it, unless he wishes to complain that those like him were brought into a criminal charge—which was your duty as a good writer to have done.

->**Fludd.**<-

Here (Reader, so that I may most rightly hurl La Noue’s words back at him) you truly have "insane and empty voices, and sounds without a mind." For if you look into the matter at hand with a deeper eye, you will see nothing but the turgid bubbles of a sterile wit, or rather the husks of *Folly*; you will not see the essential seeds of Wisdom with their kernel. For, I ask you, what do these futile words do toward the refutation of that book of ours, which was published with the greatest right against Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath who accused Fludd of being a magician and heretic</note>? Is this the whole strength of La Noue (that perverse judge, I say) to shatter our work? What? Does he think to demolish a bronze wall with naked words that concern the matter little or not at all? By the claws (as I said) we recognize the Lion. We perceive (I say) a wineskin full of wind, but empty of good wine.

As for the reasoning behind the Title and the names explained in it, I shall speak more fully in its proper place, God willing, when I deal with the same subject with Gassendi (whom I find to be more learned, more just, and more modest than this judge of ours). For why say more with one who proposes all these things as if through Gassendi's mouth, and not his own?

### Text 8. La Noue, ibid.

That he has promiscuously confused some people with others was done by design, so that by the company of the good, he might defend the cause of the evil. In the work itself, besides a continual <term>logomachy <gloss>a dispute over words</gloss></term>, there is almost nothing to the point; everything is full of insults against Christian modesty. This modesty he dilutes by negation or dissonant interpretation, despite the prudent <term>indications <gloss>proofs or evidences, from the Greek "tekmeriois"</gloss></term> and the illustrious marks of a restrained mind which he had laboriously built up in entire books long ago—such as those ideas that the Soul of the World is God or the Holy Spirit, that the soul is mortal but for sin, etc.

->**Fludd.**<-

But who made this clear to you, you clever Judge? Certainly, Judas was not numbered among the disciples of Christ so that he might defend the cause of the evil by the company of the good. Therefore, that supposition of yours is false. But let La Noue prove that I have joined the evil with the good in that list of Authors. But if he alleges Roman law—namely, that Lutherans, Calvinists, and such are Heretics, and therefore evil—I respond that this censure has weight among Romans and according to human wisdom; but before God, who is the most just Judge, and according to divine wisdom, it is nothing. As for the rest: namely, concerning my opinion on the Soul of the World, I shall dispute it copiously against these adversaries of mine in Member 4, in the examination of the "Third Impiety."

### Text 9. La Noue, ibid.

He occasionally pecks at *Aristotle’s Philosophy*; but content with a word, he hurls an insult and abstains from a more laborious refutation. Therefore, the insult is as easily despised as it is lightly and rashly cast by an unpraised and unskilled man, etc.

->**Fludd.**<-

How litigious the mind of this man is, his caviling words prove. For the tongue opens the treasury of the heart itself: and corrupt words indicate a malignant distemper of his heart or mind. But I give thanks to God that, just as La Noue voluntarily climbed onto the Judge’s seat, so in this Judgment we can find no one more unjust than he, more false, and more indulgent to his friend. But to the point.

He says I "peck at" the philosophy of *Aristotle*, but content with a word, I hurl an insult. The place in which I dealt with the errors of Aristotle regarding Meteorology *is in Book 1, Chapter 4 of The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*, where you will perceive that I—with words full of reason and confirmed by the testimony of both the Sacred Text and ocular experience—proved and demonstrated that the *Meteorological foundations of Aristotle* are most false and greatly contrary to the Sacred Page. And yet this wordy Judge says in the aforementioned text: "but content with a word," etc. Furthermore, I signaled this very thing there in these express words: "This (I said) is the cause why that philosophy..."

# To the Judgment of La Noue, Member II, Part II.

...that Heathen <note>original: "Ethnicam"; referring to non-Christian, specifically Aristotelian, philosophy</note> philosophy, he desires to prefer it to the Mosaic one, calling it true when it is in reality spurious and false, and contrary to the sense of the sacred scriptures, as will appear from these things cited by us, and is more clearly declared in our *Sacred Philosophy*. These are my words there. From which it is clear that all <note>The transcription says "rota" (wheel), but context suggests "tota" (all)</note> my *Sacred Philosophy*, or *Meteorological History* contained in the entire volume, is against the doctrine of Aristotle. I therefore challenge this La Noue of ours into the wrestling-ground <note>or "arena"</note> of true Philosophy, and let him fight with all his strength (if he dares) for the honor of his Aristotle against my reasons, both those cited against Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and philosopher who also critiqued Fludd</note> upon the aforementioned text, and those expressed in that entire Meteorological volume of mine. But certainly (as I think) he will not dare; for I perceive him to have a sufficiently glib tongue, but a mind that is slow, stupid, and dull. Hence it is that his tongue is capable of judging far more things than his mind can conceive or understand; as if someone were to say: "whether it be true or false, I shall nevertheless judge in my usual confused manner." But if his glorious rashness invites him to this controversy, I hope I shall ensure that any truly literate person perceives his errors and the weakness of his mind. For in the defense of my God, and of the sacred scriptures, and of the truth itself, he will find me most ready and most armed against those Heathen opinions of both his and his Master’s. Wherefore (to conclude by turning that last clause of La Noue most rightly back upon himself), La Noue is as easily despised, and his insulting judgment rejected, as the insult is lightly and rashly thrown at Fludd by him—namely, by a man of such given ignorance and lack of skill.

## ON THE SOUL OF THE WORLD.
->Text 10. La Noue, in the same place.<-

In this matter, however, because he establishes that God is the soul of the world, he may seem to sin only in his manner of speaking; perhaps because it is outside the sense of that most famous question among Philosophers, if indeed he establishes <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ideatemos"; likely a corruption of "ideat," meaning to form a mental image or idea</note> so that he wishes God to be present to all things as the primary principle of life, motion, and being; but that he also attributes this to God: that He enters into composition with matter in the manner of a form which we call <term>informing</term> <note>original: "formæ... informantis"; in Scholastic philosophy, an "informing form" is the principle that gives a thing its specific essence and existence by uniting with matter</note>, and makes matter itself co-eternal with God; and further, that he seems to detract from the individual properties of created things, and especially from their power of acting and efficacy—this is to be condemned not only as rashness, because it fights with <term>Scholastic doctrine</term> <note>The traditional system of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities, based on Aristotelian logic</note>, but even as Impiety, insofar as it is injurious to the nature and divine goodness.

->To this, Fludd responds thus:<-

Here our Author begins to speak in his usual way, though little to the purpose; wherefore I shall approach him more closely. From these sayings of our Author, these three *Questions*, not at all irrelevant to our matter, can arise:
1. *Can God be called the soul of the world in that He is present to all things, as the principle of life, motion, and being?*
2. *Does God exist within matter as a universally informing form, and does He act essentially in the composition toward the existence of its life, motion, and essence?*
3. *Is the first matter of all things co-eternal with God?*

->To the first.<-

<margin>Wisdom 1 & etc.</margin>
We affirm, relying on many passages of the Sacred scriptures, that God fills all things. Therefore He is everywhere and in all things. We prove this thus: The Holy Spirit of discipline fills the world. Therefore He is present through His Spirit: and by consequence, God is essentially present everywhere through the Spirit of the world by giving life.
<margin>1 Tim. 6</margin>
But this Spirit, which is one in essence with God, gives life to all things <note>original: "viuificat omnia"</note>, as the Apostle witnesses: Therefore He animates all things, and consequently also the Spirit of the world itself, and its whole. For that which animates and gives life to a thing is the soul of that thing; since from it and in it is life.

->To the second, these things:<-

We likewise affirm, led by Holy testimony, that God is present in the composition <note>the physical makeup of a created thing</note>. Truly not as a part of the composite; but as the center of any thing, whose circumference is nowhere <note>A famous mystical definition of God, often attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>. And we prove this from the following passages. And first it will be proved that He is present in the composite.
<margin>Psalm 104:2</margin>
He is clothed with light as with a garment: Therefore He is within the worldly Spirit; and from unity He constitutes the number two <note>referring to the duality of Spirit and its "garment" of light</note>.
<margin>Psalm 18</margin>
He set His tabernacle in the Sun: Therefore He dwells in the temple of the world, which is animated by His presence.
<margin>Job 22</margin>
A thick cloud is His covering: Therefore He is clothed, and wishes to be covered, by a thick garment compacted from the worldly air.
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Let the earth be opened and bring forth a Savior: Therefore He is found in the composite, and comes forth or is produced divinely from the composite.
<margin>Wisdom 1</margin>
The Holy Spirit of discipline fills the world: Therefore, regarding the composition of the earth, He immerses Himself into the earth; though not as a part of the composite.
<margin>John 1</margin>
The Word is made flesh <note>original: "Verbum est incarnatum"</note>: Therefore He mixes Himself divinely with the fleshly composite.
You are the temple of the Holy Spirit: Therefore the Holy Spirit is within the human composition.
You are the members of Christ: Therefore it is not denied that Christ is in His composite members.
From these things, therefore, it clearly stands that the Divinity is within every composition of this world.
Next, that He is present as the most essential and supreme informing form, is clearly evident from these:
<margin>Acts 17</margin>
God, not being in need of anything, gives life and breath to all things: Therefore, neither Angelic power, nor Nature; nor the Sun; nor the heaven; nor human power; nor any other created thing does this; but only and uniquely God.
<margin>Acts 17; Isaiah 44:24</note>
For the text says: God, not being in need of anything, gives life, etc. So elsewhere the Prophet: *I am the Lord making all things, and none is with me.*
<margin>Wisdom 12:1; Acts 17</margin>
The incorruptible Spirit is in every thing: Therefore Divinity is essentially in every composition, though not inclusively <note>meaning God is present but not "contained" or limited by the object</note>. Whence the Apostle: *God the father of all, who is above all, through all, and in us all.*
<margin>Judith 6 <note>referring to Judith 16 in some versions</note></margin>
You sent forth your Spirit, and every creature was created: Therefore, since every Creation is an "informing," every creature is informed by the divine Spirit.
<margin>John 1</margin>
In the word was life: Therefore God is in all created things, insofar as where there is life, there is the word, since there is nothing in the word which is not the word: for nothing foreign exists in the Divine essence. Wherefore, if life is in the word, it follows that the word (insofar as it is the sole giver of life) is that which animates any thing. Whence not unwisely the Apostle said, as a little before, God gives life to all things.
<margin>Psalms</margin>
By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit from his mouth all their power: Therefore by the Spirit of God [they are] immediately ani-

# Fludd’s Response.

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
By You <note>God</note> any thing is animated, insofar as life is the most excellent virtue of all. *But all (says the text) Virtue is from the Spirit of the Lord.* For so the universal waters were animated, when the Spirit of the Lord was moved over them.
<margin>Genesis 2.</margin>
*God breathed into the face of Adam the breath of life:* Therefore, it was the Spirit of God that immediately animated Adam.
<margin>Psalm 36:9 <note>Original citation: Psalm 30:6</note>.</margin>
*The fountain of life is with God: And all the fountains of my life are from God:* (says the Prophet) Therefore, God is the only one who immediately animates and gives life.
<margin>Psalm 104:28; Acts 17.</margin>
*When God gives, the creatures are filled with good; when He takes away their spirit, they die:* Therefore, the virtue of life is in God and from God.
Finally: *In God we live, in God we move, and in God we are:* Therefore, we have life and motion immediately from God, as from Nature naturing <note><term>Natura naturans</term>: A philosophical term for God as the active, creative force within nature, as opposed to the created world itself.</note>, and the informing form <note><term>forma informante</term>: The active principle that gives a thing its specific essence and life.</note>. Nor does this speech of the Apostle sound or seem like anything else than that of the Evangelist: *In the Word was life, etc.*

Indeed, I can draw almost infinite other testimonies from the sacred fountain to corroborate and demonstrate these things. For the entire Harmony and consensus of the Scriptures seems to confirm this same point: namely, that any creature whatsoever is animated and quickened by the Divine Spirit alone, and not from elsewhere, according to that text previously alleged: *God, needing nothing, gives life and breath and all things.* Whence elsewhere the Apostle seems to conclude most exactly: that God works all things in all, and that from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things: and consequently the act of living. Nor is there anything now for La Noue to cavil about, along with the rest of his comrades of the same grain, that I translate the Scriptures ineptly and against their genuine and proper sense to establish my "ridiculous" dogmas; since it is evident that place opens place, and text opens text; indeed, truly Book opens Book, to the confirmation and opening of our meaning.

<margin>
Judith 16:14.
Isaiah 41.
Isaiah 45.
Isaiah 44.
</margin>
I conclude, therefore, that there is no rashness in Fludd to assert that God animates, quickens, and consequently informs all things. And He does this alone, without any subalternate efficient cause or agent: since God, according to the express words of the text, *needing nothing* (seeing that it is His alone to make all things and no one’s with Him) does this alone, and by Himself, without the help or assistance of any creature: namely, He gives *life and breath and all things:* and by consequence is the informing form, inasmuch as He alone is the redeemer of man and his former from the womb, etc. He alone, and no one with Him, who creates the heavens and forms the earth: He did not create it in vain, but formed it to be inhabited. But insofar as He gives life, and breath, and all things, He is said to animate, and is the very supreme soul of all, whether Nature not natured <note>uncreated nature</note>, or Nature naturing or animating. Moreover, as He is called the "Former," that is, the giver of forms, so He is also argued to be the supreme of forms: since that which makes a thing such, is itself more such.

But as far as Scholastic doctrine is concerned: what is that to me, if I find it repugnant to the sense of the Scriptures? For (to agree with the Apostle) if I heard even an Angel descending from heaven preaching a doctrine adverse to the Most Holy Page, I would reject his doctrine, relying on a constant faith. But La Noue says it is an act of impiety, and injurious to the Divine goodness, to maintain this dogma: namely, that the emanation of God is the simplest form and the most faithful of all essences, penetrating the composition, and animating and quickening it. I truly determine that he himself is rather an enemy of the Divine Majesty and a friend of Idolatry, while he does not fear to ascribe the most excellent work in Nature to creatures and not to the Creator with such rashness; against the express text of the Sacred monument: that God works all things in all. For if it is so, that God works all things in all, as it certainly is; why (I ask) is He not likewise the author and actor of life and animation and information, since creation and quickening are easily the chief of all operations? But is this not an abominable and detestable derogation from the Divine power and virtue, to attribute those things to creatures which are proper to the Creator alone and unique? May You (Just Reader) be an equitable Judge between me and La Noue in this matter! But because this question will be more fully discussed in the fourth member of this [work], where we shake off the third Impiety thrust upon me by Mersenne, we therefore refrain from more words here.

---

### -> To the Third [Point]. <-

That the first matter of all things was not at all created, we thus prove. Whatever is created is "inactuated" <note>brought from potentiality into actual existence</note>, because all creation is a leading of power and as it were "nothing" into act; but prime matter is not inactuated: therefore it is not created. The minor premise is proved thus: That which is already in potentiality alone toward act, is not inactuated; but prime matter is already in potentiality alone toward act: Therefore it is not at all inactuated. Furthermore, that it is in potentiality alone toward act is elicited from this: insofar as it lacks form: and by consequence it seems to be held for nothing, since it is reserved in the mere divine power, and is esteemed as such by the wise, no differently than the divine act is held for His lucid emanation, namely, by means of which, and by whose presence, all things are created out of nothing; that is, out of a non-existing act; but out of a certain formless matter. In the creation of the world, therefore, the potentiality of this formless matter was produced into act, and from prime matter—that is, a thing plainly potential and as it were nothing—it was produced into second matter or water, out of which the world was then immediately fashioned, according to this doctrine of the sacred page: *His almighty hand created the world out of formless matter.* Wherefore it is not ineptly held as the principle from which the world is fashioned, and in which God, by means of His Word, is said to have created heaven and earth; according to this sense of the Mosaic text: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth:* and again that of the Evangelist: *In the beginning was the Word.* For this word "beginning" seems to denote neither a beginning of time; nor of place; nor of order: since before the fabric of the world there was no time, seeing that it is distinguished by solar motion: For before creation all things were complicitly <note>enfolded</note> comprehended in eternity: wherefore time is excluded from that archetypal state; nor place; because no "located thing" was found before creation: nor order; insofar as all things existed as nothing but a rough and confused mass of darkness. It follows, therefore, that in the beginning, and from this formless principle, *through the Word,* which was in that dark beginning, and outside this principle insofar as it is in itself—seeing that it is by itself pure light, in which there are no darknesses at all—this world was first of all created and formed in this manner: After this formless matter was informed, illuminated, and created by the presence of the lucid rays of the holy emanation, it was changed (as was said) into second matter or the species of waters, from which thereafter by dividing water from waters, by the spagyric <note><term>spagyrica</term>: Alchemical; specifically the power of separating the pure from the impure or dividing elements.</note> virtue of the Word or the Spirit, heaven and earth were produced. Hence this text: *He revealed the foundations out of the darkness, and brought back the deadly shadow into light, God stretched out the North over the empty space, and hung the earth upon nothing.* That is, out of nothing or formless matter (according to the aforementioned saying of the wise man) or a thing existing in the divine potentiality alone, or the void and empty, by the presence of His Spirit or Word He effected, or led into act, the world, divided into heaven and earth. For once the Word was made and the Spirit appeared; [all things were] animated, informed, and [brought] to life...
<margin>
Wisdom 11:17.
John 1.
Job 12:22.
</margin>

# To the Judgment of Lanouius, Member II. Part II.

...was adorned with light, called formless matter or the deadly shadow, and migrated into the appearance of waters. And then the Spirit of the Lord was said to be carried over the waters, or to brood upon the Universal waters, from which afterwards, by the power of the Word, the heaven and earth were made; these are, to this very day, animated and sustained by the Word, and remain in the Word. Which the Apostle also proves with these more expressive, though fewer, words:
<margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin>
For it escapes them (he says) that the heavens were of old, and the earth consisting out of water and through water, by the word of God, etc. <note>Original Latin: *Latei eos... quod coeli erant prius & terra de Aqua & per aquam, conſiſtente verbo Dei.*</note> Nor is it enough for Lanouius and his associates to assert that I, in this place, translate the Scriptures partly (as he himself says) ineptly and against the genuine and proper sense, and partly impiously to establish my "ridiculous dogmas." Rather, in the usual manner of true Philosophers, I would wish they did not merely affirm this, but demonstrate with arguments and firm reasons another sense of the previously cited Scripture passages—one more genuine and proper than my own—so that all these texts might equally, elegantly, and aptly cohere and agree as one. Then, indeed, I shall either yield the floor to them and acknowledge my error, or, supported by better reasoning, I shall prove the contrary. Otherwise, I boldly pronounce such naked assertions of theirs to be "insane voices" (to use Lanouius's own words) and "sounds without mind." Finally, all those most skilled in the Mysteries of Nature seem to support our opinion not a little, for they hold the view that prime matter <note><term>materia prima</term>: The fundamental, formless substance from which all physical things are created.</note> is as if nothing, and is reserved within the divine power beyond human grasp—as is sufficiently explained in many places in my works, and especially in my *Cabbala*. From what has been said, therefore, it is clear that the world was created out of some pre-existing matter, and therefore the prime matter of all things was itself not created.

## Text 11. Lanouius in the same place.

And indeed, that which he himself foresees in his own doctrine to be a consequence—that God must be called the author of sin—carries no small force and weight in proving that impiety.

->Fludd.<-

My adversary now compels me, rightly and to the point, to open my mind on this doubt: namely, whether God is the author of sin or not. I say, therefore, that I do not oppose the Church Militant on earth in this question, and consequently I affirm with the Church and the Scholastic theologians that, although God is the author of life and motion in all things, yet that act rooted in God is directed and working only toward the function of life or the observation of the law, and not toward evil or sin. For that act or motion depends not on God (who is direct and just), but on the obliquity <note>Crookedness or deviation from a straight line.</note> of the creature, which, because of the corruption of its nature, turns that divine act—as if by reflection or reverberation—into evil, namely toward the violation of the law or sin. Thus we see a ball struck against a wall rebound against the motion of the one who threw it (which was direct), and it is reverberated by a certain rebellious resistance. This is not said to come from the thrower, but from the hard, resisting wall. Up to this point we agree with the theologians, and yet a non-negligible doubt enters my mind regarding several passages of the sacred text. If Lanouius and his companions can truly—and not just in appearance—resolve this and completely remove it from my breast, I shall indeed owe him great thanks.

For at first glance it will seem, if those testimonies of the Divine page which I have mentioned are diligently weighed, that the famous distinction of the Scholars—*the evil of punishment and the evil of fault* <note><term>malum poenae & malum culpae</term>: A traditional theological distinction between suffering (punishment for sin) and the moral act of sinning itself.</note>—is quite frivolous and empty. The sacred testimonies or authorities are of this kind:

<margin>Isaiah 54:16</margin>
> *Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy.*

If you reply that God created this "waster" or prince of darkness for the punishment of the impious, and consequently to produce the "evil of punishment" and not "of fault," certainly that assertion will not satisfy the curiosity of some. For they can press the point in this manner: Is God not likewise the cause of the "evil of fault," since He produced into the world the author of sin and fault, namely the prince of darkness? But you will say that God did not create the Devil to perform the duty of evil. As if, indeed, all future things were not reserved in the ark of His foreknowledge and providence, or as if any of the creature's actions could be hidden from Him! Hence, elsewhere it is said more expressly:

> *I am the Lord, and there is none else besides me, forming the light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil. I the Lord doing all these things.* <note>Original: Isaiah 45:7</note>

And again:

> *All things were known to God before they were created, and after they were finished He beholds all things.*

Therefore, it seems that God created His privative <note>Acting by absence or negation, like darkness being the absence of light.</note> minister to sow unbelief through the world, which was the fountain and origin of sin. And although the cause was just and the best for God, yet to us, and regarding us mortals who suffer, the effect of the same seemed evil. For from the transgression of the law, sin arose, being the child of disobedience. However, the Apostle explains the cause of why God did this—namely, that He introduced incredulity into the world—in these few words:

<margin>Romans 11:32</margin>
> *God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that He might have mercy upon all.*

For without the dominion of unbelief, faith would be established in the world forever; and if faith were dominant on earth, what need, I ask, would there be for mercy? Did not also the just man Job suffer the torments of that privative destroyer? And that was not for the cause of any fault, but by God's command, for the sake of testing alone. Were not also many thousands of men punished with death for the sin of one man, namely David, though they had not shared in the fault of their King? And yet, according to this word of the Prophet:
<margin>Daniel 4:32</margin>
> *Who shall ask Him, why hast Thou done this?*

Therefore, when Job acknowledged that God had struck him without any fault—because he was a just man and after God's own heart—he burst out into these words, compelled by a zeal for piety:
<margin>Job 34:10</margin>
> *And yet (he says) far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.*

Furthermore, Good and Evil, Life and Death, Poverty and Riches are from God. But if Lanouius says that "evil" here is understood as the "evil of punishment," then I would have him observe these words:
<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:14</margin>
> *Consider the works of God, and that no man can correct him whom He hath despised. In the good day enjoy good things, and beware of the evil day; for as He made the one, so He made the other, so that man should not find any just complaint against Him.*

From which it is clear that God has ordained days, both favorable and unfavorable, indifferently for any man.

> *With Him is strength and power, His is the one who errs and the one who leads into error. Who makes counselors go in dē—* <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

# Fludd’s Response.

...into madness, and makes the judges foolish; He overthrows the most powerful, increases nations and destroys them; He takes away the heart of the leaders of the earth, making them wander like drunkards and grope in the dark for lack of light, etc. <note>original: "in dementiam, & Iudices stultos reddit... palpents in tenebris deficiente luce." This is a paraphrase of Job 12:17-25.</note>

But my opponent will always reply that such things are brought upon men because of their sins and impieties. But what (I ask) will he say about Pharaoh, whose heart Jehovah confessed He had hardened so that he would become disobedient and obstinate? What do the Apostles say to this?

Even when Rebecca’s children were not yet born, and had done nothing either good or evil, it was said to her—not because of works, but because of Him who calls: *The elder shall serve the younger;* <note>original: "Maior seruiet Minori."</note> according to that saying: *Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.* What then shall we say? *Is there injustice with God? Far from it!* For He said to Moses: *I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, etc.* For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: *For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. O man! Who are you to answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, why have you made me thus? etc.*

By these words, he seems to expressly argue that God Himself is the cause of the hardening of the heart, and consequently the author and occasion of sin, or the "evil of fault." Hence the Prophet says elsewhere:

<margin>Isaiah 63:17</margin>
> *Why have you made us wander, O Lord, from your ways? You have hardened our heart so that we would not fear you.* <note>Fludd cites this as "Ef. 63. 10." but the text matches Isaiah 63:17.</note>

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
> And again elsewhere: *Who has believed our report? Therefore they could not believe, because God blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.* <note>Isaiah 6:10, quoted in John 12:39-40.</note>

<margin>Romans 11:32</margin>
> Furthermore, the Lord’s Prayer says: *lead us not into temptation.* In short: *God has concluded all (as was previously alleged from the Apostle) in unbelief, that He might have mercy on all.*

But lest anyone should reply—if this is the case—what should be thought of those other passages of Scripture which seem directly to oppose this opinion? The Apostle, expecting such a reply from worldly men, seems to refute and remove it by this verse immediately following:

<margin>Romans 11</margin>
> *O the depth of the riches of the Wisdom and Knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, that it should be repaid? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things.*

By these words he seems to argue that whatever is done even by Satan, as a minister of God, is effected from God Himself, through God, and in God. For Satan himself attributed his every deed to God, saying: *Stretch out your hand against Job, and he will curse you.* By this speech he acknowledges that he himself is nothing but the hand or the instrument <term>organum</term> in which God moves to execute His will.

It can therefore be concluded from these points that all things are to be attributed to God, since He is the one acting in all things indivisibly. It should not be seen as a grave impiety for anyone to ascribe all things to God, as much as it is to falsely attribute to creatures those things which radically belong to God alone. Among these is the belief that there is some peculiar act in the Devil that does not originate from God, and consequently exists immediately through Him, since the essential act of God is of itself without division in every thing. For by this reasoning, if the act of the Devil were of itself and originally in the Devil and alienated from God insofar as it is evil, we would be making the Devil's act co-eternal with God. This is because if it did not draw its origin from God, it would necessarily have to be a principle co-eternal with God, contrary to the good act of God. It would be a far greater impiety for anyone to assert this than for Fludd to affirm that Prime Matter is not a created thing.

---

Nevertheless, as I have said, I do not write these things as positive doctrine; rather, I raise them as an argument for the sake of debating this point proposed to me by Lanouius. For he says that I have translated the Scriptures partly ineptly and partly impiously, against their genuine and proper sense, to establish my "ridiculous and erroneous dogmas." I desire, therefore, that he bring the texts of Scripture we have cited here back to their more genuine and proper sense, so that I may finally discern his skill in the exposition of Scripture. For whatever I have produced in this place, I have done solely for the sake of disputing and discussing this question with Lanouius. As for me, I know that all sin and evil do not proceed directly from God, but from the crookedness <note>original: "obliquitate"</note> of the creature. This happens in no other way than in a <term>bombarda</term> <note>An early type of cannon or mortar.</note> or engine of war loaded with an iron ball. The action of the fire was not intended to demolish a wall or a house; rather, its intent was that the rebellious and resisting weight of iron, which denied the ignited fire a path to the open air, should be expelled from the cannon so the flame might be granted greater liberty. Therefore, the destruction of the wall or house is not to be attributed to the ignited powder—which, without the resisting ball, would effect no harm—but to that rebellious and hard ball which, being ejected by the fire, is the cause of ruin or evil by its own blow and action.

->**Text 12, Lanouius, ibid.**<-

He speaks no more religiously regarding the Angels, whom he interprets as emanations and virtues of God, either denying they are separate intellectual substances and signifying that God works through them in various ways, etc., or he trifles and prepares to deceive with a novelty of speech.

->**Fludd.**<-

I did not say all Angels were emanations of God, but only that Great Angel in whom is all angelic power and virtue. By his rays and outflow, all subordinate Angels, created out of "otherness," are animated and shaped into various properties. The passages from Holy Scripture confirming this very thing are as follows:

<margin>Wisdom 7</margin>
> *The Spirit of Wisdom is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation or flow of the glory of the Almighty, and a spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the brightness or splendor of eternal light, etc.*

Therefore, the Holy Spirit of discipline is an emanation. Furthermore, that this Spirit is called a "creature" in respect to its emanation or flow into created matter, you have here:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1</margin>
> *God created Wisdom in the Holy Spirit: And again: Wisdom was created before all things.*

Moreover, that this Spirit was that Great Angel who went before the Israelites in the desert, we are taught by these words:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 3</margin>
<margin>Wisdom 10:17</margin>
> *My throne is in a pillar of cloud, says Wisdom. And elsewhere: Wisdom was a covering for them by day, and a starry light by night.*

<margin>Exodus 23:20</margin>
Now, Exodus testifies in many places that this same office was sometimes attributed to Jehovah and sometimes to the Angel. Nor is it a wonder, because in that very Great Angel was the name of Jehovah; that is, Jehovah Himself, essentially and presidentially. For the text says: *do not provoke him, for my name is in him.* Therefore it is evident that this principal Angelic creature is nothing other than the Divine nature itself, clothed in a luminous spirit as if in a garment. Whence, just as He who is clothed is called "Identity," so the garment...

# Regarding the Judgment of Lanovius, Member II. Part II.

<margin>Book *On the Divine Names*, chapter 6.</margin>
...then that worldly or Spiritual [substance] which is put on, together with that Divinity which puts it on, is called by the more learned—and not ineptly—"Otherness," or that which consists of two. For this reason <margin>Dionysius, *On the Divine Names*, ch. 6.</margin> St. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century Christian theologian and Neoplatonist.</note> calls the Angels **Algamatha**, which is to say, the purest mirrors looking upon the splendor of divine light. An Angel, he says, is the image of God, the revelation of hidden light, a pure and most lucid mirror without blemish. How (I ask) does this description of an Angel differ from the one Solomon attributed to that greatest and chief Angel—namely, the Spirit of Wisdom? **It is** (he says) **a certain emanation of the brightness of the Almighty, and the radiance of eternal light, and a mirror without blemish of the majesty of God and the image of his goodness**, etc. <margin>Wisdom 7.</margin> From which it is evident that all the lower or subordinate Angels, insofar as they have their formal essence from that highest Spirit, are likewise called (along with their source) "most polished mirrors," like the purest and clearest spirits who receive the ray of the brightness of divine light just like mirrors receive the likeness or image of a living thing. By means of this ray they are informed and put on the nature of Divinity. Therefore, an Angel is called the "image of God" by Dionysius, just as Solomon called the Spirit of Wisdom the "image of the goodness of God": like a mirror in which the Divine glory and power are perceived. By these things it is clearly indicated that the most clear worldly Spirit—which is created by the presence of divine light and produced from divine power into action—becomes the external consistency of the Angelic nature, by reason of which it is called a "creature." Indeed, the holy emanation itself, immersing itself into the worldly Spirit, is called an "Angelic Creature" by the wise man. I say "Angelic" <note>original: "Angelica," derived from the Greek *angelos*, meaning messenger.</note> insofar as it is sent out from eternity like a messenger for the creation of the world. Its internal part, however, is the very act and life infused from the fountain of eternity.

We conclude, therefore, that angels are called "separate substances" in respect to their external part; but in respect to their internal part and the divinity that dwells within them, they are not so at all. For that which is an emanation from the fountain of eternity cannot be divided or separated from its source, since the divine essence is inseparable and indivisible. For although it seems to be distinguished into persons by reason of its attributes and properties, it is nevertheless only one God and a single divine essence. Through this truth, all creatures, and especially Angels and men, have union with God.

### Text 13. Lanovius, in the same place.

> I add nothing of those things which he brings forth from the Cabbala <note>The Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism often adapted by Renaissance Christian scholars like Fludd.</note> concerning the names of Angels, their distinctions, properties, ministries, etc., since those were rejected long ago by the judgment of the Church.

->To whom I respond.<-

Abbot Trithemius, the monk Archangelus [of Borgonovo], and Reuchlin—most expert Cabbalists, one of whom dedicated his books to the Emperor Maximilian, another to Pope Leo—indeed, many other most learned men have made exact and clear mention of the names and ministries of Angels in their volumes. Yet, their books were not condemned by those Christian princes or by the Pope himself; rather, they are considered so innocent and free from evil by profound and skilled philosophers that they have liberty everywhere throughout Europe even to this day. As for the condemnation by the Roman Church, it is not to be cared for so much, since it is false and unjust, its judgment being obscured by the voice of ignorance. And thus it happened to the Church what is commonly said of humans: namely, *to err*. To condemn a cause simply because it is unknown to the judges is a species of rash madness. For without doubt, there are more things hidden from the world than are open to it. But because the truth is hidden, is it therefore right that it should be condemned and sent into eternal exile from the minds of mortals before it is revealed to the profane common people or understood by worldly men? Or because the external and political Church does not understand the mysteries of that mystic and internal Church—no matter how excellent and precious they are, dealing as they do with the secrets of the kingdom of God and mystic Wisdom—must they therefore be rejected and condemned by Christians? Did not Christ and his Apostles place a difference between the sons of God and those of the world? Between the Wisdom of God and that of men? Did he not say in open and express words with what malice the sons of God would be harassed by the impious worldly ones, even at the very altars? But leaving these things aside, what will this unjust Judge of ours say, who thinks he can triumphantly kill with a single word, accompanied by no reason or sufficient argument? What, I say, will he say to the Good Emperor Maximilian—to that Roman Monarch, I mean? Does he believe that if the Emperor had not understood Trithemius’s sincerity in his art and the integrity of the art itself, and had not known the man’s doctrine, religion, and good life—being a man of such eminence in the affairs of the political Church—that he would have allowed those books to see the light under his Name and Patronage if the dogma had been as damnable as Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a French polymath and priest who was a fierce critic of Fludd.</note> and Lanovius try to make it? But perhaps he will say that Maximilian was what they call a "secular" man, and therefore did not look upon matters pertaining to the Church with such diligence. So be it. But what will he say to Pope Leo, under whose protection and presidency (or that of others) that Cabbalistic work, containing so many names of Angels, has seen the light for so long? Certainly Lanovius seems in this text of his to accuse Maximilian of ignorance and Leo of negligence, or rather partiality—and even to ascribe impiety to both of them, who were willing not only to tolerate but even to approve with unanimous consent and the invincible edict or decree of the Church books so impious, or filled (as Mersenne says) with so many impieties. From these things, therefore, it is right to conclude that Lanovius thinks himself far more elevated in mind and deeper in knowledge than these princes. But it is not the knowledge itself (which in itself is pure and sincere) that is to be condemned, but the "spurious artist" (such as Lanovius and Mersenne are) who practices that knowledge in a spurious and adulterous way. Nor is the Cabbalistic discourse on the mysteries of Angels to be rejected, but rather those who receive that discourse poorly.

### Text 14. Lanovius, in the same place.

> Most of all he deserves censure for what he invents about the triple demon, divided threefold for every man; however, since this collapses at its foundation, it would be superfluous to push it further.

->To him I say.<-

Does Fludd deserve censure most of all because he brought the truth to light? For if man (insofar as he is composed of all the frameworks of the world, is called a <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," a central concept in Fludd's philosophy where the human body reflects the structure of the entire universe.</note>) participates in the intellectual portion of the empyrean heaven—for that heaven is called "intellectual and angelic" by the Fathers of the Church—by means of which he understands and produces rational effects; and in the ethereal or vital portion, from which he draws the influences of life; and finally in that Elementary portion, by which he vegetates, grows, and enjoys the powers of natural faculties: if, I say, these three distinct actions or virtues in one man...

# Fludd’s Response

...specific virtues are found—as they certainly are in him—and act from their own root, producing various effects in a single man, then we must believe that these functions or acts proceed radically either from God or from elsewhere. If from God (namely from whom, and in whom, and through whom all things exist, as the Apostle <note>original: "teste Apostolo"; a reference to St. Paul, likely Romans 11:36.</note> testifies), then God effects these things in both the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the universe as a whole.</term> and the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "little world," referring to the individual human being as a reflection of the universe.</term> by means of his Angelic ministers, for through them he works all things in heaven and on earth in Jesus Christ. Indeed, he is accustomed to carry out his word <margin>Ps. 103:20.</margin> and all his pleasures through them, according to the words of the Psalmist: *Bless the Lord, you his angels, you mighty ones who do his bidding, obedient to his spoken word; his ministers who do his will,* etc. Do we not also read, according to the doctrine of the Church Fathers, that there are other Angels who stand before the face of God in the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure light or fire.</note>, who receive the luminous influences from God and communicate them to the Angels of the lower orders? Do we not find in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> that seven Angels were assigned to the seven stars? And also that the government of the four winds was committed to four Angels by God, and that the devil has dominion in the air, to whom many legions are subjected? This is therefore clear evidence that every region of the world has Angelic or organic Agents of the first order, which differ greatly from one another in their condition. Why should there not also be various agents within man himself, since he is composed of these same particles of the world? 

Indeed, we prove this same thing more easily through common experience: it cannot escape anyone possessed of reason that at everyone's birth there is present a good and rational Spirit, and likewise an evil and natural or beastly one, since we see the same man at one time prone to contemplating good things, and at another to devising and performing evil. Are these two extremes alone in him, with no middle ground intervening? For there is a Spirit in which the virtue of free will swims; and there is a Spirit which urges and entices this middle Spirit toward evil, and on the opposite side, another which leads it toward good. Experience, I say, testifies to this. But why do we sing to the deaf? For we have expressed this with a broad thread of discourse, both in my *Mystical Anatomy* and in the treatise against Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and theologian who was one of Fludd’s primary intellectual rivals.</note>. Against this, our good corrector—or rather, trifler—can produce not even a single iota of reasonable argument, except to say that the foundation of the thing itself collapses. Therefore, since he can refute nothing in that Subject, he pretends that pushing it over is superfluous. Thus, in the preceding text, he has a similar escape: "I add nothing regarding these things," he says, "since they were rejected long ago by the zeal of the Church," etc. Thus, whenever he has nothing to answer, he seeks miserable refuges and hiding places; as he says in Text 1, "The entire system of Fludd's Physiology, besides being inconsistent, totters from its foundation." And in Text 2 he says, "He translates the Scriptures against their true and proper sense," etc. And in Text 3 he says, "This impiety is condemned by the censure of the Sorbonne," etc. Therefore you see, (*Candid Reader*), how sterile and how wretched are the escapes of this man who wishes to appear so great a personage and Judge. As for the claim he uses in this last text—that my opinion collapses from its foundation—I am utterly ignorant of it; nor do I sufficiently perceive what this haughty Judge, sitting on his terrifying tribunal, is saying or what he wishes to be understood: and he himself, unless I am mistaken, understands it less than I do.

## On the Book Titled *The Highest Good*.

### Text 15. Lanovius in the same place.

The book titled *The Highest Good* <note>original: "Summum Bonum." A text defending the Rosicrucians, published under the name Joachim Frizius, but widely attributed to Fludd.</note> lies about its author: it is certain from the style that it is not Joachim Frizius, but Robert Fludd, who stitched on this addition, and other signs are scattered throughout that prove it.

### Fludd.

Who reported this to him? Truly, I see that he has stolen not only this, but also the entire Subject of his Judiciary Letter from the labor of Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a philosopher and scientist who critiqued Fludd's work.</note>. Therefore, I shall give an account of that matter to Gassendi in his own place, and not to this man. But here, in passing, I would have the Reader warned that the invention of these three Judges in refuting my works is so sterile that they are even forced to take or feign the writings of others as mine, so that they might find a wider field to oppose. For they can bring nothing of weight against my genuine and proper works.

### Text 16. Lanovius ibid.

But to begin with the Title, Impiety shines forth in it, because he makes the "Highest Good" <note>original: "Summum Bonum"</note> the object of Cabbala <term>Cabbala: A form of Jewish mysticism that Fludd and other "Christian Cabbalists" integrated into their philosophy.</term>, Alchemy, and the Brothers of the Rosy Cross. But if he understands it as the ultimate end which they propose for themselves in common with others (if that is indeed the case), he childishly catches at an ambiguity outside the purpose.

### Fludd.

Although I have asserted elsewhere that this is not my work but that of an intimate friend, nevertheless, I shall respond to all the objections of Lanovius, the "Theologian-Soldier" who attacks me with the sword of malevolence (objections which are, quite rightly, frivolous). To the matter, then. It is clearer than light how prone this author is to rash judgment before the subject to be judged is rightly understood by him. "Impiety," he says, "shines forth in me, because I make the 'Highest Good' the object of Cabbala, Alchemy, and the Brothers of the Rosy Cross." But he speaks rashly, since he still seems to doubt the subject. For he says: "If he understands it as the ultimate end, etc." Thus, since this is so, his "Impiety" does not shine so brightly. But this is his habit: even though he himself does not know what I understand, he nonetheless adjudges a great Impiety to me. Regarding that Highest Good of Theologians, Cabbalists, Philosophers, Magi, and true Alchemists—sought so much by the Wise as the palm of eternal Wisdom and affected by all the pious with a Tantalean thirst <note>A reference to the myth of Tantalus, signifying an unquenchable longing for something just out of reach.</note>—I say that in effect it is one and the same thing. However, it is held by Philosophers to be the true Wisdom which they hunt; by Theologians to be the Divine Essence and the Word of the Almighty, in whose light they themselves desire to walk and to teach others; by Cabbalists to be the highest principle of a single nature in a double appearance: namely, the dark and the lucid Aleph <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In this context, it represents the primal unity of God.</note>; by Magi, to be the highest mystery of Nature’s miracles; and by true Chemists <note>i.e., Alchemists.</note>, to be the cornerstone. And in this it is declared that there is nothing in the world but one and the same Truth, at whose goal men aim by various arts and differing sciences. Therefore, every various art has obtained a different name for the thing they seek with such great effort, taken from the truth of the found thing's appearance or property; although the thing is in reality nothing but one. Thus, by Theologians it is recognized as the divine light; by Cabbalists, as Angelic Virtue; by Magi and Philosophers, as essential Wisdom; by pious Alchemists, as the gold to be bought from Christ <note>A reference to Revelation 3:18: "I counsel you to buy from me gold refined in the fire."</note>. ### To the Judgment of Lanovius, Member II. Part II.
