Consider also: in the acquisition of common gold, are not various techniques usually employed? For whenever the fissure of a rock is reached, penetrating the stone with iron strength, one arrives at a pure vein of gold: the granules of gold are usually purified not by washing away the superfluous or sandy material, but sometimes by the art of smelting and the intensity of fire, the pure gold is separated from heterogeneous things. It also happens not infrequently that the composite mass is tested by *aqua regia* <term>Aqua Regia: "Royal water," a highly corrosive mixture of acids used by alchemists to dissolve and test the purity of gold.</term>, so that the true may be discerned from the false; and yet there is but a single thing for the sake of which all this is done, namely, common gold. In a like manner and reasoning, these and other various formulas of inquiry correspond to one another: of which the first is **Theology**, which penetrates the center of the abyss with the sharpness of the mind, so that in the midst of darkness it may see and salute the Highest Good of all things, and then afterward publish its profound mystery to the world, and warn worldly men by preaching, so that they may walk in the light of this truth alone. The second is **Philosophy** and **Magic**, which strives to wash through the obscure veil of truth with the waves of truth, and to reserve the pure kernel spiritually for itself. The third is **Alchemy**, which, by the fervent heat of the fire of divine genius, distinguishes, separates, and collects the essential and central from the husk or superficial, and discerns the truth from the fiction. Finally, the fourth is **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: A tradition of Jewish mysticism that Fludd and other "Christian Kabbalists" adapted to explore the hidden meanings of Scripture and the nature of God.</term>, which reserves the extracted kernel for itself and hides it with obscure veils, lest the secret of God be made open or uncovered to the common people. Wherefore, as we see that *aqua regia* (as the *Chemists* <note>original: "Chymistæ"; here referring to alchemists.</note> call it) certainly separates gold from other metals, yet leaves that gold at the bottom of the vial stained with blackness and obscure; so indeed the gold of God is revealed to the *Kabbalists* by sharp inquiry; yet they make it appear dark to the common people, so that they may see and not understand. Do we not likewise see the same house constructed either from well-fitted wood alone, which work belongs to the carpenter; or from stones alone proportioned by the stonemason's art; or from bricks formed from clay and hardened to firmness by the power of fire? From which it is clear that the same effect can be produced by different arts. Why, likewise, should we not arrive at the fulfillment of that unique Highest Good by various ways or arts?

We conclude, therefore, that this demonstrates extreme ignorance in *Lanovius*, when he affirms that there is Impiety either in *Fludd* or in *Joachim Frizius* <note>Joachim Frizius is often considered a pseudonym for Fludd himself or a close associate.</note>, if they asserted that the end of acquiring truth is the same for *Magic*, *Kabbalah*, and *Alchemy* as it is for *Theology*: even though the method and formula of inquiring and acquiring it may differ.

->Text. 17. Lanovius, ibid.<-

The experts will judge concerning Alchemy: there is no one who does not detect empty boasting.

->Fludd.<-

I see he understands Alchemy as adulterated or spurious: for he is utterly ignorant of what the true art is. But more on these things at length below.

->Text. 18. Lanovius, ibid.<-

In Kabbalah he has betrayed his vanity (a common evil) and his ignorance: nor is it possible that anyone who stumbles and hallucinates as shamefully as *Fludd* does could be at all skilled in Hebrew.

->My response to this.<-

Where (in the name of God) have I betrayed my ignorance in Kabbalah? And furthermore, how sharp is his own genius, that he can discern my lack of skill in the elements of the Hebrew language even beyond the inner sanctuaries of truth? But come, *Lanovius*, and listen! Are you yourself well-acquainted with the essential and formal Kabbalistic characters, you who so lightly object to the ignorance of others in superficial matters? Certainly: from your writings it can be perceived more clearly than light that you and your companions have never tasted even the slightest bit of those holy or Hebrew letters. Truly, I will test in a few words the depth of *Lanovius* in the Kabbalistic art; indeed, I shall reveal who is truly in the Kabbalistic art?

*Lanovius* himself says near the end of his judicial Epistle: "As for what you ask regarding Kabbalah, it requires a more diligent inquiry than I can promise through today’s occupations. To speak briefly, I anticipate that nothing can be hoped to be added to the sciences from it, since it languishes miserably around the details, and both those parts concerning *Marcauah* <term>Marcauah (Merkavah): "The Chariot," a branch of Kabbalah focusing on the mystical vision of God's chariot-throne in the Book of Ezekiel.</term> and *Berefcith* <term>Berefcith (Bereshit): "In the Beginning," the branch of Kabbalah dealing with the mysteries of Creation.</term> are defiled by many fables, and not a little deformed by the dreams of idle men: so that if anything illustrious or solid could be secreted from them, it could by no means be compared to those things which our *Theologians* and *Philosophers* teach on the same matter."

<margin>My response to this.</margin> In this context of speech two things can be discerned: namely, the lack of skill of both *Lanovius* and *Mersenne* <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath and priest who was a fierce critic of Fludd’s Hermetic philosophy.</note> in the Kabbalistic art, and nonetheless their supreme boasting. For *Mersenne* says these things in *column 281 of his Volume on Genesis*: "If anyone is wise, I advise him not to spend good hours in the reading of the Kabbalists, unless he wishes to lose them; I speak from experience, for if it happens that any good is joined with their trifles and fables, we will have it deduced more clearly, briefly, and subtly in Philosophy and Theology," etc. These are the words of *Mersenne*: In which he has not obscurely confessed his own ignorance in the Kabbalistic art; and nonetheless, by his rash and unjust judgment, he proceeds to invade and condemn my art, however unknown it is to him. But who can enter or penetrate the museum or storehouse of nature without his own genuine key? We know the wolf by his hide, and knowledge by words. But why (I pray) does he attempt to deter everyone from Kabbalistic science, or from the inquiry into the Kabbalistic art? Is it because he himself (according to his own confession) is unskilled in that art? For these are his words: "I speak from experience," etc. As if it were impossible for the literate to progress beyond the sharpness of *Mersenne's* genius: Here he humbly seeks and asks *Lanovius* to instruct him further in Kabbalah. The words are clear: "Regarding Kabbalah," he says, "what you ask," etc. And so, like the blind leading the blind, this man, powerless in Kabbalah, seeks inconsiderately. This notwithstanding, he did not blush to correct, indeed even to condemn, the Kabbalah of *Giorgio Veneto* <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Franciscan friar and author of *De Harmonia Mundi*, a key text for Christian Kabbalists.</note> and *Fludd*—he who, having wiped away all shame, was not afraid to publicly proclaim his own ignorance in that art.

But now, we shall proceed to the investigation of his Master's strength in the matter of Kabbalah. The aforementioned text, therefore, also denotes the ignorance of *Mersenne's* Doctor or Master in Kabbalah. For first he says: "As for what you ask regarding Kabbalah, it requires a more diligent inquiry than through today’s oc—"

...specific virtues are found, as they certainly are in him, and act from their own root, producing diverse effects in one man, then we must believe that these functions or acts proceed fundamentally either from God or from elsewhere. Therefore, since he can find nothing to converge in that Subject, he pretends it is superfluous to pursue it. water, some through mountains and precipices, others through more level ground, and yet the city toward which they tend is one and the same. Consider this: in the acquisition of common gold, are not various techniques usually employed? For sometimes, by the iron strength of a tool penetrating a fissure in the crag, one reaches a pure vein of gold; at other times, by washing away superfluous or sandy material, the grains of gold are purified; sometimes by the art of smelting and the intensity of fire, pure gold is separated from foreign substances; it also happens not infrequently that a composite mass is tested by **strong waters** <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; likely referring to nitric acid or "Aqua Fortis," used to separate gold from silver.</note> so that the true may be discerned from the false. And yet, there is but a single thing for whose sake all this is done: namely, common gold. In a similar way and for the same reason, these various methods of inquiry—and others of this kind—correspond to a single end.

The first of these is **Theology**, which penetrates the center of the abyss with the sharp edge of the mind, so that in the midst of darkness it may see and greet the **Highest Good of all things** <note>original: "Summum omnium rerum Bonum," Fludd's term for God as the ultimate goal of all study.</note>, and then afterwards publish its profound mystery to the world, warning worldly men through preaching to walk in the light of this truth. The second is **Philosophy and Magic**, which strives to wash away the dark veil of truth with the waves of reality and reserve the pure spiritual kernel for itself. The third is **Alchemy**, which, by the fervent heat of the fire of divine genius, distinguishes, separates, and collects the essential and central from the husk or the superficial, discerning truth from fiction. The fourth, finally, is **Kabbalah**, which reserves the extracted kernel for itself and hides it behind obscure veils, lest the secret of God be opened or uncovered to the common people.

Therefore, as we see that **Royal Water** <term>Aqua Regia: A mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, so named because it can dissolve "noble" metals like gold.</term> (as the Chemists call it) certainly separates gold from other metals, yet leaves that gold at the bottom of the flask stained with blackness and obscured; so indeed the Gold of God is revealed to the Kabbalists by sharp inquiry, yet they make it appear dark to the common people, so that *they may see and not understand.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 6:9 or Matthew 13:13.</note> Do we not likewise see the same house constructed either from well-fitted wood alone (which is the work of a carpenter), or from stones proportioned by the mason's art, or from bricks formed of clay and baked to firmness by the power of fire? From these examples it is clear that the same effect can be produced by different arts. Why, likewise, should we not reach the fulfillment of that single Highest Good by various ways or arts?

We conclude, therefore, that this demonstrates extreme ignorance in Lanovius when he affirms that there is Impiety either in Fludd or in Joachim Frizius if they assert that the end of acquiring truth is the same for Magic, Kabbalah, and Alchemy as it is for Theology—even though the method and formula of inquiring and acquiring it may differ.

### Text 17. Lanovius, in the same place.

> Those skilled in Alchemy will judge: there is no one who does not detect empty boasting.

->Fludd.<-

I see he understands Alchemy to be adulterous or spurious; for he is utterly ignorant of what the true art is. But more on these things at greater length below.

### Text 18. Lanovius, in the same place.

> In Kabbalah he has betrayed his vanity (a common evil) and his ignorance; nor is it possible for one to be truly skilled in Hebrew who blunders and hallucinates as shamefully as Fludd does.

->To this I reply.<-

Where (in the name of God) have I betrayed my ignorance in Kabbalah? And how sharp an intellect must he have himself, to be able to discern my lack of skill in the elements of the Hebrew language even beyond the inner chambers of truth? But come, Lanovius, and listen! Are you yourself acquainted with the essential and formal characters of the Kabbalists, you who so lightly charge others with ignorance in superficial matters? Certainly, it can be perceived more clearly than light from your writings that you and your associates have never tasted even a tiny bit of those true, holy, or Hebrew letters. Truly, I will test the depth of Lanovius in the Kabbalistic art in a few words—nay, I shall reveal who he really is in the true Kabbalistic art.

Lanovius himself says near the end of his judicial Letter: "What you ask regarding Kabbalah requires a more diligent inquiry than I can promise given my current occupations. I will say briefly beforehand that nothing can be hoped for as an addition to the sciences from it, since it languishes miserably around trivialities, and both those parts concerning **The Chariot** <term>Marcauah: Ma'aseh Merkabah, the "Work of the Chariot," a branch of Jewish mysticism focused on celestial visions.</term> and **The Beginning** <term>Berescith: Ma'aseh Bereshit, the "Work of the Creation," the branch of Kabbalah dealing with the origins of the universe.</term> are polluted by many fables and deformed not a little by the dreams of idle men; so that if anything illustrious or solid could be extracted, it could in no way be compared to what our Theologians and Philosophers teach on the same subject."

To this I say: In this context of speech, two things can be discerned: namely, the lack of skill of both Lanovius and Mersenne in the Kabbalistic art, and yet nonetheless their supreme boasting. <margin>column 281.</margin> For Mersenne, in his volume on Genesis, says: "If anyone is wise, I counsel him not to waste good hours in the reading of the Kabbalists, unless he wishes to lose them; I speak from experience, for if any good thing happens to be joined with their trifles and fables, we shall have it more clearly, briefly, and subtly deduced in Philosophy and Theology," etc. These are Mersenne's words, in which he has admitted his ignorance in the Kabbalistic art quite clearly; and yet nonetheless, by his rash and unjust judgment, he proceeds to attack and condemn my art, however unknown it may be to him.

But who can enter or penetrate the museum or storehouse of nature without his own genuine key? Out with it: we know the wolf by his words and his knowledge. But why (I pray) does he try to deter everyone from Kabbalistic science or from the inquiry of the Kabbalistic art? Is it because he himself (according to his own confession) is unskilled in that art? For these are his words: *I speak from experience,* etc. As if it were impossible for the learned to progress beyond the sharpness of Mersenne's wit! Here he humbly petitions and asks Lanovius to instruct him further in Kabbalah. The words are clear: "What you ask regarding Kabbalah," he says, etc. And so, like the blind leading the blind, this man, powerless in Kabbalah, inquires thoughtlessly. Notwithstanding this, he did not blush to correct—nay, even to condemn—the Kabbalah of **Francesco Giorgio** <note>original: "Georgii Veneti"; a reference to the Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist author of *De Harmonia Mundi*.</note> and Fludd; he who, having wiped away all shame, was not afraid to publicly proclaim his own ignorance in that art.

But now we shall proceed to the inquiry of the strength of his Master himself in Kabbalistic matters. The aforementioned text also denotes the ignorance of Mersenne's Doctor or Master in Kabbalah. For first, he says: "What you ask regarding Kabbalah requires a more diligent inquiry than my current...

# Fludd’s Response,

And **Theology** <note>original: "Theologia"; Fludd argues that true theology must include the study of God's creation.</note> knows that the sacred text teaches the principles and mysteries of natural things: since throughout almost the entire thread of the whole Sacred Code, mention is made of snow, hail, rain, clouds, lightning, thunder, comets, winds, storms, whirlwinds, the action of the sun upon the **world spirit** <term>world spirit: "spiritus mundanus," a vital, subtle substance Fludd believed permeated the universe, connecting the divine to the physical.</term>, springs, the ebb and flow and the tempest of the sea, the changing of the air, the positions of the stars, the changes of times and seasons, the virtues of herbs and plants, the natures of beasts, and almost infinite other things of this sort pertaining to natural philosophy, as well as their origins, causes, and effects. Wherefore, (just Reader), consider with your more mature judgment whether that rash proscription of Lanovius can be held by any prudent man as good, lawful, and fit? But since Gassendi seems to make this same objection, or rather assertion, further down, I shall—God willing—dispute it there more broadly and at greater length.

From the aforementioned things, therefore (as I hope), it is clear and made manifest to all how weak and powerless is this one of those "strong" Mersennian antagonists in his battle, and how windy and empty are his assertions—indeed, destitute of both Theological and Philosophical virtue. Consequently, whether they can harm Fludd’s principles in any matter, and whether they are sufficiently valid to overturn them (as he himself seems to boast), I leave to be judged by "world spirits" whose wings of justice are raised toward God.

Now indeed (Good Reader), I see you with the eyes of my mind exalted upon a supreme tribunal to judge my cause in justice; and therefore, I shall confidently approach Mersenne’s more powerful antagonist—the one whom he seems to hold as his greatest bulwark, his strong rock, even his refuge and anchor, insofar as his whole hope is placed in him—namely, **Pierre Gassendi** <note>Gassendi (1592–1655) was a French philosopher and scientist who famously critiqued Fludd's mystical "Mosaic Philosophy" from a more empirical, atomistic perspective.</note>, with truth as my guide.

# THE THIRD MEMBER.

->In which that erroneous detection of the Principles of Robert Fludd’s Philosophy made by Pierre Gassendi is corrected, and weighed in the more equal scales of justice.<-

<image-desc>The following two points are grouped by a large curly brace to the right of the introductory text.</image-desc>

This Member is distinguished into two parts, of which:
- The first makes an open and candid judgment regarding the nature and condition of Pierre Gassendi.
- The second corrects his erroneous opinion or restoration concerning the principles of Fluddian Philosophy and washes it away with the waves of truth.

## PART I. CHAPTER I.

->Here, that wonderful hope which the powerless Mersenne has placed in the strength of Gassendi is clearly explained—as he is the one in whom the anchor of his faith is fixed, and without whose help he cannot be freed from the snares of Fludd.<-

If you (benevolent Reader) rightly remember the place in my response to Mersenne, which was titled *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* <note>original: "Sophiæ cum Moriâ certamen," a book Fludd published in 1629 against Mersenne.</note>, specifically on folio 108, a passage was cited there from column 1744 of Mersenne’s work, where he depicted the hands of a certain **God-taught** <note>original: "Theodidacti"; a Greek-derived term meaning one taught directly by God, used here by Mersenne as a title of honor for Gassendi.</note> friend of his. His words are these:

<margin>Mersenne, col. 1744.</margin>
> Let Fludd say whose hands and lines these are, which were not made according to whim, but by an excellent painter accurately looking upon the living and true hands themselves, expressed as if to life and as they truly are; and lest you perhaps complain, I offer not only the right hand of that God-taught friend, but also the left, etc.

From which it is permitted to see that those depicted hands were icons of the living hands of Gassendi. For he says, "not only the right hand of that God-taught friend of mine, etc." Furthermore, he adds:

<margin>Mersenne, ibid.</margin>
> Take care, however, lest in guessing about those hands and asserting whose they are, you wander astray in the art of **Chiromancy** <term>Chiromancy: "Chiroscopica," the art of palm reading, which Mersenne is using here to taunt Fludd, who was known to take such "occult" sciences seriously.</term> itself. For he will receive your errors excellently and publish them to the whole world, if he survives the life which he still enjoys.

Restrain your laughter, friends! For how aptly, according to the light condition of his nature, he longs to play with bubbles or feathers like a boy. But is it not a disgrace to his friend Gassendi that, although he is a prudent man in his own right and sufficiently skilled in Philosophy, he allows himself to be so seduced by that trifling man [Mersenne] that he permits his hands to be painted and sent out into public like messengers concerning a matter of little importance—nay, a ridiculous business? Truly, if this were true, as it is related as true by Mersenne, it would argue for a remarkable self-love in Gassendi; but I think Mersenne himself is rather the one sharing in that vice, whom you find elsewhere to be false and storytelling in many things—but not Gassendi, who appears to be far more prudent and modest, however much that imperious and boasting speech of Mersenne seems to bring suspicion of such a thing. Since here he expressly names his "God-taught" friend, and threatens me besides that if I displease him with my writings, that man will write against me, and by "excellently receiving my errors," will publish them to the whole world. To that same text, I wrote these words on folio 108 of my Response:

"But what sort of horrendous monster is that, and what kind of man is he among yours, who is powerful enough to strike such dread or terror into Robert that he would guard against the danger from him? You are deceived, Marin! For you shall feel, and the rest of your sort, however malicious, shall perceive that Robert rejects words of that kind, however haughty. They shall feel, I say, if I am stirred up unjustly and injuriously, what kind of man I am." These were my words at that time.

But now, what need is there for words? **The wolf is in the story** <note>original: "Lupus enim in fabula"; a Latin idiom equivalent to "speak of the devil," used when the person being discussed suddenly appears.</note>. Behold the man! Behold the God-taught friend of Mersenne, in whom he most confides! Behold him, whose help he humbly petitions to refute Fludd’s objections! For his words in his Letter are these:

> "Having shared counsel with friendly and learned men, etc. Having heard the others, I also wished to consult my Gassendi by letter, etc. I asked him, moreover, what he thought of those works..."

# To the Gassendian Exercises. Section III. Part 1.

...he might write back in earnest. For I conjectured that, out of the curiosity he has for touching upon every Philosophy, he had surely also penetrated that one under which Fludd hides his impieties, etc. <note>original: "impietates suas occultat"; Fludd is quoting his critics' accusations that his mystical philosophy is a cover for un-Christian ideas.</note>

---

->And again.<-

But behold, while Fludd, in responding to me, wished to hide himself still in the meanings of Scripture as if in lurking-places; my friend Gassendi has so led him out and uncovered his **Cabala** <term>Cabala: A form of Jewish mysticism. Here, Fludd’s critics use the term to describe his complex, symbolic interpretation of the Bible and nature.</term> that I think I am satisfied by this discovery alone, etc.

---

->And elsewhere.<-

Gassendi invites me to a more full response; yet he himself so skillfully touched upon everything that what he left behind is of no great importance, etc.

Furthermore, regarding the remarkable reputation and firm opinion that he holds of Gassendi’s sufficiency, the same man wrote these few words elsewhere to his **Patron** <note>original: "Mæcenatem"; a reference to a wealthy supporter, likely Peiresc, who supported both Gassendi and Mersenne.</note>:

> The book which treats my cause is not mine, because it was written by that friend of mine, Gassendi, who is not unknown to you. It could be said it is not so much a book as a Letter; but it is such a Letter that you might say it is to be preferred over a great book. There is no need for me to add anything in its commendation, since you know him well enough from elsewhere, and this work itself speaks sufficiently for its Author.

By which it is evident that victory is decided before the blow is struck and the battle joined. For that "good man" thinks that this Athlete or Antagonist of his is invincible: and therefore stronger than **Hercules** himself in his reasons and arguments. But the outcome will prove the deeds.

## CHAPTER II.

### In which the nature of Gassendi himself is briefly described and explained.

It is a most shameful thing for anyone to spread lies about his enemy, or to falsely and indirectly detract from his virtues. Therefore, I shall openly and sincerely reveal in a few words what I feel about this Antagonist of mine. It seems, then, that Gassendi differs greatly in nature and condition from his two aforementioned associates <note>Mersenne and Launoy.</note>. For, as I affirm directly and not without justice, while both Mersenne and Launoy are men of that sort who are most ready and very prone to speaking evil and throwing insults sharply at anyone; I see indeed that Gassendi is adorned with a far greater morality and modesty in this investigation of his. For from him, neither uncivil nor abusive words, nor quibbles exceeding the laws of philosophy, are brought forward; instead, he contains himself within the limits of an honest writer. Hence it is that he not only observes the laws of civility in writing himself, but even rebukes his friend for his immorality and curses, and for his harshness in writing, saying:

<margin>Gassendi, folios 9 and 10.</margin>
It cannot be hidden from you (Mersenne), that it is quite hard for one living in the Christian world to be called an **Evil Magician** <note>original: "Cacomagum"; from Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'magos' (magician).</note>, a Heretic-magician, or a teacher and propagator of foul and horrendous Magic: to hear that such a teacher should not be tolerated with impunity, calling upon the Prince to take punishment upon him, and even using threats that he should therefore soon be submerged in the "eternal floods," <note>original: "fluctibus æternis"; a pun on Fludd's name (Latin 'fluctus' means flood or wave).</note> etc. to say nothing of the **Atheism** and **Heresy** which you also charge against Fludd. These are surely things which could have irritated the patience of **Rufinus** or **St. Jerome**. For one of them, though he requires patience in other matters, cries out that he who bears or ignores the crime of even one heresy is not a Christian. The other says: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy." What would they have done in the face of a crime or suspicion of either Atheism or Black Magic?

From the premises, therefore, it can be seen that in his judgment he is a very just and fair moderator, teaching his friend that it is hard for anyone, however patient, to endure such great insults and shames, which are so calumnious: and consequently he proves that his own mind is very far removed from such a vice. Furthermore, Mersenne and Launoy are very rash in their judgments, having no regard for the scales of justice, but from Gassendi’s writings we gather that he is more cautious and circumspect in his judgment. Thus it happened that, although he was sharply incited by Mersenne to write against me positively and in a more turbulent and immoral manner, he nevertheless proposed to use a more modest style. Nor did he wish anything to be pronounced as absolute; but he expressly asserts that the things he wrote against me are merely **probabilities**. His words are these:

<margin>Gassendi, folios 6 and 7.</margin>
> I would wish this one thing to be allowed as a preface: that I never peddle my trifles and conjectures as the absolute truth. For although you almost forbid me from being a **Pyrrhonian** <term>Pyrrhonian: A follower of Pyrrho, an ancient Greek philosopher who advocated for Skepticism—the idea that certain knowledge is impossible and one should suspend judgment.</term>, and thus you always urge me as if I had something dogmatic to bring forward; you owe me this in return by the right of friendship: that I may be allowed to live for the day, and never to bring forth or accept anything beyond the boundaries of mere probability. In this place, I will certainly seem to attribute to Fludd an opinion for which a sensible man might be angry: however, as I greatly desire that something else resides in his mind than what I seem to gather clearly enough from his books, I declare that he can interpret it in the same way, so that he may correct this sense of mine. For why should that be denied to him? Therefore, such is my mind, that whatever my speech or opinion may eventually seem to be, I would never want it to be a prejudice against the truth or the person. Thus says Gassendi.

Do you see, then, Gassendi’s cautious condition and modesty in judging? Do you see also his candor in writing against anyone? For here he has excellently expressed his fairness and his not-unsubstantial investigation in this controversy of ours. Therefore, I congratulate myself on this good opinion of an honest man, even if he acts as an arbiter in his friend’s cause; for he refuses to overstep the bounds of a clean conscience for the sake of his friend. Moreover, regarding those things which are circumscribed by the limits of mere probability, he promises that he will condemn nothing rashly. Let him proceed then, I hope, boldly: for I shall endure the opinion of a noble man, whatever it may be, patiently and without any disturbance of mind; nor, even though I am a sensible man, will I be angry. And if he should be unable to lay aside that external appearance of accusation and bad interpretation, and cannot wipe every single stain from my writings, then let the marks of those impieties devised by Mersenne be justly and deservedly inflicted upon me.

In the meantime, however, I rejoice that I have found a man sufficiently upright, just, and skilled in Philosophy, as well as well-versed in many secrets of nature. For we no longer expect—as we have until now from Mersenne and Launoy—false judgments brought forth without reason and yet determined as truths; nor shames, nor words dripping with the rot of insults, nor quarrels in place of Philosophical reasons; but we attend our mind to the very marrow of wisdom. And since this fair Philosopher and investigator of ours grants me the permission to explain my own mind in my writings, I sincerely promise him that I will do so candidly where necessary, not with quibbles and insults that detract from a Philosopher’s dignity, but in a manner and custom befitting a Philosopher and modest Christian.

D

Fludd is transitioning from general remarks about Gassendi’s character to a point-by-point critique of Gassendi’s "Exercises," specifically defending his own philosophical principles and the authorship of associated works.</meta>

header: Fludd’s Response,

Regarding Gassendi’s remaining conditions, he seems to possess ingenious flashes of wit and humor; although these do not reach the marrow of the subject, they usually provoke laughter and jesting for the sake of the readers' or spectators' recreation. Finally, wherever he can, he strives to touch his opponent to the quick with his arguments. Nor does he neglect, where he is able, to sharply inflict deep wounds upon my Philosophy. Such efforts of his, since they adorn a philosopher, will be judged worthy of praise rather than blame by any man of letters. Therefore, let us come to his exercises.

# SECTION III. PART II.
## In which the erroneous opinion or "discovery" of Pierre Gassendi regarding the principles of Fludd’s Philosophy is corrected, and all the stains within it are washed away by the waves of truth.

If I wished to strictly survey every small detail in Gassendi’s treatise with this inquiry and examination of mine, and to respond to every sentence of almost no importance, the labor would be useless; and furthermore, it would be tedious both for me and for you (Patient Reader) to dwell on useless matters; indeed, they would be unworthy of your reading. Therefore, I have proposed to speak only of those things which pertain to me and which are most strongly brought against the principles of my Philosophy. However, since it is not commendable in a writer, nor pleasing to readers, to roll the same stone as Sisyphus <note>In Greek mythology, Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down; Fludd uses this to mean "toil in vain" or "repeat oneself needlessly."</note> or to inconsiderately repeat the same things many times, we have dealt with certain matters in the examination of Gassendi's work as "collateral"—namely, those things which do not properly lead to constructing those six impieties falsely attributed to me by Mersenne, but only concern the principles of my Philosophy. I will treat those objections of his in this part of this section. Some points, however, are like the foundation stones or calculations used to support the aforementioned six impieties. Those we shall cite in the fourth section of this Treatise, and there we will respond with precision. We shall proceed, therefore, in order, and bring those things worthy of note, as they occur to our eyes, to a strict examination.

### Text 1. Gassendi page 7.
> First I shall speak of the style of writing, and later of the argument. When I touch upon the style of writing, I do not mean the eloquence. Each of us speaks in his own way, and whether it be a **Barbarism** <term>Barbarism: In a classical context, this refers to a non-standard or "corrupt" use of Latin that violates the rules of the ancient Roman style.</term> or a **Grecism** <term>Grecism: An idiom or construction borrowed from Greek that might sound awkward in Latin.</term>, the words are of little concern, provided the meaning can remain clear.

->Fludd.<-

Certainly, I am no Oedipus <note>Oedipus famously solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Fludd is saying he is not a solver of riddles and finds Gassendi's point obscure.</note>. Therefore, I do not understand the man. I ask you (Reader) to untie, if you can, the enigma of this Sphinx of ours. If he means "false Latinity," I confess he will surely find infinite errors in my volumes. Yet this is not through my own negligence, but that of the printer and the proofreader. Do we not see several errors occurring likewise in this little treatise of Gassendi’s, despite the presence of Mersenne's diligence? I thought for certain, however, that the "Eagle would not catch flies" <note>original: "Aquilam non capturam muscas"; a proverb meaning a great person should not concern themselves with trivialities.</note>, nor that Gassendi, like some young schoolboy, would play with trifles; for I thought him so deeply immersed in the liquid of Philosophy that he would not even think of superficialities. But let us proceed.

### Text 2. Gassendi page 8.
> For not only is that work entitled *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly* Robert's own, but also that other one to which he gave the title *The Highest Good*, even though it is said to be by Joachim Frizius. My evidence is that it came from the same printing shop, at the same time, and as if in the same series as Fludd’s *Contest*; it has the same Spirit, the same aim, the same attitude toward you [Mersenne], the same style, the same words, exactly the same principles, etc.

->Fludd.<-

As if many works, in the same shop and at the same time, and by different authors, could not be printed by one and the same printer and included in one and the same volume? But this diligent inquisitor of ours discerns the same "Spirit." He certainly had need of the eyes of Lynceus <note>In myth, Lynceus was an Argonaut with vision so sharp he could see through trees or underground.</note>; but because he lacks them, he is deceived. Why does he not perceive (even while Fludd is silent) Mersenne’s own aim and similar attitude toward others? Do you not believe (good Reader) that the bold and rash censure of Mersenne against all Magi, Cabalists, and Alchemists in general has stirred the minds of many in Europe and incited them against a man too elevated on the wings of pride? As for the style and words, those are common to everyone, and my principles also have been known, accepted, and confirmed by solid arguments by many before now.

But to come closer to the matter: I confess that the author of that book is very well known to me, an intimate friend, and joined in friendship no differently than Gassendi is to Mersenne; he is, however, a Scot by nation. He, noticing partly Mersenne’s malice toward me and his blind ignorance in the aforementioned arts, and partly his insane and disordered vehemence against all practitioners of the arts—indeed, seeing them utterly condemned by him although he was ignorant of the mysteries of those arts—immediately composed that book *On the Highest Good*, and especially the **Cabala** <term>Cabala: Here referring to Fludd's mystical Christian interpretation of the Hebrew tradition, used to defend his scientific and spiritual theories.</term>, against him and sent it to me. But because one part of it was written in the Scottish tongue and the other in Latin, I likewise translated that Scottish part into Latin, and I confess I added something of my own, though not much. What? Does Gassendi believe that I wish to deny my name in my own works, when I am capable, by the grace of God, of sustaining what is mine on Atlantic shoulders <note>A reference to Atlas, who held up the sky.</note> against anyone? Or does he think it fair in a Philosopher to falsely usurp the things of another and put his name to those things which are not truly his? Truly, I judge such robbery among philosophers to be wretched and therefore I despise it, when someone is not ashamed to falsely and indirectly assume, or even sometimes to affect, the honor of another. Nor, however, would I want anyone to believe that I say these things as if I could not defend all those doctrines contained in my friend’s booklet on his behalf in his absence; for Gassendi will find me ready to respond to any objection, but because I know well enough that my friend Frizius himself, having heard the accusations against his booklet, will immediately act sharply and effectively against his adversary.

Regarding the attachment of that book *On the Highest Good* to the end of my book against Mersenne, that was done against my command; for I had expressly written that it should be printed in octavo format and bound by itself. But the printer excused himself and showed that if both treatises, since they pertain to one and the same matter, were included in one volume,

...it would be far more convenient and useful for him. In short: why should I deny what is mine? Especially since I am strong enough to defend and manfully protect both my own interests and those of others—particularly those of my friend in his absence.

### Text 3. Gassendi page 10.
But, just as Fludd, having been provoked, had some reason to be embittered and to write a Defense; so it does not seem to me that he kept his moderation when he flared up so passionately. For surely a greater degree of moderation, it seems to me, would have been more fitting for a man of letters.

->Fludd.<-
However, Mersenne found me to be far more moderate than himself: since I did not call him an Evil Magician <note>original: "Cacomagum"</note>; nor a Sorcerer of Heretics; nor an Atheist; nor a teacher of foul Magic; nor did I attempt to stain his good name or reputation with any similar insult. Rather, I attacked him for the most part reasonably, using only arguments that refuted his unjust judgment of me. But does a person inflict wounds if they merely return the lashes and cruel blows they received? Certainly, even a fly has its gall <note>A common proverb suggesting that even the smallest creature has a temper when provoked.</note>; and the wretched little worm is seen to rise up in its own defense against the enemy pursuing it. But there is a well-known proverb: even a wounded sheep fights back. Therefore, Fludd is blamed so greatly without merit.

### Text 4. Gassendi page 10.
Robert claims Wisdom <note>original: "Sophia"</note> for himself, while leaving Folly <note>original: "Moria," likely a play on Erasmus’s *The Praise of Folly*</note> to you. But I ask you: would Socrates, or any other of the Wise Men, have fled so immediately to torches and stones with such great force?

->Fludd.<-
I confess, indeed, that it is common for men to err; yet Gassendi is remarkably mistaken when he thinks I have arrogated Wisdom to myself and assigned Folly to Mersenne. For I only said (as expressed in the words of that passage) that I wished to strive with certain arguments—drawn as if they were arrows from the quiver of Wisdom, that is, of Holy Scripture—to pierce and utterly destroy Mersenne’s vain and erroneous assertions about me. I am not, therefore, so arrogant or inflated with vain self-love <note>original: "Philautia"</note> that I consider myself either a wise man or superior to my brothers in every branch of learning.

### Text 5. Gassendi page 11.
Could Christ—the Eternal Wisdom, whom he always has on his lips—have taught him this style? (Namely, that he should be driven to a foam by the stirrings of anger.) He who, when he was reviled, did not revile in return.

->Fludd.<-
That I always have Eternal Wisdom on my lips, and what is more, in my heart, is not and never shall be a disgrace to me: for through it I have life, motion, and being. I do not understand the "fifth essence of wheat" <note>Fludd is likely mocking a literalist or overly-materialistic interpretation of spiritual concepts, possibly a jab at Mersenne's "low" chemistry</note> as he himself seems to assert quite thoughtlessly. As for the bilious passion of my mind, I did not revile Mersenne; rather, I performed Gassendi’s own duty toward me: namely, I manifested his errors before the learned judges of this world. And was the Lord not just when He said: "An eye for an eye," etc.?

### Text 6. Gassendi page 11.
We must now come to the argument that Fludd treats in that twin work, but first we must have the key by which his hidden meaning may be opened. There are perpetual riddles with which he addresses you, etc. Permit me, therefore, first to elicit from Fludd's various works what principles of his Philosophy he establishes and follows. For thus, at last, it will be very easy to hunt for his mind.

->Fludd.<-
For that reason—so that he may reach the proposed work more quickly and completely—he attempts to bring into one body and harmony those long-winded things which Fludd (as he says) wrote here and there and, as it were, in a chaotic fashion. He says wisely, however, that a "key" <note>A reference to Fludd’s work *Clavis Philosophiae*, which means "Key of Philosophy."</note> must first be held, by which he might be able to open Fludd’s hidden meaning. May God grant that he obtains it! For if that key were truly known, I do not doubt that, grasping the genuine and proper sense of Fludd’s writings, he would proceed to defend them rather than accuse them so sharply. But alas! I see that Gassendi (whatever he may say to the contrary) has by no means found the true key to Fludd’s Philosophy. Therefore, I am certain that my principles will be subject to his rigid censorship. For I am entirely ignorant as to how he can solve or uncover my "riddles" (as he calls them) by means of an unknown key. I gather that he has leafed through my works from every side, and that with diligence; yet he has not attained my meaning as desired. For it is evident even from the following things that he still lacks that key to my Philosophy.

### Text 7. Gassendi page 12.
Moreover, since the principles of Fludd’s Philosophy are merely Alchemical, etc.

->Fludd.<-
He is deceived and he deceives in this matter if he understands "vulgar chemistry" <note>The common practice of laboratory alchemy or proto-chemistry.</note>; although I have demonstrated and explained those principles of Cosmic nature—not improperly, by comparing like to like—certainly parabolically and through symbols. For no "likeness" is the same as the thing itself. And although in coarse and fake chemistry the elements seem to be distinguished from one another, yet who is so stiff-necked or of such meager wit that he would wish to accept those as the mere, simple, and pure elements of nature? Nay, they are called "elements" and "quintessence" <term>quintessence: the "fifth element" or purest essence of a substance</term> not because they are truly such, but insofar as this or that portion of a thing divided by the vulgar chemical art partakes more of this or that element which our senses can perceive. Therefore, I say Gassendi is mistaken in this: that he affirms with such confidence that he has reached the knowledge of the key to my Philosophy. For if he had touched it, he would surely understand a matter a thousand times more noble than the subject of fake chemistry—created by God in nature and given as a gift to men. But, since this text is one of the chief stones or calculations from which Mersenne forged that first "impiety" which he falsely charged against me, I will say no more about it here; nor about the others. For I will speak more abundantly of those in the Fourth Member, First Part.

Moreover, this entire Empyrean region <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be occupied by the element of fire or light.</note> is itself what is called by Fludd "Angelic nature."

->Fludd.<-
It is also called by some of the Church Fathers the "Intellectual, Rational, and Angelic heaven";

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s point-by-point rebuttal to Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd defended his character and his right to respond to the attacks made by Father Marin Mersenne. # Fludd’s Response.
<meta>catchword: make [faciat]</meta>

...because of the abundance of divine light within it. Hence, it is for this reason that this sublime Spirit is called "Empyrean," <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest part of heaven, composed of pure light or fire.</note> namely because of the dominance of fire or light within it; in the same way, the angelic substance is filled with the rays of divine light. This is why angels are called *Agalmata* <note>original: "Algamata," from the Greek *agalmata*, meaning "statues," "images," or "delights"</note> by Dionysius; <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> they are like highly polished mirrors, adapted to receive the divine light in abundance.

### Text 9. Gassendi pages 43 & 44.

I notice that while Fludd, in his investigation of demons, had made Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and others into certain distinct angels, etc., he now—while he struggles against you—wants Michael, Raphael, and the others to be a single Angel, having merely received various names on account of their various duties.

->Fludd.<-

I say that all things are nothing but one in God. <margin>Romans 11</margin> *For from him* (says the Apostle), *through him, and in him are all things.* <note>original: "Ab eo enim... per eum, & in eo ſunt omnia."</note> Yet God is one and the same in himself, and yet of various wills. <margin>Ezekiel 36</margin> *Come from the four winds* (says the Prophet), *O Spirit, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again*; <note>original: "A quatuor ventis... veni Spiritus..."</note> and yet it is the same Spirit, through various ministers animated by him alone, in various properties; indeed, it even blows from every corner of the world in opposite ways. <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> Does not Solomon say that the *Holy Spirit of discipline is unique and simple*, <note>original: "Spiritus diſciplina Sanctus ſit vnicus & ſimplex"</note> that is, in his essence, but manifold in respect to his many properties and operations? <margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin> Furthermore, if all things are from God through his only son Jesus Christ, and not through the "gods" who are spoken of in heaven and on earth (as Saint Paul says)—that is, neither through angels nor through demons—then all angels of whatever kind live, move, and work through Christ. Consequently, *Christ is the one in all*, <note>original: "Chriſtus est vnum in omnibus"</note> who are distinguished from one another in both nature and name according to the various will and property of the central Worker. <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: *all things are from God, and in God*, but God is one: and all their action and operation is through our one Lord Jesus Christ. Was it then absurd for us to say that all angels, however much they differ in properties, are one in that great Angelic Spirit or Emissary, through whom alone, and in whom, they exist and work, since this same point is confirmed many times by Holy Scripture?

### Text 10. Gassendi pages 50 & 51.

I do not dwell here on how he mocks Copernicus and Gilbert regarding the motion of the earth; nor do I wonder that, being so fond of Pythagorean and Platonic symbols, he rejected the commentary of Copernicus concerning the Sun (or fire, or the "guard of Jupiter") in the center. For Fludd understands another non-volatile earth and another central Sun than the one commonly understood by us.

->Fludd.<-

Certainly, I first placed the Scriptures there speaking for me: then I proved by both physical and mathematical demonstration that the earth is naturally inclined toward rest. However, I will now bring forward another argument, stronger and more valid than the others, clearly refuting the opinion of those who want to persuade us that the earth itself, along with the others (the wandering stars or planets), moves around a sun fixed in the center. For, if the earth moved in a circle around a sun fixed in the center, it would then follow that the earth would move according to latitude, <note>In this context, Fludd is arguing that if the Earth orbited the Sun, our perspective of the celestial poles would change as we moved.</note> since in winter time we see it further from the Sun, and sometimes closer to it. But it is clear that this is quite otherwise, because the elevation of the pole, in every region of the earth, is always one and the same. By this it is indicated clearly enough that the Sun moves and is distant according to latitude throughout the turns of the year from the regions of the earth, while the earth itself remains fixed. Finally, as for the "central Sun" of the earth, we know that such a thing is constantly present to all living things; indeed, to the earth itself. Does not experience testify that a Sun of life is within plants and animals, as well as minerals?

### Text 11. Gassendi pages 55 & 56.

I observe that he wants not only Meteors, <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> but also all other things, to take their origin from the wind in such a way that, although the air is subject to the wind as agitated matter, the wind itself is nothing in itself other than an Angel, according to that saying: *Who makes his Angels spirits.* <note>Psalm 104:4; original: "Qui facit Angelos ſuos Spiritus."</note> From this, he defines the wind as an Angelic Spirit breathing secretly and invisibly here and there according to the hidden good pleasure of the Creator; though its sound may be heard, the limit of where it comes from or where it goes is unknown to mortals. It is also defined thus: wind is a certain Angelic Spirit, or subtle air, inspired and animated by the fiery Spirit of Jehovah—sometimes visible and manifest, as in lightning and flashes; sometimes invisible and hidden, like that which is heard but not seen—to execute the divine will, whether for salvation and benevolence, or for punishment and cursing on the earth, sent forth from some region of the world in a divine and secret manner. I mention these things both so that you may see the general cause of Meteors, and so you may recognize how constantly Fludd perseveres in his opinion regarding angels; and so you may judge whether in the air (which they call the Synagogue of Mages) there is a continuous celebration; and finally, so you may foresee where on earth one ought to locate either Paradise or Hell.

->Fludd.<-

I have said, and I still say boldly, that the Universal Element <note>original: "Elementum Catholicum." Fludd refers to the primary matter of the atmosphere.</note> is animated by the power of the winds, and is daily varied and changed into meteors of different kinds according to the property of the daily wind; and that the internal soul of the winds is an Angelic power, and that the power and life of an Angel is from God, namely a ray of the most holy emanation. In my volume *On the Mystery of Diseases* <note>original: "de Morborum myſterio"</note> I proved this in that place where I challenged all the philosophers and physicians of Europe who deny these assertions of mine into the public arena of philosophy. If Gassendi deigns to enter it with me for the sake of attacking my opinion, he will find me (I believe) well-equipped with arrows drawn from the quiver of truth, so that I can defend and sustain it against him and all others with Herculean strength. As for the rest, it seems to me—and likewise to all the learned of Europe (I believe)—that this reasoning of Gassendi is absurd and contrary to the sacred page: namely that, because evil exists in the air, therefore nothing good exists in it; or rather, because Satan sometimes has power in the air, therefore Jehovah does not breathe from the corners of the world; nor does he make a thick cloud his hiding place; nor does he send forth snow like wool; nor scatter frost like ashes; nor ride upon the wings of the winds sitting upon the Cherubim; nor bring forth the winds from his treasuries; nor speak in thunder; nor is the air weighed by eternal wisdom; nor are the waters bound by him in thick clouds; nor does a way for the lightning of thunder appear from him; nor does he distill drops from on high, nor infinite other things...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s rebuttal to Pierre Gassendi. Fludd is currently refuting the idea that the atmosphere (the air) is exclusively the domain of demons, arguing instead that it is a medium for divine revelation and angelic activity. He then transitions into a defense of his musical theories and the symbolic diagrams used in his works.</meta>

...[that the air] should act [as a void], but rather that only Satan or the devil performs all these things in that "Synagogue of Magicians." <note>Fludd is likely referring to a gathering of practitioners of "black magic" or simply Gassendi's group of skeptical philosophers.</note> I truly marvel that someone well-versed in Philosophy and Theology could fall into such a great error as to exclude divinity or most holy goodness from the air—which is the seat of life for lower universal things—and attribute the entire possession of it to devils and evil magicians. What? Did not the Holy Spirit descend visibly in the form of a Dove through the air upon Christ? Did he not appear over the Apostles in the form of cloven tongues, accompanied by a great rushing of wind? Did not the spiritual Christ speak to Saul from the clouds? And did not the Angels of Jehovah speak to Abraham and the other Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles? Upon what mountain, I ask, did the blessed Angels minister to Christ after the preceding temptation by the devil? What? Just because the devil had the power to tempt him in the air, were God and his good ministering Angels not stronger in that same air than Satan himself? Was not Elijah taken up by a fiery whirlwind, and carried away by the Spirit into the clouds? I certainly do not approve—hardly at all—of those Theologian-Philosophers who, with their pen as if it were a feather, delight to play so lightly and against their own conscience with such deep mysteries of God. Let Gassendi therefore seek Hell (if he pleases) in that part of the air where devils and malignant spirits dwell; but let him place Paradise in that location where God is accustomed to speak to Adam and the Elect, and to be present with the pious. I conclude, therefore, that those points brought forth at the end of that text are quite frivolous and trifling.

### Text 12. Gassendi, page 76.

> *I wonder indeed why Fludd, also a lover of musical practice, did not rather choose the division of the Fourth into tones, major and minor, and the major semitone: in this way, he would surely have accommodated himself more to the practice of singing, and would have found numbers both shorter and more elegant for the whole Octave and the whole Monochord. Nevertheless, this is to be forgiven: since he is a lover of Platonic Philosophy, he did not wish to strive for anything beyond Proclus’s invention.*

->**Fludd.**<-

May this new invention turn out well for Gassendi. It is indeed very easy to add to things already invented, and yet we shall find in the conclusion that nothing is being said now that has not been said before. For my part, I will say boldly that it is done in vain through many things which can be done through fewer. I certainly imitated neither Plato nor Proclus in that division of my Monochord; <term>Monochord: A single-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance scientists to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals and the harmony of the universe.</term> but rather, to compare it with truth and to prove its certainty, I adapted to it that musical system of Plato and Proclus, and found it to agree in all things with the intervals of my Monochord. I observed that in the exact center or midpoint of the string, the Octave <note>original: "Diapasonem"</note> sounds on either side with its whole, as 2 to 1. And again, dividing the string into three equal parts, I perceived that the third part with the whole string, or with its half part, produced the harmony of the Fifth, <note>original: "Diapente"</note> which indeed consisted of the sesquitertial proportion, being as 3 to 2. Finally, the fourth part of the string to the whole, as four to one: and consequently, being in the sesquiquartal proportion to the whole, it rendered the harmony of the Fourth. <note>original: "Diatessaron." Note that Fludd's mathematical ratios here are specific to his harmonic system.</note> And so I proceed with the others; nor indeed do I acknowledge more than six harmonies in the field of Harmony. I do not care for these trivialities <note>original: "Titiuilitia," a medieval term for nonsense or scraps.</note> and extreme curiosities of that kind. Nevertheless, in Gassendi I praise and commend the sharpness of his intellect, and honesty compels me to approve of his desire to reach manifold knowledge. I rejoice that I am dealing with such a man, from whom, being very little provoked by insults, taunts, and reproachful words, I can hear and learn something new. 

Yet, in the invention of my Symphonic Monochord and its use, I stand content, since by means of it I can compose 40 parts over one Bass song, each exactly differing from the others in sound, and can sing any part in the art of Music. And although some common musicians, being ignorant of my way of composing, may say and believe at first glance—looking only at the laws of harmony—that I am not much involved in common musical practice but only in a certain speculation of it; nevertheless, their opinion of me is known by my close friends to be quite inconsistent. For I know how, by means of the use of that Monochord, not only to sing and compose songs, but also to adapt songs so composed to various musical instruments. Indeed, I have even constructed a certain musical instrument adorned with brass strings under the direction of my Monochord, by means of which I am accustomed to bring harmony into it—however difficult it may be because of the clash of sharp and flat semitones in the composition. And this I did not do without the approval and commendation of distinguished musicians, both French and English, residing in the court of the King of England. Therefore, an exact and internal knowledge of my Monochord suffices for me; since by means of it, the mysteries of God and Nature, both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic, <note>Refers to Fludd's theory that the structure of the Great World (the universe) is mirrored in the Little World (man).</note> as well as those of song and artificial composition, can be demonstrated. I conclude, therefore, that I indeed commend Gassendi’s invention; nevertheless, I do not reject or neglect my own.

### Text 13. Gassendi, pages 87 & 88.

> *And let him call those commentaries of yours on Genesis both a "Babylonian volume" and "most famous fictions." Why should you not bear this patiently? He who elsewhere also devises so many figures of those things which he invents, so that since nothing of the sort truly occurs in the nature of things, someone might deservedly call them fictions.*

->**Fludd.**<-

He is mistaken and he misleads in that assertion of his. For I produce almost nothing that is not either a "type" of truth and a likeness of some real Being, or the truth itself. In this way, all figures invented by Euclid for the sake of demonstration could be considered fictions. Furthermore, so could those by Johannes de Sacrobosco, <note>A 13th-century monk and astronomer known for his book on the sphere.</note> describing the sphere through merely imaginary lines; and even those invented by Vitruvius for Architecture, which never existed before, but are only accustomed to occur in the practice of reality. Such things, therefore, are one's own inventions, and should not be called fictions; for those are to be regarded as falsehoods. But let Gassendi find falsehoods in my writings if he can: for I either prove the things that are therein to be true, or I will candidly acknowledge my error.

### Text 14. Gassendi, page 92.

> *It certainly occurred to me to wonder, when you had said among other things: "They extend the Monochord from the summit of the Empyrean heaven down to the base," etc. I wondered, I say, not a little with what words he would take that. And who are "they," my dear Marin? Does the one and only Robert have a plurality in his belly? For I am certain that you never received this from anyone except from Robert alone. Why then do you pretend, and falsely in this place...*

<meta>This page continues the heated debate between Robert Fludd and Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd defended his views on the nature of the atmosphere and spiritual inhabitants against Gassendi's skepticism. Here, he pivots to defending his personal reputation against charges of plagiarism and vanity, specifically regarding his "World Monochord" and his interpretations of the Book of Job.</meta>

# Fludd’s Response

...in that place you display your Latinity by saying *extendunt* <note>they stretch out</note> instead of *extendit* <note>he stretches out</note>? For I will boldly say this: that you received this division of the Monochord <note>The "World Monochord" is Fludd's famous diagram representing the universe as a musical instrument tuned by God.</note> from Robert alone, and from no one else. Thus he [Gassendi] speaks. Regarding these things, I can surely say nothing else except that Robert sufficiently indicates with what applause he embraces his own inventions, he who trumpets them abroad with such great contention, stirring up fame with his brass. I will not say that such a reproach appears childish; I will not say that such boasting appears nearly Thrasonic. <note>A "Thrasonic" boast refers to Thraso, a braggart soldier in the plays of the Roman playwright Terence; it means someone who is excessively vainglorious.</note>

### Fludd.

It is an argument for childishness, or certainly for egregious negligence or malice in someone, to twist the sufficiently clear speech of others into an indirect or bad sense, and to either neglect the meaning of Authors or knowingly refuse to understand it. I ask you, Reader, if you had ever read my book against Mersenne, <note>Marin Mersenne was a French polymath and a fierce critic of Fludd’s mystical "chemical" philosophy.</note> would you not perceive that he has taken whole pages word-for-word from my writings and expressed them in his own, and has usurped my inventions for himself under the name of plurality? For he says: "others write these things; others write those," when nevertheless all those things were composed by me alone. What? Therefore, because I accuse Mersenne of this matter—that he falsely attributes my writings to others—have I become affiliated with either childishness or Thrasonic boasting? We acknowledge Virgil to be easily the prince among Latin Poets, and yet he himself once sang in a similar case: *I wrote these little verses, another took the honors.* <note>Original: "Hos ego versiculos feci, tulit alter honores." A famous line attributed to Virgil after another poet, Bathyllus, claimed credit for Virgil’s work.</note> But was this saying ignominious to him? Or because he trumpeted this, must some Thrasonic boasting or childishness be deservedly imputed to him immediately for that reason? But let me approach even closer. I was not moved against Mersenne for any reason because he concealed my name; but because he had attributed many pages, which lie there word-for-word copied from my *Macrocosm*, to other unknown men, and not to me. For by this very act he seemed to argue and signify to the world that I had gathered those things word-for-word from those Authors to whom he had assigned them: and in this way, I had falsely usurped the works of others as my own. Let anyone who does not desire to twist my words in a bad sense read that passage, and seriously consider those things which he has read, and he will perceive immediately that this was entirely my meaning and my intention: namely, not to boast of my inventions, but rather to vindicate and defend my fame from the theft of another's late-night labors or writings. Which certainly, even with the whole world as judge, is plausible in any sensible person; nor can it rightly be called childish or Thrasonic.

## Text. 15. Gassendi page 98 & 99.

Namely, he wishes to teach you, first concerning matter, that his chaos was confirmed both by Solomon, when he said that the hand of the Almighty made or created the world out of unformed or invisible matter; and by Job, when he said that God revealed the foundations out of Darkness, brought back the Deadly Shadow into Light, stretched out the North over the empty and void, and hung the earth upon nothing, etc. There are interpreters present who take these passages far differently. However much Fludd may deride their interpretations, etc.

### Fludd.

Certainly the aforementioned texts were translated in that way by Tremellius, Pagninus, and Saint Jerome. <note>These were prominent biblical translators; Jerome produced the Latin Vulgate, while Tremellius and Pagninus produced influential Reformation-era translations.</note> But do you not see here (Candid Reader) what a miserable escape our refuter uses—though he is a Roman Theologian—when he refuses to refute those places alleged from the sacred page in any other way than by a rejection of the interpretation or translation, even that of Saint Jerome, which the Roman Church holds and esteems in the first place? For he says: *There are still interpreters who take these passages far differently.* As if indeed the interpretation of Saint Jerome were incongruous and hardly consistent with itself!

## Text. 16. Gassendi page 104.

If Fludd exhibits the World Monochord as a playful thing, and as something ingenious, I embrace it most humanely; but because he defends it with such constancy as being entirely natural, I have no reason to approve it.

### Fludd.

I do not say that I hold my Monochord to be a natural thing <note>Meaning a literal, physical object in the sky.</note>; but I do not blush at all to assert that it is a most exact symbol of worldly nature, and a type of truth itself: no differently than the heaven is represented in Circles, at this or that degree of longitude or latitude, or bodies by Geometric figures, etc. And we prove it thus: We see that, the more one proceeds step by step on my Monochord, and as if through the steps of the musical system, namely from A to B and C, the sharper the sound is always rendered; and in the exact middle, we find the natural position of the most perfect consonance, the *Diapason* <note>The Octave.</note>, to sound to the whole as two to one: and consequently it is most evident that within the interval of the *Diapason* consonance, the other two musical consonances, namely the *Diapente* <note>The Perfect Fifth.</note> and *Diatessaron* <note>The Perfect Fourth.</note>, are comprehended. However, that there are no more consonances in the nature of things, even if a sixth chord is noticed to ring out with them in some way, we have discovered and confirmed by experience. For however one might exquisitely observe all those intervals between A and a, or G and g, yet he will find no other consonance besides those. But these consonances are composed of various intervals which, being distant from one another, offer to return a different tone. And let this be by reason of the measurement of the string, to which the proportion of the air adapts itself. The Actor, however, is the vibrating Spirit itself. By which things it is argued that by ascending from the earth (in the manner of a pyramid’s ascent from the base toward the cone, which space we always find more narrow) into water, which is a thinner substance than earth; and from water into air, which is subtler than water; and from air into fire, which is rarer than air itself; and from fire into the ether, which is nobler and subtler than the element of fire; and from the ether into the Empyrean Spirit, which surpasses and excels the ether itself in purity and rarity, etc. the same proportions are designated in nature, and the same intervals in the worldly Spirit, which are found in the art or the string of the Monochord. Therefore, by diligent observation it will appear that in intervals of such a natural system, there is as if the same difference which exists in the system of sensible Harmony. The worldly Spirit is the medium or organ: the strings are the celestial rays: which the more they descend and are immersed in duller matter, the more they seem to give forth duller sounds, and more silent ones, and as if pauses or tones whispering occultly: and consequently they are more grave/low, because they are more weighed down by matter; but they are sharper/higher the more they find the Spirit or matter obedient and subtle. For there they are stronger, and give forth sounds that are more sharp and rare. The Actor is the Word, whose power is in those rays, and he strikes and vibrates them, as it were, more or less according to his [will]...

We conclude therefore, according to the aforementioned words of Solomon, that there is in the mundane Spirit a divine harmony ordered by institution, which can either be demonstrated by the contemplation of such a Monochord—since it encompasses the entire mystery of the Musical system—or there is plainly no mundane harmony at all. For the harmony of the elements is considered more in proportion than in evident sounds, since no consonance can occur without proportion; therefore both proportion and Harmonic consonance, whether natural or the artificial kind which imitates nature, can be drawn from this Monochord of mine. Furthermore, what kind of harmony exists in the World Spirit can be gathered from those intervals which the Agent in nature uses between extreme rawness and exact cooking or maturity—that is, in the overcoming or abundance of the **Sulphurous** nature in **Mercury**. <note>In alchemy, Sulphur and Mercury represent the active/combustible and passive/fluid principles of matter.</note> And by this reasoning, we see the air and the seasons altered from state to state, and as if from tone to tone, and from temperament to temperament, according to the approach and retreat of the Sun, or the movement of the winds.

Certainly, I commend the intellect of this adversary of mine, who seeks with such ardor to be illuminated, as it were, by the rays of every science, and affects such diligence. I do not envy him this good inclination; rather, I say, I commend it. But to this objection which he makes against my opinion, I respond: there is no sublunary air <note>Air below the level of the moon, i.e., in the earthly realm.</note> that does not enjoy a portion of the ether, whether sparingly or copiously. We boldly state that pure blood itself is nothing other than condensed air. Indeed, this air is more or less abundant with the influences of heaven, and insofar as it is the spiritual vehicle of celestial influences, it is the "food of life" for every creature. Whence a certain Wise Man said: *There is in the air a hidden food of life.* <note>original: "Est in aere occultus vitae cibus." A common alchemical maxim attributed to Michael Sendivogius.</note> And because flesh is made from coagulated blood, and blood from thickened air in which the virtue of life resides, Moses says that the human soul and the life of other animals is in the blood. 

Therefore, these things being duly considered, it must be observed with diligence that if air—which is the chariot of the soul—becomes "specified" before it concurs or is adapted for human nourishment (for example, if it is in wheat, or a bean, or an apple, or a sheep, or an ox, or a hen, etc.), it completely loses its "Catholic" <note>original: "Catholicam," used here in the sense of its Greek root "katholikos," meaning universal or general.</note> nature. However, before it had penetrated into any specific substance for its vivification and nutrition, the food of life was contained within it, joined with its vehicle, ready to perform the act of life and multiplication in this or that species. For the "Universal Soul of the World" <note>Anima Mundi.</note> is ready to pour out the common nourishment of life to all creatures; and the creatures themselves, with a certain "Tantalean" appetite, <note>A reference to Tantalus from Greek myth, who was eternally hungry and thirsty; here it refers to the intense "craving" of nature for life-force.</note> gape at that life-giving cup of universal nature, and greedily seek that gift of vegetation, multiplication, and preservation. 

As soon as this treasure is received by a species or an individual of a species, it suddenly leaves behind and loses, as was said before, its Universal property and name, because it is now contracted and reduced into a special or particular nature. For this reason, it is impossible for blood made from air, or flesh from blood (insofar as it is a substance from a specific juice), to migrate into the essence of another species or another specific nature. For although we see that the flesh of animals and the pulp or juice of vegetables evidently and sensibly contribute to bodily nutrition (since "like nourishes like," it is no wonder if thick blood nourishes blood, and consequently flesh nourishes flesh), we do not say that "flesh" in general belongs to the internal and specific nature of man, but only to the external. Hence it happens that the same specified juice can nourish other animals bodily as well as men, even though it does not nourish their specific nature. 

It is required, therefore, that this soul or food of life, which is given successively and immediately to every creature, be spiritually nourished and fed by the Universal Soul of the World, as if by its own Universal and non-specified "like." For such Universal food is the true fuel of life, which gives life to the species, continues it, and multiplies its "like" within it; because it is Universal and not yet specified—but rather "virginal," contaminated by no other species yet, nor infected or imbued by any foreign nature from which it is received. 

Therefore, these things being seriously weighed, it will appear for certain that as soon as the air and the treasure contained within it in bread or meat is eaten by a man, it is examined by the exact Alchemy of human nature. The purer part of the whole nourishment—namely, that aerial portion of nourishment with its treasure—is drawn from the impure and useless (now purified) to the liver <note>original: "hepar"</note>, by which and in which it is finally dyed into a bloody nature. The rest, being as it were excrementitious, is expelled either through the intestines or the bile ducts, or thrust into the Spleen, the gall bladder, or the bladder as superfluous and unnecessary for nutrition. Thus, the nourishment from specified air now being reduced into human blood...
