# To the Gassendian Exercises, Part II of the Third Section.

...then from it, flesh emerges, thicker indeed (namely from the air specified before). From these things it is clear that such a specific juice is adapted only for the structure of the human body; but for life and the spirit of animals, and especially of rational beings, it contributes very little. For since the specific nature of man consists in his internal and not his external parts, therefore another air, another ether, and another fuel for the spiritual life—the universal kind, of course—is required. <note>Fludd uses "Catholic" (catholicus) in its original Greek sense meaning "universal" or "general," referring to a spirit that pervades all of nature, rather than the religious denomination.</note> And since this universal spiritual nourishment abounds in superfluities no less than the corporeal or "specified" kind, its more smoky part is expelled, while the celestial treasure is first retained with the purer portion of its airy vehicle (which serves as its carriage). For just as there is no passage from heaven to earth without a medium, so it is necessary that the more excellent portion of that medium—like a vital spark or vehicle—be coagulated in the left ventricle of the heart and the great artery, taking on the appearance of blood. In this blood, according to the sense of the Sacred Text, resides life or the soul. <note>Fludd refers to Leviticus 17:11: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood."</note> Hence Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts are attributed.</note> said quite wisely: "The soul of man is carried in this manner: Mind in the soul, soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body. The spirit, diffused through the veins and arteries, moves the living creature everywhere." Nor is it surprising if the same appearance of blood is present in the arteries as in the veins, since both are, regarding their external nature, made of the same subject—namely, air. Yet one air differs from another in specific property, no differently than one essence of life differs from another, insofar as it is found to be foreign and taken from a specified subject; but into the arteries, it descends immediately from the universal source in its naked, universal, and virginal nature. Do we not likewise see waters coagulated or gathered from the clouds in a universal manner, and others differing from them in property, such as those seen to spring from the earth infected by the nature of various minerals? I conclude, therefore, that I have extracted the airy nature of wheat or bread, and I have perceived that, once concoction <note>An alchemical and early medical term for digestion or refinement by heat.</note> is complete, it is the chief food of the blood: and that pure blood is in effect nothing other than coagulated air. And I proved this both from the magnetic attraction of its redness, and because with slight heat, that wheaten humor, having turned to a red color, passed into air: and also because all that liquor was nothing but a volatile salt. Indeed, all Philosophers agree on this opinion: namely, that the salt of nitre <note>Saltpeter, which early scientists believed carried a vital "aerial food" necessary for life and combustion.</note> is procreated from the pure substance of the air. Finally, I have learned through manifest experience that the vegetable power of growth is situated in it. When these things are rightly considered, it is no wonder if invisible air, by the attractive power of animal nature, migrates into a bloody appearance, just as in wheat or bread it migrates into vegetable juice; which then, being thus specified, is changed into the substance of blood, both venous and arterial: and that such blood, by the excitation of the celestial sulfur’s act, is tinged into a ruddy color.

### *Text 21. Gassendi page 131.*

> But if this arterial blood were nothing else than spirit led from the air into the left ventricle through the venous artery, would that, I ask, occur?

->Fludd.<-

But how can blood be introduced from the left ventricle into that venous artery through the heart's septum, which he says is porous and perforated? For the three semilunar valves, which receive air inside through inspiration, are closed from the outside and open from the inside. Whence the way is denied for the vital blood made or converted in the left ventricle of the heart to enter and fill that venous artery; rather, that light blood is selected from the air entering and exiting. Furthermore, if he says that blood of this kind can be supplied from the Aorta; that task indeed seems possible, insofar as those two mitral valves, leading to the Aorta in the left cavity of the heart and attached at its orifice, are open on the outside and closed on the inside. Therefore, just as the entrance of vital blood from the left ventricle into the Aorta is granted, so its exit from the Aorta back into the same cavity is utterly prohibited.

### *Text 22. Gassendi, same page.*

> For what other reason can the texture of the arteries be more solid than that of the veins, unless it is because they are the vehicles of a subtler and hotter humor?

->Fludd.<-

This proves my case. For if that arterial blood is subtler and hotter than venous blood, it is certain that it has its origin from somewhere other than the venous source. For if such blood proceeded from a hepatic source <note>The liver, which traditional Galenic medicine held was the source of all blood.</note> as if from an elemental one, then I do not see by what reasoning it would be rendered hotter in its nature than that blood in the vena cava. But if he says that it receives this addition of heat from the heart, as if from an ethereal source, I say this is impossible; first, because the nature of the heart by itself is not hotter than the liver. For if this were so, a man would always be in a fever. Second, if the blood received an addition of heat from the heart, then that addition would not be natural, but acquired. Indeed, if such a circulation of blood were to occur—namely, from the venous kind into the arterial (as he himself says)—then, by reason of this, the blood would be of equal composition in substance throughout the entire body, and not at all different in heat. Therefore it follows, as if confessed, that this kind of arterial blood arises from the universal source of life or forms, both by reason of its subtlety and its heat. But be that as it may; (as he says later) let it be that the subtler part of the blood—by penetrating the mediastinum of the heart as if by *diapedesis* <note>The passage of blood cells through the intact walls of the capillaries.</note>—enters its left cavity, and the remainder is sent into the arterial vein to nourish the lungs: but I ask of him, whether it be proportionate in nature that heavy blood, and as it were the more fecal part of the vena cava (for he says the subtle and lighter part is extracted), ought to concur for the nutrition of the lungs; when rather light blood is required for such a work, so that the substance of the lungs might be rendered lighter and more agile in its motion and act. For this reason (the Anatomists say) blood is introduced through the right auricle of the heart so that it may be prepared and thinned there, by which it is rendered a more suitable nourishment for refreshing the lungs: in which lightness and not heaviness is to be sought, so that they may more easily move up and down. But Gassendi wants thicker blood to be required for the nutrition of the lungs than for that of the flesh, as is held below in text 24.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s debate with Pierre Gassendi regarding the anatomy of the heart. On the previous page, Fludd discussed the "universal spirit" and how it enters the body. Here, he moves to a technical anatomical argument: whether blood passes through the central wall of the heart (the septum) or through the lungs, citing his colleague William Harvey.</meta>

# Fludd's Response.

...or with a certain blunt iron instrument, he had discovered porous passages in the septum <term>septum: the muscular wall separating the right and left sides of the heart</term> of the heart, which he calls "a thousand doors in the septum," though they are hidden. From this, he concludes—along with the doctors and surgeons who were present at such a dissection—that there is a transmission of blood from the right chamber to the left, even if it is imperceptible. He uses this against me, as can be seen from the text immediately preceding.

But who is ignorant, if even moderately trained in anatomy, that there are hidden passages or cavities in any of the fleshy parts of the whole body? It is through these that sweats, as well as scabby, itchy, and leprous excretions, and "morphea" <note>A skin condition involving localized patches of discolored or hardened skin.</note> and jaundice, etc., are pushed from the center toward the surface. I remember a certain surgeon boasting that he had penetrated, using a probe or a spatula with a certain irregular dilation, that wonderful "net-like plexus" <term>rete mirabile: a complex of small blood vessels</term> formed by the intertwining of the vein and artery which descends from the preparatory seminal vessels to the testicles. Because of the delicacy of the structure, this is actually impossible without violating the hidden passages, unless it happens rarely in some specific individual. 

Should we be ignorant of the fact that flesh, composed of three kinds of fibers, can be made looser and more spongy through twisting, dilation, or extension? This is no different than how a string for a lute or one made of hemp is made more hollow and porous through contraction. I believe the same thing happened during that diligent examination of the heart's partition: while those porous parts were being tested in so many ways with a metal tool. Indeed, by turning the probe here and there, we must believe that fiber is very easily stretched and divided from fiber, and a gap is made in proportion to the size of the spatula or probe. 

Furthermore, this inquiry has been frequently undertaken with great diligence by many of my colleagues, and especially by **Dr. Harvey**, a most expert anatomist. <note>original: "D. Harueo Anatomico expertissimo." This refers to William Harvey, who had recently published his discovery of the circulation of the blood in 1628. Fludd was one of the first to publicly support Harvey's theory.</note> He himself, for the sake of his case regarding the circulation of the blood, performed experiments on this matter until he was exhausted; yet, even in one out of many corpses, he never found any such thing. Neither did I, nor others who have scrutinized the septum of the heart with eyes as sharp as a lynx’s. 

Therefore, it must be concluded that even if such a thing appeared in one corpse or another in **Aix-en-Provence** <note>original: "Aquis-Sextiis." This refers to a specific anatomical demonstration witnessed by Gassendi in that city.</note> (assuming it happened without the violation of the spatula), this particular instance does not imply a universal rule. For in one man, only one kidney is found; in another, no spleen; and many other things occur that are foreign and unusual compared to ordinary human composition. But should we conclude for that reason—namely because of some defects or additions of parts in one man—that all people must necessarily be that way? Certainly, one or two examples do not prove an argument, nor does **a single swallow prove the arrival of summer.** <note>A variation of the common proverb "one swallow does not make a summer," meaning a single instance doesn't establish a trend.</note> Therefore, we will partly place no faith in the experiment brought forward by Gassendi, and partly, if it were granted to him, we say that one particular does not demonstrate a general rule. 

In general, we recognize—and we speak from experience—that Gassendi’s assertion is utterly false. Accordingly, we do not blush to assert that the septum of the heart was not ordained by Nature for the function named by Gassendi. For if this were established as law, it would follow that there would be no difference between arterial and venous blood. Indeed, what is worse and more absurd, his opinion expressed in the following text, based on that experiment, argues the contrary by reason of its impossibility. For he gives the following reason for his assertion in the next text:

### Text 30. Gassendi, same page.

> It is indeed likely that a subtler portion of the blood is sucked out, as it were, through this septum and filtered by compression, while the thicker part, along with the "sooty" residue <term>fuligine: "sooty vapors," a traditional term for waste products of metabolic "burning"</term> left there, enters the open arterial vein to nourish and sustain the substance of the lungs, etc.

### Fludd.

I revealed the absurdity of this proposition above regarding **Text 22**, but since a fuller revelation of this matter is appropriate for resolving this doubt, I will speak a little more clearly on this point. Supported partly by the authority of anatomists and taught partly by my own inquiry, I understand that the right chamber of the heart is called "bloody" because it contributes to the purification and thinning of the blood. Just as it has various organic parts, so its "ear" <term>auricula: the atrium of the heart</term> serves to hold the blood sent from the *vena cava* into that chamber. 

But the *vena cava* attached to it transfers blood from the liver to that chamber, so that there it may be better prepared and purified by the **third concoction** <note>In ancient medicine, "concoction" was the process by which the body "cooked" or refined food into blood and then into tissues.</note> according to the needs of the nourished part, which is the lung—the substance of which is lighter and more airy than the other parts of the body. For if the lungs were nourished by the same thicker blood as the other parts (which are heavier in weight and substance), they would be less fit to perform their required duties, which consist of continuous motion. 

From this it is clear that a light substance naturally requires a lighter nourishment. For we are taught by experience that "like" is better nourished by that which is similar to it in both substance and quality. Is it not commonly known that hepatic or venous blood, in its thick substance, creates heavy flesh? Who then can believe that this blood—not yet purified in its heavy nature (since it is quite heavy, as can be seen from the flesh into which it thickens)—could produce something light? 

But what is even more absurd: Gassendi is not content with that venous blood in its thick nature making and nourishing the light substance of the lungs; he requires an even thicker and more dreg-filled blood to perform that task! For he says that the subtle and pure part of the venous blood is extracted and filtered through the heart’s septum to create arterial blood. Therefore, what is left over after the extraction is made must necessarily be thicker and more earthy. Consequently, he seems to conclude that "like does not make like," but the opposite: namely, that the thick, solid, heavy, and earthy makes that which is thin, light, spongy, and airy. Thus (which is repugnant to all Philosophy), air would have to have a friendship with earth, even though those two elements are most opposed to each other in quality and substance. Therefore, how erroneous Gassendi’s opinion is in this matter can be discerned, if I am not mistaken, even by the blind.

### Text 25. Gassendi, page 137.

> To Fludd’s first question: While I would not deny that some "Vital Spirit" enters the heart with the air, who could believe that the whole of life, or the whole of the vital blood, is gathered entirely from the air? Indeed, if that were true, why do we not live on air alone, as they tell fables about **chameleons**? <note>A common ancient and medieval belief was that chameleons lived solely on air.</note> Will Fludd say that the foods we take serve only to elaborate the blood that is in the veins? What then will become of the Spirit of Life, which is also contained in foods?

### Fludd.

An answer was given to this doubt previously regarding **Text 20**: namely, that both that ethereal juice elicited from foods along with the air itself, as well as that which is simply attracted or drawn from the **Universal Air**, passes into the substance of the blood after its coagulation. However, because the condition of air mixed with ether—due to its "specification" within foods, whether animal or vegetable—is foreign to the essence or nature of the...

<summary>Fludd argues against Gassendi's claim that blood passes through the heart's septum, citing William Harvey's anatomical research to prove the septum is solid. He also challenges Gassendi's theory on lung nutrition, arguing that light organs like lungs require refined, airy nourishment rather than "thick" waste-blood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s philosophical and anatomical debate with Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd was discussing how the vital spirit is distinct from the physical nourishment provided by food. He continues here by arguing that while food builds the "tabernacle" (the physical body), the true "food of life" is drawn from a universal, spiritual source in the air.</meta>

...nourished specifically, and as a consequence, it is adapted only to nourish the tabernacle or body of the nourished creature. Therefore, we must believe that the immediate food of life is to be drawn and received from the Universal fountain of life, or the Universal—that is, common—element <note>original: "elemento Catholico, vel communi." In this context, "Catholic" refers to something universal or all-encompassing rather than the religious denomination.</note>; for the nourished creature previously had the root of its life in that simplicity. Finally, I say that the Spirit of life which is in foods—insofar as it is already specified and has taken on a particular nature—is very easily turned into the nature of natural blood, intended for the generation of the body, the multiplication of flesh, and the growth of its other parts. Hence it happens that, by means of food, the thin human body is thickened, and blood and flesh are multiplied within it. 

But it is not turned into a vital and animal <note>In 17th-century medicine, "animal" refers to the "anima" or soul/mind, relating to nerves and movement.</note> nature. It is alienated from this because of the specification of the foods, from which the Chemistry of nature is extracted. And this is why it is observed that the excessive use of food puts the vital spirits to sleep and renders them less agile. But where a sparse diet is present, there we see both the vital and animal spirits flourish and be refreshed more greatly. For the heart and the brain, always drawing the fuel of life from the Universal fountain, render a person more lively and "greener" (if I may say so) <note>original: "vitidioremq;" (viridiorem). Fludd uses "greenness" to signify vitality and life-force.</note>; such a person's body is not overly fattened by foreign and specified food. Indeed, the fumes and soot of a foreign nature hinder those spirits of life rather than helping them at all. 

But if someone should say with Gassendi: if this is so, why does a creature not live on air alone, like the Chameleon? To this I bring an objection: that thin air alone cannot nourish solid bodies. Therefore, more substantial bodies are required for this work, in which the four elements are compacted, so that like can better be procreated by like. In hunger, then, which destroys the composite <note>The "composite" refers to the unified human being of body, soul, and spirit.</note>, there is a consumption of the body; it is not a defect in the vital spirits. Furthermore, even if it were as Gassendi says—namely, that a subtly crafted part of the blood is the subject of the "vital juice" <term>latex vitalis: a term for the fluid or essence of life</term> both in the heart and the arteries—nevertheless, I see no reason why someone who eats pork would not simply attract and add a porcine condition to their life, etc. That the matter stands differently is clear: and consequently, the specified juice of foods, however much it may contain air with the vital ether, contributes very little to life and the vital spirits, but only to cherishing and sustaining the body, which is the organ of life.

### Text 26. Gassendi page 138.

What will Fludd say about fish, which truly live, and yet are so far from leading a life by air that they lose their life by air—or rather, the air extinguishing it? Does their life not consist of something other than inhaled air?

->Fludd’s Response.<-

It must be known that among animals, some consist of a greater portion of fire, such as quadrupeds and man himself. In those where fire has dominion, they require a more thin and airy food of life. For air approaches more closely to fire in nature. From this it happens that thick and condensed air <gloss>it</gloss> usually... <note>Fludd notes that dense air is harmful to fire-dominant creatures.</note> while thin air is very pleasing to their life. 

Hence it is that, although water is nothing other than dense air, nevertheless, insofar as it is contrary to fire, it quickly suffocates fiery creatures. But on the contrary, cold animals, such as fish, require a thicker medium in which to live, or from which they may take or swallow the food of their life. I would therefore like Gassendi to know that, although water is a thicker medium than subtle air, nevertheless, insofar as it is nothing other than thick or condensed air, it must also contain subtle and rare air within itself—not differently than how thin air contains vapors, clouds, and waters or rains within itself. 

But I will teach Gassendi that the matter is so, and I am instructed by a certain common experiment. When I was staying in the city of Nîmes <note>original: "civitate Nemoßiana"</note> in Languedoc, I had gone outside the gates on a certain burning summer day, and wishing to swim in a certain river not far from the city for the sake of washing and refreshing myself, I submerged my head with my whole body in the waters. During this act, I struck together two flints which I held in my hands; from their collision, I heard a horrendous noise under the waters. This certainly could not have happened if air (which is the medium of the sense of hearing) were not in the waters. 

Now, the reason why fish die so quickly in the air is that common air is a spirit too thin for their vital sustenance, and too hot in its quality. For since this air is composed of moisture as the passive part and heat as the active part, there is too little moisture in the air, and that which is there is too thin to sustain the nature of aquatic creatures; and vice-versa, there is too much moisture in water for the subtle spirits of terrestrial creatures. This is also why men ascending to the other extreme—namely, to a place closer to the sphere of fire, such as Mount Olympus and places even higher in the world—can scarcely live or refresh the spirits of their life because of the thinness and rarity of the air in those places, and indeed because of the excessive heat, as experience has proven. 

But I will touch on the matter in a few words. Prudent Mother Nature has circumscribed each of her products within certain limits, within which, as in its own medium, she has left the true and genuine food for the sufficient sustenance of each life; but outside or beyond those limits, she has placed destruction. Therefore, all things must either remain in their native seat according to the prescription of their Mother, or incur the danger of their life. It is no wonder, therefore, that fish lose their life outside the medium appropriated to them. Finally, it is clear from the dilation and contraction of the hearts of recently killed fish that they inhale air just like other animals, since they similarly have their own lungs <note>Fludd likely refers here to gills, which he identifies functionally as lungs.</note>. Their life, therefore, comes from nowhere else than from that air of their own proper medium.

### Text 27. Gassendi, same page.

What will he say about the fetus in the womb? Does it not truly live a life? And yet it does not draw it from the air, since its nostrils and mouth are closed.

->Fludd’s Response.<-

Here lies a mystery. For since blood is from air, and can very easily be reduced into vaporous air by internal heat, there is no doubt that air, occultly enclosed in both arterial and venous blood, is gradually excited by the heat of the body so that, in the form of a subtle vapor, it provides food for the fetus, convenient and sufficient to sustain that life which it has in the womb until its organs are fully completed and it emerges as a perfect infant, capable of living a perfect life. For then it immediately begins to kick, and having broken the membranes in which it was enclosed, it seeks an exit so that it may acquire other nourishment and other air, which it desires for respiration. 

Wherefore it is probable that, in the meantime, that subtle and airy vapor of the arterial blood in the woman provides the fuel for life and the specific Spirit, just as the venous blood supplies the growth of the body. Furthermore, there is no doubt that nature has established infinite porous passages in the body and its membranes, insensible and hardly perceivable by human eyes, through which even Macrocosmic air <note>The air of the great world (the universe) as opposed to the Microcosm (the human body).</note> secretly penetrates and is introduced even to the center of the body. By means of this, joined together with the smoke of that Microcosm, the nourishment of life and vegetation is provided to the fetus. Finally, we say with the wise man <note>Likely referring to the Book of Job 10:10-12.</note> that the Spirit of the Almighty is even in the center of the seed, which originally gives life to the fetus, and whose task it is to fashion its composition. Whence elsewhere: "As you have poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese, you have clothed me with breath," etc. Is it not clear enough, then, that the fetus draws its life from air?

<meta>This page continues the heated debate between the English physician and mystic Robert Fludd and the French philosopher Pierre Gassendi. Fludd is defending his theory that the "vital spirit" is a celestial substance drawn from the air, while Gassendi attempts to provide more mechanical, biological explanations for respiration. In the previous section, Fludd argued that the true food of life comes from a universal spiritual source rather than physical food alone.</meta>

### Fludd’s Reply, Text 28. Gassendi, same folio.

Finally, if plants also live, as is the common opinion, do they breathe through a mouth or a nose? Do they draw the ethereal Spirit <note>original: "Spiritum æthereum." Fludd refers to a celestial, life-giving substance believed to permeate the air.</note> into a heart and arteries with the air? It is enough if they truly contain life within themselves, even though no respiration is necessary for them to have it.

->Fludd<-

Here Gassendi seems to be fighting his own shadow. For what does this have to do with our purpose? I am discussing animals; he, however, discusses plants. But let him wander off course <note>original: "extra oleas," literally "outside the olive trees," a classical idiom for straying from the subject.</note> as much as he likes. Does he really believe that there is no inhalation or exhalation except where there are nostrils and a mouth? Surely Gassendi will understand—if he wishes to look at the matter with a slightly sharper gaze—that air is inhaled through the pores of every part of the entire body, and consequently, it must necessarily be exhaled. Thus, it should also be known that the appetite of every living thing—be it animal, vegetable, or mineral—is most ready to attract and drink in that gift of life granted to it by the Powers Above, by which it lives and is clothed and adorned with the power and quantity appropriate to its species. 

Therefore, this statement of Gassendi’s is ill-considered: *it is enough if they truly contain life within themselves, even though no respiration, etc.* As if, indeed, anything could live without a medium, or as if a celestial nature could be introduced into a body without an aerial vehicle! But I would have him understand that a spark of life is granted to every composite being endowed with life for its existence, which seeks its like and always gasps after it. And for that reason, by a certain magnetic force, it continually attracts its like from heaven to itself for its help and comfort. Since this cannot be obtained without a medium, it secretly attracts the air, and with the air, that power of life. Therefore, air also concurs in the composition of a plant, which by coagulation is condensed and grows into a woody mass. This is evident from the fact that almost the entire wood is found to be converted into air by burning. Thus, that celestial, Universal <note>original: "Catholica," used here in its Greek sense of "universal" or "all-pervading."</note> power—ready to be converted into any species of any nature—is specified so that it grants life and vegetation to the species it occupies. Now, finally, Gassendi lays down four reasons, or foundations, to demonstrate why a human might breathe.

->*Text 29. Gassendi, page 139.*<-

*If these things be so, why should a man not be able to breathe? First, so that the seeds of heat lurking in the blood may be excited and cherished, in the same way that a flame is usually drawn from a coal by the power of bellows. This has always seemed to me the primary necessity of respiration in living things that move.*

->Fludd<-

In this, he seems expressly to support my opinion. For my view is that a spark of life added to a spark is the cause of the multiplication and preservation of the ray of life.

->*Text 30. Gassendi, ibid.*<-

*Second, so that—lest this heat be stretched too far—there may be a certain continuous arrival of cooler air, by which it may become more tempered, etc.*

->Fludd<-

As if indeed Gassendi, since he seems to be such a great Alchemist <note>original: "Alchymista." Fludd is likely being sarcastic, as Gassendi was generally critical of alchemy.</note>, does not understand that the fifth essence of life <note>original: "quintam illam vitæ essentiam," or the Quintessence—the purest, most balanced element beyond the physical four.</note> is of such a temperate quality that it can bind even any irregular Element that breaks out from the limits of temperament with the chains of peace and harmony! For this fifth Element, by reason of its exact balance, is the master, guardian, and ruler of the other four—provided that its entry into the body is not denied or violently hindered. What? Does Gassendi believe that a man breathing long enough in a dry bath, where the temperature of the air is actually quite scorching, cannot live for lack of that cooling? Experience certainly testifies to the contrary. Truly, heat is required more for the necessity of life than coldness, since life consists in radical moisture and innate heat <note>term: "radical moisture and innate heat" (humidum radicale & calido innato). In ancient medicine, these were the two "fuels" of life; aging was seen as the gradual drying and cooling of the body.</note>. Furthermore, that celestial light or fire in the blood is not so burning; rather, on the contrary, it is very temperate. Besides, its aerial vehicle is moist, by which that fiery dryness is taken away, and it is internally warm, which in effect usually cools less.

->*Text 31. Gassendi, page 139.*<-

*Third, so that a purer portion of the air (let it be the ethereal spirit if you please) mixed together with the blood may create arterial blood, which for this reason becomes more subtle and spiritual, etc.*

->Fludd<-

In this, we both agree. For it falls exactly within my opinion, and he speaks as if with my own mouth, as is clear from the preceding sections. And yet, nevertheless, he says these things against me.

->*Text 32. Gassendi, ibid. and page 140.*<-

*I wonder, however, why Fludd should fear confusion in a human work from this, he who himself mixes light and Spirit into all things without fear of confusion.*

->Fludd<-

Why should I fear confusion there, where the power of all nature is found, all its harmony, and the perfection of life, peace, freedom, and divine goodness? Is there any confusion where the celestial light or fire—the spark of being—meets with its own Spirit in a symphonic proportion of life? Here the vital or innate heat rejoices and delights in its radical moisture. Therefore, no confusion is to be feared in this place, and consequently, those words are empty.

->*Text 33. Gassendi, page 140.*<-

*Fourth, so that the soots <note>original: "fuligines," referring to the waste products or "smoke" produced by the "fire" of the heart.</note> or impure remains of the blood purified in the heart may be coughed out? For unless they were poured out into the air by exhalation, they would immediately suffocate the heart itself, just as smoke usually does to a lit torch unless you give it the freedom to exhale.*

->Fludd<-

It must first be granted that hepatic blood <note>original: "sanguis Iecorarius," blood originating from the liver.</note> is prepared and purified in the left chamber of the heart in the manner that Gassendi describes. As if, indeed, the more dross-filled portion of the blood could be so easily reduced into a vaporous soot that it could be expelled through exhalation! Secondly, it must first be granted that such blood is "sifted" (as he says) through the septum of the heart for such a task. Both of these points we utterly deny. Then he concludes that unless such impure soots of the blood were poured out into the air by exhalation, the heart would be suffocated. But would anyone believe that the Spirit emitted from the lungs by exhalation is the grossness of the blood? That exhaled spirit is actually far thinner and lighter, while the blood-dross is far denser and heavier; indeed, it is denser than the blood itself, or rather thicker than the thickness of the air previously inhaled. These things are impossible.

He dismisses the idea that the primary purpose of breath is to cool the heart or expel "sooty" blood waste, insisting instead on a mystical, balanced "quintessence" as the source of life.</summary>

# To the Exercises of Gassendi, Section III. Part II.

But now he approaches the examination of the third question, which is this: Why were four seminal vessels <note>original: "vasa seminaria." These are the blood vessels (veins and arteries) believed at the time to supply the materials for the creation of seed/semen.</note>—that is, two arteries and two veins—bestowed upon man for generation?

### Text 34. Gassendi, pages 140 & 141.

And perhaps it might not be absurd to attribute life to the seed (certainly, I myself once dreamed that the "little soul" <note>original: "animulam." A diminutive form of 'soul,' suggesting a tiny spark of life.</note> of the child was nothing other than a small portion of the soul of its parent; though I always excepted the **Rational soul**, since sacred faith dictates that it is not passed down by the parents but is drawn from nothing and infused into the body by God alone). Nevertheless, I do not know how I could be persuaded that all the blood which flows from the arteries into the seed is the life-giving soul, rather than just a certain "flower" of its most refined breath.

->Fludd.<-

<margin>Job 33.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 9.</margin>
What? Is it because we said that the food of the soul or life is drawn from outside that it is therefore not from God? Nor do I remember ever reading that axiom in the Sacred Pages—namely, that the soul is not drawn from the parent, but is drawn from nothing and infused into the body by God alone. I do not say that I have read that the soul was created from nothing, but throughout the Holy Scriptures we read that God and the Word are the fountain and spring of lives. But if the breath of life is from God, if life is in the Word, if the inspiration of the Almighty gives life to all things, it is absurd to believe that nothing can be in God, who is all in all and the absolute truth. For what is more foolish than that? In God we live, move, and have our being: therefore, do we live in "nothing"? But why and how, I ask, since the soul is life itself, is it said to be made "from nothing"? 

But he admits that the rational soul is from God, but not the vital soul. Yet the sacred text says this: *The Spirit of God made me, and the inspiration of the Almighty gave me life.* And elsewhere: *As you do not know the way of the Spirit, nor how the bones are formed in the womb of a pregnant woman; so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things, etc.* Therefore, the Spirit of life and growth is from God. Whence also the Prophet says: *Behold, I will send spirit into you and you shall live, and I will give you sinews and flesh, etc.* By these it is proved that the divine power, which gives life to the father, is also the immediate author of the multiplication of the father's species. 

Finally, I did not say that the whole of the arterial blood is the power of life, but I affirmed that the celestial secret of life lay hidden in such blood, and that it took on the specific nature of the thing nourished. Afterward, flowing from the artery through that wonderful network <note>original: "plexum." Likely referring to the pampiniform plexus, a network of veins and arteries in the spermatic cord.</note> with its spiritual vehicle or "most refined arterial flower," it mixes itself with the subtle physical substance emitted from the venous vessel. To this physical substance, it relates exactly as the soul does to the body, or heaven to the earth. For it builds itself a physical palace in the mother’s womb.

<margin>Psalm 139.</margin>
<margin>Job 10.</margin>
Whence the Psalmist says: *You possessed my kidneys from the time you covered me in my mother’s womb.* And Job: *Did you not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews; you showed me kindness with life, and your visitation preserved my spirit, etc.* From these it is clear that the divine power, or the author of life, is in the seed and works to construct the human palace, and that human life is preserved by his constant visitation.

### Text 35. Gassendi, page 141.

I had hoped Fludd would explain to us (as the logic of the problem he proposed seemed to promise) why there were four seminal vessels rather than two? Why one of the veins should be drawn from the emulgent branch <note>original: "ramo emulgente." This refers to the renal vein.</note>? etc.

->Fludd.<-

Was it not enough for me to have said that a fetus cannot be formed except from the exact mixture of the spiritual sperm with the specific physical sperm? For this reason, a venous vessel was required along with an arterial one on both sides, so that the complete mixture of the species might be conducted to both testicles, and also so that the right side of the fetus and the members contained within it might differ from those on the left. As for the fact that one spermatic vein springs from the renal vein, this happens because of its convenience with the other parts touching it—namely, so that the position of one should not get in the way of the other.

### Text 36. Gassendi, page 141.

However, I would ask whether that arterial blood is still corporeal enough that some of it could suffice to form the physical parts, at least the more delicate ones? And does not the venous blood also contain some ethereal spirit and "blessed Light," which might be spent upon the soul?

->Fludd.<-

I said before that only the "flower" of the arterial blood is enclosed in the arterial vessel, in which I say the spark of life exists just as the spirit is in the body. Therefore, the purer flower of the arterial blood is the seat of the human spirit. Regarding the second part of this text, I also said before that this specific spirit has no commerce with the essential spirit of the parent, but only—for the reason mentioned above—concurs to create the "natural faculty" and the liver-blood <note>original: "sanguinem iecorarium." Blood produced by the liver, which ancient medicine believed was the source of nutrition.</note> of the person nourished, or the fetus. Gassendi objects to many other small reasons of mine there, but since they are of no consequence, I knowingly and wisely omit them as frivolous, so that I may move on to more mature matters. Nevertheless, I must respond to the "tail end" of that chapter (to repel all disgrace from myself), since I feel the spurs of his assertion piercing to the quick. It is this:

### Text 37. Gassendi, page 143.

See, consequently, how brilliantly he plays with the spiritual and mystical bread in the British Churches and others of that kind, near the end of the book.

->Fludd.<-

<margin>In the Treatise on the Soul of the World.</margin>
These are my words: "And we say that the Host <note>original: "hostia." The bread used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> commonly used is nothing but a mere type <note>original: "typus." A symbolic representation or foreshadowing.</note> of the true Rock and the spiritual body of Christ, and not the essential reality itself. But in our British Churches, the matter is handled far differently, for they distribute bread and wine in their Lord’s Suppers in memory of his body and blood suffering death, he who first offered and revealed the mystery of the resurrection to the world by means of that divine spirit, etc." 

What (I pray) can be gathered from this? How am I "playing so brilliantly" with the spiritual and mystical bread in the British Churches when I assert that they administer the bread and wine not as the real body and blood of Christ, but in memory of them? On the contrary, I would rather be playing with it in the Roman Churches—if I desired to play with any religion (which is far from my mind!)—since they are accustomed to wrongly take the host (namely, the wine and bread) for the real body and blood.

Here, in the following chapter—namely the 20th—Gassendi, not without justice, dismisses and wards off from me that suspicion of **Atheism**, **Heresy**, and **Evil Magic** <note>original: "Cacomagiæ." <meta>This page continues the heated intellectual exchange between the English physician Robert Fludd and the French philosopher Pierre Gassendi. Having previously discussed the biological mechanisms of life, the debate now shifts toward Fludd’s personal character, his religious orthodoxy, and his mystical definitions of angels and "Genii" (guiding spirits). Fludd is defending himself against charges that his blending of alchemy, Neoplatonism, and Christianity is a dangerous form of heresy.</meta>

# Fludd's Response,

### Text 38. Gassendi, page 144.

As far as I am concerned, I do not take him for an **Evil Magician**, <note>original: "Cacomagum." From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'magos' (magician), a term used to distinguish dark sorcery from 'natural magic.'</note> nor do I believe him to be entirely an **Atheist**. However, I suspect that he does not merely disagree with our religion, but for that reason ought to be called by us a **heretic**—that is, one who is **heterodox**, <note>original: "έτερόδοξος"; someone holding an opinion different from the established or "orthodox" doctrine.</note> and so forth. For it is clear even from this that he is not an Atheist: he is constantly singing the praises of some divine nature, and he employs the testimonies of Holy Scripture not just occasionally, but everywhere.

### Fludd.

At this point, I confess that I owe him no small thanks for his just and honest opinion of me in certain matters.

### Text 39. Gassendi, page 145.

But because he understands the divine nature in that particular way of his—because he is the author of its "composition" with that spirit he has described; because he makes such a compound into the Christ or the Messiah; because he wishes for angels and souls to be "particles" of the same, and other similar things which follow from what has been said so far—since these things are clearly **heterogeneous** <note>original: "heterogenia"; meaning foreign or fundamentally different in kind from the sacred religion.</note> to our sacred religion, who would not think his opinion more dangerous than Atheism itself?

### Fludd.

<margin>Ephesians 1. Colossians 2.</margin>
If I should say that the Word was made flesh, and much more, was united with the spirit in the composition of the world; that such a compound is the Messiah; that the limbs of a man are the limbs of Christ, and his body the temple of the Holy Spirit; that the Church is the body of Christ, and the "fullness of Him who fills all in all"; that in Christ "dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily," and that an incorruptible spirit is in every thing; furthermore, that Angels and souls gush forth from the same fountain of life (for in the Word is the life and being of all things) and depend upon it by an inseparable bond: (For the Spirit of God, which gives life to all things, and consequently to Angels as well as souls, is not divided or separated from that indivisible essence which sent it out, nor consequently is life separated from the Word in which it exists)—if, I say, I should say these things, I assert boldly that all of them are in no way **heterogeneous** to sacred religion, but **homogeneous** <note>of the same kind or nature.</note>; since assertions of this kind harmonize with Holy Scripture. Therefore, by the highest right, I ought to be excused and vindicated from that erroneous and imaginary censure and opinion of Gassendi. But, since this has been more broadly demonstrated and proven elsewhere, I will not add more in this place.

### Text 40. Gassendi, page 146.

Nor am I the sort who would wish to provoke the leader, but rather I would greatly desire him to be **educated** (however much he might be expected to receive this wish of mine with loud laughter) etc.

### Fludd.

Truly, I am as far as can be from receiving Gassendi’s wish with loud laughter; on the contrary, if he can educate me in the truth in any way, I will acknowledge myself bound to him by the tightest debts of friendship and gratitude. I would most gladly submit myself to the laws of his teaching in the manner of an obedient disciple. But to speak seriously, according to my good conscience, what I feel about his "discipline" in the present Treatise, I will reveal in a few words: I see that he wanders so far from the mark of truth that I would not dare, at first glance, to throw myself headlong into his school or truly commit myself to his way of teaching. For why should I leave the fountain of truth? Or why should I gape so greedily at a doctrine so foreign to the truth? I do not doubt, certainly, that far better and more profound things lie hidden in the "memorial chest" <note>original: "memoriali... arca." Fludd is suggesting Gassendi is keeping his real, deeper knowledge secret while publishing only superficial material.</note> of Gassendi, but he does not wish to reveal them (relying on a better prudence, no doubt, than that of Fludd) to a cruder world. He delights in publishing commonplaces, because worldly things please worldly people best; but the more secret and difficult things (which are hated by worldly people because they exceed their grasp), he wisely reserves for himself. If I had done the same from the beginning, the people of the world would not be pursuing me now with such great injuries. Truly indeed the Wise Man said: *He who increases knowledge, increases sorrow, etc.* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:18.</note> Therefore, again and again I say, if Gassendi can pour something divine, and not worldly, into my bosom, I will act as his obedient disciple. Nor will he find me ungrateful, but I will gladly repay what I have received with a similar coin. You see therefore (kind readers) that I have received Gassendi’s wish, contrary to his expectation, not with laughter but with a grateful mind. For a splendid and polished morality persuades and commands us to act modestly with those who are benevolent and modest.

->Now he proceeds in chapter 12 to the inquiry of my mind concerning the **Genii**, assigned to every man: In which are these things:<-

### Text 41. Gassendi, page 148.

Since he understands by the name of **Genius** <note>In this context, a "Genius" is a guardian spirit or a spiritual essence linked to a person from birth.</note> that texture composed of light and spirit, etc., just as by the name of **Magus** <note>Magician or Wise Man.</note> he understands no one else than a **Rosicrucian brother**, <note>original: "fratrem Cruci Roseum." The Rosicrucians were a secret society of mystics that Fludd famously defended.</note> who, having used the Philosophers' Stone, obtains among his other duties the power of divination.

### Fludd.

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
Whoever arrives at the knowledge of true Wisdom can very easily divine concerning future things. For, by means of Wisdom herself, Solomon says: *He knew all things, both present and future and past; and even things hidden as well as manifest—indeed, even the very thoughts of men.* Therefore, if the Rosicrucian brothers have reached the mystery of true Wisdom, I say truly that they are **true Magi**—that is, Wise Men—and not **Evil Magicians**. But as far as the "texture" of the Genius is concerned, I confess that I said the Angelic nature was forged from divine Light and created spirit; and I shall attempt to prove this openly, first from the opinion of the Fathers of the Church, and then afterward by the testimony of the more excellent Philosophers. Basil, Origen, Gregory, Augustine, along with several others, and among the more excellent philosophers, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and alchemical texts were attributed.</note> with the School of the Academics, acknowledge that Angels are forged from spiritual bodies and internal light. Hence Augustine expressly affirms in his book on Genesis that demons are "aerial and fiery animals"; and consequently he assigns to them external aerial bodies and internal bright or fiery ones. And again he says elsewhere that Angels had aerial bodies in their creation, formed namely from the purer part of the upper air, and suited for acting rather than being acted upon; and he adds that the wicked Angels, by reason of their fall, were changed—as far as their external part or body is concerned—into the nature of a thicker air, by which they might be rendered more subject to torture and fiery torments. Similarly, we are taught by Basil what sort of bodies the Angels have, where he says *that they are thin and aerial spirits.* Furthermore, Artephius <note>A medieval author of alchemical texts.</note> also says that the external part of a devil is air, and he makes his internal part fire. And for that reason he argues that it is very easy for him—namely, in respect to his aerial exterior—to communicate with the bloody and aerial part of the spirit in man, and to produce in him hot and burning diseases. But Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian mystic.</note> also seems to assert this same thing, where he calls Angels **Algamata**, <note>original: "Algama-ta"; from Greek 'agalmata,' meaning statues or cult-images, here used to mean "most polished mirrors" reflecting the light of God.</note> that is, **most polished mirrors, receiving the light of God.** As if he had said they are the clearest air, or spirits... <margin>In the Great Key of Wisdom.</margin><margin>On the Divine Names, ch. 6.</margin>

# On the Gassendian Exercises, Member III, Part II.

...most pure, receiving the divine splendor, by means of which they are animated, moved, and live. Hence it is that he himself defines an Angel as the image of God, a manifestation of hidden light, and a pure and most lucid mirror. And Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and Church Father who wrote extensively on the nature of angels.</note> says that they are intellectual spirits having light (acting as their soul) from the primary light. From these things it is clear that the internal nature or root of the mind of Angels is the splendor or emanation of God, while their polished spiritual exterior—according to the opinion of the aforementioned Fathers—is the most polished air, or a pure portion of the superior air.

---

->Text 42. Gassendi, page 150.<-

I wonder why Fludd suspects that this Magus <note>Gassendi is referring to a specific "wise man" mentioned in Fludd's earlier writings, possibly the one who warned Mark Antony about Octavian.</note> could have been from the society of the Magi who came from the East to adore Christ the Lord. For we are certain that their Magic, or divine wisdom, was not human or diabolical.

->Fludd.<-

<margin>chapters 22, 23, & 24.</margin>
But those three Magi were pagans; why could not this pagan likewise reach the secret of their mystery just as well as they did? For as those three foretold the coming of Christ, like the Sibyls, so also this one foretold the future misfortune of Antony on the part of Octavius. Is Gassendi then certain that the conjectural science of this Magus or Pagan Sage was diabolical? It is surely harsh for any upright man to judge this. As for the rest of this kind, I do not see why I should dwell on them; and so I pass on to say something of what follows. But I ask the Kind Reader to reread that Treatise of mine on the **Triple Genius** <note>A "Genius" in this context refers to a guiding spirit or guardian angel assigned to an individual.</note> assigned to every man, and he will see clearly <note>original: "ad oculum" — literally "to the eye."</note> whether in these chapters of his he has brought any weight that might break the strength of my opinion. For his arguments are trivial (as I judge) and do not pertain to the marrow of the matter. Therefore, I will descend to the examination of chapter 25, in which he makes an inquiry concerning the fictitious names of Angels. But it seems to me here that he excuses his friend as if by tearing out his hair <note>A Latin idiom suggesting a desperate or strained effort to make a point.</note>, and brings almost nothing to the point, except that he frankly confesses with me that it is permissible to give names to new things or things not yet named. Whence he does not deny that Angels can be called by various names devised according to their properties. Then he proceeds thus:

---

->Text 43. Gassendi, page 146.<-

However, the question is this: whether those who first called the Angel of Adam *Raziel*, the Angel of Noah *Thophiel*, etc., were divinely inspired, and whether they were not rather later Magi and Cabbalists <note>Followers of the Cabala (Kabbalah), a school of Jewish mysticism that explores the relationship between the eternal God and the mortal universe.</note> who wished to play and mock the gullible common folk, having devised such names with a certain cleverness in imitation of those one may observe in the scriptures.

->Fludd.<-

<margin>Why Wisdom 10; Wisdom 7:17; John 16.</margin>
Before I come to the solution of this doubt, I would like to understand from Gassendi himself whether he believes that none of the later Magi and Cabbalists were just as divinely inspired as those first ones? If it is granted: it is certain that Adam, with the Holy Spirit of discipline teaching him, had the knowledge of imposing appropriate names on creatures—not only earthly ones but also those heavenly ones—consistent with their properties, and he undoubtedly left that knowledge to his chosen successors through the Cabbalistic way. The sacred text says: *Wisdom brought Adam out of the mud of the earth and gave him the power of containing all things.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 10:1-2.</note> Likewise, did it not include understanding the names of Angels? Furthermore, Solomon, who lived around the middle age of the world, said this: *The spirit of wisdom gave me true knowledge of those things that are, and to know the thoughts of men: and whatever things are hidden and unforeseen I have learned: for the artisan of all things, wisdom, taught me.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21.</note> Moreover, that same good spirit imparts the same notice and knowledge to the Prophets and Apostles. Furthermore, concerning Christ, who was full of the said spirit: *Do we not know that you know all things?* <note>John 16:30.</note> and to the Apostles: *To you it is given to know the mysteries of God, etc.* Therefore, to know all hidden things. Whence elsewhere: *Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you.* Does Gassendi doubt that in these later ages there are some chosen ones among the living to whom God has entrusted this kind of mystery, since it is written that the tabernacle of God shall remain among men forever? 

But why more words? The ancients, by reason of the properties observed in Angels, wisely gave them such names; the **Essential name** of an Angel, however, is unknown by mortals. But he says that the fictitious names of Angels were devised by later Magi and Cabbalists for the sake of "playing" and "mocking the gullible common folk." Heavens! What kind of wise men were these who only wanted to give fictitious names to Angels in derision of the people? Does he believe that Reuchlin, Archangelus the Cabbalist, Abbot Trithemius, and that good man Pico della Mirandola, <note>Fludd lists famous Christian Hebraists and occultists: Johannes Reuchlin, Trithemius (a polymath monk), and Pico (a famous Renaissance philosopher). He argues these men were too serious for "games."</note> and others of this kind, were so malicious toward men that they would waste their work and oil <note>original: "operam & oleum" — a classic idiom for wasting effort and the lamp oil used to study late at night.</note> in writing just to mock men and deceive the common folk by playing—and that in imitation of those whose sacred things they remembered? O, how poor in brotherly charity! And how unworthy of a learned man is that opinion, which so rashly tries to judge all Magi and Cabbalists indiscriminately! But it is no wonder, since he thinks the whole art of the Cabala is nothing but a mere fiction and game invented to exercise human wits, as will appear more clearly below.

Then in chapter 26 he touches upon and treats the immortality of the soul. He says it is clear that the soul, in our common and Christian sense, is not estimated to be immortal. Hence he brings out Epicurus' <note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose followers were often accused of believing the soul dies with the body.</note> opinion on the mortality or immortality of the soul, but because he brings forth almost nothing but mere words, I leave those things untouched in this place. Then he follows, namely in chapter 27, with my **Microcosmic Harmony**.

You had looked down upon it (namely Fludd’s Microcosmic Harmony) <note>Fludd’s "Microcosmic Harmony" is his theory that the human body and soul are tuned like a musical instrument to the frequencies of the universe.</note> as a thing of no value, nor did you think it worthy of spending time in refuting it. # Fludd’s Response

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin> namely, that from its own heaven and earth and elements, and by a similar proportion of harmony, its parts—specifically the soul, spirit, and body—are constituted: why, I ask, should I not depict the harmony of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," or human being.</note> through the harmony of the Macrocosm? <note>The "Great World," or the Universe.</note> For the Macrocosm is not improperly called the son of the Archetype and the image of God; and the Microcosm is the son and likeness of the Macrocosm. Why, then, should both not observe the same Harmony? Is it because the musical consonances of the Fourth, the Fifth, and the Octave <note>original: "Diatessaron, Diapente, & Diapason"</note> concur to compose the Macrocosmic Harmony that they must therefore be excluded from the composition of the Microcosmic one? As if there were not the same proportion of light and spirit in man as there is in the greater world! Or as if one small monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used by Fludd to illustrate the mathematical and musical proportions of the universe.</note> could not be divided and distinguished into as many tones, semitones, and consonances as that great one which outlines the Harmony of the Macrocosm? Then he [Gassendi] introduces these points:

### Text 46. Gassendi, same page.

> I will first concede that there is some harmony between the soul and the body in man, from which surely both the consistency and the proper disposition of the whole composite arise. But by what argument, above all, can that proportion be confirmed, from which here too are made the material and formal pyramids? <note>Fludd used diagrams of intersecting pyramids—one of Light (Formal) and one of Matter (Material)—to show how spirit and body interact.</note>

### Fludd.

If he concedes this, it is enough! For if there is a certain harmony between the luminous soul, the spirit, and the body, does Gassendi not think that such a harmony can be understood in a spiritual Monochord, which our material or visible one represents exactly? Does he believe that such a harmony can actually be depicted—the luminous soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body—or heard or understood by the ears of the mind? Furthermore, Gassendi cannot, I think, be ignorant of the fact that light, or the central fire (if he prefers that term, since I notice the word "light" sounds poorly to him), distends and subtilizes the spirit the more lively, intense, and active it is in man; and consequently, it conforms the proportion of the suffering spirit to the condition of its own virtue or act. Since this is so: why, I pray, could we not, by means of equal pyramids (one of which is formal and the other material), depict the harmony of harmonies, by making the ray of each pyramid at the bottom in the place of the Monochord, as if fused from spirit and light? 

But Gassendi will say: why then do you make the ray of the pyramids pass from the top of the head all the way to the pubic bone? I answer: because, just as we perceive in the Macrocosm that the Rational heaven occupies the highest place, the vital the middle, and the natural or elementary the lowest; so, since in the Microcosm the head is the seat of the intellect and reason, the highest-pitched sounds <note>original: "peracutos sonos"</note> of the Monochord are attributed to it, the high sounds to the heart as the seat of life, and the deep sounds to the lower region and the liver. I do not refer that Monochord to the body, as Mersenne and Gassendi think, but to the difference of proportions that exist between the internal spirit and the luminous soul, which governs and leads it as it wishes into this or that state of harmony. 

Do we not see even in temperaments <note>original: "complexionibus," referring to the four humors.</note> that the choleric person has a more subtle and fiery spirit, and consequently one more dilated, than the phlegmatic person, etc.? Yet that is the harmony of temperaments, which can also be very easily depicted by the demonstration of the Monochord. But here I am dealing with that harmony which exists between the passive spirit and the active divine sulfur. <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, solar, and masculine principle.</note> Therefore, the Empyrean virtue <note>Refers to the highest, most fiery heaven.</note> is most rightly ascribed to the highest-pitched tones—that is, those sounding subtly and powerfully. For as the intellect surpasses all things, so the Empyrean spirit is the sharpest of all, insofar as it abounds in fiery light, as is apparent from its name; for it is certain that the more powerful the fire is, the more subtle and sharp the spirit becomes. Next, the vital spirit differs from that one insofar as it is more "spirited," and consequently is not adorned with such a great presence of light. Hence in the pulse, the Systole and Diastole are discerned, in which action and passion are found equal. But where there is a great dilation of the heart, there joy, gladness, and hope are usually present; but where the heart is too contracted, there sadness, fear, and vexation follow, or perturbations of the dense spirit, both in the Elementary kingdom of the Macrocosm and the Microcosm. Finally, because in the elementary region matter dominates more than form, we have marked it with the deeper tones. This is my intention in the Microcosmic Harmony, and the reason for comparing it with that of the Macrocosm; which no one can deny unless they are unskilled, malevolent, or knowingly rejecting and mocking the truth. Any prudent person, therefore, if they have considered these things realistically and with a sincere mind, will perceive that the rest of Gassendi's subsequent talk contributes little or nothing to the purpose; indeed, he does not seem to understand the matter at hand.

Now he has moved on to the examination of my chiromancy <note>Palmistry.</note>, or rather disputing against those things said by me there, and thus he rises up in defense of Mersenne:

### Text 47. Gassendi, page 181.

> Perhaps Fludd will defend himself here by saying that once, while living in Avignon, he divined by the art of Geomancy <note>A method of divination using patterns of dots; literally "earth-divination."</note> that the mistress of his housemate had a wart on her left eyelid. But let his conscience be sworn: did he not come to the knowledge of that wart by some other way than Geomancy?

### Fludd.

What I wrote is true. And from my soul I call God to witness that I accomplished this solely by the help and rudiments of Geomancy. Indeed, so that you may be more secure from this doubt and more certain of the matter, I will tell you the mode of operation: I assigned the figure of the First House to the petitioner; I applied the figure of the Seventh House to the beloved girl. The geomantic figure was "Puella" <note>The Girl.</note>; since its significance was fused from "Puella" and "Populus" <note>The People.</note>, it denoted a woman of light and inconstant condition, with a face not so much fat as quite beautiful, delighting in vineyards and green places, and having a spot or wart on the eyelid of the eye. Behold, Gassendi; I speak the truth before God, that I performed these things by the art of Geomancy alone.

The rest, which he further adds in the same place, I omit on purpose as being of no importance. Soon after, he makes an inquiry into my Cabala, <note>Jewish mystical tradition, often adapted by Christian Renaissance thinkers.</note> which seems to him very narrow; but in my eyes, it is very broad and fantastic.

### Text 48. Gassendi, page 184.

> He says: that if you are ignorant of Cabalistic characters—for instance, not understanding that they are the first principles of things, the elements, called as it were "hylements" <note>A pun on *hyle* (matter) and *elements*.</note>; which were inscribed on the face of matter [hyle] by the finger of God—the Cabalists confirm this when they say:
>> God wrote his law into a fiery globe, by means of dark fire, upon white fire.
> See now, for it concerns you, whether you ought to bash your head against a wall because you have not been initiated into these mysteries.

# To the Gassendian Exercises. Member III. Part I.

->Fludd.<-

But let us now see what our "good inquisitor" <note>Fludd’s sarcastic nickname for Pierre Gassendi, who was critiquing Fludd’s work on behalf of Marin Mersenne.</note> has to say about plucking that kernel from the shell? And how does he explain and interpret that passage for his friend—a passage most true in its own sense, yet quite difficult to understand? Thus he spoke then:

->Text 49. Gassendi page 186.<-

> Do not ask me then what they mean, for example, etc. For I would say, since those men have two substances near the end of the work: one white, namely "virgin’s milk," another black, namely the "crow’s head," from which, when the former has obtained fixation through the intervention of the latter, that red stone arises; I would say, I say, the meaning is that the whole law of God—that is, the pre-description of the Philosophical work—tends toward this: that a fiery globe, namely the stone, be formed from dark fire, namely the crow’s head, impressed upon white fire, such as virgin’s milk.

->Fludd.<-

Behold your "good interpreter"! But oh, how wavering is his talent! And how readily he can fabricate, and with such confidence transmute a truth unknown to him into a chimera! Is it not clear from these things how deep Gassendi is in the mystery of natural Alchemy? As if the beginning of all things were his "Philosopher’s Stone": or as if those fiery characters of the divine word—by whose holy and purely formal letters this world with all its structures was formed—were of as little consequence as our interpreter seems to assert. But I see that he has understood neither the divine word nor Fludd’s alchemy (to say nothing of common alchemy). Therefore I marvel at the man; that he nevertheless proceeds with such confidence and such audacity to attempt to crack open <note>original: "enucleare," literally "to de-kernel" or explain.</note> things that he expressly confesses in plain words to be utterly ignorant of. A blind man, clearly, chosen and summoned to lead the blind. Then he proceeds thus:

->Text 50. Gassendi page 187.<-

> But if those men <note>Fludd and his fellow Rosicrucian sympathizers.</note> found out, they would call down curses <note>original: "diras," furies or dire curses.</note> upon me. Therefore, let us act more simply, and let us suppose that we know nothing of those things which these men keep hidden in their minds.

->Fludd.<-

Do not fear them, my Gassendi! For <unclear>surely</unclear> <note>original: "nimo", likely "immo" (nay/rather).</note> in place of curses, he promises you a blessing from them. For I know well enough that they will not be moved against you by envy or ill-will, but by piety and mercy: so that they wish well to you and your people for a good understanding, and pray for a sounder mind in sound bodies for you all.

---

### Regarding the fragments on the "Highest Good."

Although I am not bound to defend a book whose core was not crafted by me: nevertheless, because I translated the larger part of it from the Scottish language <note>Fludd likely refers to English or a Northern dialect, as the work in question, "Summum Bonum," was attributed to Joachim Frizius but often suspected to be by Fludd himself.</note> into Latin, and even added something of my own, I do not see why I should not descend into a friend’s cause: to bring something to light against the quibbles of adversaries, (until he himself responds more fully for himself, which I know will happen soon). For he is sufficient to defend himself and sustain his own cause: especially since nothing at all is written in that book which cannot be understood without so many quibbles or exclamations, and explained without any stain of error. And certainly: if this <unclear>offspring</unclear> <note>original: "foetus"</note> were mine, I would acknowledge it as my own child.

For what (in God’s name) is found in it so abominable and horrific as they seem to make it out to be? Is there anything in it except plain truth, confirmed by the harmony of the sacred scriptures and their full consensus? Just because something is taken not according to the mind of Mersenne and Gassendi, but as it truly is, must it therefore be held as erroneous and rejected? For it is one thing to debate the sense of scripture morally, and another mystically: since the moral sense behaves differently than the mystical. What? Because mystical wisdom and its mystery are revealed to few, should they therefore be mocked by those who occupy themselves solely with the moral sense? Let Mersenne understand first, and let Gassendi understand too, what the secret of the mystical Church truly is, before they judge it so rashly and in a worldly manner.

I would have them know that just as they themselves are theologians and members of the political and external Church (which consists of the multitude of theologians administering it), so also the mystical Church is observed by those who understand the mystery of God, not according to human tradition, but according to the precepts of Christ. In this, therefore, that worldly or political Church differs from this mystical and spiritual one. For to the chosen men of the mystical Church, Christ said this: <margin>Matthew 13</margin> "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given": namely, to the men of the political Church of the Jews. Furthermore, concerning the gathering of the <margin>Ephesians 1</margin> mystical Church this: "Now you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens of the Saints and members of God’s household: built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with the chief cornerstone being Jesus Christ himself, in whom the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built into a dwelling place for God in the Holy Spirit." 

I would not have them, therefore, condemn so lightly that "Highest Good" of Joachim Frizius: since it is not that imaginary stone of the counterfeiters and bastards (as this good inquisitor falsely believes), but that supernatural and cornerstone, which is the head and summit of all the goodness of this world. For the Apostle says: <margin>Ephesians 1</margin> "He gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body, and the fullness of him who fills all in all." Wherefore, O Gassendi! I would have you know yourself, and you will also most easily recognize who and of what sort that true cornerstone is, upon whose base you are entirely built. For once this is known, you will soon cast away those errors of yours, and at the same time utterly abolish all the quibbles undeservedly poured out of error against the mystical Church. What more? Once the veil of ignorance, which is most hostile to worldly men, is set aside, you will without doubt hold both me and Frizius excused in all things.

---

### From the Book on Magic.

In the first chapter of his inquiry, he seems to abound more in the flashes of a witty talent (which as quickly as they arrive, immediately vanish into smoke) than in the fruit of solid and sincere prudence. For just as actors in comedies strive to move the spectators to joke and laughter by their gestures; so also Gassendi therein, playing as if with a feather, uses empty words that contribute absolutely nothing to the matter. For example:

->Text 51. Gassendi page 191.<-

> I add nothing here about that remarkable promise of the title, etc.

And here he consumes a whole leaf, mocking the title of the book *On the Highest Good*, and *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*. And at last he concludes thus: page 192.

> As soon as I saw the title *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*, I immediately hoped that I would see twins

<meta>This page continues Fludd’s vigorous defense against Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd mocked Gassendi’s "interpretation" of alchemical symbols like "virgin’s milk" and the "crow’s head."
