# Fludd’s Response,

...battle lines drawn up here and there: I thought of stations, signals, conflicts, weapons, wounds, slaughters, and other such things; but observing nothing of the kind thereafter, I nearly cried out: <note>original: "ᾧ διὰ κεφαλῆς καὶ ἐγκέφαλον οὐκ ἔχει!"</note> **"He who has a head but lacks a brain!"** It also happens that sometimes a page must swell with a pompous title: as when, in this place, we read *The Highest Good* <note>original: "Summum Bonum"</note> expressed in such grand characters. Who would deny that effort should then be made to ensure that the argument the foot-and-a-half-long title promises is illustrated by a definition, distributed appropriately, and that everything within it coheres—leaving nothing lacking and nothing superfluous? For unless this is done, why is it necessary for the mountain to go into labor only to give birth to a mouse? etc.

### Fludd.

O charming wit! O intellect of wondrous virtue, which attempts to procreate something out of nothing! O delightful brain, which longs to play and replay again and again with nothing at all, as if with a feather! I perceive that Gassendi here is playing the role of <term>Davus</term> <note>A common name for a cunning or blundering slave in Roman comedy; here Fludd suggests Gassendi is acting the fool or the meddler.</note>, so that I might perform the duty of <term>Oedipus</term> <note>The mythical solver of riddles.</note>! But I should like him to say: what did he expect from that title, *The Contest of Wisdom with Folly*? Imaginary visions appropriate to a fantastic brain? Or the real truth? That is, a refutation of foolish assertions and errors, drawn from the treasury of wisdom? Do not the testimonies of the Sacred Scriptures everywhere in that response of mine thrust Mersenne’s <note>Marin Mersenne, the French polymath who originally attacked Fludd, prompting this defense.</note> falsehood into the pit of oblivion so deeply that they cannot be redeemed from there, neither by him nor by his friend Gassendi? But I shall omit those things as if they were old wives' tales, so that I may proceed to more mature and better-digested matters.

### Text 52. Gassendi page 189 & 190.

For to a few, Magic, Cabbala, Alchemy, and the <term>Rosy Brotherhood</term> <note>The Rosicrucians, a mysterious spiritual and cultural movement that Fludd defended.</note> appeared to be entirely one and the same thing—or rather, the same <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythical monster made of disparate parts; here used to mean a ridiculous or impossible illusion.</note>. And consequently, those who are truly Magi, Cabbalists, Alchemists, and Brothers of the Rosy Cross all aim at a single mark and all profess the same art. And on the following page, namely 191, he has this:

This art is properly none other than Alchemy itself. The goal sought by others is none other than the so-called Philosopher's Stone, with those effects of its own. For it is properly Alchemy by whose operations they hope to reach that blessed stone; but <term>Cabbala</term> <note>A form of Jewish mysticism that involves interpreting the hidden meanings of the Hebrew scriptures; Fludd integrated this into his Christian Hermetic philosophy.</note> properly serves to supply the vocabulary by which the mystery may be hidden; Magic declares the effects that are brought forth from it; finally, the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross designates that blessed state which they strive to attain by the benefit of the stone. And this, finally, is the *Highest Good* which gave the title to the work. Clearly, all these craftsmen, if they should attain the stone, look up to no other greater good, by which they may lead every age well and blessedly.

### Fludd.

How poorly (good Reader) these things hang together! For in the former text, he calls the matter he treats—namely Magic, Cabbala, Alchemy, and the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross—a "chimera"; but here he asserts it to be the "Stone of the Wise," which the said sciences with one voice proclaim to be the "Highest Good." But is that Highest Good, so greatly desired and celebrated by pious Philosophers, Prophets, and Apostles, a chimera? Bah! How impure is that mouth which, having no reverence, dares to call the true <term>Cornerstone</term> <note>A reference to Christ, often identified by Fludd and other Christian alchemists with the Philosopher's Stone.</note> a "chimera"! Truly, I find it necessary to pray for the blinded Mersenne, Lanovius, and Gassendi, as Christ once did for the Jews: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do or say." Since Gassendi understands nothing besides "vulgar" Alchemy, all that he brings forward into the open collapses and vanishes of its own accord, even if I remain silent. Truly, I cannot but disapprove that he speaks so lightly even of Cabbala: namely, that its own property is merely to supply words by which the mystery of the art may be hidden.

For that is not the end of Cabbala; but rather that, while we read the sacred letters (which are truly formal and difficult for the intellect), we may understand through them the marrow of truth and perceive the twin sense of God essentially speaking. Does not St. Paul testify that the letter kills, but the spirit gives life? What goodness or truth, therefore, can those draw from Cabbala who are occupied only in the letter? And this is the reason why Gassendi, by no means discerning the kernel of Cabbala, believes its essence to consist in nothing but bare, fictitious words by which the world is deceived. Truly, may God turn Gassendi for the better, so that he may think and write otherwise! Meanwhile, however, I marvel how a man of letters could judge so rashly concerning such a noble thing; indeed, I believe he only wished to wander <term>outside the olive trees</term> <note>original: "extra oleas vagari"; a classical idiom for going off track or exceeding the limits of a subject.</note> for the sake of his friend. But so that he may see his error most clearly, let him hear the words of <term>Reuchlin</term> <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a major German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew who introduced Cabbalistic study to the Christian world.</note>, and I advise him not to despise this twofold opinion, lest by mocking and condemning Reuchlin’s teaching, he appears to make himself greater than he truly is, and thus in turn be mocked and despised by the learned world. For how great a difference there is between profound study and a superficial inspection of the Cabbalistic art, no one can judge who has not seen its interior, even "through a lattice-window" (as they say). Now, the words of Reuchlin are these:

<margin>Reuchlin, Book 1 of *On the Cabbalistic Art*.</margin>
> By the Cabbalistic art of contemplation, nothing more desirable has ever been bestowed by God upon the human race—at least to those who live on earth and excel others in talent and flourish in mind—nothing more advantageous for the salvation of souls, nothing more fit for attaining immortality, by which the human mind may ascend more closely to <term>Deification</term> <note>The process of becoming god-like or united with the divine.</note> in accordance with nature: this is the height of blessedness, which the Greeks call <note>original: "τέλος"</note> <term>Telos</term> <note>The end, goal, or ultimate purpose.</note>, whether it pleases you to call it the extreme, or the ultimate, or the end; from which it happens that we, absolutely wanting for nothing, live fortunately, tranquilly, and happily without impediment forever: when, quite skillfully, through certain symbols—all earthly things being rejected and the matter of things removed—we have plucked form from form, until we have ascended to the first, all-forming and formless Form.

From these things, you can gather (Candid Reader) whether Gassendi has dealt well with the true Cabbalists, when he left behind these words written to their disgrace?

<margin>Gassendi, Chapter 7, *On the Origin of Cabbala*, page 218.</margin>
> And by this reasoning, there was a struggle among the Rabbis over the mass of volumes (meaning the Cabbalistic ones), as to who among them all could devise more and more ingenious things, etc.

But how fabulous that tradition of Gassendi's is can be seen more clearly than the noonday sun from the aforementioned words of Reuchlin, whom all the learned of Europe recognize as a true and renowned Cabbalist; whereas we have reason to suspect Gassendi’s skill in the Cabbalistic art.

### On Magic, Chapters 2 and 3.

In those chapters, truly, he brings forth nothing of great weight; indeed, he seems to offer little or almost nothing against Frisius’s opinion <note>Fludd often referred to himself using the pseudonym "Joachim Frizius."</note> on Magic, but merely exhausts himself in excusing his friend. Yet I shall repeat something from them.

<meta>This page continues the heated intellectual debate between the English physician and mystic Robert Fludd and the French philosopher Pierre Gassendi. Fludd is defending his concepts of "Magic" and "Alchemy" against charges of sorcery and intellectual fraud. He specifically addresses Gassendi’s critiques of his work and his relationship with the ideas of Marin Mersenne.</meta>

# To the Exercises of Gassendi, Member III, Part II.

### Text 53. Gassendi, page 202.

I do not deny that potions and medicines are prepared by a destructive art, but these are no more "Magical" than are robberies, murders, and similar crimes.

### Fludd.

And yet, it is through that magical power of herbs, roots, stones, and metals that such effects are brought about: therefore, they should not be called Magical without merit.

### Text 54. Gassendi, Chapter 4 & page 404.

To return to you, Mersenne, this is the species of Magic which you rightly condemn. For whether demons mingle themselves in it, or whether the mere depravity of the mind torments weak souls, this entire hodgepodge is to be rejected, etc.

### Fludd.

Regarding the first part of this text, I say that this does not excuse Mersenne for condemning Magic with such a general term. If he had instead named it <term>Cacomagia</term> <note>From the Greek 'kakos' (evil) and 'magia' (magic); specifically refers to "evil magic" or black magic involving malevolent spirits.</note>, I would most easily agree with him. For many great and wonderful things, which have nothing in common with Evil Magic, can be performed by Natural Magic alone: namely, by the power of herbs, stones, etc., collected and prepared under the proper constellations. Venerable Antiquity testifies to this, and the daily experience of our own age confirms it. Yet, by Mersenne’s harsh censure and judgment, all these things are condemned. But did not Solomon excel wonderfully in this species of Magic without any stain of sin? His own confession certainly affirms this openly.

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>

> *For He (says Solomon) gave me true knowledge of those things that exist, so that I might know the disposition of the world, and the powers of the elements, the beginning, the end, and the midpoint of times, the alterations of the turning points and the changes of the seasons, the cycles of years and the positions of the stars, the natures of animals and the rages of wild beasts, the force of winds and the thoughts of men, the differences between plants and the virtues of roots; and I learned whatever things are hidden or unforeseen. For Wisdom, the worker of all things, taught me.* <note>This is a translation of Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21, a cornerstone text for Christian Hermeticists who argued that "Magic" was simply the deep study of God's creation.</note>

Mersenne busies himself with condemning these and all similar things because they exceed his grasp. But, good God! How few of Nature’s mysteries would be open to men if nothing were brought to light except what Mersenne can comprehend. It is indeed held for certain by the Wise that more secrets of nature lie hidden from mortals than are open to them; nevertheless, I am most convinced that many things were known to those Wise ones which are entirely hidden from Mersenne, and are therefore condemned by him. And this is why he rashly accuses and condemns Roger Bacon, Abbot Trithemius, Marsilio Ficino, and Agrippa of Evil Magic, even though their entire intention was focused on licit and Natural Magic, as Frizius has excellently proven. Furthermore, I concede to the second part of the quoted text: for all those in whom evil demons mingle are indeed practitioners of Evil Magic. For this reason, they are not to be tolerated in the Commonwealth, but severely punished; just as they are vigorously barred from the sacred fellowship and banquet of the good Magi. For the good Magi are accustomed to perform their wonderful works with the cooperation of the good spirit of divine wisdom, whereas the evil ones do so through commerce with evil spirits. It is not the Magi, therefore, but the practitioners of Evil Magic who are to be condemned.

### Text 55. Gassendi, pages 205 & 206.

Furthermore, since I have spoken of you; is it not necessary that I also speak of Fludd, so that we may see clearly—when he praises Magic, and when he defends what you have rejected—what kind of Magic he is actually talking about? Thus, from what was previously deduced, it is now elicited that he understands nothing by the name of Magic other than his own Alchemy.

### Fludd.

Now let Fludd beware! For here our diligent Inquisitor has arrived at the investigation of Fludd’s Magic. But what does he think of Fludd’s Magic? That it is Evil Magic? No. What then? He determines it to be his Alchemy. Gassendi is quite certain of this. For he has found the "key" to Fludd’s philosophy and perceived that its foundations are purely Alchemical. He concludes this because Fludd’s "chaos," his "heaven," and his "elements" are extracted by the chemical art from bread or wheat, and because the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, believed by alchemists to be the life-force or celestial spirit latent in matter.</note> of wheat is the subject of his Stone. These things, I say, he saw from afar with his sharp "Lyncean" eyes <note>A reference to Lynceus, the Argonaut famous for his superhumanly keen sight.</note>, and believed them as certain (as he seems to assert expressly elsewhere). Truly, Gassendi is as far from knowing the mind of Fludd regarding the subject of Alchemy and its preparation as the "Cabbalistic letter" (which he claims to know) is from the spiritual and luminous character of that same Art. But since I have previously confessed that my "Philosopher’s Stone" (or the stone of the lovers of wisdom) is that spiritual Universal Stone which the Scriptures everywhere call the <term>Cornerstone</term> <note>original: "Lapis Angularis"; Fludd identifies the goal of alchemy with Christ, the "cornerstone" of the Church, signaling a spiritual rather than metallic alchemy.</note>—and I know this is also beyond the mind of either Mersenne or Gassendi—I verified this in my cleansing of the first stain of impiety. Therefore, I shall proceed to what follows.

### Text 56. Gassendi, same place.

This is undoubtedly the art by which it is permitted to attain knowledge of the Divine Word, of Angels, and of all other things, in the manner and sense described by us above. If you seek an argument from this passage, see how he reveals his mind quite clearly in these words:

> Sometimes (he says) this art (Magic) leads to a supernatural mystery, by producing the incorruptible spirit of the creature—the quintessence most full of the divine ray—out of darkness into the sight of mortals through true and not false chemistry. By means of this, the ancient Magi (not practitioners of Evil Magic, as the ignorant think who are practiced only in the worst and evil wisdom) brought so many and such great things to light. They were the truly wise, namely those who received the gift of wisdom from God, such as those three Magi or wise men who came from the East, etc.

### Fludd.

I will accept that sentiment as plainly my own, even though it was written by my friend Frizius and only translated by me from the Scottish tongue into Latin. For I do not in reality disagree with his opinion, since I say that the incorruptible spirit of God existing in every thing—serving as the basis of existence in place of the Cornerstone—can be drawn out of darkness to aid the needy through true chemistry (that is, by the mediation of the fire of divine genius). I hold that this art, by which such a treasure is obtained, is not human but divine; and that the Magic of the Brothers of the Rosy Cross <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics and healers Fludd famously defended.</note> is concerned with such a subject, namely the most noble Stone rejected by the worldly, which is the operator of all the wonders of this world. Indeed, they themselves openly profess the same in their Epistle published by Frizius:

<sig>F 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Will you</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Fludd distinguishes between Natural Magic (the study of divine properties in nature) and "Cacomagia" (black magic), defending himself against Gassendi's claim that his philosophy is merely literal alchemy. Fludd identifies the true "Philosopher's Stone" as a spiritual, Christ-like "Cornerstone" and links his work to the traditions of Solomon and the Rosicrucians.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s defense against Pierre Gassendi. Having previously discussed Magic and Alchemy, Fludd now turns to the definition and origin of "Cabbala" (Kabbalah), defending a work written under the pseudonym Joachim Frizius. He argues against Gassendi’s "cold" and purely historical interpretation of Jewish mysticism, asserting instead its divine and secret nature.</meta>

# Fludd’s Response.

<margin>page 52. On the Supreme Good.</margin>
"Do you wish," (they say) "O most wretched one, to be made blessed? Do you wish, O proud one, to be elevated above the circles of the world? Do you wish, O ambitious one, to rule in heaven over this earth and your dark body? Do you, being unworthy, wish to perform all wonders? Know therefore the rejected stone <note>A reference to the 'stone the builders rejected' from Psalm 118:22, often used by alchemists to signify the Philosopher's Stone or Christ.</note>, and learn what it is before it is sought."

Here you see how the Brothers of the Rose Cross <note>original: "F. R. C." for Fratres Rosae Crucis</note> apply this Stone—produced and acquired through Divine Alchemy—to true Magic, whose office is to perform wonderful operations. This aligns with the duty you previously assigned to Magic. For you said its duty is to declare the effects that arise from Alchemy. Here, therefore, Gassendi finds the mind of Frizius confirmed, as expressed in the preceding pages. But I do not wish to dwell on these things. For soon (as I hear) my friend Frizius himself will respond to all these matters. Nor will I say more of Magic: for I find the arguments here so weak, and the excuses brought forward for Mersenne so cold, that the reader needs no other response than Frizius’s own text.

### Gassendi’s Inquiry into Frizius’s Kabbalah.

Here he attempts to remove and totally overturn Joachim Frizius’s definition of Kabbalah.

#### Text 57. Gassendi, pages 211 & 212.

He defines Kabbalah (he says) as the oral reception of the mystery of God and nature from another: or the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the health-giving contemplation of God and the separate forms <note>In this context, "separate forms" refers to angels or spiritual intelligences existing apart from matter.</note>, etc.

He derives it not from Moses alone, but even from Adam, through the Patriarchs, Judges, Kings, Priests, Prophets, and even to Christ and the Apostles, and their successors as long as the world shall be.

->Fludd.<-

### At last, in Chapter 7, page 215, he begins the refutation thus:

### Gassendi, page 215.

"Behold, I will reveal in a few words what I conjecture regarding Kabbalah. Since the sacred books are contained in two kinds of subjects: histories and laws, etc."

This is erroneous. For the chief thing which the text treats is the mystery of God and His mystical wisdom, which is not obvious to any casual reader. Solomon intended this when he said, "It is the glory of a king to conceal a thing." <note>Proverbs 25:2.</note> And Christ, when he was transfigured on the mountain, said: "Tell this to no one." Here, therefore, this "complete Kabbalist" of ours <note>Fludd is speaking sarcastically of Gassendi.</note> leaves the subject in a gross error, for he ignores what is truly the subject of the entire Kabbalistic Art. He proceeds by inventing I know not what "old Talmudic Kabbalah" and a "more recent Rabbinic Kabbalah," either historical or legal. Indeed, he devises strange inventions so that he might drag the effect of this art (as if by the hair) toward some historical, political, or moral duty. Of the mystery of God, however—which Solomon, the Prophets, and Christ hid in parables—he does not even think. It is evident, therefore, that this man was nourished in the political Church of the world, so that he might banish into eternal exile that mystical Church, and God Himself represented in mystery, from the senses and souls of the Hebrew doctors and sages.

But is there anyone skilled in the true Kabbalah who believes that Kabbalah was invented (as he says) so that the circumstances of events known at the time would not be obliterated by the passage of time? That it exists because histories lack details of persons, things, places, times, and actions? Or that it exists because laws lack the many rites concerning the practice of judgments, sacrifices, and the like, as they were handed down by Moses, the Elders, and the Priests? I would ask that his following reasons be read, and it will appear how the rest hang together. Specifically: are those men the only Kabbalists who are called <unclear>קבלני</unclear> <note>original Hebrew: 'Mekubbalim', meaning 'receivers' or 'men of tradition'</note> by the Talmudists, that is, men of speculation? And is the exposition of the name of that Angel who preceded the Israelites correctly transferred to the name Michael, because by the transposition of the letters of that word (as found in Reuchlin) it is read as <unclear>מיכאל</uncall> <note>Michael</note> or into the Angel Metatron, because of the name of God in him? For just as the name of God, <unclear>שדי</unclear> <note>Shaddai, 'The Almighty'</note>, shows a numerical value of 314, so also does the name <unclear>מטטרון</unclear> <note>Metatron</note>? <note>This refers to Gematria, a system where letters have numerical values. Both Shaddai (Shin=300, Dalet=4, Yod=10) and Metatron (Mem=40, Tet=9, Tet=9, Resh=200, Vav=6, Nun=50) sum to 314.</note> What is the point of all this? What does the investigation of the essential name in Kabbalah have to do with Histories or political Laws? Indeed, from this assertion of his, he does not hesitate to pronounce such a judgment to disparage the honor of the Kabbalists:

#### Text 58. Gassendi, page 218.

"And by this reasoning, in a mass of volumes, there was a contest among the Rabbis to see who could invent either the cleverest or the most numerous interpretations."

->Fludd.<-

<margin>page 191.</margin>
Thus, [according to Gassendi] the origin of the Kabbalah of the Rabbis depends on the exercise of their own genius and the multitude of their inventions, as they showed off either the sharpness of their wit or their excellence in finding many commentaries. Consequently, Kabbalah was invented so that everyone might exercise his wit and excel in a multitude of inventions; even though he previously stated, among other things, that the purpose of Kabbalah was properly to serve in providing terms by which a mystery might be hidden.

But let us despise that judgment of the "spurious Kabbalists," so that we may return to the aforementioned definition of Kabbalah brought forward by our friend, and see what the more skilled Kabbalists thought about the origin and duty of the true Kabbalah. Leo Hebraeus says:

<margin>Dialogue 3 on Love.</margin>
> "That the most excellent discipline of Kabbalah arose first from Adam, through vocal tradition alone, because it was forbidden to be recorded in written monuments: whence it was called 'Kabbalah' by the Hebrews, as if you were to say 'reception.' Then it passed to the most wise Enoch, and from him it reached the most celebrated Noah. He is said to have left this divine science—along with a great deal of knowledge of other divine and human disciplines—to Shem, who was wiser than his other children, and to the great-grandson of Eber, as if it were a most rich inheritance. These two are then said to have instructed Abraham in letters, who took the surname 'Hebrew' from his ancestor and teacher Eber. From Abraham, then, through Isaac, Jacob, and Levi, the account of this most high science is said (as some believe) to have finally reached that race of most wise Hebrews who were called Kabbalists." So says Leo Hebraeus.

<margin>Book 1, On the Art of Kabbalah.</margin>
Reuchlin says this concerning the origin of Kabbalah: "If it is common in human and, as it were, viler crafts, that men receive by hearing and believe those who they think are endowed with singular learning above others: shall we then think that in the science of the highest and divine things—which we can scarcely reach by our own strength—the tradition and reception of Holy men should be despised? This is what is called 'Kabbalah' in Hebrew. For Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the health-giving contemplation of God and the separate forms, which those who are granted a heavenly inspiration receive..."

Fludd cites authorities like Leo Hebraeus and Reuchlin to argue that Kabbalah is a secret, oral tradition passed down from Adam through the Patriarchs to preserve divine mysteries.</summary>

# To the Gassendian Exercises, Member III, Part II. 45

<margin>Thus Reuchlin.</margin>
...by divine inspiration, they are rightly called *Kabbalics* <note>original: "Cabbalici"; Fludd uses Reuchlin’s specific terminology to categorize levels of mystical practitioners</note>; their disciples we shall call by the name *Kabbalaeans*; and those who otherwise attempt to imitate them are to be named *Kabbalists*. Thus says Reuchlin.

<margin>Book 1, On the Art of Kabbalah.</margin>
Finally, the same Reuchlin, in the first book of *On the Art of Kabbalah*, recounts the succession of those who received the Kabbalah <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, which Fludd believes was passed down orally from Adam</note> from Adam all the way to the College of the Prophets.

From what has been said, therefore, it is clear how contrary the opinions of the true *Kabbalaeans* are to those of the supposed and spurious *Kabbalists*, who call the true Kabbalah a "chimera" <note>A mythological monster, here meaning a foolish fantasy</note> and a thing of so little importance that it serves only to provide words with which to hide a mystery. Finally, he concludes thus:

<margin>Gassendi, page 220.</margin>
> O, if that good Patriarch Jacob—who endured the profession of a shepherd for so long and with such patience—possessed that Kabbalah which Fludd understands: what fable is there, then, that should not be believed immediately?

<margin>Genesis 28.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 1.</margin>
But he [Jacob] did profess the **Cornerstone**. For he recognized the stone which he set up as a monument so that it might be the house of God: and consequently, a temple of the Spiritual Stone, or Christ. He possessed, therefore, that stone which Fludd intends, and which Frizius <note>Joachim Frizius, the pseudonym under which Fludd wrote the work being defended here</note> understood through the Hebrew word *Aben* <note>original: "AbN" (Eben), meaning stone. Fludd identifies the stone Jacob slept on with Christ, the "Cornerstone" of the Church</note>. Hence the mystical Church is called the body and fullness of Him who is the head over the whole Church, who fills all in all. From these things, therefore, it is clear whether Gassendi is as "superexcellent" in Kabbalah as Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and priest who was a fierce critic of Fludd’s "occult" philosophy</note> trumpeted him to be before his patron, bursting forth into these words:

> My dear Gassendi has so led Fludd out, and so uncovered his Kabbalah, that I consider myself satisfied by this discovery alone.

That is a fine speech, if it had come from a man who understood the true Kabbalah; but how can his "dear Gassendi" uncover my Kabbalah when he does not know what it truly is? And by what reasoning can Mersenne judge someone’s strength in a science of which he himself is utterly ignorant? For he admits that he "lost his oil and labor" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort</note> in the investigation of Kabbalah: and consequently, he deters others from a genuine investigation of it with strange discouragements. But concerning men of that sort, Reuchlin says this:

> Certain sophists <note>In this context, deceptive or shallow thinkers who rely on logic rather than spiritual insight</note> worthy of ridicule, through their own temerity—or, if you prefer, their negligence in learning—have falsely asserted that Kabbalah is a diabolical and heretical man, whence they say all Kabbalists are heretics. Restrain yourselves, I pray, from laughter if you can, though it is ridiculous; but I would wish to stop laughing at these monsters and portents of men. Kabbalah is not to be sought by the crude touch of the senses, nor by the imperious arguments of logical art, for its foundation is established in the "third region of thoughts," where there is no pressing judgment, no evident proof, no demonstrating syllogism—nay, where human reason itself does not rule; but rather a certain nobler knowledge, where the light of the mind, falling upon the intellect, moves the free will of believing. Thus he says.

Truly, Mersenne boasts that he will utterly overturn the Kabbalah: and certainly he promises a great thing, but time will show what he will actually provide. In the meantime, I warn Mersenne and his associates to first learn to understand what the mystical Kabbalah is, and what its living and spiritual characters—expressed and written in the Word of God—truly are, before they rail against its dignity so rashly, harshly, and inhumanely. For it is not the art itself, but the artist, who is poorly understanding and ignorant, that should be condemned.

## Inquiry into Frizius’s Alchemy.

In this inquiry, Gassendi argues as if he were an Alchemist. I truly wish I had found him to be a true and suitable Chemist, so that I might have been more deeply instructed by him in this art. For I am not ashamed to be taught by a learned man who deigns to open anything new to me; indeed, I would accept it with a grateful mind. But in truth, I doubt I shall find Gassendi to be such a man as could teach me true Alchemy. For he is (as it seems to me) entirely ignorant of the mystical Kabbalah. Therefore, my hope will be in vain. But to the purpose.

I do not wish to consume too much time in refuting trivialities. For, if I wanted to examine every such thing strictly, I would produce weariness not only for myself but for the reader as well. Therefore, I will prepare myself here for more material and real matters. Furthermore, enough will be said about Alchemy, regarding Gassendi’s inclination, in the fourth Member of this Treatise: and all the objections of Gassendi and his associates will be plainly removed by infallible arguments. We refer the benevolent reader there. Nor shall I say anything to his petty objections made against the **Brothers of the Rose Cross** <note>original: "F.R.C." (Fratres Rosae Crucis)</note>; for (I know well) Frizius has already responded effectively in a short time. I shall therefore conclude by responding individually to every objection touching me, so that I may heal the wounds inflicted upon me by the Gassendian slanders.

## On the Letter sent by the Brothers of the Rose Cross and annexed to Fludd’s Epilogue.

### Text 59. Gassendi, page 262.

That letter added to the end of the book, which he says was written by the Brothers of the Rose Cross, is written in <unclear>diverse</unclear> and divine characters. He calls them "Brothers" here, and yet before, when about to cite the quoted fragment, he said it was written by "a certain man illuminated by wisdom," etc.

### Fludd.

Here he best demonstrates his "profound" insight into mystical Kabbalah: for he takes the characters of those letters for the divine and formal ones signified by true Kabbalists; and thus he wrongly takes the "dead letter" for the "living one." Certainly, my friend gave that letter to me, just as it had been given to him by a certain close friend. I speak the truth before God and the world; and I acknowledge, indeed I know for certain, that a most living sense lies hidden beneath those dead letters. I would gladly know, however, what Gassendi means when he reports that in one place I attribute that letter to the Brothers of the Rose Cross, but in another to "a man illuminated by wisdom"? Perhaps he is trying to build a case for a contradiction? But even if we suppose I did this, he will not achieve his intent. For all the men illuminated by wisdom could not have written the exact same letter, in the same interval of time, on the same paper, with the same characters, and with the same pen; but one alone, by the consensus of all, had to perform this. Therefore, when I ascribe the aforementioned Letter to the R.C. Brothers, I also mean to include their **Scribe** <note>original: "Amanuensem"</note>, so that I may name all the men illuminated by wisdom at one and the same time.

# Fludd’s Response,

when I speak only of a certain man illuminated with wisdom, I then understand him to be the one who composed it <note>The letter in question</note> with the knowledge and consent of the rest. Who, therefore, does not see that Gassendi’s intention is vain? As for the Brothers of the Rose Cross <note>The Rosicrucians, a mysterious semi-legendary secret society of sages</note>, I truly do not wonder why they do not more sharply attack those "flies" brought forth from the corruption of the arts, since they recognize that "eagles never catch flies" <note>original: "Aquilæ muscas nunquam capere"; a proverb meaning great minds do not bother with trivial matters</note>; indeed, they are accustomed to ignore them. Nevertheless, I shall ensure that from this very letter of theirs, Gassendi is answered in no different a way than Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and philosopher who was a fierce critic of Fludd’s mystical views</note> was previously.

> They say: "He who adds knowledge, adds sorrow, because in much knowledge there is much indignation. We speak from experience. For all the worldly; and the boastful braggarts <note>original: "Thrasones," a reference to Thraso, a boastful soldier in Roman comedy</note>, the vainglorious, the pompous, the talkative, and the empty, blaspheme undeservedly; they speak ill of us even regarding things unknown to them. But we do not wonder that the ungrateful world has persecuted the professors of the true arts along with Truth itself, etc."

Here they depict Mersenne, and also Lanovius <note>François de La Noue</note> and Gassendi in vivid colors. These men, since they understand absolutely nothing of the divine mystery of God and Nature, mock the mystics and think that among worldly men nothing is less known than that mystery of God; therefore, they believe it remains hidden even to this day. They admit nothing into the nature of things except what appears to be within their own grasp. But if they knew themselves rightly through the fear of the wise, they would immediately understand that the Kingdom of God is within us <note>Luke 17:21</note>, and is consequently the worker of all miracles. Truly, according to the Evangelist: "That wonderful Light is in the darkness, but the darkness did not recognize it; it came into the world, and the world was made through it, and the world did not know it." <note>John 1:5–10</note>

But leaving these matters to the response of Frizius <note>Joachim Frizius, a pseudonym often used by Fludd himself</note>, I shall proceed to my own. I see that Gassendi has acted as the most diligent servant and minister of his friend; and he has performed the office of Inquisitor so strictly that he has not passed over even a corner of my works. Indeed, by searching and prying into everything, he even brushes over that little apologetic work of ours issued against Dr. Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius, an early chemist and critic of the Rosicrucians</note> with a critical examination. Compelled by a certain admirable love (like that of Pylades for his Orestes, or Damon for his Pythias), he offers the very marrow of that work, along with its errors (if any are found in it), to Mersenne’s consideration.

### To the Epilogue at the end of the Book on the Highest Good.

->Text 60. Gassendi page 264.<-

Therefore, regarding that first part concerning various defenses of Scripture, we do not disapprove of it in such a way as to deny that a mystical sense lies hidden beneath the Historical one; for indeed, this variety of senses was taken by Fludd from our own Theology. What we cannot bear is that the mystical sense is translated into a single Alchemy: that whatever is said about Christ and his precious blood is made to refer to a single Ethereal Spirit and the Philosophical Stone; and that whatever is preached about the resurrection and the happiness which the blessed will enjoy in heaven, all of it must be understood as referring to the Brothers of the Rose Cross. For what else is this but to hold the profession of Christianity in loathsome mockery?

### Fludd.

<margin>Ephesians 2. 1 Corinthians 10. 1 Corinthians 12.</margin> Truly, I did not take the sense of the Sacred Scriptures from Roman Catholic Theology, but from a serious consideration and observation of the texts themselves. For if you look into the aforementioned Theology with a more inward eye, you will find it contradicts the truth in many places of the sacred Text. Should we then believe the Truth itself, or a poorly established Theology? Truly, whether they tolerate the translation of the sense of the Scriptures to my "Alchemy" or not, I do not care—unless they first truly understand what my Alchemy is. If, however, after it is well known, they do not approve that whatever I have said about the Spiritual Christ should be referred to the Stone of the Wise <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, let them reject it as they please. *For below, that is in the fourth Part, I shall open my mind regarding the true Alchemy.* Meanwhile, I affirm that I consider all those to be truly Brothers of the Rose Cross who are well-grounded in the Christian faith, confirmed in the knowledge of themselves, and who recognize that they are built upon the true **Cornerstone**, which is the Spiritual Christ—that rock, and the head of every man; indeed, one body having many members. For hence all are called sons of the Most High. Therefore, if I am asked who or what kind of person a true Brother of the Rose Cross is, I will say boldly, as I firmly believe: it is you who recognizes with certain faith that you are born from the heart and the depth of that blood (in which the divinity of life dwells), founded upon the **Cornerstone**, and finally summoned forth from the Catholic Rock <note>The "Universal" Rock, playing on the word "Catholic" meaning universal</note>. Such, I say, is a true Brother of the Rose Cross, or mystically, a Theologian of the Church; wherever he may live, and under whatever sect of Religion, or in whatever political Church. And of these, there is without doubt an almost infinite number, among men of both high and low condition. Whence Christ says indefinitely: *he who trusts in me has eternal life.* "In me," that is, in that **Cornerstone** upon which your fleshly temple is founded, and which is the source of your life. For in him we live, <margin>2 Corinthians 13.</margin> move, and have our being. Hence the Apostle: *he who speaks in me is not weakened, but is powerful in you.* Therefore, that imaginary, loathsome mockery of Gassendi's is banished from here.

->Text 61. Gassendi page 264 and 265.<-

I omit how Fludd, as he almost always does elsewhere, utterly rejects the literal sense, abusing the interpretation of that passage: "The letter kills," so that he may substitute a "vivifying spirit," namely an ethereal one.

### Fludd.

Whatever my friend may have written in that Treatise of his, I know he can sustain it, and I will also speak for him at this step regarding the extraction of the first Impiety. As for the "killing letter" and the "vivifying spirit" <note>2 Corinthians 3:6</note>, do we not know the ceremonial law to be a symbolic representation of the Law of Christ? How many parables and enigmatic senses, I ask, involve the true meaning of the Scriptures? "So that they may have ears and sense," says Christ, "yet not understand, you shall speak to them in parables." Did not Solomon involve and hide the mystery of eternal wisdom in parables and riddles, and say that it is the part of a wise man to conceal a thing? Furthermore, he interprets my meaning sinisterly. For by the "vivifying spirit," I do not understand that ethereal one, but the uncreated soul of the thing itself, by which it is animated and illuminated. This he himself has confessed elsewhere in many places of his book; however much he now feigns otherwise. Thus, therefore, when <margin>Ezekiel 37.</margin> I cited: *Come, O Spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again,* I did not assert that the air...

Fludd is transitioning from discussing the nature of the "Cornerstone" and the Rosicrucian Brotherhood to a deep theological and mystical interpretation of the blood of Christ, defending his view that the "vivifying spirit" is an internal, spiritual reality hidden within the physical world and the literal text of the Bible.</meta>

# To the Gassendian Exercises, Part II of the Third Section.

...[I denied] that that vivifying spirit <note>The "spirit that gives life," a central concept in Fludd’s mystical physics</note> was air or wind; but I said it was the life and act of the winds. Therefore, as a conclusion, I say that the Spirit resides under the letter <note>The "letter" refers to the literal, surface-level meaning of Scripture</note> no differently than the soul resides in the body. For just as the soul is hidden under the veil of the body, so is the Spirit under the letter. Thus, just as it is impossible to know what the soul is unless it is stripped of the body's veil, so also this Spirit can in no way be known or recognized unless you remove the husk of the letter. For once the tabernacle of both is laid aside, their splendor and glory immediately appear, so that they may be seen and known exactly as they are in themselves.

### Text 62. Gassendi, page 265.

> I ask only regarding what he [Fludd] has in this book concerning that passage of John, *the blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin* <note>original: "sanguis Iesu Christi filii Dei, emundat nos ab omni peccato"; 1 John 1:7</note>: in these words he holds—let it be added—that Saint John does not intend human blood, but that divine and mystic blood; hence he speaks of the blood of Jesus Christ, born of God, and not human blood, etc. I ask you truly, was Christ the Savior, as the Son of God, not also a true man? Did He, as God and not as Man, have the blood which He would pour out on the altar of the Cross? Was this blood not truly human, even if, from that ineffable union, it excelled all other blood? Was any other blood able to cleanse us from all sin? Who, then, is this other gore, not human but mystic, which, according to Fludd's mind, could provide this?

### Fludd.

<margin>John 6</margin>
I say that the sense of the scriptures is not about the external, visible, corporeal blood, but about that internal and spiritual blood lying hidden within the external. Neither do they deal with that palpable external flesh, but with the internal and spiritual or invisible flesh. This, indeed, I judge to be confirmed by these testimonies of the sacred book: *Christ said, he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.* <note>original: "Dixit Christus, non meam qui manducat, & bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam æternam, & ego resuscitabo eum in nouissimo die."</note> And soon after in the same place, He acknowledges that His flesh is the bread descending from heaven, of which if anyone eats, he shall not die. Indeed, He adds that He Himself is that living bread. Shall we believe, then, that the Savior understood common flesh or bread? What? Did flesh as commonly understood descend <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> from heaven? *For flesh and blood* (says the Apostle) *cannot possess the kingdom of God.* <note>original: "Caro enim & sanguis... regnum Dei possidere non possunt."</note> Since this is so, how can either flesh or blood, according to the common sense, descend from the kingdom of the heavens? Furthermore, <margin>John 6</margin> Christ says, *It is the Spirit that gives life, the flesh profits nothing;* <note>original: "Spiritus est qui viuificat, caro non prodest quicquam"</note> although He had said a little before, *he who eats my flesh has eternal life.* Likewise: *If anyone eats of this bread, he shall not die.* Therefore, it is evident that Christ does not speak of corporeal or external flesh or bread, but of spiritual or internal or mystic flesh and bread. And for this reason He finally concludes *that His words, which He had spoken, are Spirit and life.* According to this sense also, the Apostle said, the letter—that is, the external— <margin>Romans 2</margin> kills; the Spirit—that is, the internal—gives life. And elsewhere he says: *When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which* <margin>Romans 7</margin> *were through the law, worked in my members to bring forth fruit unto death; but now we are released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.* Therefore, it is clear that worldly flesh profits nothing, but the spirit does. Hence the Apostle says, a Jew is not one outwardly, *nor is that* <margin>Romans 2</margin> *circumcision which is outward in the flesh, but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart and Spirit.* And elsewhere more clearly: *Do not be ignorant that our Fathers were all under the cloud, and all ate the same spiritual food,* <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> *and all drank the same spiritual drink: for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.* Since, therefore, it is manifest that Christ spoke of spiritual flesh and blood not subject to death, it is also evident what kind of body He gave to His disciples to be eaten, and what kind of blood to be drunk, in the holy Communion <term>Synaxis</term> <note>From the Greek 'synaxis,' meaning a gathering or assembly, specifically referring here to the Eucharist or Holy Supper</note>: namely, not that real and palpable or external flesh of His, or that visible animal body, nor blood understood properly and commonly, but spiritual and mystic blood, and a spiritual and plainly celestial body. Which Christ hinted at not obscurely, saying: *I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom.* Thus it is necessary to believe that, since such a drink is to be drunk in heaven, even that which He gave to the disciples was of a celestial and spiritual nature, not truly elementary and common. Indeed, this is also clear from that speech of Christ which He held with the Jews who did not perceive spiritual things, and who said: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" Likewise to those disciples of His, murmuring among themselves: *this is a hard saying.* For He says in the same place: *My flesh is food indeed, and* <margin>John 6</margin> *my blood is drink indeed. This is the bread descending from heaven; he who eats this bread shall live forever, etc.* From what has been said, therefore, it is clearly established that, according to the Apostle, there are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies, and that there is a spiritual body and an animal body <note>In the sense of 'anima' or 'soul-animated,' meaning the biological body</note>, and consequently animal blood, and within the animal, spiritual blood. For blood itself is not the soul or the life of man, but that spirit of incorruptible and immortal life which is in the blood. Indeed, the soul or the life of the flesh itself is in the blood, as Genesis testifies. Therefore, while that external corporeal blood is poured out, that internal spiritual blood is also poured out together with it, and the life which flowed from the Word. For in the Word from all eternity was life, and that Word was Christ, the life and the truth: that incorruptible Spirit, I say, which gives life to all things, as the Apostle testifies, and which is in all things, as Solomon affirms. Hence we are called *the temple of the Holy Spirit, and members of Christ.* <margin>1 Cor 15; Wisdom 12</margin> But let us come to the parts of the text.

**Text.** *I ask you* (he says) *was Christ the Savior, as the Son of God, not also a true man?* I answer: Far be it from us to deny it, but at the same time we say that Christ indeed died insofar as He was man, but through His death He would have done nothing for us unless He had risen from death through the Spirit existing in Him—divine, vivifying, and immortal. Hence the Apostle: *If Christ has not risen, our faith is vain;* <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> *for you are still in your sins.*

**Text.** *Did He, as God and not as Man, have the blood which He would pour out on the altar of the cross?* I answer: that He indeed, insofar as He was man, had animal or visible blood, but that was only the seat of that celestial and spiritual blood; in the center of which moves the spirit of incorruptible life, giving life to all things and making them rise again: *In this very thing* (says St. Paul) *we live, move, and have our being.*

**Text.** *Was this blood not truly human, even if, from that ineffable union, it excelled all other blood?* I answer: It was truly human. But it must be understood that man is composed of the internal and external: and the internal is quickened and preserved by that incorruptible Spirit. Hence the Apostle: *If* <margin>Romans 8</margin> *His Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead, dwells in you, He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of His Spirit dwelling in you.* We say, therefore, that this blood was human, animal, and also that mystic and internal blood, in which was the incorruptible [life]...

**Text.** Could any other blood have the power to cleanse us from all sin? I answer, no. Thus Gassendi has here, according to the mind of Fludd, that mystic blood—not understood in the common way—explained. ->Text. 63. page 267.<-

Behold, since Fludd was so well-disposed toward the Rosy Cross Brothers <note>The Rosicrucians, a mysterious and controversial secret society of the 17th century</note>: since once, twice, and a third time he wrote an *Apology* for them: since he not only offered them secret vows, but even openly and with a loud voice cried out to them as if to "Baal, Baal" <note>A mocking reference to 1 Kings 18, where the priests of Baal shouted to their silent god</note>: since he hoped they would appear as gods from a machine <term>deus ex machina</term>: and since he could profit nothing at all from these things (evidently those so-blessed men did not have the leisure to turn aside for him); nevertheless, he thought their Arrival, and the Restoration to be made by them in these times, was of such great importance that, just as a new star arose when Christ was born long ago, so for the Brothers now about to emerge, those two stars—one in the Swan <note>Cygnus</note>, the other in the Serpent-bearer <note>Serpentarius/Ophiuchus; referring to the supernovae of 1600 and 1604</note>—recently appeared.

->Fludd.<-

Let Gassendi, swelling and triumphing with mocking laughter, understand that Fludd, however much provoked and irritated, is nevertheless peaceful; and he can very easily bear scoffs and derisions of that sort, proceeding from a worldly, vainglorious, and boastful <term>Thrasonic</term> <note>Referring to Thraso, a braggart soldier in Roman comedy</note> man. Therefore, speaking more sparingly, I say: it is human to suffer as much as it is to err. I, however, do not err at all, even though I suffer much. And I suffer more because of that immodesty which Gassendi exercised against me in this recited text, than because of any lack of knowledge concerning men most skilled in the deeper mysteries of Nature. But what else would a Man, ignorant and estranged from the inward mysteries of Nature, do? Nevertheless, are those God-taught men <term>Theodidacti</term> <note>A term Fludd uses for the Rosicrucians or divinely inspired sages</note> familiar to me? And what have I profited from them as teachers? I have no intention of depositing this into Gassendi’s bosom; this at least I say again and again: I have by no means erred in that I studiously sought their familiarity. For I did not affect the Name of the R. C. Brothers, but the truth itself which they possess, and the virtue which they cultivate, and with which they are endowed. And I undertook to defend this with an Apologetic style, not three times (as Gassendi falsely sings) but only once. Meanwhile, however, that virtue has come to me as I desired (thanks be to God), and I feel it being increased in me steadily and by degrees. Wherefore the argument is that I have not cried out so many times "Baal, Baal," as Gassendi, with sufficient unhappiness, calumniates me. For such an invocation is futile. But my invocation—since it is directed not in the Gassendian or Papist manner to Mortals or Saints, through painted images and those sculpted from stone and wood or made by hand, but to the living God himself—therefore (I return immense thanks again and again to my Creator) it is salvific for both my body and soul. Let Gassendi, therefore, take care of himself. For he, I know not who, gropes in the thick darkness of the Papacy; therefore he will arrive at a spark of light either never, or only very slowly. Truly, let him invoke his handmade Saints, but without benefit. Let him trust in the host and wine, or his fabricated Mass, but without fruit. Let him boast of great things in his words and writings, but with small enough strength. Let him, finally, cling to his worldly Exercises. And why not? For a worldly man must necessarily do worldly things. Wherefore I do not envy him at all, nor do I deride him, but rather I pity him, as a Brother in Christ however much erring and weak. Furthermore, just as I myself have never invoked Creatures or Mortals, lest by such an Idolatrous action I should sprinkle a stain upon my soul, so I will never invoke them in the future, lest I repent too late of that lethal error. He, therefore, when I sought virtue as a suppliant from him—choosing the spiritual kernel and leaving behind the husk—at last took pity on me and imparted the same to me through certain means. And certainly, I feel it (as was said) multiplying little by little in my heart, so that I am not ignorant of what I am in my own internal self. Therefore, since I have received so great a reward or recompense, I do not repent having written that *Apology* for the sake of truth. > All worldly men, and glorious Boasters <term>Thrasones</term>, vaunting, pompous, talkative, and empty, undeservedly blaspheme and even speak evil of us regarding things unknown; but we do not wonder that the ungrateful world has persecuted the professors of the true arts with the truth itself.

<margin>Luke 4. Luke 10.</margin> The Spirit, and guardian of the human mind, which abounded miraculously in Christ. Indeed, as the Holy Scriptures testify, it was poured out upon Him without measure. Whence also He baptized with the Holy Spirit: and He returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit: and He exulted in the Holy Spirit, etc.

<margin>John 6. 1 Cor. 15.</margin> **Text.** Could any other blood have the power to cleanse us from all sin? I answer, no. But yet I add, that His animal <note>original: "animalis"; Fludd uses this to mean 'physical' or 'belonging to the lower soul,' as opposed to the higher spirit</note> and external blood accomplished nothing. For physical flesh and blood profit nothing, by the authority of Christ Himself. Nor shall they enter the kingdom of God. Indeed, not even Christ Himself, in that fleshly and bloody state of His, ascended into the kingdom of His Father; but rather in a glorified, spiritual, and heavenly body. Therefore, it was that internal blood of Christ, full and overflowing with divine spirit and power, which performed that saving work of cleansing. For the Spirit, which dwells in that spiritual blood, alone gives life; <margin>2 Cor. 5:16. Rom. 16.</margin> whereas the external blood and flesh are, in themselves, dead and inanimate. And this is why the Apostle denies that he now knows Christ according to the flesh, but rather according to the spirit and power: whence he says elsewhere: it is the power of God unto salvation for every believer. He does not say human flesh or blood, but divine power. Thus Gassendi has here, from Fludd's mind, that divine mystery explained, understood in a way that is not common. For Christ was preached in mystery by His Apostles, as the scriptures testify; and even Christ Himself spoke to His disciples in parables.

### Text 63. page 267.

Look, since Fludd was so well-disposed toward the Rosy Brothers <note>The Rosicrucians, a mysterious and legendary secret society of sages</note>: since he wrote an Apology for them once, twice, and a third time: since he not only offered them secret prayers, but even cried out openly and with a loud voice, like "Baal, Baal" <note>A reference to the priests of the pagan god Baal in the Bible, used here by Gassendi to mock Fludd as a desperate idolater</note>: since he hoped they would appear to him like gods from a machine <note>original: "Deos e machina"; a theatrical term for a sudden, miraculous intervention</note>: and since he could profit nothing at all from these things; (evidently those blessed ones did not have the leisure to turn aside to him) nevertheless, he thought their Arrival, and the Restoration to be made by them in these times, was of such great moment that, just as a new star once rose for the birth of Christ: so for the Brothers about to emerge, those two stars—one in the Swan <note>Cygnus</note>, the other in the Serpent-bearer <note>Ophiuchus</note>—recently appeared.

Therefore, speaking more sparingly, I say: it is human to suffer as much as it is to err. However, I do not err, though I suffer much. But what else would a Man, ignorant of and foreign to the inner mysteries of Nature, do? Nevertheless, are those God-taught men <note>original: "Theodidacti"</note> familiar to me? And what have I profited from them as teachers? For I did not crave the *Name* of the Brothers of the R.C. <note>The Rosy Cross</note>, but the very truth which they possess, and the virtue which they cultivate, and with which they are endowed. And I undertook to defend this with an Apologetic style, not three times (as Gassendi falsely sings), but only once. # To the Gassendian Exercises, Section III, Part II.

<margin>John 15.</margin>
...heard from the sacred font, yet never reached a knowledge of its essence? Hence Christ says to those who recognized the true Cornerstone—and therefore adore him—against those who hate them:

> If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. <note>John 15:19</note>

Truly, let Gassendi say whether humility is to be preferred to pride or not; but perhaps he will assign the first place to humility. Therefore, he will find it necessary to sing a palinode <note>A poem or song retracting a previous statement; a formal retraction.</note> and, in turn, excuse me, whom he so greatly accused in the preceding text. For I, led by the love of wisdom to acquire knowledge of the same, most humbly subjected myself to the professors of wisdom, and prayed that I might be led into the inner shrines of wisdom, and that the sun of truth would deign to instruct me therein. And I did this not with a false heart—namely, full of worldly cunning, hiding one thing in my breast while, like some hypocrite, pretending another before the world—but I did so as much in soul as in body, that is, both internally and externally. I acted so that the degree to which I burned with the love of Wisdom and the desire for knowing her might be known to all everywhere, and that my humility might be made public.

Furthermore, I know well enough that Gassendi himself was captured by such a great curiosity for knowing things that, upon hearing the rumor of the virtues of the Rosicrucian Brothers <note>original: "Fratrum R. C."; referring to the Rosicrucians, a mysterious esoteric society Fludd famously defended</note>, and understanding those things concerning the miracles of Nature published by them in their fame and confession, there soon flared up in his mind a remarkable appetite and a thirst greater than that of Tantalus <note>A mythological figure punished with eternal hunger and thirst</note> to understand and learn the things they produced. But his proud mind was an obstacle, preventing him from submitting himself to them; and so, in the manner of hypocrites, he professed one thing before men, but held another in his heart. Whether this be true or not, I propose it to be judged first by his own conscience, and thereafter by God, the Searcher of hearts and deeds. Now, however, since he can attain his wish by no path, he mocks those Brothers; he cries out against them, blaming, vituperating, and accusing them—like the fox cleverly and craftily disparaging the grapes simply because he cannot reach them. Indeed, he even seems to hate all those who pursue the said Brothers with love because of the gifts granted to them by God, or who desire their Knowledge. And among the rest, this Gassendi—now despairing of his hope—delights in greeting and harrassing me with loud laughter and mockery (though it is vain and empty), and he ridicules my humility in seeking knowledge with more than a little falseness. But so be it! Let the difference appear between the humble confidence of Fludd and the lofty and proud distrust of Gassendi. Let Gassendi’s troublesome and boasting calumny shine forth, and let Fludd’s humble and restrained patience—though now appearing to sink—triumph at last. For *Blessed* (says Christ) *are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.*

<margin>Matthew 5.</margin>
> Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you and say all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account, etc.

This, I say, is spoken by Him who is the true Cornerstone <note>original: "Lapis Angularis"</note> whom we adore—not that spurious and false Philosophers' Stone <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> of Gassendi. That Rock, I say, the true and spiritual one, which Gassendi, puffed up with pride, seems to reject with such a taunt.

<margin>James 4.</margin>
> But God resists the proud (says the Apostle), but gives grace to the humble.

There was no reason, therefore, for Gassendi to mock me so much for seeking knowledge from those taught by God <note>original: "Theodidactis"</note>, since he himself has nothing that he did not receive from elsewhere. Let him, therefore (according to the command of Christ), first cast the beam out of his own eye, so that he might more rightly see the speck to be pulled from his brother’s eye. For why should he exalt himself so much in the affairs of others? Why should he so insult his brothers? Furthermore, in what matter, I ask, is he so excellent? Is there anything sent out in his booklet against Aristotle that surpasses all human wits? Is he the only Daphnis <note>A legendary Sicilian shepherd; here used to mean a uniquely famous or peerless person</note> in the woods known from here to the stars? Are his celestial observations so rare that they are adored even by the wisest? Finally, are his *Exercises* against Fludd’s philosophy so magnificent and wonderful that he should finish them with such a glorious conclusion—a sign, surely, of the greatest self-love <note>original: "Philautiae"; vanity or excessive self-love</note>—and sing a triumph before the victory, claiming the paean for himself, repeating that "Io Paean! Io Paean!"? <note>A Greek shout of victory or triumph</note> 

But I wish Gassendi to understand, along with the whole Christian world endowed with learning, that the modesty and morality in the preceding parts of his writing have restrained the rigor and sharpness of my pen and tempered it until now; but if in the future he tries to crush me with taunts, he himself—and the other birds of his feather—shall feel what kind of man I am. For I have hitherto abstained from an examination of his booklet against Aristotle, likewise from an inquiry into his celestial observations; but if he provokes me further, I will show that his strength in the arts and philosophy, as well as his "omnipotence" in phrasing and method of refutation (as he, puffed up with self-love, believes it to be), is the very essence of weakness. This I will do so that it may appear most clearly in the eyes of all wise men—French, German, and our own countrymen alike—that his writings are sterile and of almost no importance. And I shall achieve this by my own sharp wit. The incivility and immodesty of his last text forced me to publish these things to the world. For I am a sharp enemy and adversary to those elated by pride and self-love, and to those leaping over the laws and limits of civility; but to the modest and civil, I declare myself bound by every law of mercy and humanity—nay, I am their servant. But let us look at the conclusion of this very text of his.

> Nevertheless (he says), he thought their arrival, and the restoration to be made by them in these times, to be of such great importance that just as a new star arose when Christ was formerly born, so for the Brothers now about to emerge, those two stars—one in Cygnus, the other in Ophiuchus <note>original: "Serpentario"</note>—have recently appeared, etc.

Here he imagines marvelously. For I did not presage, from that celestial figure in my published *Apologetic Discourse*, the arrival of the Rosicrucian Brothers; rather, I predicted that great changes in Religion were coming, and I said that the Religious would at last carry off the palm in the end. I erected that celestial chart for the hour and minute of the Great Conjunction <note>An alignment of Jupiter and Saturn, historically viewed as a herald of massive political or religious shifts</note> made between Saturn and Jupiter, and from it, in a few words and generally, I predicted the future commotions of the Europeans, the slaughters of the Bohemians, and the miseries of Prussia <note>original: "Borussiae"</note> and Pomerania inflicted upon them by sword and famine. I foretold that the sword, famine, and plague would rage almost everywhere throughout Europe. I predicted that the hearts of Princes and Nobles would be prone to ambition and hidden dissimulation; that men would plot frequent treasons; and that there would be tremendous thunders and unusual floods. Finally, just as I observed that all these things had to happen because of the dominion of Saturn over Jupiter, so I also perceived that at length, in the course of time, Jupiter—overcoming the malice of Saturn and marked by justice and Religion—would arrange all things in harmonious peace, etc. And truly, subsequent experience has proved that all these things have already happened in the predicted places, and it will prove they are still to happen. For the force of a conjunction of the superior planets extends for thirty years; so that, although war, plague, famine, floods...

### To the Gassendian Exercises, Member III. Part II.

He heard from the sacred font, yet he never reached a knowledge of its true essence. Hence Christ, speaking to those who recognized the true **Cornerstone** and therefore adore Him, says against those who hate them: <margin>John 15:</margin> *If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.* <note>original: "Si de Mundo essetis..."</note>

But, Gassendi might ask, is humility to be preferred over pride or not? Perhaps he will grant humility the first place. Therefore, he will find it necessary to sing a recantation <note>original: "Palinodiam canere," meaning to publicly retract a previous statement</note> and, in turn, excuse me, whom he accused so vehemently in the preceding text. For I, led by the love of wisdom to acquire knowledge of the same, most humbly subjected myself to the professors of wisdom, and prayed that once I was introduced into the inner shrines of wisdom, they would deign to instruct me in it. And I did this not with a false heart—full of worldly cunning, hiding one thing in my breast while pretending another before the world like some hypocrite—but I did so in both soul and body; that is, both internally and externally. I acted so that the fire of my love for Wisdom and my desire to know her might be known to everyone everywhere, and that my humility might be made manifest.

Furthermore, I know well enough that Gassendi himself was captured by such a great curiosity to know things that, upon hearing the rumor of the virtues of the <term>Rosicrucian Brothers</term> <note>original: "Fratrum R. C."; the Rosicrucians were a secret society of sages and alchemists</note>, and understanding what had been published by them concerning the miracles of Nature in their "Fama" and "Confession," there soon flared up in his mind a great appetite and a thirst greater than that of Tantalus to understand and learn the things they produced. But his proud mind was an obstacle, preventing him from submitting himself to them; and so, in the manner of hypocrites, he professed one thing before men while holding another in his heart. Whether this is true, I propose should be judged first by his own conscience, and then by God, the Searcher of hearts and of all things. Now, however, since he could not achieve his wish by any path, he mocks those Brothers; he cries out against them, blaming, reviling, and accusing them, like the fox who cunningly and craftily disparages the grapes simply because he cannot reach them. Indeed, he even seems to hate all those who follow the said Brothers with love because of the gifts granted to them by God, or who hunger for their Knowledge. And among the rest, this now-despairing Gassendi longs to mock and harass me with laughter and ridicule, though in a vain and empty way, and he laughs most falsely at my humility in seeking the sciences. But so be it! Let the difference appear between the humble confidence of Fludd and the lofty and proud distrust of Gassendi. Let the restless and boasting slander of Gassendi shine forth alongside the humble and restrained patience of Fludd; though it seems to sink down now, it will triumph in the end. For *Blessed* (says Christ) *are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.* <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> *Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you for righteousness' sake, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for my sake, etc.* This, I say, is spoken by Him who is the true **Cornerstone**, whom we adore—not that base and false <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> of Gassendi. That Stone, I say, is the true and Spiritual Rock, which Gassendi, swollen with pride, seems to reject with such a taunt. <margin>James 4.</margin> *But God* (says the Apostle) *resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.* There was no reason, therefore, why Gassendi should mock me so much for seeking knowledge from the <term>Theodidacts</term> <note>Those taught directly by God</note>, since he himself has nothing that he did not receive from elsewhere. Let him, therefore, (according to the command of Christ) first cast the beam out of his own eye, so that he may see more clearly to pull the speck out of his brother's eye. For why should he exalt himself so much in the affairs of others? Why should he so insult his brothers? Furthermore, in what matter, I ask, is he so excellent? Is there anything in his little book published against Aristotle that surpasses all human genius? Is he alone "Daphnis in the woods, known from here to the stars"? <note>A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues, mocking Gassendi's self-importance</note> Are his celestial observations so rare that they are worshipped even by the wisest? Finally, are his *Exercises* against the Fluddian Philosophy so magnificent and wonderful that he should end them with such a glorious conclusion (a sign, surely, of the highest <term>Philautia</term> <note>original Greek: extreme self-love or conceit</note>), and sing a song of triumph as if before the victory, claiming the palm for himself, repeating that cry, "Hail the healer! Hail the healer!"? <note>original: "iö pæan! iö pæan!"; a Greek hymn of praise or victory</note> But I would have Gassendi understand, along with the entire learned Christian world, that the modesty and morality of the preceding parts of his writing restrained and tempered the rigor and sharpness of my pen until now; but if in the future he attempts to crush me with taunts, he himself, and the rest of the birds of his feather, shall feel what kind of man I am. For I have refrained until now from examining his book against Aristotle; likewise from investigating his celestial observations; but if he provokes me further, I will show that his strength in the arts and Philosophy—as well as his "omnipotence" in phrasing and methods of refutation (as he, swollen with self-love, believes)—is the very essence of weakness. This shall appear most clearly in the eyes of all wise men, whether French, German, or our own countrymen: that his writings are sterile and of almost no importance. And I shall achieve this by my own sharp wit. The incivility and immodesty of his last text has forced me to publish these things to the world. For I am a sharp enemy and adversary to those elated by pride and self-love, as well as those leaping over the laws and limits of civility; but to the modest and civil, I declare myself bound by every law of mercy and humanity—indeed, I am their servant. But let us look at the closing statement of this very text of his.

> Nevertheless, he says, he thought their arrival and the restoration to be made by them in these times was of such great importance that, just as a new star rose when Christ was born of old, so for the Brothers now about to emerge, those two stars—one in the Swan <note>Cygnus</note>, the other in the Serpent-bearer <note>Ophiuchus/Serpentarius</note>—have recently appeared, etc.

Here he imagines marvelously. For I did not presage, from that celestial figure in my upright Apologetic discourse, the arrival of the Rosicrucian Brothers; rather, I predicted great future changes in Religion; and I said that the Religious would at last carry off the palm in the end. I erected that celestial chart for the hour and minute of the **Great Conjunction** made between Saturn and Jupiter, and from it, I depicted in a few words, and that generally, the future state of Europe. But elsewhere, namely in a Treatise destined for this alone, I expressed the future effects of that conjunction more copiously and specifically: in which I predicted the future war of Italy and the Piedmontese, the commotions of the French, the disasters of the Bohemians, and the miseries of Prussia and Pomerania, inflicted upon them by sword and famine. I foretold that the sword, famine, and plague would rage almost everywhere through Europe. I predicted that the hearts of Princes and Nobles would be prone to ambition and hidden dissimulation; that men would plot frequent treasons; and there would be tremendous thunders and unusual floods. Finally, as I observed that all these things had to happen because of Saturn’s dominion over Jupiter; so I also perceived that at length, in the course of time, Jupiter—overcoming the malice of Saturn and distinguished by justice and Religion—would arrange all things in harmonious peace, etc. And indeed, that all these things have already occurred in the predicted places, following experience has proven, and will yet prove them to come. For the force of the conjunction of the superior Planets extends itself to thirty years; so that, although war, plague, famine,
