# CHAPTER III.

## In which he responds to each specific part of this fictional Impiety.

->Point 1. Mersenne.<-

Fludd is convicted of feeling and teaching, among other things:
**First, that the whole of Holy Scripture refers to Alchemy and Alchemical principles.**

->Fludd.<-

<margin>Ephesians 2:19</margin>
Fludd responds that the base and foundation of all Scripture is the Cornerstone <note>original: "lapis Angularis"</note>, namely Jesus Christ, which stone is that "Supreme Good" which is the foundation of true, divine, and mystical Alchemy. Through Christ (says the Apostle), we both have access in one spirit to the Father: therefore you are no longer guests and strangers, but you are citizens with the Saints and of the Household of God, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with the Cornerstone itself being Jesus Christ. In Him, the whole building and structure grows into a Temple for the Lord, in which you also are built together into a dwelling place for God in the Holy Spirit, etc. Now, however, it must be known that the duty of spiritual Alchemy is to separate, through mortification, that entire dark fabrication which is corruptible and vile, and thus to lay down the tabernacle of gloom and ignorance, so that the incorruptible spirit—once shrouded in darkness—may be liberated, flourish, and multiply within us. This is mediated by that fiery spirit, full of grace, which God kindly rains down and multiplies from a grain into a mountain. This, therefore, is that true Alchemy which I embrace: by its mediation, that Cornerstone, which is the basis of my life and soul, can be multiplied in me, even unto the new regeneration and resurrection of my dead self, from the old human nature dead in Adam, into a new and living man in Christ, or that Cornerstone. Hence the Apostle says: God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus: but we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence may be of the power of God and not from us. We are humbled but
<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
not confounded: always carrying about the mortification <note>In this context, "mortification" refers to the "killing" or refining of the lower, physical nature to reveal the spiritual.</note> in our body, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies, etc. And although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
<margin>2 Corinthians 5:1</margin>
If our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens. If anyone is a new creature in Christ, the old things have passed away;
<margin>John 12:24</margin>
Behold, all things are made new, etc. The hour comes that the Son of Man should be glorified: unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, etc. <note>original: "nisi granum frumenti..."</note> By these things, we perceive the mystical separation of the world from the unclean, the light from the dark, the fleshy from the spiritual, and the multiplication of the shining divinity in the separate and free spirit—an Alchemy of the divine Word performed within the human body. Through the manifestation of this Stone, the righteous shall shine like the Sun in the kingdom of their Father. By its mediation, the body of Christ was transfigured and his face shone
<margin>Matthew 13:43. Matthew 17.</margin>
<margin>The Sun, etc.</margin>
like the Sun, etc. I conclude, therefore, that the sense of the Holy Scriptures is none other than that explained through the "Theo-philosophical" Cornerstone, which we understand as the Word, Jesus Christ the Messiah, or Eternal Wisdom; as you will find more clearly explained in the final portion of this section. Truly, I have responded accurately enough to this point above in Text 20, Member 2, Part 2; therefore, I pray you inspect that.

->Point 2. Mersenne.<-

**It does not matter to Fludd what religion you are—Roman, Lutheran, or any other.**

->Fludd.<-

But in what place did you find this opinion of Fludd’s? This is indeed not the least of your "Babylonian fictions." As for that writing concerning the "Supreme Good," it is not mine, but should be attributed to my friend Frisius Scotus <note>A pseudonym or associate of Fludd's; "Scotus" implies he was Scottish.</note>, as I candidly confessed to Gassendi. Indeed, if you read that very writing, you will not find such an assertion brought forth there; rather, he seems to assert in his Epilogue that there are men in every sect of religion who are essentially engaged with the mystical wisdom of God, and who aim as directly as possible at that same goal of the Supreme Good. I would wish for any literate person to read that Epilogue of Frisius with diligence; they will perceive immediately whether this rash judge—or rather, the herald of an unjust judgment—proclaimed the truth when he taught that "it does not matter to Fludd what religion one becomes." But since a fuller response has been given to that same calculation of Lanovius in Text 19, Member 2, I will refrain from further words in this place.

->Point 3. Mersenne.<-

**Fludd feels and teaches that he alone is "Catholic" who believes in the "Catholic Stone"—that is, the Philosophical Stone—by whose power men may cast out demons and speak in new tongues.**

->Fludd.<-

I truly believe that all miracles can be performed by the power of the highest Cornerstone, or the Theo-Philosophical Stone—which is the spiritual Christ—and that he alone is a "Catholic" <note>Fludd is playing on the word "Catholic," which means "universal." He argues that true Christianity is a universal, mystical truth rather than just a denominational label.</note> who believes in that Stone, and that he who does not believe in Him is a reprobate and an infidel. But more on these things below.

<meta>This page continues Fludd’s rebuttal against his critics, specifically focusing on the third and fourth points of accusation regarding his views on the nature of God, the Ethereal Spirit, and the Sun. He is defending himself against the charge that he makes God part of a material "composition" (mixture) with the world.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>
<header>Fludd’s Response</header>

Finally, it is more likely that the Divine Virtue itself inhabits the Ethereal Spirit; this is to be gathered from the fact that His seat is said to be in the heavens. And Christ says: *The true bread is He who descends from heaven and gives life to the world. I am the Bread of Life,* etc. But heaven, insofar as its purity surpasses the nature of the element of fire, or the Fourth Essence, is called the Fifth Essence <note>original: "Quinta essentia"; in medieval philosophy, the quintessence was a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>. It is certain, therefore, that the more a creature abounds in goodness and purity, the fuller of Divinity it becomes. For God alone is good, and creatures possess no goodness except that which they participate in from that source of all goodness. Hence Augustine seems to recognize that as much light as something has within itself, so much of Divinity does it claim for itself. Furthermore, the Ether is called, as it were, "fiery air": from which comes that notable and most true axiom: *In the Light is the Deity, and in the Deity is the Light.* <note>original: "In Lumine numen, in Numine lumen."</note> Hence that text of the Prophet previously cited: *Clothed in light as if with a garment.* If, therefore, Gassendi, along with Mersenne and Launoy, have ears, let them hear these things, and let them truly understand what they have heard; then they will perceive that I have spoken not of the alchemy of men, but of the Spagyric <term>Spagyric: from the Greek words for 'separating' and 'recombining,' used by Fludd to describe God's creative power to organize the universe like a master alchemist.</term> power and operation of the Divine Word. If they mock this, the Creator of all will also look upon their impiety in that mockery, and in His own time He will not let it pass unpunished. I conclude, therefore, that even this limb <note>Referring to the previous "part" of the accusation.</note> seems to waste away and be plainly deadened, and therefore it must be cut off along with the preceding one. For it is of no value or weight in building up this charge of Impiety. I proceed, therefore, to the third part.

## Part 3. Mersenne.

->That God therefore makes a composition with this ethereal spirit.<-

## Fludd.

<margin>John 1.</margin>
This is false. For I have not made God a "composition" <note>Mersenne accused Fludd of Pantheism, suggesting God is just a part of a physical mixture.</note>, but I say that the act and life of God, and consequently His essence, is in all things, since without it nothing can exist. Whence St. John says: *By him all things were made, and without him nothing; in him was life, etc.* He Himself fills heaven as His own seat: and by His presence in it, He animates and vivifies its Spirit, according to that word of the Apostle, *God vivifies all things.* Hence the Text says elsewhere: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit from His mouth, all their power.* But life is the most essential power and act. What? Do I make God a part of a composition because of this? Not in the least. For just as God in His essence is indivisible, so He cannot be called a "part," but He is in all things, and through all things, as the most essential act of life, insofar as He vivifies all things. He is thus in all things in such a way that He is also outside all things, with no divisibility of His substance preceding it. Thus by His word all things were made, and by His Spirit life is applied to all: in which general act His word is not divided from the Speaker, nor is the Spirit in any way disjoined from either one.

<margin>
4 Esdras 16.
Acts 17.
</margin>
Hence Esdras says: *The breath of God Almighty made all things, and searches out all things in the hidden places of the earth. Thus in God we live, move, and have our being;* and yet God is in us, and we are in God, not as a part in a composition. Therefore I conclude that God is "in" the composition of the Creature, not as a part of the mixture, but as the eternal composing act—not mixed with the compound, but mixing its particles by number, weight, and due measure, tempering them and uniting them as if with the glue of love: so that, although He is present to all things for their existence, yet in Himself, and through Himself, He remains and is simple, without any stain from the composite thing.

<margin>Pimander</margin>
Hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismegistus"; the legendary founder of Hermeticism, whose text 'Pimander' or 'Poimandres' Fludd frequently cites as equal to Scripture.</note> says: *The Word, standing by the moist nature, cherished it.* But Mersenne will say that Hermes Trismegistus is an impious author. But does not Holy Scripture have this written even more expressly? Namely: *The heavens were of old and the earth consisting of water and through water by the word of God.* This sounds the same as that Psalm mentioned before: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, etc.* But to immerse myself even more deeply into this matter: I will produce Scriptures that support my meaning. For in them we are expressly taught how the essence of God is always present in animating, tempering, and proportioning the mundane Spirit according to His will.

<margin>
Job 28.
Wisdom 7.
Wisdom 7.
</margin>
Job therefore says: *God by his wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs the waters in measure, makes the decreed laws for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders, etc.* From these we can see how the Spirit of God, which is the bright emanation of the Almighty, animates, composes, dissolves, and alters the mundane Spirit, from state to state, and from species to species: and how by reason of such diverse works, it is called "manifold" by the wise man, and yet in itself it is "simple."

<margin>Jeremiah 51.</margin>
Likewise, how it is called "multiform wisdom" by the Apostle; surely insofar as it puts on and produces many species in the Spirit, and out of the mundane Spirit. Whence also the Prophet says: *He who made the earth in his strength, and prepared the world in his wisdom, and by his prudence stretched out the heavens; when he gives his voice, the waters in heaven are multiplied; when he lifts the clouds from the end of the earth, he makes lightnings and rain, and brings forth the winds from his treasures.* In these things we see how the eternal wisdom is in the mundane spirit, and works in the composition of meteors out of the mundane spirit, and much more in that ethereal one: because it is fuller of purity, goodness, and vivifying rays.

<margin>Proverbs 8.</margin>
Does not the Text elsewhere also openly narrate and explain how the Spirit of wisdom, existing in the mundane Spirit, is the composer of all things out of it? *Jehovah possessed Wisdom* (says Solomon) *in the beginning of his way, before any time, when he fitted the heavens, there she was with him, composing all things.* Finally, when the Word was made flesh, did not Divinity enter into the composition?

<margin>
Ezekiel 35.
Psalm 139.
Job 10.
</margin>
When the earth was opened, so that the Savior might be brought forth; did not divinity then inhabit that earth? Much more truly does it inhabit the clear Spirit of heaven, whether it be of the world or of the creature. For heaven is as much in the heaven of both cosmoses as it is in the earth. Behold, says Jehovah, *I will put my Spirit into you, and you shall live.* Here you see the soul of the composite, or the Spirit of the creature, animated by a divine act. And elsewhere: *You possess my reins, from when I was covered in my mother's womb.* Have you not poured me out like milk? Here it evidently appears that the vivifying power of God is in the composite, as if composing and vivifying all things in it, and that it has its place in the Spirit of life, which is ethereal.

We conclude, therefore, that this limb of this Chimera of Impiety is too weak and founded upon nothing, and therefore it must necessarily collapse and vanish of its own accord. Therefore, to the fourth point.

## Part 4. Mersenne.

->That He resides especially in the Sun, from where He is vibrated forth for the generation and vivification of all things.<-

## Fludd.

And why not? For His seat is said to be in heaven. Furthermore, the Psalmist narrates in express words: that God placed His tabernacle in the Sun. Does this not seem consistent with the truth, that any thing claims as much of God for itself as it has light within it? And does not daily experience teach us that a vivifying outflow descends from the Sun every year into the earth and sea, by means of which all things germinate, and are refreshed by a vivifying and vegetative heat? But, by the testimony of Scripture, God is the only one who vivifies all things, and is the bread...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s defense of his philosophy against the accusations of "impiety" leveled by Marin Mersenne and Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd argued that the purity of the heavens and the Sun allows them to participate more fully in the Divine nature. Here, he moves toward a central theological dispute: whether God acts directly in all things or through secondary, natural causes.</meta>

<header>Regarding the Impieties, Member IV. Portion I. Part II.</header>

...and the bread of life descended from heaven, and that bread is the spiritual Christ, as Saint John testifies. What then? Shall we believe that Divinity is absent from the Sun, when we see such wonderful effects of life descending so abundantly from that tabernacle of his? For where the goodness of God is present, there the Divinity itself—or the divine essence—cannot possibly be absent; since "the Good" and "God" are interchangeable <note>original: "conuertibilia"; a logical term meaning two terms that refer to the same thing and can be swapped.</note> and inseparable. Therefore, since it is certain that the source of life and multiplication descends through the solar vents, it must also be established that divinity is undoubtedly present there in abundance. It is the proper nature of divinity to give life, and inspiration, and all things; consequently, God has, as it were, stored the treasure of life in the sun, so that from its sanctuary—as if from some treasury chest—He might liberally rain down the gifts of life upon His creatures.

I do not say that God is so enclosed within the sun that He is nowhere else; for He is present everywhere, and He can grant the happiness of life to all, even to those dying or completely dead outside the path of nature. This is seen when He said, *Come, O Spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain that they may live again.* <note>A reference to the vision of the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37:9.</note> However, He made the Sun the tabernacle of natural life, or a vessel full of His glory. By its outflow, not only are individual creatures animated, moved, and preserved, but also the Elements and the general Spirit of the world, from which creatures draw their immediate food of life. Hence the sacred text cited above: *God in His wisdom sets a weight for the wind and measures out the waters,* etc. Therefore, this point of the argument falls away without needing any further push. To the final part.

### Particula 5. Mersenne.

->That God is, in this manner, the form of all things, and thus performs all things such that secondary causes <term>Secondary causes: In medieval philosophy, these are natural things (like fire or plants) that appear to cause effects, though theologians debated if the power actually came from God.</term> do nothing by themselves.<-

->*Fludd’s Response.*<-

Here indeed a very great task presents itself to be completed: for in this lies the entire knot of dissolving and wiping away these "Impieties"; indeed, it is the revelation of the truth itself, which has been hidden and obscured for a long time. For what (I ask) is a more serious cause of such impiety among worldly men, and of such ignorance of the true God, than falsely attributing to Creatures those things which in reality and essentially belong to God? Or what, by the Immortal God, is more futile or more foolish in the Christian world than to assert that action, motion, and life exist in and of themselves within things that are plainly dead?

From this comes the origin of Idolatry; from this comes the neglect of God and a vain confidence in creatures. From this, finally, comes the ignorance of the Divine Majesty. Although He is within all things without limit, and all things live and exist in Him, the ungrateful world does not acknowledge this. Instead, it falsely ascribes the act of life, motion, generation, and preservation either to "Nature," or to a "created soul," or to some "radical spirit" (as they call it), or to "innate heat," or to the heart, or the blood, or the ether, or the Sun and stars, or other created things of this kind. Thus, the world tends to use the effect in place of the essential cause and the sole efficient power—substituting the creature for the Creator himself—not listening to the words of the Evangelist: *All things were made by Him, and without Him was nothing made. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men, which was in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. He was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not,* etc. For this reason, He makes a distinction between those who recognized this eternal light working all in all, and those who were ignorant of it and denied it; calling one sect the "children of the world," and the other the "children of God" through adoption or grace.

# CHAPTER III.

->In which one most famous question regarding the Universal Act is discussed.<-

These things having been rightly considered, it is clearer than light how empty those nurseries are which Mersenne sowed in the sandy and sterile soil of Gassendi to build up this charge of "Impiety." But, because the very structure of that "Impiety" rests on a subject of a question that is difficult to discuss—by whose proper resolution and explanation that immense error among Europeans, introduced from Heathen Philosophers <note>Referring primarily to Aristotle and his followers.</note> into the Christian world, will be manifested and opened up—I judge it first of all worthwhile to reveal it to the world. This is so that any religious person may be called back from Idolatry to the true worship of God; that is, moved from the admiration of the creature to the adoration of the Creator. For what else (I ask) is it but a foul kind of Idolatry to attribute to creatures that which by highest right belongs to the Creator alone? The question is as follows:

> Does God work all in all immediately as the sole and only agent in the world? Or does He act only as the principal efficient cause, by means of subordinate causes or creatures that act by themselves?

Gassendi, agreeing with the doctrine of Aristotle, affirms along with his disciples Marin Mersenne and Launoy, that God does not act alone in all things. Instead, they think He acts only as the *principal* efficient cause, and not as the intermediate or final cause. Hence, according to the opinion of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle used to walk about while teaching.</term>, they admit infinite subordinate causes in the world that are efficient essentially and through themselves—and consequently, which are separated and distinguished from that principal act which is in God.

The "Calculations" <note>original: "Calculi"; here meaning points of an argument or formal propositions.</note> of Gassendi, upon which this opinion is founded, are of this sort:

### Proposition 1. Gassendi, page 100.

Fludd wants to teach you that the immediate agent by which all things were created is the uncreated light, or the divine Word, which flowed immediately from the Father. But here, as far as I can guess, the point escapes your mind. For I know the question for you is about the Principal creative cause, of which kind is the divine Word, being the same with the Father and working together with Him. But since God the Father works all things through His Word, or guided by Wisdom (about which nothing has been said), the question is whether God produced anything through the mediation of the Sun, Light, or some other creature, or by Himself alone, or His Word? This is like asking not whether a man writes with a hand (for that is assumed), but whether he writes with a pen, or with the finger alone? (Though why do we take him seriously, since he always speaks in his usual manner?) Again, he brings forward many passages to prove that the uncreated Light, or God alone, works all things in all things.

### Proposition 2. Gassendi, pages 112 & 113.

The Aristotelian opinion, if we look at nature, is not so repugnant to Scripture that it cannot be tolerated;

...it may be. Let Scripture teach, as Fludd contends, that God is the author of both the Winds and the Lightnings; even if this is true regarding the Principal Cause. For otherwise, just as God produces these meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just space rocks.</note>, He also allows **secondary causes** <term>secondary causes: The natural processes or physical laws through which God (the Primary Cause) is thought to work.</term> to produce them; and there is nothing contradictory in these being the same causes that Aristotle identifies. But perhaps Fludd will not admit that there is any secondary cause at all, since he wishes the **Acting Principle** of any thing to be a **particle of God**, and thus for God to be the unique and immediate cause of all things. Yet, to overlook for a moment that this overturns all accepted Theology and Philosophy; it is still necessary for Fludd to admit various states of matter as causes, which is why the enclosed particles of God produce these specific effects rather than others. Furthermore, these are the very causes that Aristotle would defend. And he certainly would not say their effects are Angels, or the flashes of Jehovah, since he did not know these words of Scripture, etc.

### Calculation 3. Gassendi, page 126.

Thus there will be no action of the Creature, but of God alone, whether you distinguish it as being mediated, immediate, or in any other way whatsoever. Thus every action, whether of Virtue or of Vice, will not belong to man, but to God alone, etc.

### Calculation 4. Gassendi, page 101.

God thus works all things in all, so that He should not also be judged the cause of evil actions, etc.

These are those "calculations" which Gassendi has objected against me (attacking the omnipotence and sufficiency of the Divine Virtue or act), drawn from my works in defense of Mersenne. And from these at last, this "good" Mersenne of ours—as if drunk and emboldened by I know not what milk—has wisely (as he thinks) constructed the square of his Impiety; and acting as a diligent herald, he concludes his proclamation thus:

> God (he says) is in this way the form of all things, and so acts in all things, that secondary causes do nothing by themselves.

By which he seems to imply that natural causes, acting as secondary ones, can act by themselves—that is, without the immediate act of God or the Word. Consequently, he makes causes that are essentially acting and efficient to be distinct and separate from the divine act. If this were indeed true, then that saying of the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> would be utterly false: *God works all things in all* <note>original: "Deus operatur in omnibus omnia"; from 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note>; that is, in both natural and supernatural things alike. However, it seems to me that supernatural things cannot be considered unless they are understood within natural things. For, just as the Angelic nature cannot be considered outside the world (since it could not have existed without the created world), so too it is not granted to mortals to know what God truly is, except *a posteriori*—that is, as He is revealed through His creatures—as was shown in my preceding discourse on the 4th calculation of the first Impiety.

My opinion, therefore, leads me to believe that God works all things in all, both mediately and immediately, without any opposing or hindering distinction; and that without His act, there is no motion in the world, and consequently no effect. And we shall clearly explain this whole matter from the testimony of Holy Scripture. Therefore, to the point. If

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>

<margin>John 1</margin>

God is the only and unique one who, by the witness of the Revelator, is *Alpha and Omega*, the beginning and the end, the center and the circumference, then every act—from the beginning to the end, as well as from the center to the circumference—is of God alone *who is all things in all*. But that divine essence, which is Alpha and Omega, is one, continuous, and indivisible: for it is the holy and undivided Trinity. Therefore it follows that God Himself, and no other, is the sole actor and mover, *through all things, and in all things*. For if *God fills all things*, as the sacred page testifies; if the *Spirit of Wisdom fills all things*, as Solomon affirms; if that *incorruptible Spirit is in every thing*, as is confirmed by the same; if *He himself is more mobile than any thing*, as is testified elsewhere; then He cannot but be the unique actor in all things. Whence the Apostle says most rightly in a universal sense: *God works all things in all*. And, *from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things*. Finally, if *in the Word is life*, if *God through the Word gives life to all things*, if *in God we live, move, and have our being*: then it is God alone who essentially works or acts in every thing, since without life and action, any thing is dead. Therefore, by this infallible assertion of the Apostle we say that, although there be many who are called gods in heaven and on earth; *yet to us there is but one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him, etc.* It is as if he had said that, although to those worldly men instructed in worldly or ethnic <note>pagan</note> philosophy, there are said to be many "gods" and authors acting by themselves—namely, Angels, demons, stars, Elements, etc.—nevertheless, by true Christians it is acknowledged that there is only one God the Father, from whom (as the principal efficient cause) and one Son of His, Jesus Christ, through whom all things are essentially acted upon and made in the world, as if by the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. Consequently, things are not done through secondary and subordinate causes acting by themselves, as Mersenne falsely concludes, nor through nature, the Sun, Light, or any other creature, as Gassendi unjustly contends in the manner of infidels in his 1st Calculation.

That God therefore works in the world solely through the Son, without any assistance or help of any creature cooperating with Him by itself, we shall prove by many passages of Scripture harmonically sounding together in the same tone.

<margin>Acts 17</margin>
The Apostle says, *God, needing nothing, gives to all life, and breath, and all things.* Therefore He acts by Himself, needing the help of no creature whatsoever to produce, enliven, and move all things in any way; and consequently, neither Angel, nor Sun, nor stars, nor Element acts, but He alone through those instruments of His.

The Prophet says, *I am the Lord, making all things alone, and no one is with me.* Therefore no creature is co-assisting, but He alone acts in the organic creature through His eternal Wisdom, which (as Solomon witnesses) *fills all things and is in every thing*, and the essence is not divided from Him. And this divine wisdom is that Spiritual Jesus Christ, who (as the Apostle witnesses) *fills all things, and through whom all things are*, or who is that holy Word *from whom all things are and without whom nothing is made*, as the Evangelist says. If therefore the divine essence fills all things, then without doubt it is within all things, since without it all things are empty and void. If He is "more mobile than any thing," then in the bodies in which He dwells, He never rests, but works alone by Himself; for He alone is the agent or efficient cause. If the divine essence, distinct in three persons, be individual and indivisible, then it is whole in itself, however much it may be through all things, and in all things, and outside or *above all things*, as the Apostle says. Consequently, He acts and works *all things in all* by His own act of mobility, as he concludes elsewhere. From these things it is clear how vain it is to appropriate or attribute an act separated from God to a creature—whether Angelic, stellar, simply Elemental or Meteorological, or composed of the elements—and consequently to assert that a creature works anything by itself, that is, out of its own proper nature, and not by means of the immediate divine act. <meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s systematic rebuttal of the charges of "impiety" leveled against him by the French scholars Marin Mersenne and Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, the debate centered on whether natural phenomena (like wind or lightning) are caused by physical laws or by God’s direct action. <header>To the Impieties, Member IV. Portion I. Part III.</header>

For without the divine, the creature can do nothing; but the divine act, as it is within all things, so it is more mobile than any thing, and its mobility is universal: seeing that He is the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the center and the circumference, as much of the whole as of the parts. Consequently, He is all in all, not otherwise than how a whole multitude is seen to be contained within unity. We conclude, therefore, not incongruously (as the Apostle said), that **God works all things in all**, <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note> though Mersenne quite indiscreetly claims that some creature acts through itself as a "secondary cause" <term>secondary cause: In Aristotelian philosophy, the idea that God created the world but that physical objects have their own inherent powers to cause effects.</term>, and that God is only said to work all things as the "primary cause." As if, indeed, God were not the Omega as much as the Alpha, the end as much as the beginning—or rather, that in the end and conclusion, He is all in all?

For if any Creature acts through itself, it certainly follows that it possesses the principle of that act either through itself and from itself, or from elsewhere. If from elsewhere, then it must be either from the divine fountain, or from some principle that is co-eternal with God. If the former be granted—namely, that it is from the divine fountain—then every emanation is continuous and not divided from its source, extending itself continuously like an Alpha to its Omega or end. For the essence of Divinity is indivisible: and consequently, it is God through Himself, and not the creature through itself, who works all things in all. He is **Nature naturing** <term>Natura naturans: Literally "Nature naturing," a term for God as the active, creative force within the universe.</term>, who effects all things both universally and particularly in **Nature natured** <term>Natura naturata: Literally "Nature natured," referring to the created world and its physical manifestations.</term>, with no violation or division of His act having been made. But just as there is **one Spirit** who fills all things, so indeed is it a **unique Spirit** who works all things.

Yet, by reason of the variety of the "organs" <note>In this context, Fludd means physical bodies or natural structures through which the spirit acts.</note> through which and in which He acts, and because of the meager understanding of the human race (which is more occupied with sensible things than with spiritual and invisible ones), we say that this or 그 <note>original: "hunc aut illum"</note> Angel, or nature, or star, or heaven, or wind, or Element, or elemental quality, or meteor, or fire, or composite bodies, act and work through themselves, this or that. In which assertion, indeed, there is a derogation from the Creator, and an idolatrous arrogance of the divine act by the creature. It is not, therefore, the Angel who acts through himself, but Jesus Christ, or Eternal Wisdom, acting through the Angel and in the Angel. Nor is it the Sun or star, but Jesus Christ or Divine Wisdom, by means of the Angelic organ in the star, and the wind, etc., who works those things which are done in this world both universally and particularly: and consequently, no creature acts through itself, but through Jesus Christ. Whence the Apostle spoke most excellently and correctly: *There are those who are called Gods in heaven and on earth, but to us there is one God the Father (that is, the fountain of Divinity) from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ (or the holy emanation of the divine Majesty) through whom are all things, who is all in all.* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 8:5-6.</note>

To the rest, a clearer response is given regarding Text 11, Member 2 of Part 2 of this Treatise, where the text of Lanovius <note>Claude de Lalouvère (1597–1670), a Jesuit mathematician and critic of Fludd.</note> is as follows:

<margin>Lanovius in a Letter to Mersenne.</margin> *And that which he himself foresees in his own doctrine to be a consequence: that God must be called the author of sin, etc.*

Furthermore, see my response to Lanovius, Text 10, Member 2, Part 2, where you will find all these things explained more clearly.

Finally, for a fuller discourse on this question, see my Treatise *On the Mystery of Diseases* <note>original: "De Morborum Mysterio"</note> page 283, where this question is proposed and treated affirmatively, namely:

->**That God is the sole and unique actor and operator in the world.**<-

## Member IV. Portion I. Part III.

### In which the marrow of the third Impiety is treated; which is this:

->*Mersenne in his Letter.*<-

> Thirdly, (Fludd feels and teaches) that the Composite of God and that Ethereal Spirit is the **World Soul** <term>Anima Mundi: The "World Soul," an animating spirit thought by some philosophers to permeate all nature.</term>. That the purest part of this Soul is the Angelic nature and the Empyrean heaven, which is understood to be mixed into all things. That Demons also are particles of the same essence, but tied to malignant matter. That all Souls, as much of Men as of Brutes, are nothing other than particles of the same soul. That this same Soul is the Angel Michael or Metatron <note>Metatron is a powerful angel in Jewish mystical tradition, often identified as the "Prince of the Countenance" or the celestial mediator.</note>.

* This is that imaginary Impiety, which he himself falsely fashioned against me in the third place or order. It is (I say) imaginary and false: its members hang together very poorly. For first he affirms that the "composite of God and the ethereal Spirit" is the World Soul, and then he says that the purest portion of that Soul or composite of ether is the Angelic nature and the Empyrean heaven. As if, indeed, the Empyrean heaven and the Angelic nature were not—as much in dignity as in place and time—prior to the creation and constitution of the firmament or the Ethereal heaven? But concerning these things, I shall speak more clearly below. I shall therefore approach those "calculations" of Gassendi which he selected from my works to build the third corner of this impious tower.

# CHAPTER I.

## Here the Gassendian calculations are reviewed, and a response is given to each of them.

->*Calculation 1. Gassendi, pages 51, 52, & 53.*<-

Unless, therefore, those things are to be understood regarding this visible heaven; regarding what thing, finally, are they to be understood? Truly regarding no other than that **Ether** described above, or the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: Also known as the "quintessence," the pure, celestial substance that makes up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements.</term>, and that blessed son of the world, the **Philosophical Stone**. And first, indeed, what was said above regarding the operation upon Wheat and similar things, etc., can look toward this and be easily accommodated. You see, I think, where those things related from Fludd are tending, etc. Moreover, because the chief mystery of **Alchemy** lies hidden here: I therefore point out a few things. Consider the matter in which the germ of gold (for what other could you understand than common gold itself?) purged of its filth, as if from darkness, and rendered as open and spongy as possible, is included in a glass vessel, which is to be **Hermetically sealed**. This, if it is then exposed to the rays of the stars, but especially of the Sun, etc.

->Fludd.<-

He is mistaken. For I did not say that that pure Balsam of Wheat, or of bread, was in truth the quintessence, or that blessed Stone of the true Alchemists <note>original: "Lapis illum verorum Chymicorum benedictum." The "Philosopher's Stone" was the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and granting eternal life.</note>. Rather, by way of comparison, I likened it to the ethereal substance in which Divinity chooses to dwell—seeing as its seat is called "heaven," which is surely a substance more worthy than the rest of the world—because of its purity and the excellence of its stages of preparation. And indeed, if God, according to the sense of Holy Scripture, is the only Good; and if creatures receive that goodness they possess from the creator, it follows from this that the more a creature participates in His goodness, the richer and fuller it is of the presence of Divinity. But in the Balsam of Wheat, a greater healing power is found than in its other elements. Therefore [it is more divine]. Finally, we did not call this Balsam "heaven" or the "quintessence" because it is truly such, but insofar as it overflows more with power and is closer to that nature than those other elements of wheat. That relationship was therefore symbolic and typical, just as Christ is likened to the vine, to bread, and to other such things in the Scriptures. As for the practical application he fabricated, the question is: were glass vessels known in the time of Hermes? Or was the "Hermetic seal" <term>Hermetic seal: A method of sealing a glass vessel airtight by melting the neck, attributed to the legendary founder of alchemy, Hermes Trismegistus.</term> fused from common glass? Or was it achieved by the fire of a furnace? I doubt it.

<header>Regarding Impieties, Member IV. Portion I. Part III.</header>

...we move, we exist <note>original: "mouemur, sumus." A reference to Acts 17:28: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being."</note>, and similar things. Nevertheless, because Gassendi seems to interpret the matter quite differently, I believe his opinion must be utterly rejected by our theologians.

->Fludd.<-

I take him at his word. For what more should be thought concerning the central World Soul? What further could be devised to confirm the World Soul as established by Fludd, than that it is God, who intimately flows into all things through His essence, presence, and power? But is it, as he says, merely for the sake of existing through preservation, and not for creating and multiplying through generation—or rather, the administration of the soul and the primitive life? Yet he admits that God is present in His essence as a principle effective for acting. But is any act more effective than life itself? Since, therefore, God gives life to all things, the question is: when? Is it after creation or generation, or in the very beginning and moment of it? But his own words will convict their author. For he says that God is present to creatures as a principle effective for acting. Therefore, He is the vital act: the beginning, the middle, and the end, both in the world and in its creatures. For, as He is the beginning, He gives the start of life, which is the office of the essential Soul itself; in the middle, He acts toward existence and preservation; in the end, He takes away or receives back the Spirit of life. Therefore the Psalmist says: when God gives to the creatures, they receive life; when He takes back their Spirit, they expire <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 104:29-30.</note>. In God's hands, therefore, is the Spirit of every living thing, according to that saying of the Prophet, who gives and receives back as it seems good to Him. In short: by His word all things were made, and in the Word was life. But who has considered this? Not without reason, therefore, did Saint John say: The world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not.

But why do I speak, when Gassendi (though in this matter blinder than a mole) seems to himself to be certain that Fludd understands it quite differently? For this reason, he judges that Fludd's opinion must be entirely rejected by theologians. And why? Because (he says) it is clearly elicited from what was said above what Fludd understands by the World Soul. And what, I pray? Surely the Balsam of Wheat and its quintessence <term>quintessence: The "fifth element," or the purest, most concentrated essence of a substance.</term>, which Fludd makes the Philosopher’s Stone. But how can this be, since the latter is particular, while the former is universal? Fludd's mind, therefore, is elsewhere. Yet Gassendi, after a diligent inquiry into Fludd’s philosophy, perceived its foundations to be merely alchemical; and that his Ether, and consequently his quintessence, is the Balsam of Wheat. Truly, Gassendi understands one thing, while Fludd intends another. It is no wonder, therefore, that this "good and diligent searcher" errs, since like a blind man, with the door bolted and the key missing, he gropes in the dark. But let us hear what follows; for he selects that very thought of mine, expressed clearly enough in these words:

->Point 5. Gassendi, page 120.<-

It follows, he says, that God gave both life, and inspiration, and all things, and consequently that He Himself, clothed in light—or rather, dressed in the clear Spirit of the World, which He illuminates by His presence—is the World Soul, insofar as He animates, inspires, and gives it life. And that Mundane Spirit, which He puts on like a garment, is the Spirit of the World; and the earth, both celestial (such as the stars) and sublunary, is the body, which He occupies by means of the Spirit, not otherwise than the human soul occupies the human body, with the spirit carrying it, etc.

->Fludd.<-

What does he conclude? Namely, that Fludd understands the world soul far differently than the theologians mentioned in the place cited before. But does he not say himself in express words that God intimately flows into all things through His presence, essence, and power, as a principle effective for acting? Does he believe this is done otherwise than by the mediation of the Mundane Spirit? Do the Scriptures not say: He sits upon the Cherubim and flies upon the wings of the wind? And again: He is clothed with light as with a garment? And the saying is: Light within Light, Light within the Divinity? And Augustine says: That anything can claim for itself only as much of God as it has light within itself? Furthermore, does the sacred Text not say: A thick cloud is His tabernacle? And, Come, Spirit, from the four winds? And, Wisdom assigns a weight to the air? Indeed, we can collect infinite other things from the Sacred Text, evidently proving that God is everywhere within the mundane Spirit and its bodies. Yet, he says, Fludd feels otherwise. For his principles are alchemical. Therefore let us see how he proceeds.

->Point 6. Gassendi, page 121.<-

Now from these things I gather two points that are least of all to be approved by our theologians. One is that Fludd calls God into "composition" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "composition" implies that God is a component part of a larger whole, which theologians viewed as a threat to His simple, transcendent nature.</note>, first with that mundane or ethereal spirit; and then, by means of that, with all other things, as their true form and act, etc.

->Fludd.<-

I do not despise their theology; yet I do not adhere to it so strictly that I would repudiate the Truth for its sake. But the Truth says: in the Word is life, and life is the Soul of things. Therefore, since man is constituted of soul and body, the more central part of his soul must not be excluded from man's composition. Did God not breathe the breath of life into the face of Adam? Was that breath of life, then, flowed in from the Word, not so annexed to man that it cannot be divided or separated from God? Since life is always in the Word, and the divine essence is in no way divisible, and the Holy Trinity is individual and continuous, as was said above. Furthermore, are we not called members of Christ, and the Temple of the Holy Spirit? Is God not in us, since in Him we live, move, and exist, according to the rule of the Apostle? And what, I pray, would a creature be, unless God by His presence made it such as it is? Is there any other act prior to God who informs all things? Is not "form" the first act, by means of which name and being are given? Does God Himself not alone work all things in all? I (says Jehovah) creating the heaven, and establishing the earth, and making all things, and none with me. Finally, since that sentiment of David is most true—that by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit from His mouth all their power—and the chief of all powers in the world is life or soul; it follows that this itself is an efflux of that Spirit which proceeded from the mouth or essence of Jehovah, who is no more divisible from it than a ray of the sun is from the sun. And by consequence, the soul and form of the heavens, and even of the whole world, is from God, through the mediation of the Spirit, which is in the Word and is called life. Therefore that unique and Universal Soul exists in God Himself, and through God Himself, in the mundane spirit, by means of which all things, though diverse in species and property, are animated, live, and exist as they are. Hence, I (says the Lord) creating the heavens, forming the earth, giving breath to the people, and to those treading the earth. But why should I speak? All these things will be "chemical" to Gassendi. Therefore I proceed to what follows.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s defense against the criticisms of Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd argued that God is the vital principle or "World Soul" that animates all creation. Here, he responds to Gassendi’s logical objections (Calculi 7, 8, and 9) regarding whether such a view implies that God is divided into parts, moves through space, or is limited by physical matter.</meta>

# Fludd’s Response

->Gassendi’s 7th Point of Argument, pages 122 and 123.<-

If God were part of a composition <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "composition" refers to anything made of parts, such as body and soul or matter and form.</note>, it would follow that the Divine Simplicity would be completely violated. Indeed, it is not only an imperfection to be composed of parts, but also to enter into the composition of another thing, and so on. It adds that God could not possess the nature of a "Pure Act" <note>original: "purissimi Actus." A theological term meaning God is fully realized existence with no untapped potential or "becoming."</note> if He contained a "potency" <note>Potentiality or the capacity to be changed.</note> through which He might be halted, bound, limited, or modified by matter. Not to mention that God would be infinitely divisible if all the things in the world possessed distinct portions of Him, glued to distinct portions of matter.

->Fludd.<-

The incorruptible spirit (says Solomon) is in every thing. <note>original: "Spiritus incorruptibilis (ait Salomon) inest in omnire." A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 12:1.</note> But in what way? Namely, that in Himself and through Himself, He is simple; and yet, by His presence, He gives form to the Spirit of the Creature, from which—along with a suitable body—a "composition" is made. Thus, in Exodus, we frequently see an Angel named, and again the name of Jehovah accepted for that same Angel; namely, the Creator within the angelic creature. This is why it is called "alterity" <note>A state of being "other" or "different."</note>, as if consisting of two things. But Jehovah, through Himself and in Himself, is always "Identity" <note>Oneness or sameness.</note>; although the creature exists from Him, through Him, and in Him. For He Himself exists outside of all composition, in and through Himself, and He shall remain forever as that one and the same Being in whom all things reside.

But I would like Gassendus to say whether the infinite can truly be divided into parts? Furthermore, simply because God is said to be within all things, must He be divided into parts because of the sheer number of those things? We see the sun shine in infinite places, or illuminate countless rooms at once; yet it is not divided into parts. What then? Because a single candle illuminates different places, and fire performs various actions in different tools, is their flame immediately and necessarily forced to be divided? Gassendi's argument, cited in the preceding text, sounds quite hollow: namely, that God would be infinitely divisible if He animated all things with His influx of life, because the pieces of matter to be animated and "informed" <note>In the sense of giving "form" or life to matter.</note> are distinct from one another. For in this way (he says), God would be bound and limited, etc. But, if he were to weigh this matter on a fairer scale of the mind, he would notice that He who gives and withdraws life according to His own pleasure does not give life as if He were "included" or trapped in a place; rather, He gives it as one who is exclusively outside all things, yet includes and permeates all things. Hence a certain Philosopher truly said: *God is a center whose circumference is nowhere.* But let us proceed to the following.

->Gassendi’s 8th Point of Argument, page 123.<-

Secondly, the idea of "Transportability" <note>original: "Vectilitate." The quality of being carried or moved.</note> is rejected because Divine Immutability <note>The theological doctrine that God cannot change.</note> would be violated by it.

<margin>Psalm 104.</margin>
->Fludd.<-

I ask Gassendi: has "emanation" <note>A flowing forth from a source.</note> not occurred through a divine emission? For the Spirit of Wisdom is called a "flow" or an "emanation of the brightness and power of the Almighty." Since this stands, do you not see a kind of motion in the divine Spirit? Wherefore the Holy Text testifies that the Spirit of Wisdom is "more mobile than any mobile thing." <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7:24.</note> But the Father, from whom that Spirit emanated, remains fixed and immobile in Himself; even though this Spirit, emanating from that Divine fountain and always continuous with it, is carried along as the Scripture witnesses. For it says: *He set His tabernacle in the Sun.* And elsewhere: *the thick cloud is His dwelling.* And again: *He ascended above the Cherubim, and flew upon the wings of the wind.* <note>Psalm 18:10 and 104:3.</note> This is not because He does not know how to move by Himself, but because it pleases Him to use His Creatures according to His will, both in heaven and on earth, while leaving the divine immutability unharmed and inviolate. Hence this Spirit is called "simple" by Solomon, and yet "manifold"; namely, because of the multiplicity of operations it performs in the nature of the world, just as it is accustomed to work in many ways within the human spirit according to its will. Finally, it is said in sacred words in express terms: *the thick cloud is His vehicle or chariot*, etc. Therefore, this opinion is undeservedly rejected.

->Gassendi’s 9th Point of Argument, page 123.<-

Furthermore, Fludd admits, as I see, that God fills all places—but look, he still conceives of a local motion within Him. He thinks that this "God of his" sometimes dilates and becomes thin, and sometimes contracts and, as it were, multiplies.

->Fludd.<-

How childish these things are! If Gassendi does not produce stronger arguments than these, he will undoubtedly be unable to overturn the foundations of Fludd’s Philosophy. Therefore, it is necessary for Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, the French polymath who initially prompted Gassendi to critique Fludd.</note> to find a more robust reader for himself. But to the point. Does it follow that because God is in every place, I must necessarily conceive of local motion in Him? And what, I pray, is more futile than to believe that He, who is outside all things, can be grasped as if He were a "located object" contained in a place? We say, therefore, that God is everywhere, and consequently in every place; but not "inclusively," like a content in a container or a located thing in a location. Thus it is said, in the Prophet, that *God comes from the South*: So Christ shall come from the East in the clouds: So God breathes from the North. We answer in the same way; that God indeed sends out His power—namely, that holy emanation by which He created all things—yet in the end He says He will take away His Spirit. Sometimes He shows His face in His benevolence, and sometimes He hides it, so that evil may befall creatures. Indeed, His power is proven by the Scriptures to be both "contractive" and "dilative." Thus, by His breath, He is said to contract water into ice and snow; and again, by sending out His word, He dilates and dissolves it. Sometimes also He condenses the Worldly Spirit, contracts it, and makes it opaque; and again, He thins it, making it rare and clear. Sometimes He makes it frozen with cold, and sometimes He makes it glowing with His heat. And if this is not as much Gassendi's God as it is Fludd's (for he says: *he thinks that God of his*, etc.), then he will choose, I well know, the devil for his own. For the Scripture names no other God who can, or is accustomed to, bring about this effect. He is surely the one who "assigns weight to the air, and weighs out the waters by measure, and makes a path for the lightning of the thunder." <note>Job 28:25-26.</note>

<margin>page 51.</margin>
But he says elsewhere that there is a "Synagogue of Sorcerers" in the air; therefore, it is no wonder if he mocks this God of mine, or considers Him the devil: in this way judging good to be evil, and vice versa. And hence, mocking that God elsewhere, he says this: *Whether Christ, the eternal wisdom, whom Fludd always has in his mouth*, etc. From there, you conclude quite unwisely as follows.

<meta>This page continues the debate between the English physician Robert Fludd and the French philosopher Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd defended the idea that God is present in all things without being "composed" of parts. Here, Fludd addresses Gassendi's objections regarding the physical properties of "rarefaction" (thinning) and "condensation" (thickening) as applied to the divine presence.</meta>

# Concerning Impieties, Member IV. Portion I. Part III.

### Point of Argument 10. Gassendi, page 124.

*Since, therefore, the ray—whether of light or of God—is carried from one place to another, it leaves that part of God from which it is sent forth "thinner" <note>original: "rariorem" (rarer/thinner), referring to the process of rarefaction.</note>, and it makes that part in which it is received "thicker" <note>original: "densiorem" (denser), referring to condensation.</note>. I ask you, is there any theological ear that could bear this patiently? As if indeed God could be conceived as being so weak in one place that He must subtract something from Himself to be strengthened in another? Oh, what perpetual distractions, excursions, and tearings-away <note>original: "reuulsionesque"</note> there would be in God, if He were to endure such agitations like some stormy sea!*

->Fludd.<-

<margin>Psalm 36.</margin>
<margin>Job 22.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 147.</margin>
<margin>Job 38.</margin>
<margin>Job 10:9.</margin>
Scripture testifies everywhere that God is the Author of expansion, rarefaction, and condensation, and likewise the immediate cause of multiplication. We say, therefore, that God is not altered in Himself, but always remains immutable. He is not expanded, but He *expands*; nor is He multiplied, but He *multiplies*. For how can that which is infinite be said to be multiplied? Or how can that which is impassible <term>impassible: incapable of suffering or being changed by external forces</term>—if I may put it that way—be truly thinned or thickened in and of itself? Therefore, God, the worker of all things, is said to be contracted, expanded, or multiplied only insofar as it is His will (which the effect follows immediately) to increase or decrease multiplication through the worldly spirit within creatures, and to liberally bestow or withdraw His gifts, goods, or the fruit of His blessing. Furthermore: since God alone is good, and nothing is to be held as good except Him—insofar as it partakes of God's goodness in a greater or lesser proportion—then I ask, can we not rightly say that this goodness of God is multiplied in this or that thing according to that proportion? Moreover, grace (according to the Apostle) is given in a greater measure to this person than to that one. Is not the Kingdom of God also said to be multiplied, like a grain growing into a massive tree? Was not Christ himself said to have "grown in grace"? Is He not said to have been full of the divine spirit, or filled with the Holy Spirit? "If you light my lamp," says the Psalmist, "you will make my darkness shining." Do you see here the multiplication of divine light within a human being? But let us come closer to the matter. We did not say that God contracted Himself in His substance or essence, but rather in His hidden property, in order to fulfill His will regarding "privation" <note>In this context, "privation" refers to the absence of light or form, which Fludd associates with the physical "contraction" of matter.</note>. Read (Good Reader) chapter 7, book 1, section 1, tract 1, volume 1 of my *Universal Medicine* <note>original: "Medicinae meae Catholicae." Fludd's massive work on the intersections of theology, alchemy, and medicine.</note>. Hence the text: "God made darkness His hiding place." Or as it says elsewhere: "He made darkness His secret place," or, by contracting a thick cloud out of the subtle air, He made a tabernacle for Himself. And elsewhere: "God covers the heavens with thick clouds," etc. That is, God, by His "contracting" property, reduced a thin and transparent nature into something opaque and thick. Hence the Psalmist: "He sends forth snow like wool, He scatters frost like ashes, He casts down His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold?" And Job: "By His breath, the mighty God produces ice; by the breath of God, the frost is congealed." If, therefore, God works all things in all, is it not evident that He produces these weather phenomena by His will and this "contracting" property? Furthermore, His "expanding" property and will are recognized in these words, for it follows in their text: "At His cold..." etc., and then: "Sending forth His word, He melts them; as soon as He blows His wind, the waters flow," etc. By these words, he denotes that God, in His expanding property, scatters and dissolves—by thinning them—those things which He gathers together in His contracting property. Why are more words needed when the effect confirms the cause? Does not that suffering man <note>A reference to Job.</note> express this more clearly: "Wisdom fits the weight to the air, and weighs the waters by measure, for He binds them in thick clouds," etc. And regarding the Microcosm <note>The human body/being as a miniature version of the universe.</note>: "You have poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese," etc.

<margin>Psalm 72.</margin>
But tell me, what "theological ear" is so chaste that it would refuse to hear and patiently bear these things when they ring with truth? None indeed (I think), unless it be one that either does not understand, or by pretending, does not wish to understand. Where does that wretched and almost painful cry of the exclaimer now lead? *Oh, what perpetual destructions, excursions, and tearings-away there would be in God, if He were to endure such agitations like some stormy sea!* For He does not, I say, endure them; He *acts*. Nor is He agitated; He *agitates*, and He does whatever He wills, remaining immobile and firm within Himself without any alteration. He is no different than an earthly Emperor who commands, and his subjects—though sometimes with great turmoil—fulfill the mandate. Hence the Psalmist says: "The Angels of God, most mighty in strength, carry out His word, listen to His voice, and do His pleasure." Thus, God is called a "consuming fire" in that property by which He consumes, holds, and disturbs the air through the mediation of His Angels or His organic ministers. Thus the Text says: "The waters saw you, O God, and they were afraid. The clouds poured out water, the upper clouds gave forth a sound; as your thunder sounded in that sphere, the lightnings illuminated the habitable earth; the earth was moved and trembled. Your way was through the sea, and your path through the great waters," etc. Do you see now how God acts and agitates by His "expanding" property? But on the other hand, in His contrary property, "by the breath of God the frost congeals; who can stand before His cold?" What then? Because of these things, are we to say there are "perpetual excursions, distractions, and tearings-away" in God? Truly and indeed, yes—if He were to *suffer* the agitations like a stormy sea. But from what has been said, it is right to conclude the opposite: God acts through His will and word, either by disturbing or by peacefully moving the creature according to His pleasure, while He Himself remains immobile and immutable within Himself, just as the center of a circle remains immobile even when the circumference is moved. Now he comes to those inconveniences that would follow if there were a single "Soul of the World" by which all things in the world were animated.

### Point of Argument 11. Gassendi, page 124.

*As for the Soul of the World, I pass over what the entire school <note>The "School" refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the universities.</note> will object against Fludd: namely, that not all bodies in the world are animated; nor do all things that are animated live, feel, move, and understand through one and the same soul.*

->Fludd.<-

Let his entire Theological School object whatever it can against this opinion of mine, and I will easily draw a sufficiently valid response from the treasury of truth. But who taught Gassendi that any body exists in the world without a soul or essence? For although a thing may not commonly appear to be "animated," nevertheless it has its own life within it; otherwise, it could not possibly exist in the nature of things. Indeed, the earth itself is filled with the seeds of life. Gold, which is extremely compact and immobile by reason of its weight, possesses an essential life by which it lives. Otherwise, it would not progress through the stages of maturation from the state of lead. Indeed, it is established by experience that lead—after it has been exposed for many years upon the roofs of palaces, exalted to a greater perfection by the "cooking" of the sun, and abounds with grains of gold. Even the dregs of tin in Cornwall, after the separation of the pure metal, when piled up in a great heap, in the space of some...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s response to Pierre Gassendi. On the previous page, Fludd began explaining how the divine presence does not require physical "thinning" or "thickening" to move through the world, but rather acts as an immutable source of life. Here, he extends this to the growth of minerals and the nature of the "Universal Soul."</meta>

...to resume the strengths of years, to grow back, and are known to be filled again with good metal of the same kind, from which it is afterwards extracted again, and so on. Furthermore, that both stones and any other bodies have a living salt and an essence peculiar to their species cannot seem strange to anyone who is knowledgeable. For hence it happens that today, in certain mines, stones and their related types are found which did not appear there in previous centuries. We conclude, therefore, that any composite thing has its own life or soul; even if that soul in some things is deep, imperceptible, and very hidden because of the compact nature of its body, as in minerals. In others, however, it is more evident and manifest. Let this infallible axiom therefore stand: **God gives life to all things.** For if He gives life to *all* things, then is any tiny particle of the world to be excluded?

To the second part I respond: if many artificial tools <note>original: "organa factitia"</note> can be seemingly animated and given life by a single fire—acting in various ways and forming various effects through art—shall the same power be denied to the **Light of Lights**, whose proper nature it is to give life and work all things, while He Himself remains unmoved? For the same spark of fire or portion of flame acts in a rocket <note>original: "pyrolobo," an early term for a fire-throwing projectile</note> to lift it high; in a cannon <note>original: "Bombardo"</note> it acts to explode a ball for the destruction of a creature; in an oven for the baking of bread; in a house for the lighting of a room; in a pot for the boiling of food; in water for the raising of vapors; in wood to burn it; in metal to purify it by way of melting. In a lantern, by its breath, it causes images to move; in a chimney it turns a wheel; and thus it acts differently in different things. So too the sun: in one instrument it heats intensely; in another it evaporates without great heating; in another it causes growth; in a burning-mirror <term>burning-mirror: a concave mirror used to concentrate sunlight to start fires</term> it burns; in horse dung, by way of corruption, it gives birth to snakes <note>Fludd refers to the then-common belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter.</note>. In short: according to the variety of things it meets, it produces various forms of operations. What then shall we say of that infinite power which is in that unique **Word**, in which life radically exists? Therefore, this proposition of Gassendi is most false and absurd: that those things which are animated in the world are not animated by one and the same Universal <note>original: "Catholica," meaning universal or all-encompassing</note> soul.

### Point of Argument 12. Gassendi, pages 124 & 125.

*And if indeed he admitted particular souls in addition to this universal soul of his, the matter might perhaps be tolerated: but to attribute the functions of all things to one alone—which, since it is itself a certain whole, contains all particulars as if they were some small parts of itself—there is none of our learned Doctors who could bear it.*

->Fludd.<-

<margin>
1 Timothy 6.
Judith 16.
Isaiah 42.
2 Corinthians 5.
1 Corinthians 8.
Ephesians 6.
Acts 17.
</margin>
Truly, it is absurd to assert this so irrationally. For, if God Himself through His Word gives life to all things, as Paul says; if He alone sent His spirit to creatures and they were created, as the Book of Judith holds; if God, creating the heavens and establishing the earth, gives breath to the people and spirit to those walking upon it, as the Prophet says; if from one God are all things, as the Apostle intends; if there is one God the Father from whom are all things and we in Him, and one son of His, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him, as the same Apostle says; if finally there is **one Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all**, according to the teaching of Saint Paul—in whom we live, move, and have our being—will it not then be absurd, or rather something worse than sacrilege, to attribute to creatures some other peculiar souls besides those drawn from that unique fountain of life? I do not know, therefore, how this good Inquisitor of ours <note>Fludd is mockingly referring to Gassendi as an "Inquisitor."</note> can affirm and prove that all creatures have their own peculiar souls either through themselves and from themselves, or from elsewhere. They cannot have them from themselves, because they have a beginning: therefore they have them from elsewhere. If therefore from elsewhere, it is either from God (who animates the world and is the act of the world-soul) or from some other principle that is co-eternal with God. To establish such a [second] principle will seem irreligious, indeed impious and utterly atheistic to all godly people. Therefore, they have them from God, the sole and unique giver of life; and consequently, there is only one soul of the world, from which the rest proceed. 

If therefore Gassendi concedes that these souls are originally from God, then he must confess that they are either divided and as if separated from God, or continuous within God. But they cannot be a division from God, since the divine essence from which they draw their life is indivisible. We grant, therefore, that souls are distinct from one another in their own way, but no one can say they are divided from God without—contrary to the intention of all theologians—wishing the divine essence itself, or the indivisible Holy Trinity, to be divisible. Forced by logic, therefore, he must acknowledge that all souls are continuous in God, and consist through His son Jesus Christ, or His Word, in which there is life, and consequently in which we live. For it is clear from what has come before that there is only one Father of all; therefore we all have life from Him. And although He is above all things—and consequently not "included" within the creature—nevertheless He is through all things and in us all: hence in Him we live, move, and have our being.

<margin>Wisdom 12.</margin>
Hence Solomon spoke not unwisely: *An incorruptible spirit is in every thing.* And the Apostle: *Your members are the members of Christ.* But Christ is the Word in which is the life of all. Let Gassendi respond to these things if he can. And if he can reasonably and truly erase these things, I shall write no further. Nor shall I rely on divine omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence hereafter, if there are other principles of life besides God alone, or if there is such "passibility" <note>the capacity to be changed or acted upon</note> in the divinity that it can be divided into parts really distinct from one another. For if His power or spirit, according to the teaching of the Psalmist, gives power to any thing, and consequently its soul, it is absurd and erroneous to believe that that essential power can be divided from the giver and not be continuous. Therefore, whether Gassendi and Lanovius and Mersenne <note>Fludd’s primary intellectual opponents: Pierre Gassendi, François de La Noue, and Marin Mersenne.</note> can bear it, or can patiently hear that all peculiar souls have an inseparable dependence and union with that thrice-great Animator of the greater world—whose nature it is to give life to all things presently and essentially—whether they bear this or not, I say, I do not care, since I am a faithful servant and worshipper not of fiction and error, but of truth.

### Point of Argument 13. Gassendi, pages 125 & 126.

*Thus indeed there will be no creature that is not some small God—suppose, composed of God, etc. Thus there will be no necessity at all that we worship any other nature than our own divine nature; for even if some other greater Gods existed, they would not be more "Gods" than we are, etc. Thus there will be no reason why idolatry should be forbidden to men, since the essential form of both wood and stone would be God. Thus demons themselves will be Gods, and to be worshipped with equal right. Thus no soul will be more mortal or immortal than another, nor consequently will the soul of a beast be said to perish more than that of a man, etc. Thus there will be no action of the creature, but only of God, whether mediately or immediately, etc. Thus every action, whether of virtue or of vice, will be not of man, but of God alone, and therefore God alone, at least in part of Himself, will have to be affected by either reward or punishment—here unhappy, there blessed, here a fool, there a wise man, etc. It is clear how these things are not to be borne.*
